News.title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
News.content:
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.

He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.

News.title: Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife
News.content:
Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area and were taken to Dover for processing.

Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and start slashing at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille LibertÃ©.

As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Danny Tommo shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat.

"Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."

It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat.

"We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Tommo told his followers.

Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

News.title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
News.content:
They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.

Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.

As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight.

UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad.

Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than â¬4,000 (Â£3,400).

Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for â¬750 (Â£650).

She described its clinic in DÃ¼sseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".

The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.

It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.

The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.

Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.

She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before.

"I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."

News.title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
News.content:
Two influential economic bodies have warned the UK's ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth put the country in a tougher position ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.

The UK is one of several countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.

The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) also told the BBC that Britain and the US needed "the courage" to take action on debt.

Rising borrowing costs are limiting governments' room for maneouvre as pressure grows for more spending on defence and support for people facing price rises.

The OECD said it expected the UK economy to grow by 1% next year, slightly less than the 1.1% it had been forecasting for 2027.

However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected in 2026, and upgraded its forecast for growth this year from 0.9% to 1.1%.

Taken together, higher growth in 2026 but marginally lower growth in 2027, adds up to an upgrade in the growth forecast for the UK.

Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase, not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".

"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

News.title: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tent
News.content:
TV critics have described Nigella Lawson as the "icing on the cake" of The Great British Bake Off, after the show returned for a new series on Tuesday.

Lawson has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced she was leaving earlier this year after nearly a decade in the programme's famous tent.

The Telegraph said Lawson gives the Channel 4 series a "new lease of life", while Digital Spy agreed she was a "brilliant addition" to the line-up.

But the Independent was cooler on the launch episode as a whole, saying the show "wastes Nigella's prodigious charms and misses a chance for a true revamp".

The return of Bake Off saw Lawson join fellow judge Paul Hollywood, who has appeared on the programme since its launch in 2010, and presenters Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding.

Former Bake Off winner Giuseppe Dell'Anno told BBC Radio 4's Today that Lawson "did produce a step change" to the show and was a "nice fit with the ethos of the programme".

"She was doing her best by capturing the vibes of a cake, the feelings, what it makes you think of, which was very nicely balanced by Paul being very technical and scrutinising," he said.

"I think, however, that she will get better over time, because my gut feeling yesterday was that she was still in new territory."

News.title: Netanyahu calls Macron's remarks on West Bank in UN speech 'grotesque'
News.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly.

"Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter.

Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day".

There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation".

The source told the Jerusalem Post, external that the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sÃ©vi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank."

Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire

"Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?"

After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering."

"On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank.

"Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria."

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality".

Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said.

Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it.

The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

The settlements are illegal under international law.

News.title: Drug deaths in Scotland rise 11% as country struggles with worst rate in Europe
News.content:
Deaths related to illicit drugs rose by 11% in Scotland last year to 1,133 as the country struggles to tackle the worst fatality rate in Europe.

National Records of Scotland (NRS) said the figure for 2025, external was 116 higher than the previous year, bringing the total deaths in a decade to more than 11,000.

After adjusting for age, there were 214 drug-related deaths per million people.

NRS defines drug-related deaths as those where the underlying cause was drug poisoning, a controlled substance was in the body at the time of death, and drug use led directly to the death.

Efforts to save lives over the past year have been hampered by criminal gangs mixing powerful synthetic opioids such as nitazenes with existing drugs including heroin, cocaine and fake Valium pills.

News.title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of threats and intimidation
News.content:
Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.

The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in legal documents filed this week.

The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.

In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.

In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the case had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.

"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.

"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."

Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.

Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.

In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".

They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."

News.title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says
News.content:
The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation, including from Russia, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation".

The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.

Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.

In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign.

"The Kremlin spends around Â£1.3bn each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly.

"They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.

"We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community â creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.

"On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'

He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.

To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.

The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".

There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham.

When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".

Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".

News.title: Farmers' fury as race for £233m funding compared to 'scramble for Oasis tickets'
News.content:
The National Farmers' Union (NFU) is calling for the government to explain why the scheme opened and closed so quickly, with so many farmers left out of pocket.

It said it wanted "clarity and urgency" from the government and added that it had made "repeated warnings of a lack of sufficient budget".

NFU vice-president Robyn Munt said: "The rapid uptake of the scheme comes as no surprise. Its closure in less than six hours shows the scale of demand there is from farmers to deliver for the environment and to invest in farm resilience.

"The current cashflow pressures facing farmers and growers only exacerbates that demand as they look for certainty and clarity for the year ahead."

Vicki Hird, agriculture lead at the Wildlife Trusts said "the scramble for green farming schemes was worse than the dash for Oasis tickets".

She added: "The budget has been inadequate for far too long and the Treasury must recognise this and allocate far greater funds to ensure climate resilience in farming in the next budget."

The SFI scheme is vital for many farmers who have turned large swathes of their land over to nature-friendly schemes, such as planting hedges, creating wildflower margins and protecting the soil.

When the scheme was suddenly closed without notice last year, there were concerns that some farmers might turn their backs on environmental work if they could not access the payments and demand for Tuesday's scheme was expected to be high.

News.title: Off sick? You need to phone your boss, back-to-work adviser says
News.content:
People off sick from work should keep in phone contact with their boss, government-appointed back-to-work expert Sir Charlie Mayfield has said.

Getting bosses and workers to have a conversation, rather than simply exchanging emails and sicknotes, could help get people back into work, Sir Charlie, who is leading the Keep Britain Working taskforce, said.

His latest report said health-related economic inactivity was costing Britain around Â£210bn a year in benefit payments and lost output.

Talking on the phone was just "one piece of the jigsaw" he said on Wednesday.

The report calls for more workplace support, external for people with health conditions and disabilities and the establishment of a Workplace Health System alongside the NHS.

But improving communication was also a way to "rehumanise" the workplace and help prevent people dropping out of work altogether, Sir Charlie said.

The report does not suggest that someone struck down by flu needs to croak through their symptoms over the phone or that bosses need to provide down-the-line sickbed sympathy if an employee is off with food poisoning.

"I'm not worried about a day here and a day there. It is more about longer term issues," Sir Charlie told the BBC's Today Programme.

But he said Britain was doing a "poor job" of handling sickness in the workplace, leading to more people becoming disengaged and dropping out altogether.

"I have met so many people who have said to me, 'You know, I was signed off sick and I was off sick for a month, two months, three months, and I had almost no contact with my employer'," Sir Charlie said.

Around 300,000 people leave work every year with a health condition, much of which is preventable, the report said.

Sir Charlie said employees sometimes feared talking about long-term health issues with their employer.

"But the fear is also felt by employers as well because they're afraid of causing offence or creating a complaint or a grievance," he added.

Fear on both sides can create a distance and lack of understanding, he warned, with longer absences making it much more likely a worker will drop out of the labour force altogether.

"If you can keep more people in work, there's a massive opportunity for us to add billions to the economy and, frankly, to people's livelihoods," Sir Charlie said.

"To get that, though, you need to have people talking to each other, and you've got to more actively manage sickness and ill health in the workplace."

Employers need to do more, he said, and employees need to engage with it.

Other ways for bosses to support staff include ensuring access to treatments such as physiotherapy and talking therapies, he said.

News.title: Inmates deny attempt to murder Sara Sharif's father
News.content:
Two prisoners have pleaded not guilty to the attempted murder of Urfan Sharif, who is serving a life sentence for killing his 10-year-old daughter, Sara Sharif.

Steven Sansom, 47, and Adam Watson, 39, were charged last month following an attack in Belmarsh Prison on 1 January 2025, which reportedly left Sharif with cuts to his face.

Sharif and Sara's stepmother, Beinash Batool, were sentenced to life imprisonment for murdering Sara at their home in Woking, Surrey.

Sansom and Watson appeared at the Old Bailey via video links from HMP Wakefield on Wednesday.

The hearing was told how Samsom reportedly invited Sharif into a cell at Belmarsh, where Watson was waiting, at which point Watson allegedly took hold of him and punched him repeatedly before Sansom applied pressure to his throat.

Prosecutors then claim Watson passed an object to Sansom, which was used to make cutting motions to Sharif's throat.

The pair also deny wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, and unauthorised possession of two weapons in the form of a tin lid, and a pen attached to a handle.

News.title: Pornhub investigated over its age checks
News.content:
Ofcom has launched an investigation into Pornhub owner, Aylo, over whether the site's new age checks are effectively stopping children from accessing adult content.

The regulator said in May that Pornhub started using a new age verification process for some users, which relies on a third party, in this case Apple.

It said it had concerns that Aylo "may not have conducted sufficient due diligence and testing" before implementing this new process, and so it "may not be highly effective" at preventing children from seeing pornography.

Under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA), sites that host pornographic material must use highly effective age assurance to ensure whether a user is over 18.

The BBC has approached Aylo for comment.

Ofcom says as part of its investigation it will consider how Aylo implements its age verification processes and whether it conducted the "necessary due diligence" before it was implemented.

It will not investigate how Apple operates its age checks.

George Lusty, Ofcom's Director of Enforcement, said: "Online age checks are a vital protection to prevent children from encountering inappropriate or harmful material, including pornography.

"We expect tech firms to ensure age checks are highly effective before introducing them. Anything less could leave children at risk."

Under the Online Safety Act, Ofcom holds the power to fine non-compliant companies up to Â£18 million or 10% of their annual global turnover, whichever is greater.

This probe is just the latest clash between the regulator and what is one of the world's most viewed porn sites.

In October 2025 Pornhub said traffic from UK users had plunged by more than 75% following the introduction of more robust age checks by the OSA.

Some have questioned whether people were simply using Virtual Private Networks (VPN) to get around the checks instead.

In January, Pornhub announced it would restrict access to its website in the UK, blaming the tougher checks, with only people who had previously made a Pornhub account able to access its content.

Aylo said that updates to the Act requiring age verification had "not achieved its goal of protecting minors" and had "diverted traffic to darker, unregulated corners of the internet".

However, in May, it said it would be making the site available again for some UK Apple users who had confirmed their age with the company's most up-to-date version of iOS, its mobile operating system.

News.title: Council leaders wary of radical plan to redraw Scotland's local government map
News.content:
Council leaders have been voicing their concerns about proposals for the biggest shake up of local government in 30 years.

Some have warned that Scottish government plans to potentially streamline the number of authorities from 32 to six will not save money.

Others have questioned the potential impact on rural parts and the "absurd" timeline.

Under proposals for a new two-tier system, external, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth.

Between 120 and 160 community authorities would also be created, contributing to local issues such as licensing and town centre improvements.

News.title: Prince and Princess of Wales share a laugh with Tom Cruise at film premiere
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales renewed their friendship with Tom Cruise at the premiere of the Hollywood star's latest film in London on Tuesday.

Cruise took the hand of Catherine, Princess of Wales, as they talked and laughed on a black carpet - instead of the traditional red - before the royal gala screening of Digger in Leicester Square.

Cruise has known the prince and princess for a number of years and also met William's mother, Princess Diana, and attended her funeral in 1997.

Catherine wore a pair of Diana's pearl drop earrings to the premiere on Tuesday, as well as the late Queen Mother's amethyst sautoir necklace.

News.title: Neighbours 'broken' over family's house fire deaths
News.content:
Neighbours of a mother and three children killed in a house fire have said their community has been "broken" by their deaths.

The fire at the house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, "spread rapidly" in the early hours of Tuesday morning. An injured man who was outside the house when fire crews arrived remains in hospital.

Cards addressed to the family, as well as teddy bears and photographs, have been left close to the scene by bereaved relatives and shocked locals.

Loti Nambobe, who is taking care of the family's dog after the fire, said: "It's a community. It's broken. It hurts."

A joint investigation involving Merseyside Police and Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service is expected to continue into this afternoon, with a mobile incident room set up close to the scene in the hours after the fire.

The Bishop of Liverpool the Rt Rev Ruth Worsley and Bishop of Warrington the Rt Rev Simon Robinson said they were "deeply saddened to hear of the devastating incident".

"Our thoughts and prayers are with their families and loved ones at this unimaginably difficult time," they added.

Bootle MP Peter Dowd said: "My heart goes out to the family and friends of the four who lost their lives in a house fire in Bootle.

"Their loss is beyond words. This shocking event will touch everyone in our community."

Silversea passengers can now choose from four new suite options on the brand’s cruises.

The line has organised its 17 suites into the categories, starting with Panorama and Vista Oceanview suites, featuring large windows with expansive ocean views.

Passengers can opt for Premium Veranda, Deluxe Veranda, Superior Veranda, Classic Veranda and Veranda suites, each with a private balcony.

The next grade is the Residence category featuring Junior Grand, Signature, Silver, Premium Medallion and Medallion suites. Each has separate bedroom and living spaces.

The fourth option is the Villa Category, with Otium, Master, Owner's, Grand and Royal suites. These are the brand's most expansive cabins, with large living spaces and terraces.

All suites include butler service, 24-hour in-suite dining, wifi, dining, drinks, port fees, taxes and tips.

Residence guests get extra perks such as priority embarkation and early access to reservations.

Villa guests can also have a private transfer when they book an airfare with Silversea, alongside dedicated planning support plus priority on excursion bookings. These guests will also have private consultations with the chef and spa manager, their own dining experiences such as afternoon tea and will get a Technogym exercise bag in their suite. Additionally, Villa guests can stay on the ship for longer at the end of a cruise.

The changes will apply on sailings departing on or after 1 January 2027 across both the brand's classic and expedition cruise ships.

Bert Hernandez, president of Silversea, said: "Guests choose to sail with Silversea time and time again for the intimacy of our ships and the personal attention that comes with it.

“Our new suite categories let us build directly on that foundation.

“Whether that’s with early access to spa and dining reservations or dedicated time with the ship's head sommelier – we’re strengthening the personalised service that has always defined Silversea, while maintaining and expanding on the inclusions guests know and love."

The Justice Department argued in a court filing Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the authority to bar CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House on “national security” grounds, urging a federal judge not to suspend the restrictions.

The three outlets filed a lawsuit after Trump abruptly revoked their reporters’ White House access on Friday, arguing the restriction amounts to a “blatant violation” of the First Amendment. A hearing on their request for a temporary order restoring that access is scheduled for Wednesday.

In the DOJ’s telling, the ban doesn’t violate the First Amendment, because, it argued, “access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.”

“CNN, MSNOW, and Politico have long been granted privileged access to White House grounds,” department attorneys wrote in the court filing. “But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”

Letters were sent to the three outlets outlining a “non-exhaustive list” of incidents in which their reporters “have threatened national security and spread falsehoods,” the filing states.

open image in gallery The Department of Justice argued President Donald Trump can bar reporters from the White House on national security grounds ( Reuters )

The letter cited stories on President Trump’s White House ballroom, weapons stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and Russian sanctions.

The president has previously invoked national security in justifying other actions, including the construction of his massive White House ballroom and of his planned 250-foot victory arch.

Trump abruptly announced on Friday that the three organizations were being banned from the White House “effective immediately.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

By the following morning, CNN, MS NOW and Politico all said that their journalists had been stopped from accessing the White House grounds, with some reporters stating that they were asked to hand over their badges.

open image in gallery Flyers hang in the White House briefing room in Washington, DC, on September 21, following Trump's media ban ( AFP via Getty Images )

On Monday, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and several of his top aides, arguing that the ban violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as well as the First Amendment, and calls for the press passes to be restored.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit states.

“No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here,” it continues.

The 80-year-old president has long had an extremely combative relationship with the press, accusing reporters of unfair and biased coverage, lobbing personal insults against them and insinuating that those he opposes should be punished.

Trump previously curtailed The Associated Press from accessing certain presidential spaces in 2025 after the outlet continued using the “Gulf of Mexico” despite Trump rebranding it as the “Gulf of America.” In 2018, Trump also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass following a contentious news conference.

English winemaker Chapel Down has revealed a boost from strong demand among millennial drinkers as it upgraded its profits guidance.

It came as the Kent-based company cheered a “high-quality” harvest so far this year as it benefited from warm temperatures in the UK.

Shares in the company lifted higher in early trading on Wednesday.

Chapel Down told shareholders that net sales grew by 19% to £9.4 million in the half-year to June 30, compared with a year earlier.

open image in gallery Chapel Down said it saw a ‘continued strong performance’ in the third quarter of the year (Gareth Fuller/PA) ( PA Archive )

It said this benefited from growth in both retail and hospitality venues, while international sales jumped 66% on the back of growth in the US.

Boss James Pennefather told the Press Association that it has benefited from “millennials” choosing to drink sparkling wine at “informal occasions” such as birthday celebrations.

The firm saw growth supported by more venues selling its wine by the glass, as well as new listings from operators including The Gordon Ramsay Group and Handpicked Hotels.

Chapel Down said that it saw a “continued strong performance” in the third quarter of the year and has “confidence” in its trading plans for the final three months of the year.

As a result, it said adjusted earnings are now on track “to be materially ahead of market expectations”.

Meanwhile, net debt is also expected to be lower than market predictions after capital spending was lower than originally expected.

The company also said it believes its 2026 vintage will be “high quality” after completing more than half of its grape harvest for the year.

Mr Pennefather said: “The English region is coming into a multi-decade period of good temperatures for our vines, which were still green and in good condition after very little rain.”

Shares in the company were up 5.4% at 48.5p.

UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland has provided a health update after surviving an ATV crash while not wearing a helmet.

Strickland initially shared a video of the immediate aftermath, showing his head and body scratched up, before later posting footage of the crash as it happened.

“Guys, I’m in a real bad place,” he said. “I let my buddy ​drive, he ‌rolled us going, ‌like, 60 (mph). We rolled like six times.

“That was from my head smacking the ground, going 60, did not have a helmet on. I’m ‌an idiot.”

Strickland’s friend Chris Cornell, a cinematographer for the UFC, collapsed after both he and Strickland emerged from the flipped vehicle, and was subsequently taken to ER.

The American middleweight has since taken to Instagram and played down any fears that either sustained a serious injury.

“I think I’m OK,” he said. “Chris Cornell went unconscious for a little bit, he’s in the hospital but I think he’s going to be alright, he just went to sleep for a little bit.

“Honestly, the most f***ing fun I’ve had in a very, very long time. My wallet’s a little sore, Rainbet said they’d cover it so that’s nice. But that was the most fun thing I’ve done in a very long time.

“I hope Chris is OK - I’ve never seen anyone go unconscious before, so that was interesting.”

open image in gallery UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland ( Getty )

Strickland, 35, has a history of controversy in the past, with a litany of sexist and racist remarks landing him in hot water.

It is also not the first time he has been involved in a motor vehicle crash, with a motorcycle action in 2018 forcing him out of the octagon for two years.

A two-time middleweight champion, he is yet to book a first title defence of his second reign after dethroning Khamzat Chimaev in May.

America’s aging air traffic control network continues to face widespread disruptions because it relies on outdated telecommunication systems, obsolete Compaq computers, and replacement components bought on eBay.

In the latest example of these technical vulnerabilities, thousands of flights across the heavily populated Northeast were delayed or canceled on Monday after dual failures: a circuit breakdown at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and a fiber-optic line severed by a construction crew near New Brunswick, New Jersey.

"The architecture of our telecom is still a 40-year-old architecture, which means you could have a switch go down and a line be cut yesterday and the Northeast goes down," U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday.

open image in gallery The recent disruption shows how fragile the national air traffic control network has become ( Getty )

The recent disruption shows how fragile the national air traffic control network has become after decades of delayed modernization, inadequate funding, and fragmented temporary fixes.

Despite billions of dollars spent or approved, the Federal Aviation Administration remains dependent on legacy, incompatible equipment that can turn a single component breakdown or severed cable into widespread travel chaos—a risk officials warn will persist without a far larger structural overhaul.

In January 2023, every departing flight across the US was grounded for the first time since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks when a contractor accidentally erased computer files associated with a vital pilot messaging database. The resulting outage impacted 11,000 flights before technical teams resolved the issue.

In September 2025, a telecom failure triggered by a contractor cutting fiber lines disrupted communication systems at two Dallas-area airports, resulting in delays for more than 2,000 flights and hundreds of cancellations, affecting 100,000 American Airlines passengers alone.

open image in gallery "The architecture of our telecom is still a 40-year-old architecture, which means you could have a switch go down and a line be cut yesterday and the Northeast goes down," U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday ( Getty )

A series of significant technical problems prompted Congress last year to approve $12.5 billion to modernize national air traffic control systems. On Tuesday, Duffy stated that he is seeking an additional $30 billion to complete facility repairs and finish overall system upgrades.

"These incidents will continue to happen unless we get the resources and actually build the architecture fit for the 21st century," Duffy said.

Across the Atlantic, Britain has similarly experienced major air traffic control outages this month, leading commercial airlines to openly question the overall resilience of its systems.

The FAA has been forced to utilize 3D printing techniques or search eBay listings to acquire replacement components for its legacy equipment. In several other instances, the agency can no longer procure spare parts.

In 2024, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA must take "urgent action" to address its aging air traffic control network, warning that one-third of existing systems are unsustainable.

open image in gallery A view shows United Airlines at the tarmac at Newark International Airport, as the skyline of New York is seen in the background ( Reuters )

The agency's more than 300 air traffic facilities cannot communicate directly with one another and run on isolated analog computers. "Every facility is a silo," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters in a recent interview. "We're behind 20 years."

Bedford explained that FAA control towers effectively run on individual Compaq computers. The computer brand, acquired by HP, stopped manufacturing hardware in 2013.

The agency also continues to rely on legacy telephone networks and three telecom systems that lack interoperability, sharing a "clunky connection" that regularly forces flight delays, Bedford noted.

Simultaneously, the US manages the world's most complex airspace while navigating a chronic workforce shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers.

A major technological transition is expected in late 2027, when air traffic control moves from analog to digital communications. The FAA then plans to shift facility operations from individual computers to cloud infrastructure.

The FAA has attempted to modernize its aviation infrastructure for decades, but those initiatives have consistently fallen short of expectations.

In 1982, the agency published its first comprehensive master plan to improve air traffic control services, estimating it would cost roughly $10 billion through the late 1990s.

open image in gallery Officials investigate the scene on where cars were damaged after a Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway and struck vehicles on September 6 at Miami International Airport ( AFP/Getty )

By 1995, the Government Accountability Office reported that estimated costs had escalated to at least $36 billion in the push to consolidate facilities and standardize computer hardware and software systems.

Another overhaul project named "NextGen," launched in 2004, was initially budgeted at $15 billion. However, a report last year revealed it suffered extensive delays and cost overruns while delivering a less ambitious outcome than envisioned more than 20 years ago.

"FAA has delivered a delayed, over budget, and less transformational NextGen than originally planned," said the Transportation Department Office of Inspector General.

The agency has also worked for years to phase out a long-criticized, decades-old practice where air traffic controllers track aircraft using paper flight strips.

The transition to modern digital tracking at 49 major airports began in 2022 but will take the agency until at least 2028. The FAA noted that 18 major airports have successfully phased out paper strips so far.

Street signs along one of Britain’s most crudely named roads have been reinforced with concrete to deter souvenir-hunting tourists – but locals are “very proud” of their address.

Minge Lane, in Upton upon Severn, Worcestershire, has been highlighted in a new survey ranking the nation’s most cheekily titled locations.

Other places on the list include Norfolk's Sluts Hole Lane, the New Forest's Sandy Balls, Shitterton in Dorset, and Yorkshire’s Wetwang.

Jeremy Owenson, the mayor of Upton upon Severn, said that Minge Lane residents embrace the moniker so wholeheartedly that they organise an annual summer festival named after it.

“We’re very proud of (the name)… There is an informal festival with loads of bands and a bit of fancy dress,” he said.

“People get down to the local pub and generally have a good time. It’s a fun celebration to embrace the name Minge Lane rather than worrying too much about it.”

open image in gallery Minge Lane plays host to an annual festival ( PA )

Mr Owenson, who is also deputy leader of Malvern Hills District Council, said that the street's popularity among amused visitors has previously led to the road signs being stolen.

“The new names have been concreted in to make sure they can’t be taken,” he said.”

“It is something that is regularly photographed by people.”

He said that Upton is a “big tourist town” with lots of festivals, and he hoped that those taking a photo on Minge Lane would “spend some money in the town before they leave”.

People living on the lane are used to it being a tourist drawcard, he said.

open image in gallery Hornyold Road in Worcestershire is also on the list of the places with the rudest names ( PA )

“I know people who have lived and still live on Minge Lane and they are proud of it.

“It is derived from an old Anglo-Saxon word and it is something people are proud of.

“Everyone gives a wry smile, but they are certainly proud of it.”

Butthole Lane in Shepshed, Leicestershire, another cheeky road that made the list, also has a historic reason for its name.

Peter Grainger, a resident of the road for 46 years, said: “The reason why it is called Butthole Lane goes back to 1066, there was a royal decree that you had to practice shooting arrows, and you shoot arrows into a hollow, which is a hole. They are called butts.

“There was a hollow, which is gone now because they built houses, but that is why it is called Butthole Lane.”

open image in gallery Cock Hill Lane in Birmingham ( PA )

Asked if he would ever want the name changed, Mr Grainger, a town councillor, said: “No, not at all, I would be against that.

“There are only seven houses on Butthole Lane and everyone is happy and proud of the name, and why not?

“Some people have a laugh at the name and you have to explain the reason why it is called that. It is history that we shouldn’t lose in this country.”

Bell End in Rowley Regis in the West Midlands, which also made the list of rudest place names, was the target of complaints in 2018 and residents started a petition to change it.

They claimed that children would be bullied at school and called on Sandwell Council to rename it because they had become a “laughing stock”.

The petition attracted only 100 signatures but a rival campaign – titled “Leave the Historic Name of Bell End Alone!” – received more than 4,800 supporters. The road name was never changed.

open image in gallery Bell End in Rowley Regis ( PA )

Rude road names can be distracting for drivers

More than half (53 per cent) of Britons think that the UK has some of the funniest road and village names in the world, but they can also be a distraction for drivers, with cheeky road names putting off two-thirds (65 per cent) of drivers, the new survey found.

Six in 10 (60 per cent) admitted missing their turn or exit due to laughing and one in three (33 per cent) nearly having an accident.

Of people surveyed, 63 per cent said they have taken a detour to witness a funny street name, while 58 per cent have pulled over to take a picture of a humorous sign.

Asda Car Insurance visited some of Britain’s most distracting roads this month, temporarily putting green velvet “modesty” curtains over the signs, in a bid to help keep drivers’ eyes on the road.

A portrait of beloved documentary presenter Sir David Attenborough has broken a world record – after being made out of pumpkins.

Measuring an astonishing 218.19 square metres, Sunnyfields Farm in Hampshire has broken the Guinness World Record for the largest mosaic created using squashes.

The display, which marks Sir David's 100th birthday, used around 11,000 squashes and pumpkins, taking 18 people around five hours to complete.

Sir David was selected to feature on the display after the farm took to social media to ask the public who they would like to see on this year's mosaic.

While hundreds of suggestions poured in, Sunnyfields director Thomas Nelson described the number of requests for Sir David as “overwhelming”.

open image in gallery Sir David Attenborough was described as ‘the perfect fit’ for this year’s mosaic ( Sunnyfields Farm )

Explaining what he believes lies behind the requests, Mr Nelson told The Independent: “David means so much to so many families across the UK and the world... he has been part of our living rooms; him and the causes he has championed for his entire life.”

In-house artist Andrew Béga, who designed the portrait, agreed: “Attenborough – given the icon that he is, was just the perfect fit.”

Guinness World Records senior adjudicator Pravin Patel confirmed the new record at Tuesday's unveiling.

But this is not the first such achievement for Sunnyfields Farm.

Over the past decade, its owners have staged various pumpkin displays, first entering the record books in 2023 for a Tim Burton-inspired mosaic depicting Jack Skellington's famous moonlight stance.

The farm beat its own record in 2025, creating a 212 square-metre mosaic featuring Ozzy Osbourne, commemorating the Black Sabbath frontman who died earlier that year.

But putting on this year’s display was a much harder feat, as extreme weather continues to affect pumpkin farmers across the country.

open image in gallery Pumpkin farmers across the country have reported significant drops in yield after a dry summer ( AFP/Getty )

“It has been very tough,” said Mr Nelson. “The heat and lack of rain have been unprecedented. The best conditions for pumpkins are lots of sun and lots of water.”

As a result, five back-to-back heatwaves and prolonged drought conditions have taken their toll, with this year’s pumpkins being on the smaller side.

But these challenges have not deterred Sunnyfields Farm.

Discussing next year’s display, Mr Nelson said: “There is always scope to go bigger and better.

“We can't say we have given too much thought to it, though it's best not to put limits on what you can achieve.”

News.title: Yemen’s factions battling Iran-backed Houthis share a common enemy but not common goals
News.content:

Yemeni factions fighting the Iran-backed Houthis are united mainly in one thing — their opposition to the rebels who control the country’s north and have recently advanced along its Red Sea coastline.

But beyond that, the groups fighting under the banner of Yemen's internationally recognized government are divided by geography, foreign patronage and competing visions for what their country should look like if the Houthis are pushed back.

In a month of intense fighting that saw the Houthis' biggest land grab in years, factions of the anti-Houthi coalition lost their hold of Mokha, a strategic city on the Red Sea, and islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait further south. The advance ended a truce that had been in place since 2022 and had calmed a devastating civil war.

Neighboring Saudi Arabia is trying to weld the factions — amounting to thousands of fighters — into a more unified force, but their divisions have raised questions about their ability to halt the Houthi offensive that now has the rebels perched on one of the world’s busiest waterways.

The Houthis' unified command and goals have helped their swift expansion, rather than any single military advantage, said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington-based think tank.

“For the Houthis, that makes it so much easier to fight this battle: one coherent movement on one side, and a loosely linked umbrella group on the other,” he said.

Here is what we know about the anti-Houthi factions:

The factions have been shaped by Saudi-Emirati rivalry

Saudi Arabia formed a coalition to fight the Houthis in 2015, a year after the rebels overran the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, driving the government into the south.

In the south, an array of militias and armed groups arose over the years, ostensibly to back the government against the rebels.

Over the years, rivalries grew between Saudi-backed factions and others backed by the United Arab Emirates, as the two regional powerhouses competed for control over the coalition as well as Yemen’s coastal regions overlooking strategic shipping lanes.

The factions repeatedly clashed on the ground. After Emirati-backed southern separatist factions intensified clashes last year, Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes against a suspected Emirati weapons shipment to southern Yemen. In January, the UAE said it pulled out of Yemen’s war, ending its support for factions on the ground.

Bringing fighters under one umbrella is proving difficult

Now as a single patron, Saudi Arabia is trying to absorb under its command and funding structure the factions that spent years operating with other loyalties. Some commanders have been reluctant to give up autonomy and their own revenue sources.

A main faction is the National Resistance Forces, established in 2017 and long backed by the UAE. With an estimated 30,000 fighters, it has been considered one of the best-armed factions, according to the Washington-based Middle East Institute.

It was the main group holding Yemen’s Red Sea coast but not the only one.

The Giants Brigades was also part of the command overseeing the coast. Also once funded by the UAE, it broke with other Emirati allies last year and is now backed by the Saudis.

Mistrust between the two runs deep. The National Resistance Forces is made up largely of Yemenis from the north, led by a commander related to the country’s former autocrat, Ali Abdullah Saleh, who died at the hands of the Houthis in 2017. The Giants Brigades is dominated by tribesmen from the south who are mostly Salafis — an ultraconservative movement within Sunni Islam — and who hold bitter memories of Saleh’s rule.

Officials say leadership disputes and lack of coordination between the factions were a major factor in their defeat by the Houthis as they moved along the coast.

The Saudis are trying to build a new Yemen command

Saudi Arabia also has been trying to build an umbrella group to unify Yemeni factions, called the National Shield. Established in January 2023, it reports to Rashad al-Alimi, the Saudi-based chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

The National Shield is dominated by Salafi fighters with close ties to Saudi Arabia. It also includes tribal fighters, with some absorbed from the previously UAE-backed separatists.

Composed of three divisions with tens of thousands of fighters, it operates in the sprawling central province of Hadramawt and areas in southern and eastern Yemen. The group also controls Yemen’s main land borders with Saudi Arabia and Oman.

The National Shield is not yet trying to bring the National Resistance and Giants into its forces.

There is also an official Yemeni government military. But it was weakened for years by the UAE, which saw it as too close to Yemen’s branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islah party. Instead, the UAE built a network of other groups as proxies.

Now, army forces as well as Islah-connected armed groups are stationed in the oil-rich region of Marib, one of the current front lines with the Houthis.

Southern separatists have threatened government forces

For years, one of the strongest forces against the Houthis was the Southern Transitional Council, an umbrella group of armed factions that sought to restore southern Yemen as an independent country, as it was from 1967-1990.

The UAE funded and armed the council, which fought the Houthis but also frequently clashed with the government, based in the southern port city of Aden.

The council's leadership was dismantled in January when the UAE quit Yemen. But its cause still has supporters, and earlier this month, a group of them attacked a convoy of the Yemeni defense minister, Lt. Gen. Taher al-Aqili, in the southern province of Dhale. The minister was unhurt.

Overall, the renewed fighting risks a full-scale return to the civil war that killed more than 150,000 people and forced millions from their homes. Already, nearly 130,000 people have been newly displaced and hundreds killed.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

News.title: France releases infertile Asian tiger mosquitoes to fight dengue threat
News.content:
French cities are fighting the growing threat of diseases like dengue, chikungunya and Zika in mainland Europe by releasing millions of sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes.

Terratis, a new company in the southern city of Montpellier, is breeding infertile males on an industrial scale as a long-term solution to the rapid spread of the disease-carrying insects.

The sterile males are bred at a factory in the southern city of Montpellier and then released in urban hot zones where the mosquitoes are most prevalent. After they have mated, females reproduce only empty eggs for the remainder of their lives.

“By using this technique, the mosquitoes will have no descendants and then, in theory, we can reduce the population with each generation,” said Clelia Oliva, the founder of Terratis.

“We are confident of being able to achieve a reduction of between 70 and 90 per cent in the towns in which we are releasing the sterile mosquitoes.”

The company, which started only two years ago, has experienced a dramatic surge in demand in the last few years as France tries to deal with the invasive species.

News.title: ‘42 surgeries in 48 hours’: Doctors face extreme pressure in South Sudan
News.content:
Dr Mathiang Agany had no idea what was coming.

On a humid morning in April, scores of patients were rushed into his basic hospital in rural South Sudan after a shoot out between rival gangs. As the most senior doctor, Dr Agany, a maternal health specialist, had to perform 42 surgeries in just 48 hours.

Working alongside a second surgeon, a nurse and an anaesthetist, Dr Agany, 44, carefully extracted bullets from the vital organs of nine patients.

In 22 cases, he glued together fractured bones; and in four others he clamped damaged tissues shut and repaired torn organs.

Over the same 48 hour period, he also delivered seven babies through emergency c-sections.

“You are tired... but you can relax later,” he told The Telegraph over a video call.

“My job [was] to keep people alive”.

Separate to the ruinous four-year civil war in neighbouring Sudan, the violence plaguing South Sudan is inter-communal, a self-perpetuating cycle of cattle raiding, territorial disputes and revenge attacks carried out by armed youth militias from pastoral communities known as Titweng (“cattle guard”).

Young children were among the victims, including a four-year-old boy, whose leg was fractured by a gunshot, and a nine-month-old baby girl whose chest was grazed by the same bullet that killed her father.

Sports.title: Who is Morgan Gibbs-White’s fiancee Britney De Villiers? Meet the model and TikToker
Sports.content:
Next

BRITNEY De Villiers has built a huge social presence while supporting her footballer fiance Morgan Gibbs-White.

The South African model and influencer regularly shares fashion, family life and football-related content with her army of followers.



Who is Britney De Villiers?

Britney De Villiers, 26, is a model, content creator and law graduate from South Africa.

As of September 23, she boasts more than 273k Instagram followers and over 621k on TikTok.



She shares everything from fashion and beauty content to glimpses of life with Nottingham Forest star Morgan Gibbs-White and their kids.

Her social media accounts have also documented the couple’s trips around the world, including holidays in Dubai, Italy, Portugal, Monaco and St Tropez.

Britney and Morgan reportedly met through a mutual friend in 2019, when they were both 19.

She later explained that their young age was why they waited several years before getting engaged.

Britney has also regularly supported Morgan from the stands and has not been shy about backing him online.

After he was initially left out of Thomas Tuchel’s latest England squad, she shared a statistic with her Instagram followers highlighting his chance creation in the Premier League.



Her post read: “Morgan Gibbs-White is the only player to have created five+ chances in a single Premier League game this season.”

What was Britney De Villiers’ viral TikTok with Morgan Gibbs-White?

Just days later, Morgan received the call he had been waiting for.

The 26-year-old was drafted into the England squad following Cole Palmer’s withdrawal.

But Morgan had already headed off on a family holiday to Dubai with Britney and their young ones.

Just two hours into the trip, he had to pack his suitcase and leave to join up with the Three Lions.



Britney went viral after making light of the situation with a TikTok in which the couple mimed Gotta Go My Own Way from High School Musical 2.

Morgan played Vanessa Hudgens’ character Gabriella as he waved goodbye with his suitcase.

Britney captioned the clip: “When he gets a last minute England call-up 2 hours into the family holiday.”

She joked that he must have been in a particularly good mood to agree to make the video, which quickly picked up more than 100,000 likes.



When did Britney and Morgan Gibbs-White get engaged?

Morgan proposed to Britney during a romantic trip to Lake Como in June 2025.

She announced the news on Instagram with pictures from the Italian beauty spot and simply wrote: “Forever.”

Britney later joked ion TikTok: “It only took six years and two babies. Don’t lose hope girls.”

The couple share two sons together. Their eldest, Greyson, was born in 2023, and Hayes followed on August 8, 2025.

On becoming a father for the first time, Morgan told BBC Sport: “It’s the best feeling in the world. No feeling can describe it. It’s the hardest thing in the world as well.



“[Life] has changed for the better. It’s calmed me down and chilled me out. It’s another purpose to do well in football and do well in life.

“Ever since he’s been with us, everything I do is for him. Every decision I make now I think twice about.

“Now he’s getting to the age where he’s got personality and is starting to express himself. He has this belly laugh going, I’m loving it.”

At the time of writing, Britney and Morgan have not publicly announced a wedding date.

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim’s Man Utd sacking payoff revealed with Portuguese boss receiving just HALF of Erik ten Hag’s fee
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED have saved £8.5m after Ruben Amorim was hired by Milan in the summer.

United’s third-quarter results in May showed the club were set to lose £16.7m in maximum exposure figures after the Portuguese and his team were sacked in January.



But United’s end of year financial results released on Wednesday show Amorim’s appointment at Milan in June cut the cost of his exit payout and saved debt-ridden United from paying the full amount of his remaining contract.

The full year results show United paid out £8.2m in “exceptional items,” primarily driven by severance packages for Amorim and his backroom staff, along with final corporate restructuring fees.



When managers are dismissed, standard contracts don’t pay out the full remaining salary upfront in a single lump sum.

Instead, the club continues paying their weekly wage until the contract expires or until they land a new job.

When United chiefs dismissed Amorim after his outburst at Leeds in January, they faced a maximum liability of £16.7m to cover him and his coaching staff through June 2027.

But Amorim joining Milan meant United’s obligation to pay his contract ended after just five months out of work, capping the losses at around half that figure.

His Milan role saved the club a repeat of their payout fiasco after sacking Amorim’s predecessor Erik ten Hag.

The Dutchman received £15million at the end of his disastrous reign at Old Trafford in 2024.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

But the mammoth payday only came after United chiefs elected to offer the manager and improved contract that summer, rather than allowing him to continue through the final year of his deal.

He lasted just 14 games after the new contract was signed – a move that cost United as much as £7m.

Amorim’s successor Michael Carrick was appointed permanent manager after guiding United to a third Premier League place finish after replacing the former Sporting boss on a temporary basis.

Amorim’s Milan beat 4-2 Carrick’s side in their pre-season friendly in August in Wroclaw, Poland.

But Milan owner Gerry Cardinale held an ‘internal meeting’ with Amorim following their dismal 2-0 defeat to Benfica in the Europa League last week.



Despite his unbeaten start to life in Serie A, winning two and drawing two of his opening four league matches, Amorim’s defensive approach has been called out by Italian media.

Reports in Italy suggest Amorim still has the full support of the Milan board and they have no plans of making a change in the immediate future.

Sports.title: Man Utd finances revealed as Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s side announce £43million LOSS… but there’s hope yet for Red Devils
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED suffered a £43million net annual loss – £10m more than last year.

Despite pulling in a record-breaking £677.6m in revenue, the Red Devils’ end of year financial results saw its annual net loss widen.



But Old Trafford bosses insist ongoing cost-cutting will lead to long-term financial stability.

United’s net losses have increased to £43m from £33m last year, and borrowing is up £95m to take the total to £583m.



The loss is primarily attributed to reduced broadcasting revenue and ticket sales due to the club’s absence from European competitions this season.

Meanwhile, total revenue for the year ending June 30, 2026 increased by £11.1m.



That was despite matchday revenue being down after embarrassing early cup exits to Grimsby and Brighton caused a 40-game season, with no European football on the cards either.

United say “non-current borrowings” now stood at £577.6m, up from £471.9million a year ago.

They also have a revolving credit facility, which is akin to a credit card, and that balance stood at £110m at the end of June this year.

United’s increase in revenue was driven by an uptick in broadcasting income, which rose by £33.9m this year due to a third-place finish, compared to 15th a year ago.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The club’s wage bill fell, down to £302m, which United said was “primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men’s first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction program”.

While ticket sales, shirt deals, and cost-cutting made the core business profitable, the combined weight of debt financing, manager payouts, and past transfer accounting pushed the club £43m into the red.

Chief executive Omar Berrada said: “We are pleased to have secured record revenues and adjusted EBITDA which demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football.

“This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

“While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.



“With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men’s and women’s teams during the summer window and our men’s team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford.

“Our other main area of focus is our plan to develop a new 100,000 seater stadium.

“We have now completed the major milestone of securing the land which will form part of the proposed location of the new stadium.”



Under-fire minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe sought to reduce waste when he purchased a minority stake with the club £1.1bn in debt and later claimed United could go bust due to unsustainable spending.

Ratcliffe, 73, has slashed costs across the club, including ditching the annual Christmas party and removing Sir Alex Ferguson from his paid role as an ambassador.

Many fans have blamed the financial situation at United for the failure to match many of their rivals’ spending in the transfer market this summer.

Addressing the transfer situation in his news conference earlier this month, head coach Michael Carrick said: “The situation is what it is, in terms of finances and what we can work with.”

United have made an underwhelming start to the Premier League campaign and needed a late leveller from Matheus Cunha to escape from Fulham with a point on Sunday.



Carrick’s side have only won one top-flight clash this season – leaving them already TEN points adrift of table-topping Manchester City.
