The other four nations in Europe's big five leagues all managed over 1,000 players in the same category. Italy's players - young or old - are just not as fancied by Europe's elite.

The lack of quality coming from the Italian ranks could also be seen in the national team. Between June 2025 and February 2026, only one capped player for the national team was under the age of 24 - Inter's young forward Pio Esposito. England managed a dozen in the same period.

In 2025, Italy also gave 1.9 per cent of their Serie A minutes to eligible players under the age of 21. That was the second-lowest out of the top 50 leagues in world football. Only the United Arab Emirates Pro League managed fewer.

It also contributed to a weaker Serie A last season. Veteran players Kevin De Bruyne, Luka Modric and Jamie Vardy were among the high-profile signings. And there was a similar lack of creativity amongst the managers too.

The likes of Antonio Conte, Max Allegri, Gattuso, Luciano Spalletti and Maurizio Sarri have all been passed around the top Italian clubs without much variation. Even this summer, Sarri moved to Atalanta, while Allegri joined Juventus.

Cesc Fabregas' Como revolution - resulting in their Champions League qualification earlier this year - is exactly what can happen when tactical ideas emerge from outside that never-ending cycle. Ruben Amorim has also turned up at AC Milan and played some eye-catching football with the Rossoneri.

But there are some signs that times could be changing for Italy. Mancini's first Italy squad back contained a few positive surprises. A 34-player roster included nine uncapped players - and 11 players under the age of 23.

That includes Borussia Dortmund's 18-year-old striker Samuele Inacio, Chelsea-bound defender Honest Ahanor, now at Crystal Palace. Brentford's Michael Kayode is among the new 'young revolution'.

Image: Samuele Inacio is one of the up and coming stars of Italian football

As well as Inacio and highly-rated Inter forward Esposito - who has five goals in nine Italy caps - there is also FC Nurnberg's Ali Zoma who has 20 goals in 36 appearances in the German second division. Midfielder Issa Doumbia is also a key player at Sporting CP this season.

There's a new generation of young Italian stars.

"There will certainly be some established players. We're getting older, but we're still young, and there will also be some very young players joining the team," says Donnarumma.

"So it will be a mixture, and we need to help these young players integrate well. They can give us a great deal of help.

"They're certainly talented players who need to play and gain experience, but I'm sure Italy will return to where it belongs."

Italy have a very tricky Nations League group, with Belgium, Turkey and France competing in a very competitive Group A.

But a nation who has been lingering in the dark for so long needs just one spark.

Watch The World Football Show this Thursday on Sky Sports News to see more analysis of Italy's recent plight and a preview of Roberto Mancini's second spell at 2pm

Sports.title: Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking order
Sports.content:
The document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is safely preserved at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Nearly 150 years after fans started paying up front to watch their team, the season ticket remains a key component in the success of English football. It is also an enduring source of conflict between supporters and clubs, with tensions seemingly reaching new heights. Arsenal, like United, have continued to act against the perceived misuse of tickets, suspending nearly 74,000 club accounts since they began a crackdown in 2024. This summer Chelsea became the latest club to insist on minimum levels of attendance to retain your ticket for the following season. Bournemouth moved 600 season-ticket holders to accommodate new hospitality seats and 14 out of the 20 top-flight sides raised their season-ticket prices.

Season-ticket holders have long felt undervalued. But there is a growing sense, especially among fans of the biggest clubs, that they are falling ever further down the pecking order as economic imperatives change. It is a feeling that intensified after a World Cup that seemed precision-tooled to extract as much money as possible from the most devoted fans. One Liverpool supporter crystallised common fears when he appeared on The Overlap at the start of the season arguing that a big club would soon try to get rid of season tickets altogether. The clip went viral.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal celebrate victory over Atlético Madrid with fans in May. The club have suspended 74,000 fan accounts under a crackdown launched in 2024. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

The Football Supporters’ Association argues that clubs’ present behaviour shows an antagonism towards season ticket holders. “There’s a sense from supporter groups at the most successful teams that their club executives and owners don’t fully appreciate season ticket holders and would rather have stadiums full of one-off visitors,” an FSA spokesperson said.

“Those who only measure things by the bottom line see season-ticket holders as a group whose matchday spend is lower than the once-a-year fan who will fill their bag at the club shop and pay a bigger premium for their ticket. It’s a shortsighted vision.”

The claim that clubs want to swap longstanding supporters for one-off tourists is at the heart of many fans’ fears over season tickets and, to a certain extent, it bears out. Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management in Düsseldorf, says season tickets “come at a cost” for clubs.

“In the Premier League, demand is way higher than seat supply,” Schreyer says. “But season ticket holders get discounted seats, right? They are also more likely to be no-shows. When they do come they spend less on food, less on merchandise and they come later to the stadium. They also don’t churn, because these tickets are so scarce that nobody in their right mind would give them away. Every year the average age grows by one because there is no one new getting tickets. So for the clubs, there are a lot of economic problems from their season ticket holders.”

That, however, is only one side of the ledger. “What we should not forget is that, in the end, season ticket holders are part of a product that, in the case of the Premier League, is marketed to a global audience,” Schreyer says. “They are creating an atmosphere. Season ticket holders are also used to all the rules and the rituals and the songs, the moments that make this experience very special. So tourists want to come because they want to experience it. If you were to get rid of all the season ticket holders, you would have all the operational and coordination costs of doing it and the product would not be the same any more.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A packed Anfield. Bigger clubs have been accused of prioritising tourists over season ticket holders, who generate the atmosphere that enhances the attraction. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

There are other reasons why season tickets work for clubs, not least because they generate a largely predictable amount of revenue that turns up at the same time each year (at the very end of the season where it can be usefully deployed to help with transfer spending limits). For most clubs, it would not be feasible to replace season-ticket holders with one-off fans even if they wanted to. But with the average number of season tickets at any given Premier League fixture running at 75% of all tickets, is there a case that this number should not be set in stone? Could access to matches be broadened without killing off a part of what made them great?

“In theory, you could give all the seats to season ticket holders and still have a lot of tickets for new fans if you manage it effectively,” Schreyer says. “You just need to change the mechanism in order to get the ticket that is unused on to the secondary market.”

This is what is happening at a number of clubs, with fans being asked to return their tickets for resale if they are not being used. But these requests have often come with warnings that tickets could be removed should fans not comply. Some of the tension around season tickets is simply because clubs are not talking clearly or frequently enough with fans. “Clubs don’t communicate that well,” Schreyer says. “I don’t understand why they don’t get fans on board better. You can make things so transparent.”

It is instructive looking across the Premier League at the season-ticket policies of each club, the way they were announced and the response they received from supporters. Brentford raised prices for the first time in five years, but faced minimal pushback. Brighton’s 3% rise was backed by the fan advisory board. Chelsea and Tottenham froze prices but still found themselves at odds with their fanbase.

The season ticket is a device as old as the game itself but has grown to become a symbol of the connection between fanbases and clubs. Disputes over the importance of season tickets may prove to be a harbinger of their demise, but may equally be better understood as a sign of the dysfunction at the top of our biggest clubs.

Sports.title: Ireland manager gets prime minister Martin’s backing in row with Israel over ‘genocide’
Sports.content:
Ireland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, after Israel’s football federation accused Hallgrimsson of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy” over comments about the war in Gaza.

“I think those are unacceptable remarks; they should be withdrawn,” Martin told reporters in New York, where he is attending the UN general assembly. “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.”

Hallgrímsson sparked the row after saying before two Nations League fixtures against Israel: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”

Quick Guide How do I 

Martin said Hallgrímsson’s comments reflected concerns about the scale of death and destruction in Gaza, also citing remarks by the UN secretary general, António Guterres.

On Wednesday Hallgrímsson, preparing for Thursday’s game in Kosovo, expressed gratitude for Martin’s backing. “What I said at the last press meeting has taken the attention away from maybe what’s most important; we are playing an important game against Kosovo,” Hallgrimsson said.

“Maybe, from a ‌leadership point of view, not clever for me to take the attention like this. But to answer the question, we are thankful for all the support we get. It’s a tricky time for ​us.“

The dispute comes amid mounting controversy in the Republic over the fixtures, scheduled for 27 September and 4 October. More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter calling on the national team to boycott the matches, and protesters gathered outside the team’s Dublin hotel on Monday. Further protests are planned around the country in the run-up to the games.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) passed a motion last November requesting that European football governing body, Uefa, suspend Israel from international competition. The FAI has said it has little choice but to fulfil the fixtures or risk sporting and financial sanctions.

Ireland’s designated home match on 4 October was moved from Dublin’s Aviva Stadium to Backa Topola, Serbia, after concerns over disruption and security. The 27 September match, officially Israel’s home fixture, will also be played at a neutral venue, in Debrecen, Hungary.

Israel strongly rejects allegations that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. Hamas led the deadliest attack against Israel on 7 October 2023 when militants killed 1,221 people and dragged into Gaza 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead, according to Israeli official figures.

Israel launched a massive retaliatory offensive that has displaced virtually the entire population at least once and has killed 73,919 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy for Palestinians often linked to the country’s history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway and has repeatedly criticised Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza.

Reuters contributed to this report

Sports.title: Disney+ criticised for advert break during Women’s Champions League game
Sports.content:
Disney+ has been criticised by viewers after an advert break interrupted the second half of Tuesday’s live television coverage of Arsenal’s opening Women’s Champions League fixture.

Fans were unable to see the action for about three minutes, with some 15 minutes remaining, during Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over the Danish side HB Køge.

Some viewers saw the adverts, while others were presented with the words “commercial break in progress” on an orange backdrop.

Once match coverage resumed, the commentary team continued without commenting on the disruption, seemingly unaware it had happened. No goals were missed and Arsenal scored the winner through Mariona Caldentey’s 93rd-minute penalty.

Disney+ has been approached for comment.

The streaming platform’s Women’s Champions League coverage is produced by ESPN. Many fans vented frustration on social media during and after the advert break, and some received replies from the Disney+ Help account on X, which wrote to one fan, Emelia: “Sorry for any frustration, Emelia! Our Disney+ Standard and Disney+ Premium plans are without commercial interruption, but these plans may include limited promotional content including clips and trailers, as well as branded content or programme sponsor messaging. Live and special events may also have ads.”

However, it is understood Tuesday’s interruption was unintended and was caused by a technical issue, which Disney+ is understood to be taking steps to address.

In 2025, Disney+ secured a five-year deal to broadcast the competition exclusively across Europe, including to viewers in the United Kingdom, replacing the previous rights holders, Dazn.

The streaming platform’s coverage also drew criticism from some fans for the unusually quirky nature of its analysis show, which included the presence of a dog in the studio and a quiz about Italy, including a question about pasta. A new show called The Hangout, which aired live from 5pm until 10.30pm BST to cover the 5.45pm and 8pm kick-offs, also included guests enjoying a vegetable platter while discussing the games.

The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughes wrote on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”

It is understood Disney intends to listen to audience feedback regarding The Hangout as the season progresses.

Sports.title: Ten of the best-value deals from this summer’s transfer window
Sports.content:
1 Rodrigo Mora: Porto to Roma (£21.4m)

Even in this era of relentless transfer inflation, a fee of more than £20m does not usually represent a bargain. Roma’s move for the Porto playmaker Mora may be an exception, though. The teenager has been on the radar of Europe’s elite teams since starring for Porto’s B-team at 15, and Porto were braced for his €70m (£59.5m) release clause to be met in the summer of 2025. That didn’t happen and Mora then fell out of favour under the new head coach, Francesco Farioli. Roma swooped with an offer of €25m (£21.4m), plus a 50% sell-on fee which can be bought out. The potential move also intrigued Mora, who was eager to play under Gian Piero Gasperini. “He played a big part in my decision to come here because he likes players with my qualities, and I’m a fan of the way he wants his teams to play,” Mora said. The early signs are positive, with Mora netting his first Roma goal against Lecce as the Giallorossi made a flying start in Serie A.

2 Elliot Stroud: Mjällby to Hull (£3.5m)

Getting promoted to the Premier League is an expensive business. This summer, Ipswich, Coventry and Hull collectively spent £450m net on players. Amid such frantic investment, Hull’s move for the 24-year-old Sweden international Stroud looks like excellent business. The wide player was a standout for Mjällby as the small-town team won the Swedish title last year, earning a place in Graham Potter’s World Cup squad. Sergej Jakirovic identified him as a key squad addition after Hull’s playoff final success. “He’s a very good player; he’s very versatile,” the Hull manager said. “He can play full-back, wing-back, left-winger, and in the middle. He’s a runner too, so I think he will suit us very well.” Stroud has been a pacy creative outlet for Jakirovic’s hard-working unit.

3 Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang: Marseille to Deportivo (£1.3m)

On the face it of, paying a nominal fee to sign a striker of Aubameyang’s class and experience is a no-brainer. Still, the former Arsenal and Dortmund player is 37 and has endured a nomadic career since leaving Barcelona. An unsuccessful stint with Chelsea has been followed by two seasons with Marseille, sandwiching a year in Saudi Arabia. Aubameyang’s goal return has still been impressive, with 44 across the last three campaigns, and he has reportedly accepted a greatly reduced salary to play regular La Liga football. Dépor’s ambitious project looks the perfect fit, with Aubameyang scoring five goals in seven league games.

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has five goals in seven league games for Deportivo. Photograph: Miguel Riopa/AFP/Getty Images

4 Satoshi Tanaka: Fortuna Düsseldorf to Schalke (£900,000)

The Bundesliga’s trio of promoted clubs, in sharp contrast to their English counterparts, spent a combined £7.2m net on signings. The second-tier champions, Schalke, secured some notable names on loan (including boyhood fan Robin Gosens) but the holding midfielder Tanaka was their most expensive permanent recruit, at €1m. The 24-year-old still represents something of a gamble, his only previous experience of German football coming since January with Fortuna, who were relegated to the third tier. Tanaka still caught the eye of Schalke’s director of football, Youri Mulder, who said: “His work rate and intensity fit our game really well.” On his Bundesliga debut, Tanaka’s battling qualities helped his team hold Bayern Munich to a goalless draw, and he could be key to whether Schalke stay clear of trouble.

5 Nico Elvedi: Mönchengladbach to Leeds (£6.8m)

Leeds have a clear recruitment model: sign reliable, experienced players with strong physical attributes, preferably from the Bundesliga. The Swiss centre-back Elvedi fits that mould perfectly. Daniel Farke might have anticipated an adjustment period for a player who had spent 11 years at Borussia Mönchengladbach. Instead, Elvedi has settled quickly alongside his fellow newcomer Tarik Muharemovic, mostly playing on the left of Farke’s back three. It’s a welcome reunion for the 29-year-old with his former Gladbach coach. “It was just one year but I loved him as a manager,” Elvedi has said of Farke. “I learned a lot from him and I will learn a lot now.” He is learning fast already.

Quick Guide How last year's picks have fared Show Robin Roefs (NEC to Sunderland, £9.1m; pictured) The Dutch keeper’s commanding presence was key as Sunderland secured European football. Kept 10 clean sheets in 35 league games, with only three teams conceding fewer goals than the promoted Black Cats. Ferran Jutglà (Club Brugge to Celta, £4.7m) Made a solid start at Celta with nine La Liga goals, but struggled to make an impact in Europe. Hit a purple patch in March and is now playing more regularly as a No 9 rather than out wide. Ernest Poku (AZ to Leverkusen, £8.7m) Featured regularly in his first season at Leverkusen, but was allowed to join Besiktas on a loan-to-buy deal this summer. The winger has made a slow start in Turkey but scored in their Europa League win over Marseille. Adrian Truffert (Rennes to Bournemouth, £11.4m) The left-back settled quickly in Bournemouth’s rebuilt defence, helping his side qualify for Europe. Called up by Zinedine Zidane for the Nations League and could win his second France cap, four years after making his debut. Santiago Hidalgo (Independiente to Toulouse, £2.5m) Enjoyed a promising first season in France with nine goal involvements in Ligue 1. May need to find another goalscoring gear this term with Toulouse struggling early on. Borna Sosa (Ajax to Crystal Palace, £3m) Played in 18 games for Palace last season but managed just 99 minutes in the Premier League as he struggled for consistency. Now on loan at Cologne, and looks unlikely to have a future at Selhurst Park. Berke Ozer (Eyupspor to Lille, £3.9m) Kept a league-best 13 clean sheets in his first season, helping Lille finish third. Ozer has retained the No 1 spot despite the arrival of Paraguay World Cup hero Orlando Gill, and was voted fans’ player of the month in August. Christian Ordoñéz (Vélez Sarsfield to Parma, £6.7m) One of six Argentinian players in the current Parma squad, Ordonez has admitted to being “surprised” at the step up in quality, but has featured regularly in a solid first season in Serie A. Carlos Soler (PSG to Real Sociedad, £6.9m) Midfielder has enjoyed a much more pivotal role at Real Sociedad, scoring in the Copa del Rey final shootout victory over Atletico to help deliver a trophy. Nikola Stulic (Charleroi to Lecce, £4.3m) Signed to replace namesake Nikola Krstovic at Lecce, the centre-forward had a middling first season, scoring four of his side’s 28 league goals. • Read last year's list here Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

6 Gabriel Vidovic: Dinamo Zagreb to Paderborn (£2.6m)

Paderborn have returned to the Bundesliga with a bang after shocking Wolfsburg in the promotion/relegation playoff, smashing their transfer record (which, admittedly, was only £700,000) to sign Vidovic and the striker Marvin Pieringer for €3m each. Vidovic is a former Bayern Munich academy talent and his return to Germany’s top flight is an intriguing prospect. He was brought through at Bayern by Julian Nagelsmann but the Croatian playmaker could not become a regular there. A successful loan in Zagreb led to another chance to impress with Mainz but Vidovic barely featured and Bayern cut the loan short. After moving back to Dinamo permanently, the Bundesliga looked a distant prospect until Paderborn pounced. “His sporting CV speaks for itself,” their sporting director, Sebastian Lange, said. The 22-year-old’s arrival is a risk for a club with limited means, but the potential ceiling spotted by Nagelsmann makes it one worth taking.

View image in fullscreen Gabriel Vidovic came through at Bayern Munich under Julian Nagelsmann. Photograph: Leon Kuegeler/AFP/Getty Images

7 Giovanni Reyna: Mönchengladbach to Strasbourg (£2.6m)

As the self-styled “league of talents”, Ligue 1 functions as a development pool for young players who are sold on for hefty fees. Strasbourg, a “partner club” to Chelsea, are closely tied to this model: four of their summer signings were drawn from the vast stock of spare players at Cobham, while Valentín Barco and Emmanuel Emegha went in the other direction. Reyna, despite being 23, feels like a different prospect. He was once a heavily hyped youngster who thrived with Jude Bellingham and Erling Haaland at Dortmund, but injuries and inconsistency have stalled his career. Reyna made only four league starts in his solitary season at Gladbach but has begun promisingly in France. He scored his first Strasbourg goal in the 6-2 rout of Troyes in early September; if he can stay fit and capitalise on this new start, it may not be long before he is linked with a move across the Channel.

8 Flávio Nazinho: Cercle Brugge to Monaco (£4.3m)

An attacking left-back once touted as the next Nuno Mendes, Nazinho was called up to Sporting’s first team by Ruben Amorim but made only 11 appearances before drifting back into the reserves. An initial loan to Cercle Brugge in 2023 became permanent for €2m the following summer, and regular game time began to breed results. After recording four goals and eight assists last season, Nazinho was snapped up by Cercle’s partner club, Monaco. He has made an immediate impact, striking up a left-flank partnership with Stanis Idumbo as Filipe Luís’s side sit top of Ligue 1. Their Conference League campaign will offer Nazinho further chances to trust his attacking instincts, and potentially earn a first Portugal call-up.

View image in fullscreen Flávio Nazinho, battling here with Achraf Hakimi of PSG, joined Monaco from one of their partner clubs. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

9 Fran García: Real Madrid to Real Betis (£3.2m)

Real Betis stole a march on several Premier League clubs with a move for the prolific forward Troy Parrott, who quickly showed his worth with a winner against Real Madrid. The Ireland international cost Betis €20m, though, and the fee would doubtless have been higher if Parrott were heading back to Spurs, rather than to Seville. García, a left-back, may be this summer’s real steal, sold for £3.2m plus 50% of any future sale as Madrid cleared out fringe players. At 27, he is approaching his prime and has plenty of big-match experience, featuring more than 100 times for Madrid and playing two full top-flight campaigns on loan at Rayo Vallecano. García was, perhaps unsurprisingly, linked with Fulham this summer; Álvaro Arbeloa may come to regret allowing Betis to swoop.

View image in fullscreen Fran García faced Real Madrid this season after playing for the club more than 100 times. Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty Images

10 Ainsley Maitland-Niles: Lyon to Everton (£4.3m)

Everton experienced a traumatic transfer deadline day that left David Moyes with one senior striker and a squad desperately short of depth. They did at least wrap up a late deal for Maitland-Niles, a versatile addition at a decent price. The former Arsenal full-back’s arrival may not have soothed fans’ frustrations, but his late equaliser against Manchester United may already have repaid a decent chunk of his fee.

Sports.title: Which football stadiums have the highest and lowest Google ratings? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“As someone who occasionally has to search for stadiums to find directions and the like, I always enjoy that people take the time to rate their experience of visiting a football ground,” begins our very own Will Unwin. “Hull City, for example, have 4.3 stars from 3,655 reviews. I therefore ponder … which ground has the highest and lowest Google rating?”

Pete Tomlin comes up clutch with this answer and one of the most impressive tables in Knowledge history. “I have literally searched every home football ground in the Football League via Google and I have recorded the rating and number of votes for every one,” he starts. “The range is not particularly large – the highest recorded rating is 4.7 and the lowest is 4.0. Therefore, where the scores are tied, I have used the higher number of votes as the decider with the largest number of votes being the winner. Not surprisingly, the bigger and more successful clubs tend to have the higher ratings. The nine highest-rated grounds are all Premier League clubs.

“The highest overall is Anfield (Liverpool) with a rating of 4.7 from 54,546 votes. Only two other clubs have achieved a 4.7 rating: Tottenham Hotspur (26,545 votes) and Nottingham Forest’s City Ground (2,245 votes). Just behind with a 4.6 rating are Old Trafford/Manchester United (54,535 votes), Emirates Stadium/Arsenal (34,778 votes), City of Manchester Stadium/Manchester City (32,246 votes), Stamford Bridge/Chelsea (25,434 votes), St James’ Park/Newcastle United (12,116 votes) and Elland Road/Leeds United (10,066 votes).

“The highest ranked ground from the Championship is Wolverhampton Wanderers’ Molineux in 11th position with a rating of 4.6 from 7,408 votes. However, League One fares better with Leicester City/King Power Stadium in 10th position (4.6 from 7,573 votes). League Two’s highest rated ground is Exeter City’s St James’ Park – ranked 31st with a score of 4.5 from 246 votes.

The lowest ranked Premier League ground is Hull City’s MKM Stadium (4.3 from 3,676 votes) and the lowest Championship ground is QPR (Loftus Road), down in 85th position with a rating of 4.1 from 3,458 votes. Only two grounds in the Football League have been rated at 4.0: Oxford United’s Kassam Stadium (2,506 votes) and the ground in 92nd position (my club!), Stevenage’s SPORTA Arena (350 votes).

Here is the complete English list, colour-coded by division:

Firing blanks

“There still hasn’t been a 0-0 draw in Serie A this season, after four five rounds of matches,” writes Stephen Hogg. “Is this getting near a record yet?”

Chris Roe, as he so often kindly does, chimes in, writing: “I only have just over 30 years’ worth of Italian league data so, within that small sample, this is equal to the longest wait for a goalless draw (between Napoli and Carpi), which came in the fifth round of matches in Serie A in the 2015-16 season.

“In the Premier League, we had to wait until the fifth round of matches on 17 September 2023 for a goalless draw (Bournemouth and Chelsea). But, you’d not be surprised to find the 21 divisions in which a longer wait was needed for a goalless draw all happened a long time ago.

“The longest top-flight wait came in just the second ever season in 1889-90 when the first goalless draw came in the 17th round of matches. This was only beaten by the 1894-95 season in tier two, where the first (of only two goalless draws in the season) came on 23 March 1895 between Arsenal and Crewe Alexandra, which was the 25th match of the season for Crewe (and the 26th for Arsenal).

“Equalling this is a much more recent example from the Scottish third tier in 2013-14, which also had its first goalless draw in the 25th round of matches (between Airdrie United and East Fife on 22 February 2014).”

Fans wearing replica kits (part II)

Last week we led with the question: “When did fans first start wearing replica kits?” and came up with the answer of Leeds United in 1973, with the caveat that there were earlier examples of other clubs, players, managers, outlets that sold or endorsed unofficial merchandise (or at least strips that weren’t an official replica of kits issued to the players). But you have been back in touch – with dozens of responses so apologies if your email didn’t make it – with some pre-1973 examples.

“I had an Umbro Brazil strip in 1970 – I was eight – and a Celtic one before that,” add Janette and Brian Kidd. “Even earlier – five or six years old – my brother and I were given football socks to wear when we played football. Strips didn’t seem to exist then. They weren’t sold by clubs. But they did have badges and sometimes numbers of the great players. Nor were they worn anywhere but on a football pitch!”

The official Brazil kit was not sold commercially during the 1970 World Cup, so it is likely the Umbro garment differed slightly from the one issued to players. As an interesting aside, the Brazil 1970 team wore two different shirts, made by two different companies during that tournament. Torn between staying loyal to a domestic supplier and keeping up with the latest technology and trend, Brazil used shirts made by Athleta – a Brazilian company – and a almost-identical Umbro kit. The only noticeable difference between them was the manufacturers’ tag in the collar and a slight variation in the shape of the numbering. Throughout the tournament, Pelé, Jairzinho and co would wear the Athleta shirt in the first half, then swap to Umbro in the second half – that is except during the final, where they wore the Umbro shirt from the start, all the way to the final whistle.

“While I can’t nail down the exact year, it was around 1970 when I had a full (kid’s) Nottingham Forest replica kit for Christmas. This predates Leeds in 1973,” declares Andy Wainwright.

“Please find pictures of my Umbro Manchester United child football kit, circa 1967, complete with grass stains,” parades Simon Crompton. “It may not have had any official branding but when I wore it I was, of course, George Best. I passed it to my daughter explaining its significance, but hastily reclaimed it when she outgrew it.”

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Simon Crompton

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Simon Crompton

“It wasn’t at a match but Alan Hull famously appeared on the Old Grey Whistle Test in 1971 wearing a Newcastle shirt,” notes John Morrow (and others).

“I bought a replica Chelsea 1965 shirt from Frank Blunstone’s sports shop in Lavender Hill, Battersea, that same year. He was, of course, a former Chelsea player [and aged 91, the current longest-surviving England senior international].”

“I had my first Liverpool kit in 1969,” writes Keith Foster. “John Bennett’s on the Old Kent Road had all the top teams’ kits, home and away. All probably unofficial. But kids have always wanted these. All my friends at school had replica kits of their favourite teams, but no one wore them to games. Firstly, it’s usually too cold to watch a game in just a shirt, and in the hooligan days, you’d be putting a target on your back. I used to go to Liverpool games in London with just an easily foldable silk scarf in my pocket. Better to be incognito!”

“In the 1969 film Kes, Brian Glover is wearing his ‘Bobby Charlton kit’ and one of the kids has a Burnley shirt on,” notices Roger Kirkby. “Being a kid myself back then I can remember several eight or nine-year-olds wearing the West Ham away shirt when playing football. They were definitely about it the mid-60s.”

View image in fullscreen Brian Glover in Kes. Photograph: Allstar Collection/Woodall Films/Sportsphoto/Allstar

“In 1959 as a 14-year-old in Wilmslow, my summer holiday job was packing Manchester United kit into boxes as potential Christmas presents for children,” adds Frank Close. “Until today, I hadn’t realised I was part of history.”

“I’m reminded of an anecdote recounted by Michael Parkinson (I think in his book, Football Daft), in which he tells of a Barnsley FC supporter in the 1950s who faithfully turned up to matches with a full kit of the time under his outdoor clothes,” writes David Crowe. “He dreamed of the day when Barnsley would be a man short and would appeal to the crowd to find someone to step in. Sadly for him – but probably not for Barnsley – his day never came.”

Knowledge archive

“Which English top-flight champions had the smallest ground at the time when they won the league?” pondered Roland Tye in 2014. “Might be worth dividing into pre- and post-war, dunno. I’m guessing Blackburn in the modern era.”

You guessed quite correctly for the Premier League era, Roland, as Ewood Park was in more or less the same state as in 1995, and with a capacity of just over 31,000. Highbury was next on the list, which could fit 38,419 in when Arsenal last won the league in 2004 [2026 update: Leicester had a capacity of 32,259 when they won the league in 2016]. Before that is trickier, obviously because of the changing nature of every ground and their capacities, and it’s probably best to stick to postwar, if only because it serves as a useful (if a little arbitrary) cut-off point for when records were reliable, each team had a settled home, etc. The best guess we could give you was Portman Road, home of the 1961-62 champions Ipswich, which was the smallest ground to call a postwar league title winner home, with a capacity of around 29,000.

Can you help?

“Andy Burnham and Mark Carney were in attendance at the recent Everton v Wolves Carabao Cup match,” mails Greg Hunt. “Have two national leaders attended a club match in the UK before, apart from European finals?”

“Antoine Semenyo (wearing No 42 for Manchester City) scored his second goal against Sunderland to make the score 4–2,” notes David Gregory. “While No 11s must make it 1–1 fairly regularly, what is the highest scoreline ever created by a player whose squad number matched the resulting score?”

“Manchester United and Spurs are not in Europe, and both knocked out of the League Cup,” begins Matt Walker. “They are also well off the pace in the Premier League (which neither were likely to win anyway). This means the only realistic chance for either to win a trophy this season is the FA Cup. What is the earliest point in a season a team in the top flight has been confirmed as having a trophy-less season?”

“In the Oxford United v Cambridge United League One fixture last Saturday, the goalkeepers in both starting lineups were called ‘Eastwood’,” notes Mat Hope. “Are there any other occurrences of keepers with the same surname starting opposing each other?”

Sports.title: Wamser rescues point for gutsy Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern
Sports.content:
Manchester City produced a gutsy performance to fight back and earn a valuable 2-2 draw away at Bayern Munich on their return to the Champions League. José Barcala’s side took the lead through Giulia Gwinn and an unfortunate Kerstin Casparij own goal but Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser earned the visitors a hard-earned point.

City’s head coach, Andrée Jeglertz, was pleased with the resolve of his side after a difficult first half. “It [a comeback] has happened before because we know the quality is there,” he said. “The mentality of ­winning and the belief is there. It shows ­something about this group again.

“There were definitely two phases of this game. In the first half, Bayern were very good. I think we were a bit slow on the ball … It was almost like we were surprised by the tempo. I know we weren’t but it looked like that. At the end of the first half, we got a little bit back. The trust and the belief at half-time was good so I felt that this is still possible.”

It was always going to be a challenging start for the English champions against a Bayern team who have historically thrived in the league phase of this competition. They came into this unbeaten in their last 15 home group-stage matches and on the back of a semi-final run last ­season that, according to Gwinn, had left them “even hungrier and eager for more”. Not only that but the German team have kicked off the defence of their Frauen-Bundesliga title in stunning fashion with five wins from five.

City also arrived in Germany full of confidence after an equally impressive start to the season. Their 4-2 win over Liverpool on Friday had been a further sign of their mettle, finding a way to win despite not being at their best.

Quick Guide WCL roundup: PSG peg back Real Madrid Show Paris Saint-Germain came from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw at Real Madrid in their Women's Champions League opener. Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG. Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – as Benfica dispatched Juventus 2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts. The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game for Inter with a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish side BK Häcken to a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack. Press Association Photograph: Alberto Gardin/Getty Images Europe Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

European football, however, presents a different test altogether and they came into this game with plenty of unknowns. How would they measure up after a year out of the competition? Could their injury-hit squad juggle the load of European football and domestic challenges?

Reality hit in a first half during which a refreshed Bayern took control of proceedings. Barcala had been able to make five changes to his starting XI, having completely rested Klara Bühl and Gwinn against Köln on Saturday, and they looked full of energy.

Bühl immediately stretched every sinew of City’s fragile-looking defence with her pace and guile. The 25-year-old was at the heart of everything Bayern created early on, firing a volley wide before setting up the equally prolific Pernille Harder for a half chance.

It did not come as a surprise, therefore, that the hosts broke the deadlock with 11 minutes on the clock. It was a move that cut through the heart of Manchester City as Linda Dallmann broke clear to send Gwinn on her way. The full-back saw the pitch open up in front of her, dispatching a cool finish past Ayaka Yamashita in the City goal.

View image in fullscreen Giulia Gwinn reacts after opening the scoring. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP

It was moment when the 4,291-strong crowd raised the decibel level, buoyed by their team’s domination and, perhaps also, the Oktoberfest celebrations. This was Bayern’s first outing at Sportpark Unterhaching and the raucous crowd seemed to settle in straight away at their new home.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The pressure on City continued. Struggling to find space in possession, they were guilty of playing into Bayern’s hands, channelling their attack centrally rather than trying to exploit the wide areas. Things got worse when an unwitting Casparij diverted a dangerous Harder cross into her own net to double the score.

This City side are made of stern stuff, however, and Jeglertz’s ­players were handed a lifeline just before the break, albeit in controversial fashion. As a blue smoke flare blazed on the pitch, the referee allowed play to continue while Casparij burst forward. Her cross was met by Khadija Shaw, whose shot was deflected into the path of Mead, who tapped home.

View image in fullscreen Bayern Munich and Manchester City try to stay focused despite a flare on the pitch. Photograph: Michaela Stache/AFP/Getty Images

The second half was a much more even affair as the pendulum of momentum swung between the teams. City should have had an equaliser when Aoba Fujino was brought down by Ena Mahmutovic only for the goalkeeper to step up and save Shaw’s penalty.

Despite the hosts still looking potent going forward, City could sense that the tide was shifting and found an equaliser with four minutes to play. Wamser, signed from Bayer Leverkusen this summer, arrived unmarked on the edge of the box to rifle home a finish on her return to Germany.

The substitute Edna Imade had two big chances to win it for Bayern late on but the visitors held strong. With one of their most difficult games out of the way, they face Real Madrid next week in Manchester with a chance of making another statement on the European stage.

Sports.title: Columbus Crew sack coach Federico Higuaín for ‘man’s game’ jibe aimed at female referee
Sports.content:
Major League Soccer club Columbus Crew have sacked their reserve team coach after he allegedly grabbed a female referee’s hand and told her “don’t forget this is a man’s game”. Federico Higuaín was sent off for the incident, which occurred during a MLS Next Pro league match, and was later given a two-match ban.

Columbus Crew’s general manager, Issa Tall, said in a statement: “We determined it’s in the best interest of our club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuaín from his responsibilities. After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our club’s standards of what’s expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met.”

Higuaín, brother of former Real Madrid striker Gonzalo Higuaín, is alleged to have refused to let go as he squeezed the female official’s hand after being told to stop three times at a match on 23 August. The Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA) said a “forceful grab” requires a three-game ban and criticised the MLS’s response for falling “drastically short”.

The PSRA added: “A male head coach committed two deliberate acts of physical abuse and sexism against a female official – squeezing her hand and refusing to let go after being told to stop three times. This physical intimidation was compounded by a demeaning, sexist remark to the official: ‘Don’t forget, this is a man’s game.’

“Women make every level of this game better. They should not have to endure intimidation or degrading comments to prove it. Our female officials have proven their excellence on the world stage. They deserve the same respect, dignity, and safe working environment as every other official.”

Columbus Crew did not immediately respond to ⁠a request for comment from Higuaín. The 41-year-old attacker ​played in Argentina, ​Turkey and Mexico before ​joining Columbus Crew where he made more than ​200 appearances.

Sports.title: Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle
Sports.content:
For Gianni Infantino there is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year.

Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifa abandoned its World Cup sell-off plan last month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body.

From his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence.

Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimate Fifa presidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March. That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him.

Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him.

A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight.

“As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team.

“If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.”

Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter.

The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team.

As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared.

The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino.

View image in fullscreen Victor Montagliani (right), president of Concacaf, is reluctant to walk away from his current role but would be the most credible challenger to Infantino. Photograph: Elizabeth Ruiz Ruiz/Getty Images

The AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on.

To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE.

Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing.

Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate.

“While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.”

Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward.

An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome.

“The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.”

Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues.

Thrive subsequently bought 20% of the LA Lakers last month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda.

A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there.

“All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.”

Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino before the World Cup final. Photograph: Pablo Morano/BSR Agency/Getty Images

“I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.”

There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal.

Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal.

Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino.

“It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.”

Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition, revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additional payment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associations during the next four-year cycle.

Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it.

Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since.

Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership.

Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation.

For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said.

“The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”

Sports.title: Kyle Walker is spotted 'completely plastered' alone late at night in Cannes after partying all day with wife Annie Kilner on break from football struggles
Sports.content:
A video that appears to show Burnley defender Kyle Walker 'completely plastered' and alone on holiday in Cannes has emerged on social media.

Walker, 36, is currently vacationing with his wife Annie Kilner during the extended three-week international break, having endured a difficult start to life in the Championship with the Clarets.

Kilner, with whom the full-back shares five children, posted an Instagram story of the married couple partying on a beach in what appears to be the luxury of the French Riviera.

Hours later, a football fan on social media posted a video of a man who they believe to be Walker slouched on a bench while apparently drunk in the depths of the night.

The X user wrote a caption along with the video which read: 'I just ran into Kyle Walker all alone and, above all, completely plastered right in the middle of Cannes'

Daily Mail Sport has contacted Burnley for comment.

Je viens de croiser Kyle Walker seul et surtout ivre mort en plein milieu de Cannes… pic.twitter.com/uSOoal9XpF — Ҡ. (@KiskinTime) September 22, 2026

Footage has emerged on social media that appears to show Kyle Walker drunk and alone in Cannes

Walker's wife Annie Kilner posted a video of the Burnley defender partying earlier in the day

Walker has featured six times for Burnley in what has been a nightmare return to the second tier, acting as captain with Josh Cullen on the sidelines for an extended period through injury.

However, the right-back was dropped by manager Nicky Hayen for Burnley's 1-1 draw with Derby County on Saturday.

The Lancashire club currently sit rock bottom of the Championship after eight games, and are winless following relegation from the Premier League last season.

Burnley fans have not witnessed their club win a football match at Turf Moor in the league since October 2025, and they haven't seen a victory in any competition since February.

They were moments away from ending that horrendous run against the Rams as they led through Zeki Amdouni’s first-half header as the match entered stoppage time.

But Mo Fuseini's dramatic late leveller ensured that Burnley's woes continued, and extended their stay at the foot of the table.

Walker has featured six times for Burnley in the Championship this season as they sit bottom

Wales international Connor Roberts filled the right-back spot in the back four against Derby, as Walker was left on the bench for the full 90 minutes by under-pressure Hayen.

Walker and his wife, Kilner, welcomed their fifth child, and first daughter, Royal Wish, into the world ahead of the new season back in July.

The couple plan on calling their baby daughter Wish, but wanted to keep the 'R' theme going with their brood.

Annie and 36-year-old Kyle's sons are called Roman, 11, Riaan, seven, Reign, five, and 14-month-old Rezon.

Last month, Annie, 33, revealed the newest addition to the family had arrived, saying: 'Our precious baby girl is here safe.

'Speechless with the amount of love we all feel and the joy she's already brought to our family.

Kilner and Walker share five children with the defender fathering a further two

'Hoping now we have announced our special news everyone respects our request for privacy as we enjoy these special moments.

'Thank you for everyone who has supported us with well wishes for the pregnancy and birth.'

Childhood sweethearts Kyle and Annie married in 2021, but their relationship hit the rocks in January 2024 after it was revealed that he was the father of Lauryn Goodman's daughter Kinara.

The influencer controversially messaged Annie on Boxing Day 2023 to reveal she was expecting her second child with Walker, who previously fathered her first son, Kairo, five, during a brief break-up with Annie.

Kyle's betrayal resulted in the defender being kicked out of the family home he shares with Annie, who later served him with divorce papers as their marriage fell apart.

Sports.title: Keely Hodgkinson is BANNED from wearing her 'sexy' running catsuit at the Olympics under Team GB rules
Sports.content:
Keely Hodgkinson will be banned from wearing her all-black Nike catsuit at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 due to Team GB's sponsorship rules.

The reigning 800-metre Olympic champion donned the ensemble, which pulled over her head and covered her in the sleek material from palms to ankles – except for her almost entirely bare back – for the first time at Athlos in London last week.

She crossed the finish line in one minute 56.40 seconds to mark Athlos' debut on the international stage with a commanding win.

The one-of-a-kind super suit, which seemingly takes inspiration from Cathy Freeman's iconic Sydney 2000 number, was engineered by Nike specifically for Hodgkinson.

When asked if she and all her competitors will be wearing the style in LA in two years' time, Hodgkinson gave an answer that suggested it could be a possibility.

'We might know some things that people don't,' the track star said. 'It was a test out there. This is not something we haven't seen before.'

Keely Hodgkinson will not be allowed to wear her all-black Nike catsuit at the Olympics in 2028

Hodgkinson wore the suit for the first time at Athlos in London last week and won the 800m

However, unless Nike's biggest rival, Adidas, knocks up a bespoke version for Hodgkinson ahead of the Games in the United States, then the 24-year-old will not be able to wear such a suit to defend her title.

This is due to Team GB's longstanding partnership with the German sportswear manufacturer, which spans back to the last Olympics that was held in LA, 42 years ago.

British athletes are required to wear the team racing kit, which is designed by Adidas, when competing for the nation at the Games. 'Technical' kit, such as running spikes, are an exception to the rule.

If Nike does roll out the full-body 'Zero-Distraction Speed Suit' to its other athletes, and World Athletics ratifies it for use at the Olympics, then Hodgkinson may indeed watch her competitors take to the track in the eye-catching black catsuit she brought back to life. But she wouldn't be able to race them in it.

Team GB and Adidas are expected to continue their partnership at the famous multi-sport event in 2028.

A Team GB spokesperson said: 'Supported by our partners and in tandem with our sports, we have always worked to provide athlete-centred and innovative kit that supports our teams to perform at their best at both the Summer and Winter Games.

Hodgkinson will once again have to wear Team GB's Adidas kit at the Games in two years

'We're confident and excited about what's ahead and the developments we're working towards for future Games, including Los Angeles 2028.'

Hodgkinson admitted she was a 'little nervous' to walk out in the speedsuit, which was completed by iridescent spikes, but felt the all-female Athlos meet – where she secured £50,000 in prize money for her win – was the ideal place to debut the ensemble.

Following her win, she said: 'Cathy Freeman and some other athletes from a while ago did something like this, and this is the updated new version, with the new technology.

'(Freeman) was before I was born, but I have seen the race and photos. It was really cool to draw inspiration from the past and make it your own as well. The style was a big thing for me.

'I wanted to be comfortable but I wanted to feel a little bit sexy, the back's open and that makes it feel really cool. It feels like I'm wearing nothing to be honest. I trained in it in South Africa in 37-degree heat and it was OK.'

Sports.title: Man City flop Tijjani Reijnders brazenly admits he went to Saudi Arabia for the money - insisting he doesn't want to work after retiring from football
Sports.content:
Man City flop Tijjani Reijnders brazenly admits he went to Saudi Arabia for the money - insisting he doesn't want to work after retiring from football

Manchester City reject Tijjani Reijnders has admitted that he moved to Saudi Arabia for the vast financial benefits.

The 28-year-old midfielder left Man City over the summer for the relatively unknown Saudi outfit Al-Qadsiah in a £52million deal.

He spent just a season at the Etihad and, despite a hugely impressive debut after joining them from AC Milan for £46.5m, he struggled to make a consistent impact across his 50 appearances.

Reijnders is on a five-year contract with Al-Qadsiah, who are managed by Brendan Rodgers, and is reportedly set to earn around £86million over the half-decade.

Now a month into his time there, he said: 'Once my playing career is over, I don’t want to have to work anymore.

'Of course, I probably wouldn’t have needed to work anymore after my contract at Manchester City either, but this move allows me to secure the future of the next generations of my family.

Former Manchester City midfielder Tijjani Reijnders has admitted he moved to Saudi Arabia for the money

He says he wants to secure generational wealth, thinking ahead to his future grandchildren

'I’m not going to lie about that. By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?'

He currently has one son, Xavien, with his wife Marina. Speaking about what attracted him to the club in August, Reijnders was not so quick to mention cash.

He said at the time: 'Especially the ambition of the club (is what attracted me).

'The club wants to be the biggest in Asia and what they did already in the past and what we can do now in the future, it triggered me a lot.

'And, yeah, I want to help the club to bring it to the highest level.

'I came here to try and win trophies with my teammates - we're playing for four trophies, if I'm right.

'We want to win as many as possible and we are all very eager to do that. And, personally, I hope I can help the team as much as possible with goals and assists.'

The Netherlands international has scored three goals in five Saudi Pro League outings for Al-Qadsiah, who also feature in the AFC Champions League.

They are currently fourth in the Saudi Pro League, where they have finished for the last two seasons.

The club is owned by the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, the majority state-owned petroleum and natural gas firm.

They do not have as many big names as some of their Middle Eastern counterparts but do have some respected faces from around Europe, such as former Spain and Italy defender Nacho Fernandez and Italy striker Mario Retegui.

Reijnders played three matches for the Netherlands at the World Cup.

Sports.title: BBC begin 'systematic dismantling of TV sports news' in brutal new cost-slashing with top journalists told their jobs are at risk and furious staff considering strikes
Sports.content:
BBC Sport staff have been told that their jobs are at risk with seven journalists’ jobs to be cut - including four senior roles - as part of cost-cutting across the corporation. Sports bulletins on the 24-hour BBC News channel will also be lost as part of the drive to save money, staff were told on Wednesday morning. The impending cuts - as reported by Daily Mail Sport on Sunday - are likely to mean some staff have to reapply for their jobs, with some considering strike action. Ski Sunday, fronted by Chemmy Alcott, has already fallen victim to BBC Sport cost-cutting A meeting at the BBC Sport’s HQ at Media City in Salford is due at 2pm on Wednesday to further outline the corporation’s plans for the future. At 9.30am a group of producers from the team responsible for sourcing sports stories were told their numbers were being cut from 15 to 11. One insider said: ‘This is the systematic dismantling of TV sports news at the BBC as we know it.’ Daily Mail Sport understands the staff were also told that they will not be able to work four-day weeks and will instead all be expected to work across five days. The prevailing view among staff is that they already work 40 hours across those four days and that the demand is evidence that chiefs do not understand how television operates. The news of cuts and programme losses come with director of sport Alex Kay-Jelski having already overseen a programme of change, with dozens of redundancies made last year. Earlier this month, the BBC announced it was to axe Ski Sunday while it came in for criticism for not building a studio in North America for the summer’s World Cup. A series of events have been dropped, including the Commonwealth Games, the Boat Race and the Rugby League World Cup. Football Focus was also canned at the end of last season.
