Sports.title: Disney's Alex Scott-fronted Match of the Day-style show enrages fans as they chase woke viewers with a dog on set, rotating sofa, cucumber snack bar and influencer pundits
Sports.content:
A new Match of the Day-style football show on Disney fronted by Alex Scott has left fans raging after a bizarre debut show on Tuesday evening.

The streaming platform launched 'The Hangout', with former Football Focus presenter Scott leading a punditry team of former footballer Lianne Sanderson and influencers Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess.

The aim of the programme was to bring analysis and reaction to the new season of the Women's Champions League, but it came under fire for a chaotic launch show.

A move to appeal to Gen Z viewers seems to have been made, with discussions about pasta and cucumbers front and centre of its debut episode.

An influencer dog named Barley was also introduced, with the animal asked to pick the winner of the Champions League through food.

The show featured a 'watch party' with Dutch twins Sanne and Merel van Dongen, with Sanne a former basketball player and Merel a footballer.

Disney's new Women's Champions League show came under fire for its debut episode

Fans criticised the chaotic approach to the show, which featured influencers including a dog

One particular clip saw Scott throw the coverage to the duo, and they asked: 'Do you want some cucumber?'

Scott replied 'no, a drink,' and was told that she might 'get a Coca-Cola' if she 'continued doing her work'.

She was then told the water they had could have been vodka, with Barley also present for the watch party.

Fans were left in disbelief at what was unfolding on social media, with one writing: 'Disney said they were a brand and ran with it. They thought a revolving sofa and dog would keep the attention of the girls whilst watching the football and stuck an ad mid game because no one’s really watching. You get comments about how empty the stadiums are but how are we growing the game if it's still being dressed up with a pink bow on the top?

'Then bored men with no club football will s**g it off because some football account is making fun of it.

'If we like women's football, we like it for the game, for the players, for their skill, our clubs. JUST like you would for a men's game. Disney, the fans of women's football do not need cute, we'd love impartial analysis, post-match interviews with the team that's played and less dog.'

Another added: 'Sorry the dog in the Disney studio for the UWCL coverage is finishing me like am I watching the coverage for the football or Crufts?'

There was no explanation for why Barley was on the show, though his 137,000 Instagram followers were mentioned.

Barley the dog has 177,000 followers on Instagram but was left scared while on the show

Dutch twins Sanne and Merel van Dongen spoke about cucumber and alcohol on the show

The dog seemed scared by the rotating floor, which was used to move the punditry team from their spot for half-time analysis to the watch party. Barley ran off but was offered pretzels to return.

The platform also came under fire for showing adverts during the action. One fan on social media posted: 'Disney + just showing an advert mid champions league game is diabolical.'

Viewers were able to choose what game they wanted to watch, and a three-minute round of adverts was shown during the second-half of Arsenal's 1-0 win over HB Koge.

Daily Mail Sport understands the adverts shown during the action was not an intended interruption and instead was a technical difficulty and that there are no plans at present to make wholesale changes to the show.

Disney have had the rights to the competition for two years now, with The Hangout new for this year. Live from 5.30pm to 10.30pm, Scott will rotate presenting duties with Shebahn Aherne.

Sports.title: How Cardiff City developed the best academy in the EFL with the help of 'the grandparents' - as Brian Barry-Murphy reveals sales pitch to ward off Premier League clubs and why he'll stick by his young talents no matter what
Sports.content:
They are well versed in the art of mining rich seams in South Wales. They trust the quality of their local resources. They commit to work hard and forge kinship. So, when Cardiff City sought a reset, the decision to go back to unearthing and nurturing their own talent served them well. No team in the EFL gave more game time to its homegrown players last season than Cardiff as they bounced back into the Championship at the first attempt under Brian Barry-Murphy. More than a third of all minutes played came from academy graduates. Among them stylish centre-half Dylan Lawlor, 20, whose effortless step into the Wales team last season has ensured a growing list of admirers including Bayern Munich. And the Colwill brothers Rubin and Joel, striker Isaak Davies, teenage full back Ronan Kpakio and 21-year-old forward Cian Ashford, who this month received his first call-up from Wales boss Craig Bellamy. 'When I first came here, I truly didn't realise the size of the club,' says Cardiff boss Brian Barry-Murphy. 'Our young players have a real sense of who they are and who they represent' Centre back Dylan Lawlor (pictured talking to Daily Mail Sport) is one of the jewels from the Bluebirds' academy, and has attracted interest from Bayern Munich

Your browser does not support iframes.

Three times inside the last 12 months, the Bluebirds have set a new club record for their youngest player. All of which has helped Cardiff emerge from the long shadow of the Emiliano Sala tragedy and subsequent relegation from the Premier League in 2019 and restore some confidence and self-esteem. 'This is a truly unique club,' boss Barry-Murphy tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I've been racking my brains trying to figure out if there's another capital city with only one club playing in a league run by another country. 'So much has changed in football in recent times, it has become so influenced by finance and outside factors, but at its core there is still a sense of who you're representing.' Perhaps the closest points of reference are the Basque clubs Athletic Bilbao and Real Sociedad, both of whom harness identity for sporting reasons in Spain's La Liga. 'When I first came here, I truly didn't realise the size of the club and how far its support stretches, right into the valleys where the history of Cardiff is so deeply rooted in the mines,' says Barry-Murphy. 'Our young players have a real sense of who they are and who they represent.' Modern clubs crave identity like this and spend fortunes manufacturing it. For Cardiff it is a natural advantage and although there were times when they failed to maximise it, this has changed. Three years ago, they opened the doors of an £8million academy training base in Llanrumney, to the east of the city. The previous year they hired as academy manager Gavin Chesterfield, an expert in player development at the Welsh FA, with 15 years behind him as manager of Barry Town and 20 years in higher education. 'I don't want to come across as if we've reinvented football, because we haven't,' says Chesterfield. 'We've got good players. This is an area that's always produced players. What we've done is focus on opening pathways. 'Relegation to League One (in 2025) gave us a chance to appraise exactly what we want to stand for. Senior players left and most of those places were filled from the academy. 'There's always an element of the unknown, but what is known is that academy players will give their all because they care about where they come from and they harbour a great desire. 'We're a patient model. We believe in coaching. We back our own for a bit longer.' 'One of the big things that attracted me to the job was my understanding of the players beneath the surface here,' says Barry-Murphy. 'I knew if I got the job I'd play those players' 'We don't single out players, but we do single out Rubin Colwill (pictured),' admits Barry-Murphy. 'Super intelligent guy, great person, very special' Gavin Chesterfield talks of 'Four Hs' representing the core values of his academy – honesty, humility, hard work and happiness Cardiff looked closely at past models of success, including how Southampton harnessed their academy when they slipped into League One in 2009. Chesterfield talks of 'Four Hs' representing the core values of his academy – honesty, humility, hard work and happiness. Key details of the environment created at Cardiff include first-team staff taking the trouble to learn about academy players, regular two-way traffic between the first-team base and the academy base, and a collection of staff members affectionately known as 'the grandparents' for their long service of more than 10 years who can share experiences and instill culture. 'Buzzword isn't it,' says Barry-Murphy, rolling eyes at the mention of culture. 'Very fashionable. I never mention it. It's not something you say. Just what you become. How you act every day.' Get it right and over time, cultural success should be silent and self-perpetuating, with the likes of 24-year-old Rubin Colwill in the first team to guide, advise and serve as an example of what is possible. Born in Neath, the Colwill brothers were raised with Cardiff loyalties. There is a famous family photo of them as children outside Wembley Stadium in club colours with bluebird crests painted on their faces before the League Cup final against Liverpool in 2012. 'We don't single out players, but we do single out Rubin,' admits Barry-Murphy. 'Super intelligent guy, great person, very special. Probably the most significant player for Cardiff in our time here.' And, of course, none of this can work if the talent is not backed with first-team opportunities. Rubin Colwill and his brother Joel (right) were boyhood Cardiff supporters and are now helping the next wave of players come through Barry-Murphy knows top talent when he sees it, having worked with Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers at Manchester City Barry-Murphy, with a fierce commitment to youth development after three years in charge of Manchester City's Under 21s, working with elite talent such as Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, has been thrilled to deliver them. 'It's not been difficult because the players we have are very good,' says the 48-year-old Irishman. 'When I first came, there had been a history in recent times of acquiring a lot of players for a lot of money from far-reaching fields. 'One of the big things that attracted me to the job was my understanding of the players beneath the surface here. I knew if I got the job I would play those players.' Rob Tankiewicz was 16 years and 117 days old when he became Cardiff's youngest ever player last October – a record held for 18 years by Aaron Ramsey and before him by John Toshack – only for it to pass 64 minutes later to his close friend Axel Donczew, then 15 years and 234 days old. 'That was an emotional night for everyone in the academy,' says Chesterfield. In August, Noah Anyadike claimed the record, just 15 years and 98 days old when he made his debut in a Carabao Cup tie with Norwich. 'All players are very different,' says Barry-Murphy. 'Noah is well developed physically, a big strong guy for 15, so he can cope. Rob and Axel were less developed physically but advanced beyond their years in terms of technical and tactical understanding.' Arsenal swooped to lure Donczew away in August. 'Top Premier League clubs can offer finances we can't,' says Barry-Murphy. 'Our biggest sales pitch are the opportunities, but you have to back that up with actions. 'Dylan Lawlor was outstanding last season. It's no secret he had many suitors over the summer. He has the potential to play at the very highest level. He's a very humble guy with a passion to play for Cardiff. I feel that every single day, it's incredible. 'We were confident he would stay because we backed up what we said to him at the start of last season about playing so many games.' 'Dylan Lawlor was outstanding last season. He has the potential to play at the very highest level' The test of nerve will come for Cardiff, a Category Two academy, now they are back in the Championship and hoping to push back towards the Premier League. 'The challenge of these things will come when you don't win as often as you did previously,' says Barry-Murphy. 'Then you have a choice – either stick by the young players and really believe in them and back them, or do what happened to them previously when they were pushed back a bit so they never quite fulfilled their potential the way they should. 'For me, it is not a difficult decision really.' The 'Raised in the EFL' campaign shines a light on the commitment of EFL clubs to the next generation of talent. Over 170 academy players had their professional debut in the Carabao Cup and EFL last season - while 19 of the 26 members of England's 2026 World Cup squad made their debuts in EFL competition.

Sports.title: Stars DO care about playing for England: Jarrad Branthwaite defends Declan Rice, Cole Palmer and Co after five dropouts cast shadow over start of Thomas Tuchel's post-World Cup mission
Sports.content:
Jarrad Branthwaite has defended his England team-mates amid a raft of withdrawals from the national team squad ahead of the upcoming Nations League fixtures.

Five key players have withdrawn from Thomas Tuchel's England squad before their international matches due to injury.

Cole Palmer, Declan Rice and Tino Livramento are among the absentees, along with Manchester United duo Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo.

James Garner and Morgan Gibbs-White have been called up as replacements.

Everton centre back Branthwaite, who earned his first cap under Gareth Southgate more than two years ago, dismissed suggestions that players are prioritising their clubs over their country.

The 24-year-old said: 'I think all players are fully committed to playing for England. I can speak for myself how much of a privilege is to to be in the England squad and to represent England, so I think it'll be the same for all the players.'

Chelsea midfielder Cole Palmer withdrew from the England squad to manage his workload

Branthwaite has struggled with injury issues of his own. Shortly after his first England appearance, he was linked with a move to Manchester United in the summer of 2024, but the club failed to meet Everton's £70million valuation. A groin operation and a thigh problem then sidelined him until October.

Last season, a hamstring injury delayed the start of his campaign until January, and another setback sustained in April limited him to just 10 Premier League appearances.

After a summer spent in Germany learning more about holistic fitness, Branthwaite has now played every minute of Everton's opening five Premier League matches and has earned his first call-up under Tuchel.

'When I went off with the injury (in April) I was devastated after the amount of times I’ve come back from it, and for it to happen again. To be called back up to the England squad means everything to me.

Jarrad Branthwaite is hoping to win his second cap after a solitary appearance in 2024

'All the hard work that went into the rehab to get to this point, it makes it worthwhile. I’m buzzing to be back in the England set-up.'

Branthwaite’s call-up marks an important first step in challenging Marc Guehi and Ezri Konsa for a place in Tuchel’s starting line-up, and he revealed that the German coach’s main message to him was to ‘come in and express yourself.’

'Every time you get the opportunity you’ve got to show the best account of yourself to give yourself the best possible chance to be in the squad and in the team for the future,’ he said.

‘That starts with every training session, every chance you step on the pitch and hopefully I can do that.’

England face Spain in their first Nations League fixture at Wembley on Saturday, before two matches against Czech Republic sandwich Croatia away over an extended international break.

Sports.title: Man United flop shows off bizarre recovery method which involves using FIRE to aid his recovery
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United goalkeeper Andre Onana has taken on a bizarre recovery method in a bid to improve his form.

The 30-year-old, who is still technically contracted to United but on loan at Turkish side Trabzonspor, has shared footage of cup therapy going to new heights and including fire.

Onana was seen lying on a massage bed with dozens of cups on his back – accompanied by various objects set alight.

Cup therapy is no stranger to those interested in recovery techniques, with the specialised objects placed on skin to create a suction.

The aim of the technique is to relieve muscle tension and improve blood circulation following exercise or activity.

Using fire, however, is not common. Onana was seen embracing the technique, however, with the hope it will give him a boost going into the international break.

Andre Onana has raised eyebrows with his recover technique, which includes fire - source: andreonana.24 Instagram

Onana joined United in 2023 before things went south and he was eventually loaned out

The goalkeeper is rebuilding his career out in Turkey after a calamitous spell at United – who he joined in 2023 – which resulted in him losing his place and, eventually, being loaned out.

His wages are not being covered by the Red Devils, and it is expected he will leave permanently either this summer or when his contract expires in 2028.

It's been a mixed season for the club so far, having been knocked out of the Europa League in the play-offs before losing their first game of the season – 2-1 to Amed SK.

They bounced back, though, beating Genclerbirligi 5-0 the following week, with Onana picking up his first clean sheet of the campaign.

Trabzonspor are currently seventh in the league table after six games, and achieved a 5-0 win over Galatasaray in the final match before the international break - though Onana will not be playing for Cameroon due to not being selected.

He has also formed an unlikely friendship with Liverpool legend Mohamed Salah, who joined the club after leaving the Reds and scored a hat-trick in the weekend win.

Sports.title: Eric Cantona teams up with Gary Lineker as Man Utd chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe slammed again
Sports.content:
Eric Cantona teams up with Gary Lineker as Man Utd chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe slammed again

Gary Lineker and Eric Cantona have both slammed Manchester United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe over recent days, following his latest comments bemoaning immigration

View 2 Images Eric Cantona and Sir Jim Ratcliffe's politics do not align (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Eric Cantona has joined Gary Lineker in calling out Sir Jim Ratcliffe after the Manchester United co-owner said: "Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem". The four-time Premier League winner even claims he would not have moved to Old Trafford from Leeds United in 1992 had Ratcliffe been a minority shareholder at the time.

‌



Cantona, 60, is the INEOS founder's favourite player. Ratcliffe, 73, even named the company he established to acquire a 25% stake in United, Trawlers Limited.

‌



It is a reference to Cantona's famous quote: "When the seagulls follow the trawler, it's because they think sardines will be thrown into the sea."

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

However, the admiration is very much one-sided due to their differing politics. After being asked by well-known United fan Pete Boyle in a video shared on TikTok whether he would have been willing to sign for a club part-owned by Ratcliffe, Cantona said: "No."

After being encouraged to expand on his blunt response to the hypothetical question posed, the interviewee went on to add: "Of course not.

‌



"You know what I think about all of this, with this kind of politics. I cannot understand how someone like this can say something like that when he's one of the club's owners."

View 2 Images Sir Jim Ratcliffe is not popular with his favourite player Eric Cantona (Image: Bo Amstrup/EPA/Shutterstock)

Cantona continued: "Football is a very popular sport. Football is made - all the greatest players come from different waves of immigration. Everywhere, in France, in England, everywhere.

‌



"In France, for instance, the greatest players all come from different waves of immigration. I made a documentary on that, French Football: An Immigrant History.

"Raymond Kopa, in the fifties, was the son of Polish immigrants who came to France, worked in France, and worked hard in France. And then the Italians, Italians like Platini. And then the Spanish, like me, my mother came from Spanish refugees. I cannot accept this kind of thing."

‌



These comments come days after Lineker branded Ratcliffe a 'not particularly pleasant human being' who is 'even worse than the Glazers'.

He said on The Rest is Football podcast : "I must congratulate the Glazers on finding someone even worse than them that they can blame and getting him in there and getting all the stick: Jim Ratcliffe.

"He's clearly... I don't think he's a particularly pleasant human being, and it's a bit of a shambles of a football club the way it's being run at the moment. So, well done to the Glazers on that one, deflecting everything away from them!"

Sports.title: Micah Richards doubles down on plans to quit punditry as he names successor
Sports.content:
Micah Richards doubles down on plans to quit punditry as he names successor

Micah Richards has reinforced his plans to give up punditry but the Sky Sports and BBC favourite has now named his heir apparent

View 3 Images Micah Richards has doubled down on his plan to quit being a pundit (Image: Getty)

Micah Richards is standing firm on giving up punditry in 2034. And the 38-year-old believes current Tottenham star James Maddison could be the one to fill his chair.

‌



After hanging up his boots in 2019, following a 14-year playing career which featured spells with Manchester City, Fiorentina and Aston Villa, Richards picked up the microphone.

‌



The 13-cap England star became an instant hit, making his broadcasting debut for Sky Sports and becoming a staple on the BBC, providing analysis on Match of the Day, Final Score and Radio 5 Live.

‌



He was front and centre at the World Cup in the summer for the Beeb, analysing the final alongside former team-mates Wayne Rooney and Joe Hart. Richards also makes up one-quarter of the revered CBS Sports Golazo team, covering European football with host Kate Scott, Jamie Carragher and Thierry Henry.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Micah Richards opens up about dad's death and tough decision to carry on with live BBC punditry READ MORE :

Roy Keane refuses to apologise as Andy Robertson tells Man Utd icon he went too far READ MORE :

Yet for all his popularity, Richards does not envisage himself staying in the punditry game for long. In July, he put a specific timeframe on when he'll step away. Now, he's dug his heels in and has even gone so far as to name Maddison and Everton star Jack Grealish as two who could step in to succeed him after they call it quits.

‌



View 3 Images Richards thinks Maddison could be the next in line once he retires (Image: Getty)

Speaking to The Telegraph two months ago, Richards said that he would be out of mainstream media by the time he is 46. He announced that he would not work beyond the 2034 World Cup and has informed Sky Sports, the BBC and CBS of this.

In an interview with The Times this week, Richards was resolute, confirming that this is still very much the case and explaining his decision. He said: "By then I'll have been 15 years a player and 15 years a pundit and what more could I ask for?

‌



"So it'll be, 'What can I give back to the game?' I don't want to work past my sell-by date. Fifteen years, whether you like me or hate me, that's enough time to get across my point. There'll be someone else on the sofa by then. [Jack] Grealish . . . or [James] Maddison. Definitely Maddison. He's a natural on TV. He's the next one."

Spurs midfielder Maddison has frequently appeared on Sky Sports, including a player-guest appearance on Monday Night Football in 2025. He has been hailed as charismatic and honest in these instances, much like the authentic Grealish.

Continuing about his punditry journey, Richards recalled how co-star and Arsenal legend Henry helped him analyse games at a new level. He said: "I remember having a chat with Thierry Henry.

‌



View 3 Images The ex-Man City defender credits Henry with helping him grow as an analyst (Image: Getty)

"He said, 'You've got a good football brain, but all my friends text me about is how much of a great personality you are.' Thierry said at some point there's got to be a switch, because when you talk about football, it was, 'I like what you're talking about, but we don't hear it enough.'

"I was taken aback. So I went to his house and we started watching games and he just tapped me like that [on the shoulder]. It was so patronising!

Article continues below

"'What do you see there?' 'Well, I see the defender.' He said, 'Yeah, but what are they trying to do? What is the plan? What is this tactic against that tactic?'

"It opened my eyes. I knew the stuff. But this was him unlocking it. I just look at the game completely different now."

Sports.title: Irish racing rallies behind jockey Kaitlyn Ryan, 21, after spinal cord injury
Sports.content:
Irish racing rallies behind jockey Kaitlyn Ryan, 21, after spinal cord injury

Amateur jockey Kaitlyn Ryan, 21, is receiving treatment for a spinal cord injury after a fall, with a GoFundMe set up by trainer Shark Hanlon raising almost half of its €90,000 target

View 2 Images 21-year-old Jockey Kaitlyn Ryan (Image: John Hanlon)

The Irish racing community is uniting in support of a promising young female jockey who has suffered life-changing injuries following a freak accident on the gallops.

Amateur jockey Kaitlyn Ryan, 21, is currently undergoing treatment for a spinal cord injury after being seriously hurt in a recent fall.

The Fethard, Co Tipperary native rode her first winner at Killarney just this past July, partnering the Bill Durkan-trained Eagle Fang to victory in a Qualified Riders' race. A UCD student, she rides predominantly for Durkan and Shark Hanlon and has taken part in 22 races as an amateur since her debut ride in July 2025.

Michael Owen spends more than £460,000 in one day on new racehorses for stable READ MORE :

Willie Mullins tribute to legendary dual champion hurdler Hurricane Fly after death aged 22 READ MORE :

Kaitlyn landed awkawardly after what had appeared a straightforward fall in which she landed while riding out.

She is receiving ongoing treatment for her injury and will continue to do so for the foreseeable future. She will face numerous lifestyle adjustments as she adapts to her new circumstances in order to maintain her independence.

A GoFundMe page set up by Carlow-based trainer Hanlon has set a target of €90,000 and has already surpassed nearly half that figure, with trainers, jockeys and industry figures digging deep to show their support.

View 2 Images Shark Hanlon: launched fundraiser for amateur rider (Image: PA)

Ryan comes from a family steeped in racing, having ridden ponies from a very young age, and the accident has deeply shaken the close-knit Irish racing community.

Hanlon said: "Kaitlyn's future is unknown and she faces a long journey ahead. We want to help Kaitlyn and her family through this challenging time.

"Kaitlyn is a lovely girl with a very good personality. She would always do anything you asked her to do. It's a freak accident, and we are going to try to help her as much as we can. The support from the racing community so far has been absolutely unreal."

Sports.title: Michael Owen spends more than £460,000 in one day on new racehorses for stable
Sports.content:
Michael Owen spends more than £460,000 in one day on new racehorses for stable

The former Liverpool and England striker was very active at the Tattersalls Ireland September Yearling Sale where he bought five lots with trainer Hugo Palmer

View 3 Images Michael Owen (circle): bought lot 231 for £180,000 (Image: Tattersalls Ireland)

Michael Owen spent more than £460,000 in one day buying new horses for his successful racing stable.

‌



The former Liverpool and England striker was very active on the first day of the Tattersalls Ireland September Yearling Sale where five lots were knocked down to his team.

‌



Since retiring from football, Owen has invested time and money in another passion, horse racing, establishing Manor House Stables in Cheshire. Owen won his first Classic with Brown Panther, a horse he also bred, when he captured the Irish St Leger in 2014 and secured his richest top level victory in August this year when Glacius, trained by Hugo Palmer, captured the £550,000 Saratoga Derby in the US.

‌



Owen, Palmer and bloodstock agent Ed Sackville were in Ireland on Tuesday looking for future talent to join his 135-horse stable.

Willie Mullins tribute to legendary dual champion hurdler Hurricane Fly after death aged 22 READ MORE :

Value Scope Extra: Saffie Osborne could have more reasons to be tearful at Ascot READ MORE :

They came away with five yearlings including the day’s top lot, a son of 2,000 Guineas winner Chaldean, who was bought for £180,000. The team also secured two colts by Mehmas, one by New Bay and a filly by Starman.

Palmer said: “What excites me about Chaldean is that he, like Frankel, was a champion two-year-old.

‌



"This sale has been so good to me as a trainer – my first stakes winner came from here, and then there has been Galileo Gold, Hawksmoor, Adaay Of Scarlett and Sale Shark. I love the fact that we can come here and feel that we can buy any horse in the ring, which we can’t really do at any other sale.

“It means we feel that we can buy the horses we think are the best – we are coming here with a good chance.”

View 3 Images Michael Owen: bought five yearlings (Image: Tattersalls Ireland)

‌



Owen told Tattersalls: “We bought a couple of Mehmases. The one we bought for €125,000 was vert very nice, just looked a strong, typical son of the stallion.

“We’ve had luck with Mehmas here before with Adaay Of Scarlett who has run really well this year for us. It’s always nice to go back to a proven source and we just loved him as a horse. He looks fast.”

“It means we feel that we can buy the horses we think are the best – we are coming here with a good chance.”

‌



Palmer has trained 44 winners of £1.3 million in Britain this year, including successes at the Epsom Derby meeting and Glorious Goodwood. Last year the stable had 70 wins and a prize-money haul of £1.5m.

View 3 Images Glacius: won the Saratoga Derby in August (Image: PA)

Owen said: “We’ve been flying along. It’s nice. We are up on prize-money more so than winners, which is obviously good.

‌



“We have tried to target the festivals a little bit more and some bigger races and everything’s going nicely. Every season we sort of try to make another step so we are already preparing for next season now.”

Reflecting on his yard, he continued: “It’s been a long time in the making. I bought it as an old arable farm about 23 years ago, put in a gallop, a little trotting ring and 20 boxes, and off we went.

“It’s unrecognisable compared to back then. We’ve got all kinds now and are still wanting to develop, still wanting to make it bigger and better.

Article continues below

“It’s my passion, it’s my little baby and I want to keep going.”

Sports.title: Keely Hodgkinson banned from wearing 'sexy' outfit after causing a stir
Sports.content:
Keely Hodgkinson banned from wearing 'sexy' outfit after causing a stir

Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson captured attention after unveiling her bespoke speed suit last week

View 2 Images Keely Hodgkinson showed off her new Nike outfit at the recent Athlos event (Image: Shaun Botterill/Getty Images)

Keely Hodgkinson will be banned from sporting her new Nike catsuit when representing Team GB. The 24-year-old debuted her sleek outfit during her Athlos victory in London last week.

‌



The Olympic 800m champion donned the stylish speed suit after helping Nike hone the design, which featured a topless back and a compulsory gap for her iconic ponytail. The suit immediately caused a stir as Hodgkinson ran 1:56.40, two seconds slower than her personal best, to claim the Athlos title.

‌



While the aerodynamic benefits could aid the 800m star in her rivalry with Audrey Werro, who recently won the European and Ultimate Championship titles, Hodgkinson also admitted to making aesthetic choices. She said: “The style was a big thing. I wanted it to be comfortable but also to feel a little bit sexy. The back is open. It makes it cool. I am not hot at all in it. It’s like I am wearing nothing.”

‌



Hodgkinson described how the suit made training in high temperatures easier, which could be a positive sign ahead of defending her 800m title at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. However, she will be unable to wear her custom Nike design at the LA Games due to Team GB’s long-standing partnership with Adidas.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

The Sun reports that while GB athletes are permitted to wear items such as shoes and spikes from different clothing brands, the same would not apply to Hodgkinson’s catsuit under the kit agreement. It would also ban Hodgkinson from wearing the Nike design when representing Team GB at next year’s World Athletics Championships.

‌



A Team GB spokesperson said: “Supported by our partners and in tandem with our sports, we have always worked to provide athlete-centred and innovative kit that supports our teams to perform at their best at both the Summer and Winter Games. We’re confident and excited about what’s ahead and the developments we’re working towards for future Games, including Los Angeles 2028.”

A UK Athletics spokesperson stated: “The speed suit Keely Hodgkinson wore at Athlos was a bespoke Nike design created specifically for her. We are in regular dialogue with Nike regarding all aspects of performance apparel and will continue to assess any innovations that could benefit our athletes in future championship environments.”

Despite Hodgkinson being unable to wear her Nike suit at the next Olympics, Team GB teammate Georgia Hunter Bell admitted that similar designs will be available. The 1500m runner said: “That’s going to be an option you can wear for the Olympics, when we get our kit drops for Team GB. It’s exciting to showcase it now.”

‌



View 2 Images Hodgkinson has spoken about the process of designing her suit with Nike (Image: Shaun Botterill/Getty Images)

Hodgkinson’s design looks to be the next innovative step in athletics, following on from Cathy Freeman’s bodysuit at the 2000 Olympics and Faith Kipyegon’s bespoke suit for her sub-four-minute mile attempt last year. “This has been a year in the making, with lots of adjustments and fittings. A really fun process with the Nike innovation team,” Hodgkinson said of her new design.

“It’s a mixture of fashion, speed and science, all coming together – maybe it’s the future of athletics. It’s an honour for them to choose me to put this out first.

Article continues below

“In hindsight, this is an all-women’s event – it’s all about the glitz and glamour, putting eyes on the women. It’s a moment. The perfect way to end the season.”

On her ponytail potentially impacting her performance, Hodgkinson added: “The science was like, technically with the air drag you’re slower with your hair out, but I was like, ‘That’s a non-negotiable. My hair is staying out’. I’m very much ‘look good, feel good’, mental and physical balance.”

Nike’s director of innovation apparel product design Hannah Amis said: "The large opening at the back has been a favourite of Keely’s since day one. The hood streamlines the hairline and manages the chaotic aerodynamics of hair in motion. Of course, Keely’s ponytail is iconic to who she is as a person, so we engineered an exact, strategic opening to let her hair flow out the back flawlessly."

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn lays out plans to transform rugby after darts and snooker success
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn lays out plans to transform rugby after darts and snooker success

Eddie Hearn oversaw Henry Pollock's recent contract extension with Northampton but insists he could maximise the growth of rugby if he was handed the reigns

View 2 Images Eddie Hearn has begun asserting his influence in the rugby sphere (Image: George Wood, Getty Images)

Eddie Hearn claims "it would be a stroll in the park" if he were able to get involved with rugby as he backed himself to improve the sport's landscape.

‌



The Matchroom supremo, whose greatest successes have come in boxing, is now involved in rugby having taken control of the futures of Henry Pollock and Finn Russell, arguably the two biggest names in the Prem.

‌



Russell, the Bath fly-half, is thought to be the competitions highest paid player and on Tuesday Pollock signed a new deal that sees him earn in excess of £400,000-a-year. Negotiations over the Northampton star were ultimately limited by the £6.4m salary cap for Prem clubs.

‌



That is imposed to ensure a level playing field and so that clubs do not go beyond their means in pursuit of success with three clubs already going bust since the pandemic as rugby struggles financially.

Rugby star knocked out one minute into his debut in worrying collision as medics rush to aid READ MORE :

Hearn has been vocal about scrapping the salary cap, which would give individuals the belief that they could earn huge sums from playing the sport. The Matchroom boss is due to meet with Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor in Monaco in the coming weeks to discuss ideas and insists his successes in darts and snooker show what he could do.

"We haven't really touched the surface in terms of what we could do in the sport," he said. "All I've done is done a few deals with Henry, he's come to a couple of fights and I've done a couple of Zoom calls [with journalists].

‌



"That just shows you the buzz that can be created with a little bit of hype and perception. But hype and perception are nothing without substance. The sport and the brand is the substance and it's significant in rugby. Look at what Matchroom has done elsewhere. Boxing was dead, darts was non-existent, snooker was stuck in the air. We don't fail. Our track record is second to none.

View 2 Images Henry Pollock's career is being managed by Eddie Hearn (Image: @henryjpollock)

"If we went into rugby, it would be a stroll in the park for me. It's a huge global sport steeped in history with fantastic values and tradition that just needs to be just turbo-charged."

Article continues below

Hearn admits Pollock turned down seven-figure offers to move elsewhere with the young back rower determined to remain at his boyhood club, where he won the Prem last season. But his agent insists the salary cap model is proving a hindrance.

"Let the players earn," Hearn claimed. "All they hear about is salary caps or one star player per team - marquee names or whatever you want to call it. You don't want that.

"You want to say to a young player, 'hey, come to rugby, you can be a superstar and you can earn a fortune'. You could have lost Pollock and it would have been a disaster for English rugby."

Sports.title: Max Dowman handed England reality check as Arsenal star eyes long-standing record
Sports.content:
Max Dowman handed England reality check as Arsenal star eyes long-standing record

Max Dowman is tipped for huge things but, despite talk of an England call-up, the Arsenal teenager has been reminded that players have to progress through the age grades first

View 2 Images Max Dowman is making his way through the England age grades

Arsenal sensation Max Dowman has been told that he won't necessarily go straight into the England squad with the U21s seen as his next step.

‌



The 16-year-old, who became the Premier League's youngest ever goalscorer last season, has enjoyed a rapid rise and is now being talked up for a senior spot with the Three Lions. He has been Thomas Tuchel‘s radar since before the World Cup, but is poised to play with the U19s on Friday.

‌



Lee Carsley, the U21s boss, could see a host of his players step up after five players, including Declan Rice and Cole Palmer, pulled out of the England squad that have four matches in the next 10 days, starting with Spain on Saturday.

‌



But Carsley has made it clear that Dowman's next step will almost certainly be with the U21s, not the senior squad, as the coaches attempt to ensure he enjoys a natural progression, which they believe will lead to a long lasting England career.

‌



He said: “It’s important players develop at their own pace. Max is an outstanding talent, the timing and the balance of when he comes to the Under-21s is inevitable.

“He’s going to the U21s because of his talent, but we have to make sure we do that at the right time. We have to be patient and make sure that ultimately we want them to play for the senior team for a prolonged period. So we have to make sure that we get the time right with that. We had a similar issue a few years ago with Ethan Nwaneri."

Carsley did make clear: “Thomas and I speak regularly about squad selection and obviously Max is always in the conversation because of his talent.

‌



View 2 Images Max Dowman scored twice on his first outing for Arsenal this season (Image: David Price, Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The England U21 boss, who has won successive Euros with the Young Lions, cited the experience of former team-mate Wayne Rooney as an outlier. He jumped age groups to make his senior debut at 17 years and 111 days, but that is very much seen as an exception to the rule.

Dowman still has time on his hands to make history with England. He has until March 30 to break Theo Walcott’s 20-year record as the country's youngest-ever player at 17 years and 75 days old, which he achieved when he ran out in 2006.

Sports.title: Daniel Levy's £27m Tottenham exit package explained after huge pay-off and exit
Sports.content:
Daniel Levy's £27m Tottenham exit package explained after huge pay-off and exit

Daniel Levy left Tottenham a year ago and was handed a significant pay-off fee

View 2 Images Daniel Levy left Tottenham last year (Image: David Rogers/Getty Images)

Tottenham Hotspur reportedly paid £27million to their former executive Daniel Levy following his exit from the club last year. Levy saw his 24-year tenure with Spurs come to an end in September last year.

‌



It has been reported by The Athletic that the payout from Spurs to Levy factored in his salary, as well as any bonuses and the long-term incentive plan in place at the club. It is thought that the £27m given to Levy is one of the largest amounts given to a football executive.

‌



Non-executive chairman Peter Charrington wrote an open letter to Tottenham fans at the end of last season following a major overhaul of the club’s hierarchy.

‌



He wrote: "Last September, we recognised that something seismic had to change at Spurs.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



"The Lewis family stepped in and authorised a full reset. That decision was not taken lightly, and it came later than it should have."

Since taking the reins, the Lewis family have pumped a staggering £320million into the club over the past year, most recently injecting £120million in working capital as they continue to steadily grow their shareholding.

Levy still holds around 24% of Tottenham, though his stake was diluted earlier in the summer. He was offered the opportunity to participate in a £100million equity investment but did not respond before the August deadline, seeing his share drop from 26%.

‌



Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi has also been generously backed in the transfer market, with the club signing 10 new players over the summer for a combined outlay of nearly £400million.

View 2 Images Tottenham Hotspur are yet to win a Premier League match this season (Image: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

‌



Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Savio, Jan Paul van Hecke and Tosin Adarabioyo were amongst the high-profile arrivals at the club.

The substantial outlay on playing staff is aimed at steering clear of a repeat of last season's struggles, when the club spent the vast majority of the campaign battling to preserve their Premier League status. Spurs required a final day victory over Everton to secure their survival.

Yet heading into the first international break of the season, Tottenham find themselves at the bottom of the Premier League table. Of their five top-flight fixtures so far this term, Spurs have lost three and drawn two.

De Zerbi's side return to action on Saturday, October 10 when they make the trip to face Manchester United at Old Trafford.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
