Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr fires brutal dig at fierce rival Conor Benn after Brit's devastating second round defeat by Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr brutally mocked his fierce rival Conor Benn after the Brit suffered a devastating defeat by Ryan Garcia.

Benn, 29, was crushed via a second-round stoppage in Las Vegas as they fought for Garcia's WBC welterweight crown.

Benn was dropped by a right hook in round two, and although he managed to beat the count, he struggled to fend off Garcia's subsequent attack, leading to referee Thomas Taylor bringing the fight to a stop, shattering the Brit's world title dream.

It was Benn's first fight at welterweight for four years after he had taken on Eubank Jr at middleweight, meaning he had to cut weight ahead of the fight, something his great rival had to do for their bitter showdowns.

And, Eubank Jr seemed to enjoy his foe's struggles having gone through something similar.

Taking to X shortly after the fight concluded, he posted: 'Welcome to the "fighting after cutting too much weight" club… Enjoy.'

Chris Eubank Jr aimed a brutal dig at Conor Benn after his defeat to Ryan Garcia on Saturday

Benn suffered a heavy defeat by Garcia and his long-time rival Eubank Jr seemed to enjoy it

Eubank Jr had previously posted a photo with Garcia ahead of the fight with the caption: 'Get the job done kid.'

For his two fights against Benn last year, Eubank Jr had to cut down to 160lbs.

He missed that weight for the first bout, before he came under the limit for the second.

Meanwhile, Garcia's triumph over Benn, who was taken to hospital as a precaution, was the Mexican-American's first defence of his WBC crown.

Speaking afterwards, he insisted he hadn't been at full fitness, but outlined his ambitions going forward.

'I have always had the right hand,' he said. 'But I carried a lot of injuries, so I couldn’t really show it.

'I know people question my Mexican heritage because I don’t speak Spanish. But I always feel my people with me and I do it for them. Teofimo Lopez can get it next.

'I want to clean the division out. I want Devin Haney’s a** again, too.'

Sports.title: Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL

The Wizard Of Oz is now a spectacular fantasy production encompassing the inside of the giant globe called The Sphere which looms large over the Las Vegas Strip.

Where the yellow brick road leads for Conor Benn after his one round, one minute and 25 seconds destruction by the fastest gun in Sin City is a question to which nobody had the answer as he was being ferried to hospital for precautionary checks. And may not have for some time to come.

There is no clear pathway back to the heights to which he was thrust all too prematurely and without justification this Saturday night.

Benn had no place being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia, who is emerging as the golden goose saviour of American and Mexican boxing. Nor had he done anything like enough in his patchwork career thus far to qualify for the honour of topping the bill at an arena as grand as the T-Mobile in as hallowed a home of boxing as Las Vegas.

This was a match made far away from fight heaven, deep in the casino vaults. Benn Jr leaves here millions of dollars the richer but with not so much as a scintilla of evidence that he will ever be able to mix it with the royalty of the ring, in which King Ry sits upon the throne. He has the payoff but not the legacy he craved.

For the second time in as many months English sport comes home from America with its tail between its legs. Only this clinical beat-down of an inferior boxer was aeons more humiliating than the retreat of our footballers from the World Cup. His defeat more comprehensive than that by Argentina.

Conor Benn was beaten inside two rounds by Ryan Garcia in their welterweight championship fight

Benn's humiliating defeat came after he thrust all too prematurely and without justification into the title fight

Benn had no place in being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia

Little did Benn know, in his delusion of self grandeur, that in return for securing his family’s financial future he was used as a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between the houses of Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White on their doorstep.

Garcia, younger of the two by a year but a decade wiser, knew. He tried to cushion Benn’s fall from grace by calling him a ‘good dude who I hope can come back from this.’

But as a man who likes to tell it as it is he felt compelled to add: ‘ I knew exactly how the fight would go. Rushing in against me from the start is not a good idea. Not the way to go. You need patience in this game.’

When it was pointed out to him that Benn has not stopped an opponent for more than four years he added: ‘I must be honest. I did not feel any power in his punches.’

Not that there were many of them. Benn’s charge from the first bell was suicidal against the best, fastest and hardest counter puncher in the world. He ran headlong into a hail of Garcia’s trademark left hooks. To note that he lost the first round is as understated as saying that Goliath had a bad day at the office against David. And when in the second Garcia brought into play the right hand which is now almost as deadly as the left Benn was gone in 85 seconds.

Gone crawling on the canvas and still so unsteady when reeled to his feet that the referee let him continue only so far as the next battering.

Garcia observed: ‘It could have been stopped after the first knock down. I looked into his eyes down there and they were glazed over. He was already gone.’

He echoed the pre-fight fears of many of us that Benn could be in critical jeopardy if this went on too long, saying: ‘It would not have been good for Conor if this lasted any further.’

Benn appears to have been a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White

Has he lived to fight another day? Dana White sounded less than totally convinced: ‘I’ve told Conor to go on holiday with his family and call me when he’s ready to come back. Then we can try to find the right fight for him.’

That would not be at welter after his ‘hellish’ struggle to cut his poundage. But if he can be hammered into oblivion by a 147-pounder what will become of him if he goes back up two divisions to middleweight?

No such doubts hang over Garcia. Having been saluted to the reverberating rafters of the T-Mobile by his half-brother Mexicans in the delirium of their Independence weekend celebrations, this Californian will resume his American love affair in more world title fights against the likes of Devin Haney and Teofimo Lopez.

He, not Conor Benn in his wildest dreams, is the face and the future of boxing over here.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia destroys Conor Benn with brutal second-round TKO to retain WBC welterweight title in Las Vegas showdown
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas on Saturday night, retaining his WBC welterweight title in the process.

Benn ran blindly to the slaughter - in a fight which was always a lunge too far - and was left groveling on hands and knees at the feet of the new face of American and Mexican boxing.

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the upstart son of Nigel the great.

Benn’s predictable sally forth from the first bell was as pointless, desperate and doomed to disaster as The Charge of the Light Brigade.

He was stopped in his tracks by the barrage of left hooks which have taken Garcia to the welterweight championship of the world, over which he will reign for as long as he likes.

The first round was but a prelude to the carnage to come in the 85 seconds which the first round lasted. A punishment doubled by the dynamite which also explodes from Garcia's right fist.

Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the British star

The 28-year-old retained his WBC welterweight title after the devastating display in Sin City

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by a two-fisted assault to which he had no answer. When he staggered drunkenly to his feet referee Thomas Taylor looked long and hard into his glazed eyes before letting him carry on.

The kill was mercifully swift. A combination of lefts and rights which the third man in the ring could no longer ignore.

This is a warning which his handlers must not forget. This was fight too much, too soon. As Garcia had warned he done nothing to deserve the tilt at the WBC belt his father had worn with such pride.

Nor his elevation the top of a bill in the T-Mobile arena nor in this Mecca of boxing Whether he will ever be ready to mix with the company of prize-ring loyalty is doubtful.

He was not only outclassed, out-sped an out-thought but was treated to punching of almighty power with which his dad could not gift him.

The last 24 hours before the first bell had been consumed by doom-casts about Benn’s drastic weight draining to reach the welter limit of 147 lbs.

Followed by extraordinary claims that he had put on more than two stones following Friday’s weigh-in which, if authentic, would have catapulted him into the ring three divisions even heavier than the super-middleweights.

The truth would out as his robe slipped off. But if he had gorged himself between stepping on the scales and the first bell that might done him much good. Such drastic shifts in poundage are as debilitating as dehydration.

If this was another of the mind games played by Benn and Garcia throughout the wind up and build up it seemed doubtful that any of that would have a material effect on the fight itself. Would anyone in this hardest of all games risk being beaten by indigestion.

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by an assault to which he had no answer

The referee swiftly waved off the bout after a barrage of punches from the American star

The substantive issue was Garcia’s boxing class and knock out power versus Benn’s frenzy and punch resistance.

For the high-paying fans – Benn’s long-haulers from the old country and Garcia’s Gen Z armies of groups from his two nations of identification the US and Mexico – what mattered most was that both delivered the barn-burner of a fight they promised.

Quite beautifully those three congregations fell silent together in commemoration of one boxer who never gave in, never gave up, never delivered a disappointing fight, never offended anyone, never betrayed a friend.

The giant screens in the 02 went into black and white mode for a nostalgic picture of Ricky Hatton who died too young as the previous British fighter to top the bill in what was until recently the fight capital of the world. Over to you Master Benn.

Garcia came to the ring to the strains of a patriotic Mexican song, wrapped in that country’s flag and to rapturous acclaim from the baying Amex majority in the house.

Unabashed and as expected Benn went instantly on the offensive only to be met by barrage of Garcia’s trademark left hooks.

Less than three minutes later it was all over.

Sports.title: Conor Benn shows off remarkable weight transformation after piling on 32 pounds in just HOURS, having been 'dragged to the pits of hell' during excruciating weight cut ahead of mega-fight with Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
Conor Benn has shown off a dramatic 32lb weight gain just hours after coming in one pound under the 147lb welterweight limit ahead of his bout with USA's Ryan Garcia.

The 29-year-old Briton came in at 146lb (66kg) at Friday's weigh-in for Saturday's fight, half a pound heavier than champion Garcia.

Just 12 hours later, Benn revealed on social media that he had added 32lb, taking him to 12st 10lb (80.73kg).

Speaking at a ceremonial event in front of fans later on Friday, Benn already appeared noticeably bigger, with his face and shoulders having filled out.

'Did it look hard? How did I look?' he asked. 'We'll see tomorrow night how good I really feel.'

Benn had previously said he could weigh as much as 12st 7lb (80kg) by the time he stepped into the ring on Saturday evening (around 4am Sunday, UK time).

‼️ Conor Benn has rehydrated to 178.4 pounds already.



📈 He is up 32.4 pounds (including clothes etc) in just 10 hours! 😱 pic.twitter.com/m6netuS2c1 — EverythingBoxing | Darshan Desai (@EverythingBoxi2) September 12, 2026

Benn revealed on social media that he had added an incredible 32lb hours after the weigh-in

The 29-year-old Briton had come in at 146lb (66kg) at Friday's weigh-in for Saturday's fight, half a pound heavier than champion Garcia before quickly adding it back on

Speaking at a ceremonial event in front of fans later on Friday (above), Benn already appeared noticeably bigger, with his face and shoulders having filled out

He has not fought at welterweight for more than four years, having moved up through the divisions before competing at middleweight during his two-fight rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr.

Now, for the biggest fight of his career, taking on Garcia for the World Boxing Council (WBC) title under the bright lights in Las Vegas, he has had to come all the way back down.

'It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life,' he told BBC Sport earlier this week.

'Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard.'

Whether the weight cut affects Benn's strength and power on Saturday night will be one of the central questions of his WBC world title fight.

Garcia has suggested Benn's move back down could leave him vulnerable, but Benn was dismissive of that concern when he spoke to Daily Mail Sport earlier in the week.

'You think I've been up at middleweight, mixed it with someone who's competed at super middleweight? You think I'm worried about what a lightweight can do to me?' he told this publication.

'You think I'm concerned in the slightest about this guy? I'm not concerned about one little thing he brings to the table… that silly left hook of his is useless. He can bring whatever he wants. It don't concern me.'

USA's Garcia claimed the WBC title with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making the first defence of his belt against Benn on Saturday

Benn's unusual route to this fight has been shaped by his rivalry with Eubank.

Their first meeting at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in April 2025 was the culmination of years of animosity between the two families, with Benn and Eubank Jr inheriting a rivalry that began with their fathers in 1990.

The fight itself was fought at a catchweight above 160lb, with Benn stepping up significantly from his previous division. Eubank won a close decision, leaving Benn to reflect on a performance in which he felt the occasion and the emotion had affected him.

Seven months later, the pair met again at the same venue. This time Benn won the decision, dropping Eubank twice in the final round in a dramatic conclusion to their second fight. It left them level at one victory apiece and appeared to finally close the door on one of British boxing's most talked-about rivalries.

Benn insisted the atmosphere this week is nothing like those two nights when asked whether his hatred for Garcia compared.

'This is nothing like the Eubank fight,' he said. 'The Eubank fight, there was nothing pleasant or friendly or fake about the Eubank fight. There was a lot more raw emotion in that fight and I let that get the better of me the first time. That won't happen here.'

Garcia has won 25 of his 28 professional fights, including 20 by knockout, with two defeats and one no-contest. He claimed the WBC title with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making the first defence of his belt against Benn. Benn has 25 wins, 14 by knockout, and one defeat.

Benn said of his rival: 'He just carries on like a spoiled brat, like a big child who throws his toys out of the pram. I'm not worried about him in the slightest. If anything, I'm gonna have a bit of fun with him. He's a little bit sensitive, highly emotional, and a little bit insecure.'

There is also an uncomfortable shared history between the two men when it comes to drugs testing.

Benn's original 2022 fight with Eubank was cancelled after he returned two adverse findings for clomifene, something he has consistently denied intentionally taking. Garcia subsequently returned an adverse finding for ostarine following his 2024 victory over Devin Haney, which he also denied intentionally taking.

Both men were asked at the fight's press conference whether they had concerns that the other could use performance-enhancing drugs ahead of Saturday's contest.

Neither appeared keen to make it a central issue, with the focus instead returning to the fight itself.

Benn defeated Chris Eubank Jr by unanimous decision to take revenge in their rematch at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last November

Garcia has also questioned whether Benn's career has prepared him for this level of opposition, arguing that the Briton is taking a step too far by challenging for the world title.

Benn's response was typically blunt. 'How is this too far? He quit against Tank Davis. He got outclassed by Rolly (Romero), and then got a world title shot with Barrios,' he said.

'Then there is me. Stepping up to fight the contenders up at middleweight, fight of the year up at middleweight, avenging my loss. Two big stadium shows. Just come off beating a two-time former world champion and having to make 147, which again I ain't made in four years in six weeks.

'What's he talking about? Ultimately, who cares what he thinks? I don't listen to quitters anyway.'

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn

A dazzling talent just reaching his prime will enter the T-Mobile Arena here this Saturday night with the hopes of a fighting nation resting on his shoulders.

Conor Benn, not so much. British boxing is enjoying a boom, not least with its dominance in the marquee heavyweight division.

The young man the son of Nigel is challenging for the world welterweight crown carries the burden of restoring America to its historic pre-eminence in the prize-ring.

Not just by adding to an unusually low head count of their champions but by resuscitating the excitement, the stardust, the impudence, the controversy, the brilliance and the fascination of the public over here with the hardest game of all.

Ryan Garcia is the only poster boy left to them following the retirement of Floyd Mayweather. Vitally, he has all it takes to bring a new generation of fans clamouring to his fights.

At 28 he has the matinee idol looks of a young Elvis Presley which brings the girls squealing into the crowds. A rock and roll bad-boy reputation which chimes with the lads. Showmanship within the ring and charisma outside the ropes.

Ryan Garcia will take on Conor Benn on Saturday night with the American carrying the hopes of a fighting nation on his shoulders

Garcia has reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde (left), the beautiful mother of two of his three children (above)

Benn has arrived in Las Vegas with the aim of taking the WBC welterweight belt from Garcia

Glamorous blondes vie for his favours. Even though he is resisting those temptations now he has scrapped divorce proceedings and reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde, the beautiful mother of two of his three children.

And, boy, can he box. The speed of hand and foot. The knock-out punching power. The taunting evasion. And, yes, the conceit which on occasion gets him into trouble.

The two defeats scarring his 28-fight record – against two of America’s other world champions Gervonta Davis and Rolly Romero – came when he was at his most arrogant and complacent.

The no-decision verdict which negated his stand-out victory over Devin Haney was imposed for failing a post-fight drug test for performance-enhancing Ostarine.

Like Benn he protested his innocence: ‘I’ve never knowingly taken drugs.’ His relatives revealed he had been struggling with his mental health and against alcohol. But unlike Conor he preferred taking his punishment – a $1million fine and a 12-month ban – rather than financing a protracted court case which would also have kept him under lengthy suspension.

Not that King Ry - he wears a gold crown for his ring entrances - is prone to compromising his regally unvarnished opinions. Garcia was a vociferous backer of Donald Trump in his first presidential election campaign. But given his Mexican roots he criticised Trump’s second-term deportation policy. Finally he renounced his support, denouncing the Trump administration’s handling of the Epstein Files.

A devout Christian, he called rapper Eminem a satanist and posted on Twitter: ’I don’t support the LGBTQ+. F*** you guys. Rot in hell.’

He called for a boycott of the Olympics for ‘disrespecting Jesus Christ' with the section of the opening ceremony of France 2024 in which drag queens imitating Greek gods were widely supposed to be parodying the Last Supper.

Garcia scrapped divorce proceedings with influencer Andrea in August 2025

Garcia turned down WBC offers to help with his mental health difficulties but progress has been deemed to be made, leading to him fighting and beating Mario Barris in February

The rock-and-roller came out in him when he was arrested for causing $150,000- worth of damage while trashing a room and a corridor at the ritzy Waldorf Astoria hotel in Beverly Hills. That risked a short prison term, which has not been applied.

Another suspension was imposed. This one from competing in fights sanctioned by the WBC for racist slurs live on the internet against the black community and muslims. President Mauricio Sulaiman reported that Garcia had turned down a number of offers from the WBC to help Garcia with his mental health difficulties.

Sulaiman relented last November, saying he recognised the progress made in that regard by the fighter’s large family.

Promptly, this February, Garcia defeated the highly rated Mario Barrios to claim the WBC welterweight belt, inflicting a first round knockdown on his way to a unanimous decision.

The braggadocio bubbles to the surface before fights. As soon as this weekend’s bout was announced he told Benn to his face: ‘You box like amateur trash. You're just a flashy trash can. I’m going to throw you out with trash.’

All the ingredients are there for the making of a turbulent, troubled super-star son of this angry and violent 21st century. All wrapped up in the rare skills and brave heart of a potentially great fighter.

Some indication of whether all that will be enough for him to kindle another golden age in US boxing may be seen in how he deals with Benn. The huge scale of that task is evident in this, my overwhelmingly American list of the 20 greatest boxers of all time, with Lennox Lewis the Brit who came closest to inclusion...

Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival

‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton's mother has recalled her last hug with him three days before he took his own life one year ago as his parents speak out for the first time.

Carol and Ray Hatton have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late after the boxing champion hanged himself on September 14 last year.

One year on from Ricky's death, aged 46, his mother has revealed the last time she embraced her son.

Just days before he took his own life, the boxing champion had been in an argument with his parents but the family were 'building bridges'.

Carol decided to make an unplanned visit to his gym in Hyde and gave him a 'real proper hug'.

She told ITV News: 'I pulled up on the car park because I saw his car. He asked if everything was okay.

'I said "yeah, everything's fine". I said I'd like to see a bit more of him.'

Ricky's mother said he told her he wanted to see his father Ray the next week. However Ricky died three days later.

Former world boxing champion Ricky Hatton died by suicide in September last year aged 46

Ray and Carol Hatton (pictured at their son's funeral) have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late

Ricky had previously opened up about his struggle with drug and alcohol addiction and had become estranged from his parents before the reconciled

She added: 'I'm so glad (I got to see him) because nobody knows when it's the last time you're going to see somebody.'

Ray, the boxer's father, said: 'You tell your grandkids how much you love them, you tell your wife how much you love them but I think, especially with men, don't ever be afraid of getting hold of your son and telling him you love him.'

Ricky had become estranged from his parents for around a decade before he reached out to patch up their relationship several years before his death.

He had survived previous suicide attempts and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

Ricky fell out with his parents over money and despite the dispute he still allowed Carol and Ray to see his newborn daughter Millie.

However the boxer became upset when his girlfriend Jennifer was not invited to a Christmas Day party.

Months later he received letters from his parents' lawyers saying they wanted to see their granddaughter.

But he told Manchester Evening News in 2013 that he responded by saying: 'I replied to my parents, through solicitors, and said we did not want them to have contact with Millie.'

Carol Hatton wipes a tear from her eye while reading a statement at her home after Ricky's death

Ricky had survived previous suicide attempts before he died in September last year

'We have never stopped them seeing her, as far as I was concerned they had just not been ******.

'I know that sounds harsh and I am sure they see it differently, but it is how I feel.'

He added that the situation 'was a mess', describing the family feud as 'bitter and horrible', referring to back-and-forth letters between his and his parents' lawyers.

This culminated in his father attacking him in a car park fist fight.

Angry about 'all that stuff you've written about your mum in that solicitor's letter', Ray then punched his boxing champion son in the face before Ricky hit back and his father then drove off.

But Ricky's parents are still struggling to come to terms with his death and Carol said the couple 'have to move forward' but will continue 'remembering him and loving him'.

Carol and Ray have now called for a statue of Ricky to be erected in Manchester, saying it would be a 'fitting tribute' to their son who 'brought a lot of pride' to the city.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York
Sports.content:
Cardiff's Principality Stadium now looks set to be the unlikely winner of the venue war for boxing's biggest fight - by hosting Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury in the early hours of the morning.

The local authorities could today approve lifting the stadium's 10.30pm curfew to host the fight - stepping in after rows over holding it at Wembley Stadium or Madison Square Garden in New York.

Cardiff has history of hosting late-night boxing. Joe Calzaghe fought Mikkel Kessler at the Principality in 2007 at 2am. Fury and Joshua could fight at a similar time to satisfy broadcaster Netflix's huge audience in the United States.

Netflix had wanted the fight in New York to suit their prime timezones, while Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn pitched Wembley to host under the guise that Britain's biggest fight of the century should be hosted in the UK - and he has refused to budge unless contracts are rewritten with upgraded financial offerings.

Cardiff now appears to be the compromise. The Principality Stadium has an 80,000 capacity and a retractable roof - unlike Wembley - which could be useful in late November or December. A date of Saturday, November 28 has been mooted.

The Times report a press conference is tentatively scheduled for next week pending the approval.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in November

Joshua and his camp wanted the fight in the UK - while broadcasters Netflix wanted a US host

Wembley looked an ideal venue for the fight but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

Netflix have been running s for Fury-Joshua as recently as Thursday night, clearly confident an agreement will be struck.

The streaming giant has yet to sign off on Cardiff but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last night reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Joe Calzaghe trains at the Principality Stadium before his 2am fight there in 2007

Joshua has fought in Cardiff twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in the Welsh capital in 2017 and 2018.

While Joshua has left Hearn to do the talking on his side of the deal, Fury has been publicly speaking and threatening that the heavyweight contest will be called off.

This week he suggested he will no longer be fighting Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continued.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

Provided Cardiff hits no further stumbling blocks, the Welsh capital may now offer the solution to get the fight on at last.

Sports.title: "Free agent" Ocon talking to other teams with Haas yet to confirm F1 2027 line-up
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon declared himself a "free agent" as Haas is yet to confirm its driver line-up for the 2027 Formula 1 season, but did not rule out potentially staying at the team.

Although the Frenchman has been enjoying much improved performances of late, which have gone largely unrewarded as Haas' performance has slipped away from its early-season points-scoring form, Ocon's seat has been under threat for some time.

Haas has been using its testing of previous cars (TPC) programme to identify a potential partner for Oliver Bearman next season, with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, and current reserve Ryo Hirakawa in the frame.

Ocon confirmed that he was looking for other options for 2027, while Haas continues to assess its driver pairing for next year.

Recent rumours have surfaced suggesting that the team is leaning towards Camara - currently the reigning F3 champion and second in this year's F2 standings - although team boss Ayao Komatsu stated during the Spanish GP that he had "maybe five" drivers in contention.

"Yes, at the moment I am definitely a free agent for next year," Ocon stated. "There are things in discussion that are out of my control and there are certain topics that are out of my control. So I will keep pushing until the end of the year and see how it goes."

Asked if staying at Haas was an option, Ocon remained tight-lipped and responded: "Let's see."

Esteban Ocon, Haas Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ocon added that he was pleased with his performances of late, having suffered this season with an inconsistent car in the early stages of the season.

It is unclear if this is an aerodynamic sensitivity issue or a parts quality control problem; Komatsu has suggested both could be causes, and that the team is still investigating the issue at hand.

"We know it's been an ongoing issue," he said. "It's reassuring that I'm doing a good job. Obviously, my performance hasn't been an issue this year.

"I've performed every time I had the car. I've been the last one to score in Monaco. I was almost scoring in Madrid. There's been a lot of times where I've performed when the car was underperforming. It's been clear.

"Everybody in the team has been following that very closely, trying to fix the problem. We haven't been hiding from it. But it's been quite disappointing at times, obviously, to have these kind of problems."

Bearman was asked if he felt ready to step up as the team leader should Ocon depart, and the Briton stated that he'd learned a lot from his team-mate across the almost two years spent together as team-mates.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team, Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

He pointed to Ocon's feedback in the engineering room as something that he'd taken inspiration from, along with his own improving performances on-track.

"I've been here for, well, this is my second year driving as a full-time driver, but also I've been one year as a reserve for Haas, also did a few races and FP1s the year before that, even in 2023, I did my first FP1. So I have a really good level of experience with the team," Bearman said.

"I feel like I've improved a lot in terms of my on-track performance, but also how I describe what I'm feeling in the car and things like that. And that's something I certainly learned a lot from someone who's very experienced like Esteban. So on that side, it's been really good learning for me.

"Even if I compare my feedback to 12 months ago, I'm not sure I would have the confidence to just rely on my own feedback. But I feel like I've made a good step in that regard, and it's just a normal learning process, really."

Sports.title: The initial plan for F1's next engine regulation in 2030
Sports.content:
Formula 1 stakeholders have reached an agreement on the main elements of the next engine rules cycle.

The FIA and F1 engine manufacturers have opted against a naturally aspirated option, partly because of noise restrictions at street circuits, with a smaller and simplified electronics package.

A push-to-pass overtake mode is also under consideration, along with a possible debut in 2030.

While discussions are still ongoing, the engine set to define the next technical cycle in F1 has largely taken shape. Meetings between the FIA and the manufacturers will continue to finalise the remaining details, but a substantial agreement has been reached on the key points with the focus on a simpler and lighter power unit, one that is considered closer to the traditional concept of a racing engine.

A return to V8 engines

F1 is set to move to 3.0-litre V8 architecture, but one of the issues that most divided the engine manufacturers was whether to retain the turbocharger.

The possibility of opting for a naturally aspirated engine was also on the table, a solution that would have delivered a sound particularly appealing to fans nostalgic for F1 in the early 2000s.

Fernando Alonso, Renault R25, leads Michael Schumacher, Ferrari F2005 Photo by: Motorsport Images

However, the turbocharger element will remain as part of the power unit configuration, but the reasons behind the decision go beyond purely technical considerations.

A naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V8 would have reached noise levels that would cause a major problem with some of the current F1 venues.

The issue concerns street circuits in particular: Melbourne, Miami, Madrid, Singapore, Baku and Las Vegas are venues where noise-emission restrictions are in place, and the arrival of cars significantly louder than the current generation could create major difficulties that would be impossible to overcome and potentially even put some events at risk.

This has led to the decision to retain a smaller turbocharger, a compromise that should still make it possible to achieve a considerably louder sound than that of the current power units, while keeping noise levels within limits applied at some F1 circuits.

Smaller electrical motor and lighter power units

The new V8 will not be completely detached from electrification either. The new rules look set to include a simplified 100kW electric motor, a considerably lower output than the 350kW current generation of power units.

The aim is to maintain a technological link with the automotive industry without replicating the complexity that has characterised the latest generation of power units. The direction emerging from the discussions is clear: electric power will remain part of F1, but with a less dominant role within the overall package.

Start action Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Another area where the lessons of recent years appear to have been taken on board concern the weight of the overall power unit. The target set for the new power unit is highly ambitious: to produce a complete unit weighing at least 50kg lighter than the current power units.

Push-to-pass and 2030 introduction being considered

Some aspects still need to be finalised. Among them is the system that will give drivers an additional power boost to assist overtaking manoeuvres.

There appears to be no intention to bring back the DRS used until the end of the 2025 season. The solution currently under consideration is closer to the push-to-pass philosophy adopted in IndyCar: a temporary increase in power that the driver could deploy under specific circumstances.

This will be one of the areas the FIA and the engine manufacturers still need to reach a definitive agreement on.

When the new regulations will be introduced in F1 also remains open, with the plan to debut the new rules in 2030 an option, which would bring forward the end of the current technical rules cycle that began by one year.

Reaching a decision will require all parties to find common ground, but the issues that have emerged with the current generation of power units have accelerated a broader discussion that goes beyond individual technical details. After pushing hard on technological complexity, F1 appears keen to return to a more traditional concept of a racing engine.

Sports.title: What would you like to ask Emerson Fittipaldi?
Sports.content:
On 24 September, two-time Formula 1 world champion Emerson Fittipaldi will join us in the Baku paddock to answer Autosport readers' questions ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

In a remarkable career that span across three decades with even further outings, Fittipaldi not only clinched the F1 title with Lotus and McLaren in 1972 and 1974 but also won the IndyCar championship in 1989.

Fittipaldi is one of few drivers who have raced for their own team in F1, and now looks after his eponymous son, currently competing in F2 with AIX Racing – so there should be plenty to ask him about.

Sports.title: Hadjar to partner Verstappen at Red Bull for F1 2027
Sports.content:
Red Bull has confirmed it will field an unchanged Formula 1 driver line-up in 2027, with Isack Hadjar staying put alongside Max Verstappen.

Hadjar stepped up in 2026 after a rookie season at sister team Racing Bulls, and has impressed with his speed in what has historically been a difficult second Red Bull seat.

The Frenchman, who is making his return in Azerbaijan this weekend after missing three races through injury, will stay on board for another campaign in 2027 alongside Verstappen, who recently signed a contract extension to 2030.

"We’re very excited to continue our journey with Isack," said Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies.

"Since joining us at the start of the year, he has been superb on and off track, especially considering this is only his second Formula 1 season, which made extending his contract an easy decision.

"From the very beginning, Isack immersed himself in the team, spending every minute at the factory with his engineers to develop the car, always eager to learn and improve.

"You could see from that first weekend in Melbourne that he handled the step up with remarkable composure and had earned his place in this seat."

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Despite sitting out Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid, Hadjar still holds eighth in the standings, boosted by a first Red Bull podium in Monaco to complement his maiden podium in 2025, as well as a streak of seven consecutive top six finishes in what has largely been F1's third or fourth quickest car.

"I am really excited to continue with Oracle Red Bull Racing," the 21-year-old said. "There are so many talented people at the factory, and you’re aware of the privilege of driving for such an incredible team alongside a four-time world champion like Max.

"From the moment I signed, I set out to dedicate myself to the team, and with the support of Laurent and everyone in Milton Keynes, I’ve been able to justify the faith they’ve had in me.

“I’m constantly looking to listen, learn and push myself further every single day, which only makes me more excited about what lies ahead."

Racing Bulls is yet to confirm its own driver line-up for 2027, with incumbents Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad having both impressed this season while the squad also has junior driver Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings.

Sports.title: What were Leclerc's "other opportunities" before signing new Ferrari deal?
Sports.content:
Every time Ferrari and Charles Leclerc agree to extend their relationship in Formula 1, the news comes against a background of allusions to other suitors Charles has spurned to remain with his true love.

"For that, I'm also lucky to be in the position where I've got my manager," he said on a recent episode of F1's Beyond the Grid podcast when asked how seriously he had considered a life away from Ferrari.

"And my manager is here to let me know about what are the other opportunities, what's going on around. And so I didn't have any personal talks, but my manager did.

"I mean, it's his job to be honest with me and to give me the full picture of what's going on in the paddock and what opportunities we might have. So, yes, there were other opportunities. But at the end of the day, we sat down with Ferrari and we made it happen quite quickly."

If Leclerc has a special relationship with Ferrari, the same can be said of his manager, Nicolas Todt: son of Jean, the former rally co-driver who masterminded Peugeot's rally and endurance programmes before leading Ferrari to world domination in the Michael Schumacher era, then shifted into politics as FIA president for over a decade. Todt Jr also managed long-time Ferrari driver Felipe Massa and still superintends the affairs of James Calado, a Le Mans winner with the Scuderia. He has a great many drivers on his books at all stages of the career ladder, and is a consummate player in the paddock.

But what Todt Jr enjoys to a greater extent at Ferrari than anywhere else is the ear of influential figures further up the food chain than the team principal – although he is a key ally of Fred Vasseur, having co-founded the ART GP organisation with him over two decades ago. Indeed, it's understood that Todt was instrumental in the removal of former team principal Mattia Binotto and his replacement by Vasseur in January 2023.

Nicolas Todt and Fred Vasseur Photo by: Getty Images

Having a manager so plugged into the senior echelons of power enables Leclerc to get what he wants with plausible deniability, such as Binotto's departure at a time when Ferrari's recovery trajectory underwent a major wobble, and the peculiarly communicated removal of Xavier Marcos as Leclerc's race engineer early in the 2024 season. He would not have quite the same influence if he were to shift to another team.

Equally, his influence depends not just on his performance but also his market value. If Ferrari has Leclerc locked into a contractual "golden prison", as our Italian colleague Roberto Chinchero puts it, then threatening to go elsewhere is no longer a lever he can pull.

Nobody doubts Leclerc's speed or commitment. Arguably he often over-commits, especially if the car isn't good enough. If the Ferrari is only 90% or 95% as good as the frontrunning car, Charles will try to make up the shortfall himself in the form of risk. That's why the Tifosi place him in the same rarefied space in their hearts as Gilles Villeneuve.

In recent seasons Leclerc's prime options outside Ferrari have been with Mercedes, Red Bull and McLaren, whose leaders have had to weigh up the performance benefits Leclerc would bring against the change in equilibrium it would cause. Nicolas Todt has certainly been busy doing the rounds of those teams over the past couple of years, but there is a tendency in the F1 media to get rather too excited when a driver's manager is spotted in another team's motorhome.

Sometimes a casual chat is just a casual chat. Sometimes a deal may actually be in progress, though the likelihood of this happening in plain sight is quite low. Often such encounters are staged in public purely to suit each party's agendas: for the team principal, to show their drivers they have other options on the table; for the manager, to show his client has interest from elsewhere.

To manage the internal equilibrium when it announced in January 2024 that Lewis Hamilton would be joining the following season, Ferrari also signed Leclerc to a long-term deal that theoretically reached until the end of 2029 with options, but which was also understood to have included a break point in 2026. On Leclerc's side this was to cover the possibility of Ferrari making a mess of the new technical regulations.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton Photo by: Getty Images

Instead, a more complex picture has emerged in which Ferrari has engineered a competitive car, and has been able to add performance to it in the form of upgrades – which hasn't always been true in the recent past. But it has also suffered operational misfires and blown several chances to score more points.

The dynamic in the other leading teams has also changed, though. When Leclerc signed up for the long term in 2024, this was partially because Todt knew Hamilton's move was coming, and had approached Mercedes with a view to Charles filling that vacancy. But when the break clause came into view early this season, Mercedes was perfectly happy with its line-up. The same could be said of McLaren, where Todt is also understood to have held discussions on and off with leaders including Andrea Stella and Zak Brown. When Todt was doing the rounds late last season, McLaren had two drivers in contention for the world championship.

It's also understood that Aston Martin made an approach at the end of last year, but this was at a time of yet more underperformance and internal wrangling in that benighted organisation, when recently installed managing technical partner Adrian Newey had MD and team principal Andy Cowell ousted. Given a choice between Ferrari and a farrago, Leclerc wisely chose door number one.

"I don't want to give up on my ultimate goal, which is to become a world champion with Ferrari," Leclerc said.

"And I believe in the project. I believe in every single person of the team. I think we are in a year where we've been showing innovation. We are very aggressive also in the production plan and in the upgrades we are bringing and that gives me lots of hopes for the future.

"Fred is a big reason on why I have signed again as well. I believe in Fred 200%."

Next time his contract is up for renewal, Leclerc will be over 30. Will he still have as many other opportunities then?

Sports.title: Hadjar set to make Red Bull return at Azerbaijan GP after injury recovery
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar will return to Red Bull for this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix at Baku after recovering from a wrist injury, as Liam Lawson moves back to the Racing Bulls Formula 1 team.

Hadjar had injured his wrist in training over the summer break and, following medical advice, was told to avoid driving to manage his recovery.

Lawson therefore deputised for the Frenchman at Red Bull, starting with the Dutch Grand Prix, with Yuki Tsunoda stepping up from his reserve role to fill Lawson's seat.

This lasted for three races as Hadjar prioritised his recovery, and Lawson thus stayed in the Red Bull seat for both the Italian and Spanish grands prix, with Tsunoda continuing to fill the Racing Bulls void.

Lawson scored 14 points in his three outings for Red Bull, with Monza the only scoreless round of the three as he took a series of power unit penalties - and then was forced to pit later after contact with Nico Hulkenberg broke part of his front wing.

Tsunoda finished 10th in that race, although was close to scoring a point in Zandvoort before Pierre Gasly passed him for 10th late on in the race.

"The team would like to thank Liam for his professionalism, dedication, and hard work over the past three races," read a statement from Red Bull.

"Stepping in under challenging circumstances, he delivered some impressive performances and made a valuable contribution to the team."

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

Hadjar thus makes his first appearance at the wheel of an F1 car for the first time since July's Hungarian Grand Prix, although managed to increase his seasonal points tally in that time when his Monaco Grand Prix third place was reinstated.

McLaren and Red Bull had successfully appealed against the post-race rescinding of Gasly's two five-second penalties for speeding in the pitlane, moving Hadjar back up to the podium positions.

The Frenchman also sought advice from MotoGP champion Marc Marquez, who suffered an arm fracture in 2020 - which worsened as he tried to return to competition prematurely, and the Spaniard has since required multiple surgeries on the same arm in the years since.

Marquez revealed that he told Hadjar: "I learned in the past that missing one race will not change your life. Worsening your injury because you ride too early, can change your life."

Sports.title: F1 approves shorter races for 2027 to fit revised power unit plan
Sports.content:
The Formula 1 Commission has rubber-stamped the proposed changes to reduce the lengths of races in 2027 by 15km, in line with the expected power unit changes for next season.

During Monday's F1 Commission in London, the decision to reduce the standard grand prix length from 305km to 290km was agreed upon - pending approval from the FIA's World Motor Sport Council - to reduce the cost associated with chassis changes to fit the reworked output from each of the powertrain components.

For 2027, the decision had previously been made to increase the output of the internal combustion engine and reduce the power delivered by the electrical components to rebalance the formula, and reduce the level of superclipping and energy harvesting during races.

The ICE will thus be upscaled to a 420kW figure, while the maximum power from the MGU-K is reduced to 300kW - except in overtake mode, which will remain 350kW. To achieve this, the fuel flow for the engine was increased by five percent to deliver the expected increase in power.

Read Also: Formula 1 How the 2027 F1 rule changes will work

Rather than increase the capacity of the fuel tanks to fit the increased fuel flow rate, the FIA and FOM has elected to reduce the distance of the races for next season to minimise the risk of drivers running out of fuel at the end of the race. At most circuits, this will knock around three laps off the current count.

It is unclear whether the races will remain in their shortened form for 2028, where the powertrain rules will be revised again. In 2028, the ICE power will rise again to 450kW, with an overall 13% increase in fuel flow to create a 60/40 split in combustion to electric power delivery, which will necessitate a larger fuel tank.

Marshals wave the red flag Photo by: Simon Galloway / Motorsport Images

The F1 Commission has also put other changes forward to be approved at the WMSC, including a rework to the timer for grand prix race stoppages. The two-hour limit will remain in place but, for any stoppages under red flags, races currently operate within a maximum three-hour window.

Instead, the three-hour window would be removed, instead implementing a hard stop time for any delayed or rain-affected races to account for daylight. The FIA stated that "these changes were introduced to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur."

The statement also revealed that the F1 race directors would have more power to extend practice sessions in the event of any extended red flag periods; the FP3 session at the Spanish Grand Prix lost around 30 minutes of its run-time following incidents sustained by Lewis Hamilton and Ollie Bearman.

Hamilton hit the wall at Turn 22, necessitating around 25 minutes of barrier repairs, while Bearman's late-session crash truncated the session by a further five minutes.

Furthermore, gearbox homologation has been rescinded for 2027 - which means that manufacturers can continue to develop their transmissions next season. The document also teases further minor technical regulation changes for next year, plus undisclosed sporting and financial regulations for this year.

Sports.title: Why Leclerc didn’t copy Hamilton’s driving style amid F1 2026 struggle
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc has explained why he refrained from trying to copy Lewis Hamilton’s driving style when extracting the most out of Ferrari’s 2026 Formula 1 car was tricky.

As F1 switched to new regulations for this season, Leclerc sometimes struggled with the Scuderia’s SF-26. After the Monegasque noticeably outperformed team-mate Hamilton last year, their head-to-head has been a lot more balanced in 2026.

Looking at qualifying as the best way to evaluate pure performance, Hamilton is up 10-9, while Leclerc has been 0.023s faster on average – but that figure is skewed by the fact he didn’t set a time when he crashed out of Q3 at Barcelona.

This was during the period where Leclerc struggled the most. He was outqualified four times across the Canadian (grand prix and sprint), Monaco and Catalan rounds, while scoring just 16 points to Hamilton’s 64, due to what the 28-year-old described as “something that was extremely difficult to deal with on the car” in the Beyond The Grid podcast. This was compounded by a puzzling crash in his home race, which he blamed on brake supplier Brembo.

“When things don't go well, like it did in Montreal and Monaco, it's not only about the results,” Leclerc said. “For Barcelona, it was better. And Barcelona, of course, in qualifying, I have no excuses. That's just me pushing the limit too much and too far.

“Of course, I was disappointed, but the feeling was there. So when the feeling is there, you are a lot more confident as a driver. But Montreal and Monaco, the feeling was really not there. Like, whatever the result I will have done on the Sunday, I didn't really care about this.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“What's important for me is that when I get into the car, I get the right feeling and I know that I can do my job properly by driving just naturally and not overthinking things.

“And so when you've got two races consecutive where things are getting tough and you don't have the feeling, you've got two options, really. One is to try and find a way around with the set-up and with the car and trying to fit your natural driving style more. The other is just change your driving style.

“And in my case, I have Lewis as a team-mate, who was having incredible form – and who is in incredible form – so I knew that his driving style was working. Surely it was working,” Leclerc continued, speaking ahead of the Italian Grand Prix. “So I still had that option on trying. And I push on the word ‘trying’ because it's always difficult to try and reproduce a driving style.

“It's not as easy as, ‘Oh, Lewis is doing that, I'll just do the same’. Lewis is an incredibly talented driver and has a natural driving style that is his and he's the best in the world for that particular driving style. And so to reproduce that is very tricky.

“I tried to push more into trying to find ways to have this car a bit more fitted to my driving style. And I found a few things in the data that were just not working.

“Again, in Formula 1, it's not always black and white. It's not like you sit in front of your computer, look at the data and say, ‘Oh, this is one tenth and a half of a second, let's change that and we'll gain one tenth’. It's not as easy as that. It's intuition, it's feeling, it's things that you might think, ‘Okay, this is what makes me a bit less comfortable in the car, and if I improve that feeling, then performance will come’.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Madring

“And so I saw two, three things on the Friday night in Silverstone, changed those for the Saturday in qualifying, and the feeling was a lot better and even better than it was in Barcelona. And from that moment, I felt it went towards the right direction.”

Leclerc’s Silverstone breakthrough saw him qualify on the front row for the British Grand Prix, 0.175s down on Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and 0.172s ahead of Hamilton. The Ferrari racer took the lead at the start and dominated the race to clinch his first victory since 2024.

A switch to Carbone Industrie brake discs is understood to have contributed to Leclerc’s upturn in form, which wasn’t a case of returning to the feeling he had at the Melbourne season opener, where he had claimed an encouraging podium finish.

“The car is constantly changing, so it's not like I can really go back to that feeling I had in Melbourne. It's evolving,” Leclerc clarified.

“But my goal is to get into the car and not overthink. When you overthink, you know that you are losing time on the table because our sport is not a lot about reacting on what's happening on the car. It's more about anticipating and feeling the car yours. I mean, getting into a corner, I need to know exactly the way the car will behave so I don't have to overthink about things.”

Leclerc has been the third-highest scorer since over the latest six rounds, going back to his Silverstone win, with 88 points to Antonelli’s 121 and Lando Norris’ 107; his record is tarnished by his early Monza crash only, as he finished every other race in the top five.

Meanwhile, Hamilton has scored just 66 over that period, though he was taken out of the Madring race by brake issues.

Sports.title: Antonelli has “perfect driving style” for 2026 cars – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli is enjoying an extraordinarily successful second season in Formula 1 because his driving style works perfectly with the current generation of cars, says his team mate.

George Russell is Antonelli’s closest rival at the top of the championship standings, but the second-year driver is 81 points ahead. This is a sharp contrast to last year, when Russell out-scored Antonelli by 319 points to 150.

While Russell said Antonelli’s ability was clear before this season, he believes the reduction in aerodynamic downforce and grip this year has played to his team mate’s strengths.

“Of course Kimi is extremely talented,” said Russell. “He’s an incredible driver and has been fast in his whole career.

“I think his driving style is very similar to what he had last year and I think with just how things have fallen this year, it’s kind of the perfect driving style for these cars.”

Russell believes the same is true of other drivers, including Lando Norris, who is the only driver to have won more than one round this season.

“If you look last year, there are definitely trends,” said Russell. “If you look at Brazil last year, Kimi had a really strong race and Lando won in Brazil, and they’re two drivers who are always very strong on the low grip tracks and they’re two drivers who are arguably the best-performing drivers of this season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“He’s an amazing driver and he was of course doing extremely well last year as well. Let’s see next year if it changes or not, but certainly his natural driving style suits very well for this regulation.”

Charles Leclerc echoed Russell’s view that Antonelli’s potential was clear despite his patchy rookie campaign last year.

“I wish I knew, but clearly he’s doing something that works very well,” said Leclerc. “But to be honest, it’s not that it comes as a complete surprise.

“If I look at Kimi going through the junior ranks, I think it was quite clear for everybody that he had something very special. If you look obviously at his first year in Formula 1, I think he probably faced challenges – it is not up to me to go into detail, I don’t know, but surely he had some struggles in the first year – but this year has been extremely impressive. I mean, from the first race to now, he’s been perfect and driving at a very high level against a driver that I rate extremely high as well, which is George. So he’s doing an incredible job.”

However Leclerc said there is only so much he can tell about Antonelli’s qualities from outside the Mercedes team.

“To [tell] you exactly why he’s so fast, and why he is outstandingly fast this year compared to last year, is very difficult for me. We are all here analysing the data of everybody but we can only go up to a certain amount of detail, then you really need the data of the actual car to dig into more detail.

“So it’s difficult. But his laps look a lot on the limit but somehow he manages to do the lap when it counts and that’s been very impressive to watch.”

Sports.title: Hadjar says injured wrist is “still it’s going to be painful for a while” after comeback | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar says he is still in pain from his injured wrist as he returns to racing this weekend.

The Red Bull driver, who has missed the last three rounds, said his wrist is “good enough to drive, so that’s all I need.”

He said no surgery was required on the injury and a pre-event simulator session indicated it is now strong enough for him to be able to drive.

“I have a small fracture on the outside of the wrist and it’s just quite a long process,” said Hadjar. “I didn’t need any surgery so it’s all natural and it takes some time.

“It’s still it’s going to be painful for a while. It’s going to be six weeks.

“It says that it’s strong enough at the moment to resist the tensions. I had a test on the sim, it went well. I think it’s a similar environment as the cockpit. It’s actually, if anything, nearly identical. So if it’s fine on the sim, with the adrenaline on track and everything, I think I should be okay.

“It’s just been the training sessions have not been fun because I’ve been doing basically nothing with the left limb, so it’s been a bit boring.”

Hadjar confirmed he spoke to multiple Moto GP champion Marc Marquez, who has broken many bones during his career, notably in 2020 when he made an early return from one injury only to sustain another. Hadjar said Marquez told him: “Not to race.”

Red Bull confirmed today Hadjar will continue to drive for them next season. Hadjar said the news is “good, it is nice, but it is natural.”

“I’m not here to be hopeful,” he explained. “I’m here to show what I do on track and naturally, the rest comes, so it’s normal in a way.”
