CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico sued President Trump after he made good on his threat to bar them from covering official events. Trump told White House reporters on Friday that he was fed up after what he called two years of unfair and negative coverage.

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposefully negative things," Trump told reporters Friday. "Now, if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my — into the people's house."

The news outlets accuse Trump of violating not only their right to freedom of speech under the First Amendment, but also to due process under the Fifth.

"The President has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn't like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration," the lead attorney for the news outlets, Theodore J. Boutrous of Gibson Dunn, said in a statement. "This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States."

Sponsor Message

Boutrous represented NPR and three Colorado public radio stations on similar grounds: a federal judge found a Trump executive order that banned federal agencies from distributing federal funds to public media outlets because he didn't like NPR's coverage to be unconstitutional. (Trump still succeeded in convincing the Republican-led Congress to pull back nearly all federal funding for public media.)

White House debuts an alternative

Trump famously loves the spotlight and basks in the glow of TV cameras. After all, he's a former reality TV star.

But barring CNN in particular posed a dilemma for him Monday. CNN was set to be the pool TV network, meaning it would film the president as he went about his official duties and distribute that footage to other major television networks. None stepped in to fill CNN's place, in a show of solidarity. And many of CNN's competitors are not airing video of the president from other sources. (NPR, which is a member of the White House radio pool, has also declined to broadcast audio of Trump.)

That left Trump cutting a ribbon on a new White House helipad on Monday in a video released by the administration. There was just one problem: the whirling helicopter parked in the background drowned out whatever Trump was saying. The audio was inaudible .

The White House had tried to circumvent the press pool by debuting its own streamer on YouTube, called Trump TV. While Trump is having a busy week at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Trump TV features a collection of past press conferences and official events (all with high-quality audio).

Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico are following Trump as he travels through New York. On Tuesday at the United Nations, CNN's Kaitlin Collins stood with other journalists and shouted a question about the unpopularity of the war in Iran.

Trump ignored the question, instead telling her , "You should not be here covering me." She pointed out that the United Nations had given her press credentials. Not all locations are under his — or the federal government's — control. The court case will determine to what extent the president can dictate terms of reporting on him from the White House itself.

Sponsor Message

News outlets want access restored

Previous judicial rulings appear to offer ballast to CNN, MSNOW and Politico's legal argument.

As Trump noted, there is no constitutional or legal right that requires the president to let any particular journalist — or anyone at all — to report on federal matters from the White House grounds. The administration has argued in public statements that reporting from White House grounds is a privilege not a right.

But once a journalist is given credentials to report from the White House, they cannot be prevented from returning simply because the administration does not like their coverage. That would be "viewpoint discrimination" that the courts have held violate their free speech rights under the First Amendment.

Under a 1977 U.S. Court of Appeals ruling that still holds today , reporters cannot be barred from the White House or denied a permanent White House press pass without a clear explanation from the Secret Service that incorporates due process.

Trump barred the Associated Press from the White House last year, after he deemed the Gulf of Mexico should be called the Gulf of America, but the news wire declined to follow suit. The AP sued under similar grounds as the three news outlets' lawsuit. That case is ongoing.

World.title: As Congress confronts AI, Senate lawmakers are shut off from its most advanced tools
World.content:
As Congress confronts AI, Senate lawmakers are shut off from its most advanced tools

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

A majority of the American public wants Congress to regulate AI. But as policymakers try to make informed decisions, Senate lawmakers and their staff are barred from using all but the most basic AI tools.

According to an internal communication obtained by NPR that was sent to Senate staff in the spring by the sergeant at arms, who oversees cybersecurity in the chamber, Senate staff have access to three AI chat interfaces at no cost to their offices: Microsoft Copilot Chat, Gemini Chat for Google Workspace Enterprise Plus and OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise.

But in an apparent effort to balance innovation with risk, the sergeant at arms has not currently authorized any of the more advanced AI tools that are at the center of regulatory discussions in Washington, as well as recent public debate about AI development and safety. That debate has been prompted in part by AI industry leaders' own warnings.

Sponsor Message

These more capable tools, like OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork, allow "agents" powered by advanced AI models to complete tasks autonomously at a user's request — and can be powered by models of varying cost and capabilities.

"Congress, unfortunately, has always lagged behind," said Adam Kovacevich, the founder and CEO of center-left tech industry policy group Chamber of Progress. "Right now you've got lawmakers writing rules for technology they, in many cases, never even used and that's a problem."

The agentic tools, which can be given varying levels of access to a computer's files, are considered more capable than the web-based chat interfaces that Senate staff currently have access to. The rules from the sergeant at arms state that "platforms cannot independently access internal Senate drives, shared folders, email, Teams chats, or other Senate resources."

While outside experts acknowledge there are risks of a broader embrace of AI tools by Congress, they say limiting access also has its drawbacks.

"The use of tools and technologies that have the possibility of exfiltrating data elsewhere are a significant risk for the Senate and for the House and elsewhere," said Daniel Schuman, executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan think tank focused on strengthening government institutions. "This is also true with even more prosaic tools, right — the use of Google documents or email."

Sponsor Message

"But those concerns are not the best reason for the non-approval of certain technologies," he said. "I think people want to do better, but the incentives of the way the institution is set up is a drag on progress."

Advanced AI tools are being vetted for specific use cases, according to a Senate staffer who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the chamber's cybersecurity policies. No timeline was offered for that work.

"I think security is often a pretext for slower government agencies and businesses to use," said Kovacevich. "The reality is that you've got Fortune 500 firms who have plenty of sensitive customer information and data using all these tools and using them successfully. So I tend to think those arguments are sort of pretextual objections."

The top Republican and Democrat on the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, which oversees the Senate sergeant at arms, did not address specific details about the policy in response to questions from NPR about the chamber's AI rules. But in a statement, a committee spokesperson said the policies are designed to "protect Senate data and include stronger security and contractual requirements."

"While Senate offices should have access to AI tools, subject to individual members and committee policies, it's critical that these powerful tools are adopted with adequate safety and security checks to ensure that the Senate's constitutionally protected data is secure," the statement said.

Across the Capitol in the House, AI use is overseen by the Office of the Chief Administrative Officer, a separate body. A House staffer who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss chamber cybersecurity policy said that House rules outline specific use cases in which AI use is permissible and said tools from Microsoft, OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are approved in various scenarios.

Sponsor Message

The CAO office did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Finding a path forward

Schuman suggested that if Senate leaders decided there was a need to access more powerful AI technologies, they could make it happen.

"Their senior staff can have conversations and say, 'we really want you to expedite this, we think that there's value here and you should do it.' And the Sergeant at Arms is probably going to be responsive to that," he said. "But it's also worth keeping in mind, this is a political institution."

The sergeant at arms "is going to be more reticent because they don't want to have the finger pointed at them in case things go wrong, so they have an incentive to put the brakes on most things," Schuman continued.

Meanwhile, it seems some offices are moving ahead with these tools on an ad hoc basis. Sen. Bernie Moreno, Republican of Ohio, spoke to technology news show MTS Live last week about how his office uses AI. He said his office has an AI staffer they named Albert.

"He works long hours, doesn't require a lot of pay, but it's great for research, things that would normally take somebody a long period of time to kind of vet," Moreno said. "We use it quite a bit. I personally would like to be using it a lot more, but unfortunately the Senate has some crazy rules about how we're allowed to deploy or not allowed to deploy."

"Right now, the Senate prohibits us from integrating outside systems into the Senate's," Moreno said, "but I'm hoping that, soon in fact, that they get that done next year."

Moreno's office did not respond to an inquiry about how Albert is powered and whether it complies with Senate rules.

"This is a tool that half of all Americans are using today," Kovacevich said about AI chatbots, criticizing lawmakers who refused to use the technology they are being called upon to regulate — including one senior Democrat who told Axios last week that "you don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated."

Sponsor Message

"Well, that's true, but nobody thinks heroin has an upside to be preserved," Kovacevich said. "So if your only mental model of the technology is the harm, you're probably going to write a bill that's all brakes and no steering wheel."

World.title: How an 'AI freeze' could make big AI companies bigger and hurt smaller firms
World.content:
How an 'AI freeze' could make big AI companies bigger and hurt smaller firms

toggle caption Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

As Silicon Valley executives call for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence, a growing chorus of critics has coalesced around a counterargument: halting the advance of AI will consolidate the power of leading tech companies and kneecap their upstart rivals.

The debate comes as concerns mount in Washington about autonomous AI agents escaping human control and hacking into private companies, just as current and former employees of AI labs issue dire warnings about the dangers of unconstrained AI.

Tapping the brakes on the rapid progress of AI is now something Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI executive Sam Altman, SpaceXAI owner Elon Musk, Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and Microsoft's Satya Nadella all say they support — though they don't all share a common vision for accomplishing it.

Sponsor Message

But smaller AI firms say an AI slowdown will only cement the advantages of the companies at the forefront of the industry, often called frontier labs. And other skeptics say pausing AI development would only work with the cooperation of China, which is far from guaranteed.

"If there's an industry-wide freeze, then essentially what would happen is whoever has the strongest model today is going to dominate the market share," said David Bellamy, a research scientist at the United Arab Emirates-backed Institute of Foundation Models, which develops open-source AI tools.

Bellamy estimates that the institute's AI model is about six months behind OpenAI's and Anthropic's most advanced models. He argues that keeping that gap in place will make it hard to compete in a moment when both OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing blockbuster initial public offerings.

Alvaro Bedoya, former Federal Trade Commission commissioner under President Biden, said a freeze could make the playing field more uneven by putting pressure on smaller companies in ways that could prove ruinous.

"When powerful incumbents lock up the market, the rivals, the upstarts, the scrappy players in that market, can no longer compete on product or quality and service," Bedoya said. "They are just locked out. And the options available to them are to be bought by the incumbent or to go out of business."

Sponsor Message

In statements to NPR, some middle-of-the-pack AI companies said they fear a freeze would hobble their businesses at a time when competition is as fierce as ever.

Perplexity, a San Francisco-based AI company, said skepticism is warranted "whenever a company asks to be regulated in a way that protects its market position."

Nick Frosst, co-founder of Toronto-based AI startup Cohere, said "a blanket, privately coordinated slowdown is not a neutral safety policy, it would lock in the advantage of the small number of labs that already have the most compute, capital, and distribution, while making it harder for researchers, startups, and other labs to compete."

Other critics are pushing back in the courts.

Four consumers of AI products filed a federal lawsuit last week accusing Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI of making an illegal deal to slow the pace of AI development. They allege the arrangement violates antitrust law and will slow improvements to paid AI subscriptions."

Then there is the looming China question.

Some opponents of an American AI slowdown argue that it would allow Chinese companies to speed past American AI firms.

President Trump is the loudest voice against a Silicon Valley AI slowdown, writing on Truth Social that fears about AI going rogue and endangering humanity are overblown and "the only one that is happy about it is China."

Susan Rice, who served as national security adviser in the Obama administration, has pushed for a negotiated freeze with China to stop the training and release of new models until both Washington and Beijing can ensure that leading AI cannot overtake human control.

"America should aim to win the A.I. race, provided that the race can be won safely. Ultimately, we have more in common with our fellow humans in China than the A.I. agents who might control us all," Rice wrote recently in The New York Times.

Sponsor Message

China's Xi Jinping will be meeting with Trump in Washington this week, with artificial intelligence among the many agenda items.

One persistent question has been how the U.S. would guarantee that China would comply with a slowdown, even if the two nations agreed. Some observers have compared a U.S.-China pact to a nuclear non-proliferation agreement.

In Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's recent essay calling on the industry to "pace the frontier," he recognized that Chinese cooperation was a potential wrinkle in any global agreement to slow down.

"Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities," Amodei wrote. "Therefore any agreement must either have ironclad verifiability, or must be limited enough that defection would not be militarily existential."

Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: There's growing concern that Trump may deploy the National Guard ahead of elections
World.content:
There's growing concern that Trump may deploy the National Guard ahead of elections

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

With Election Day less than 50 days away, a growing number of Democratic lawmakers, retired military leaders and civil society organizations are seeking assurance from members of the Trump administration that the U.S. military will not be deployed to or around polling places — while also preparing for such a move to occur.

Having armed federal agents — like the FBI or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — or military troops near the polls is clearly barred by federal law, but President Trump and several other key officials have recently sidestepped direct lines of questioning around the issue.

Some have even suggested that such a presence might be necessary to ensure trust in the vote, a claim that voting officials across the United States deny. Those voting officials say they plan on administering the midterm elections as usual and have been working hard to assure voters that plans are in place if armed federal officials do show up.

Sponsor Message

The concern over federal interference at the polls has led to a wave of unprecedented action by civil rights groups, unions and political organizations, including multiple lawsuits, Freedom of Information Act requests and public service announcements to voters about what to watch for on Election Day. And many are specifically ringing alarm bells over the possible involvement of the U.S. military, particularly the National Guard.

Trump's extraordinary use of the National Guard on U.S. soil has already upended democratic norms in the U.S. and unnerved civil rights groups. And experts say the U.S. Supreme Court's recent rejection of Trump's executive order attempting to limit mail voting has backed him into a corner.

"Quite frankly, as this president's options are dwindling, the idea that he might use the military becomes even more of our concern," says retired Air Force military lawyer Maj. Gen. Steven Lepper.

Lepper is part of the Former Judge Advocates Working Group, made up of several dozen retired military lawyers. The group has been tracking the president's executive orders and military deployments and has written several reports to Congress about its worries.

"Either this administration is trying to limit the ways in which votes can be cast, or they're setting up a situation where a scenario could be concocted to justify the use of military force," Lepper says. In particular, he notes the executive order declaring antifa a terrorist organization. He says that this could be used amid disruption at polling places to justify invoking the Insurrection Act — something Trump has repeatedly threatened to do.

Sponsor Message

When asked directly by a reporter in May about deploying the National Guard or ICE, Trump didn't rule it out, saying he would do "anything necessary" to make sure there are "honest elections."

NPR reached out to the White House for clarification on the comment but did not receive a direct response.

The National Guard can legally be used to support elections in many capacities — like logistical or cybersecurity purposes — when ordered by state governors. But the president deploying troops or federal armed agents to polling places is illegal.

It's a situation that would almost certainly face immediate legal challenges — like all of Trump's domestic military deployments — but, as Lepper points out, such challenges take time to work their way through the courts.

"There's no do-over," Lepper says. "There's no way the courts can basically reverse the impact of something like [election interference]."

Democrats pressure Trump administration

It's not just Lepper and his colleagues raising the concern.

In March, several Democratic members of the Senate Armed Services Committee sought assurances from Gen. Gregory Guillot, the commander of U.S. Northern Command, who would be in charge of federal troops if such an order came from the president.

When asked by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois what guardrails are in place in that situation, Guillot said he very clearly understands the laws.

"If given the order, I would look at it very closely," Guillot answered, later adding that he didn't think troops should be "anywhere near" polling places.

Last month, the Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration for failure to respond to Freedom of Information Act requests seeking records about any plans to seize ballots in the midterm elections.

In recent weeks, Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan directly pressed several military leaders and federal agencies to confirm that U.S. troops won't be sent to polling places. Only the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, has responded, saying that there are "no plans" to send U.S. troops to the polls.

Sponsor Message

Immigration enforcement

There is also growing concern about immigration enforcement agents being used to intimidate voters, something that's also illegal.

The Department of Homeland Security has told NPR that it is "not planning operations targeting polling locations." This month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents could serve warrants at polling places. And that, too, could include the military accompanying the agents, although that is also considered by most legal experts to be illegal.

An internal DHS memo from last year that was recently made public shows that the administration has outlined a way to circumvent a law that prevents the military from performing law enforcement duties, including immigration enforcement, known as the Posse Comitatus Act. The memo lays out a specific path to deputize federalized National Guard members as immigration enforcement officers — something many members of the administration, like Stephen Miller, have long stated as a goal.

"This memo is designed as a work-around to say, 'Here is how we can get this done without violating federal law,'" says Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight, the nonpartisan, nonprofit watchdog group that obtained the memo through a Freedom of Information Act request.

The memo, which NPR has read, does not explicitly say anything about elections or polling places. But Chukwu says that given the administration's escalating claims around voter fraud by unauthorized immigrants, it's important to read it in that context.

"We should be planning for this to potentially be the way that they justify deploying National Guard to the polling places around the country," she says.

When asked about the memo, DHS told NPR it "speaks for itself."

World.title: Trump is hailing his new deal with Greenland and Denmark — but a deal already existed. So what changed?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Recently, U.S. President Donald Trump said on his social media platform that for over 100 years, presidents have recognized the strategic importance of Greenland, "but NONE of them were able to do anything about it."

The president then wrote that he had "permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation." On Tuesday, a new security agreement between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland was officially signed at the UN General Assembly in New York.

However, the U.S. already had a security arrangement with Denmark and Greenland dating back 75 years. So what, if anything, has changed?

"If we try to look at the new defence agreement compared to the old defence agreement, I would characterize it as a moderate improvement for the U.S.," Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute of International Studies, told CBC News.

"But it's a moderate improvement that has come at an immense cost."

That cost, some observers say, is the damage done to the relationships between the U.S. and some of its NATO allies including Denmark and Greenland, borne from Trump's repeated threats to seize the northern island and make it part of the U.S.

"Even though I don't think this deal has a lot of new stuff in it, I think everyone should be happy that it's finally getting signed," said Imran Bayoumi, a deputy director with the GeoStrategy Initiative in the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.

But he added that the "gains are minimal" considering the harm inflicted on the direct relationships between the U.S. and its NATO allies.

WATCH | Why Greenlanders won't forget Trump's threats: Greenlanders 'will never forget that he threatened us,' former MP says of Trump | Duration closed caption 5:21 Tillie Martinussen, a former member of Greenland's Parliament, says that while the details aren't publicly known, the deal to be signed Tuesday by Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. appears to reiterate an agreement that's been in place since 1951 — just 'don't tell Donald Trump.'

Comparing the agreements

In 1951, the U.S. and Denmark signed the Defense of Greenland Treaty that authorized U.S. military presence in agreed upon areas on the island.

During the Cold War, the U.S. maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today, only Pituffik Space Base remains, staffed by some 150 U.S. military personnel.

With this new deal, it was also announced that the U.S. plans to open two new military bases.

U.S. Vice-President JD Vance arrives to speak at the U.S. military's Pituffik Space Base in Greenland, in March 2025. (Jim Watson/The Associated Press)

But under the previous arrangement, the U.S. already had the right to expand its bases. Instead, it decreased its presence in terms of numbers and size over the years, according to Marc Weller, the director of the Global Governance and Security Centre and the International Law Programme at Chatham House, a think-tank based in London, England.

"Now they have the right, in consultation with the Danes and the Greenlanders, to agree on additional bases," Weller said.

But he says both parties had already indicated they were happy to accept an expansion of U.S. bases.

"It was a non issue."

The new agreement also prohibits foreign adversaries of the U.S., like Russia and China, from establishing bases on Greenland.

But even under the 1951 agreement, that kind of scenario would have been "unthinkable," said Olesen.

"How many Russian and Chinese bases do we really see in NATO countries these days? It is sort of a given that of course it was never going to happen. But now it's on paper."

WATCH | Trump signs deal with Denmark, Greenland leaders: Trump gets his Greenland security deal, but without U.S. ownership | Duration closed caption 2:06 U.S. President Donald Trump signed a deal with Denmark and Greenland to enhance the American military presence on the island while still recognizing Denmark's sovereignty over its self-governing territory.

The new agreement gives the U.S. t he ability to veto investments in critical infrastructure and other mining sectors from geopolitical adversaries.

But Bayoumi notes that there are logistic obstacles already preventing that. He says it's very difficult to build in Greenland, and that the infrastructure to support the launch of a critical mineral extraction project just isn't there.

Not only would it be costly and time consuming to build that infrastructure, he says Greenlanders themselves have vetoed and voted against some other mineral extraction projects in the past over concerns about environmental degradation.

But if the U.S. is going to veto other countries from investing in Greenland, Bayoumi wondered if it's ready to potentially take on a broader role "in facilitating economic development in the island."

'Infinite Life' agreement

The deal also does not have an end date, something Trump described as an "Infinite Life" agreement.

Bayoumi says this is a new development, as the 1951 pact was tied to the existence of NATO. The new agreement also makes provisions for Greenland to exercise its right to determine its independence.

But Bayoumi also notes that NATO is unlikely to disappear in the near future, and Greenland independence is unlikely to come any time soon.

According to the new pact, if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark's rights and obligations under the deal.

"This would have been implied probably in the previous stages, but it is useful for the U.S. to clarify this," Weller said.

World.title: John Amagoalik helped found Nunavut. Now he’s fighting to age there
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

John Amagoalik is widely known as the ‘Father of Nunavut,’ but after a lifetime advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination he’s now fighting to age in the territory he helped create. CBC’s Juanita Taylor shares his story and explores how it has ignited a broader conversation about Nunavut’s reliance on southern facilities for elder care.

"I'll never go back," John Amagoalik said of an assisted living facility in Ottawa, where he was sent to live by Nunavut's government in February 2025.

The territory's Department of Health transferred him to Embassy West Senior Living after an infection left no choice but to amputate part of his right leg.

"The worst part was the loneliness," Amagoalik recalled in an interview with CBC News as he sat in a wheelchair at his temporary home in Iqaluit with his wife, Evie, on Sept. 7.

"The strange surroundings. That was the worst part, being so far away from home and not ... being able to be with my many grandchildren."

Amagoalik is turning 79 in November and has multiple chronic age-related issues. He also has a difficult time talking.

John Amagoalik, who turns 79 in November, is shown in Iqaluit. The Nunavut government declined his request to provide adequate funding for his care and accessible housing, so he's going to court. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

He's frail, but he's still a fighter.

After a lifetime of struggle that included being forced to attend residential schools and advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination, Amagoalik is in his last fight: to age in the territory he helped create.

"It's been my life," he said, when asked what Nunavut means to him. "And I feel fortunate in being part of it."

'Father of Nunavut'

John Amagoalik is revered as the "Father of Nunavut" for his work spanning over three decades beginning in the 1970s — earning him the Order of Nunavut and the Order of Canada.

Among his many roles, he advocated for Inuit as an adviser with the Tunngavik Federation of Nunavut before it became Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. He was also on the executive council of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in the 1980s, and served as president of what was then the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, now Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami.

Amagoalik holds a photo of himself attending a meeting of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in Iqaluit in 1983. His work over three decades helped lead to the creation of Nunavut in 1999. (Graham Shishkov/CBC)

Amagoalik led the land claims settlement process with Nunavut Tunngavik after ratification in 1993. He also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission that designed the public government of Nunavut before the territory was created in 1999.

It's the very government his Victoria-based lawyer and longtime friend, Steve Kelliher, said is now failing him. So he's helping Amagoalik take the Nunavut government to court.

Kelliher, who first worked with Amagoalik in the 1970s formulating Nunavut's future government, said his friend is still as much a force today as he was back then.

But when he and another friend, Mark Stiles of Ottawa — who first met Amagoalik in 1975 while working in the land claims office of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada — visited Amagoalik at Embassy West in March, they felt he needed their help.

Amagoalik, centre, is shown with Georges Erasmus, left, who at the time was national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, and Indigenous rights advocate Louis Bruyere at a news conference in Ottawa in May 1987. (Chuck Mitchell/The Canadian Press)

"I said, 'Well, how do you like it here, John?' And he said, 'I hate it,'" Kelliher said.

So he asked Amagoalik if he wanted help to return home. "He said, 'Do anything to get me out of here, to get me back to Iqaluit.'"

So they did.

First, they delivered a letter to the territory’s health minister, signed by Amagoalik and dated March 31, pleading to return home. Amagoalik claims he never agreed to the move being permanent.

A copy of Amagoalik's letter delivered to Nunavut's health minister in March. (John Amagoalik)

When the minister, Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster, didn't take any action on his request to return home, they formed the John A. Committee and brought in Iqaluit lawyer Anne Crawford.

The committee raised $30,000 for a consultant to develop Amagoalik's plan of care, buy medical equipment and supplies, and pay for eight to 10 hours of daily private home care from personal support workers.

It also secured an accessible unit at a subsidized rate of $2,000 a month that has space for his hospital bed and an elevator. The Amagoaliks' public housing unit has stairs that would be too difficult for him to use.

The committee also arranged air transportation donated by an airline to fly Amagoalik to Iqaluit. On June 12, 16 months after he arrived in Ottawa, he returned home.

Amagoalik’s public housing unit has stairs, making it difficult for him to access his home. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

An uncertain future

But despite all of the hard work to bring Amagoalik back to Nunavut, his future is still uncertain.

The funds raised by the committee were only meant to be for the short term, and Anne Crawford said the money is running out.

"Which we did tell the government at the time, this will not last forever. And therefore, can you talk to us about how and what we can do going forward to continue to support him and live in his home community?"

Anne Crawford, a longtime lawyer in Iqaluit, says Amagoalik is leading the way for Nunavut elders to be cared for in their communities. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

The request to the territorial government for $16,000 a month to cover accommodations in the accessible unit and up to 10 hours a day of support worker care was declined. However, the government can provide a maximum of two hours per week of personal support worker care.

The committee says its research shows that Nunavut was spending about $30,000 a month for Amagoalik’s care at Embassy West.

The Health Department told CBC News that it can't comment on his care in order to protect his privacy. Brewster, the health minister, also declined to be interviewed.

But a communications manager provided a written statement saying the government has not refused to provide publicly funded health care to Amagoalik and that it continues to work in "good faith to support him."

Victoria-based lawyer Steve Kelliher (pictured) and Mark Stiles, friends of Amagoalik, worked to bring him home to Iqaluit and are trying to secure funding from the government for his care. (Submitted by Steve Kelliher)

"So we have no alternative but to appeal to the courts to compel them to do the right thing," Kelliher said, calling the situation "despicable."

"If we've got no money, we'll go beat the bushes," he said. Amagoalik "deserves better. He's earned it. He is an exception. Who treats their leaders like that? Not the Inuit. I don't believe it."

On Sept. 16, two notices of application for judicial review were filed in the Nunavut Court of Justice on behalf of Amagoalik.

"One for judicial review of the assistant deputy minister's letter, the decision not to fund John's care and housing," Kelliher said. "And an application for urgent relief to compel them to do so until the matter is fully heard, which could take months."

Amagoalik and his wife, Evie, embrace. (CBC)

Lack of care facilities for seniors

Amagoalik's care situation is emblematic of a wider problem in Nunavut. The vast territory, which covers a total area of just over two million square kilometres and is home to roughly 40,000 people, has only six seniors' facilities spread across its three regions.

The government says it's expanding two more long-term care facilities in Nunavut.

Currently, 73 elders from Nunavut are being cared for at Embassy West Senior Living, the only out-of-territory facility contracted by the government for more complex needs.

"We don't want to continue seeing our elders getting flown to Ottawa,” said Gloria Uluqsi, president of Nunavut Tunngavik. "I think they can do better. I think we as a team can do better for our elders."

World.title: With secularism sidelined in Quebec election campaign, here's where the parties stand
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After losing her job over Quebec's controversial religious symbols ban, teacher Fatemeh Anvari says secularism is her top campaign issue in the province's election.

“Something that has to do with my personal freedoms, my rights and the rights of so many – it would be at the forefront,” Anvari said.

“I lost my teaching job only because I was wearing a hijab and the law didn’t allow that."

It’s the same story for Bouchera Chelbi, a Montreal teacher who under Bill 21 was allowed to keep her current job because of an acquired rights clause, but cannot move jobs or get a promotion.

“Because of this bill, I'm denied many advantages that anybody can have, at least anybody who's not wearing a religious symbol,” Chelbi said.

“This is not because I'm not competent enough. This is not because I'm not qualified enough. It is because of the way I choose to dress."

Ahead of Quebec's general election on Oct. 5, Chelbi says she'd like all five main political party leaders to take into consideration "that there are real human beings impacted by these bills."

WATCH | Secularism hasn’t been a big election issue. Some want that to change: Secularism hasn’t come up much this election. We asked the 5 main parties where they stand | Duration closed caption 3:50 Voters both for and against the province’s secularism laws say party leaders haven’t talked much about where they stand on the issue during the campaign. They want to hear what the parties have to say before they cast their ballot.

Supreme Court decision looming

The previous Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government passed various laws during its eight year mandate – bills 21, 94 and 9 – that banned police, prosecutors, judges, teachers, other school employees , and publicly-funded daycare workers from wearing religious symbols at work.

The ban even extends to parent volunteers at schools.

The CAQ also banned prayer rooms in schools and universities, barred public institutions from serving exclusively kosher or halal menus , and put restrictions on group prayers in public.

One of the reasons secularism hasn’t come up much in this campaign may be because everyone’s waiting for a Supreme Court decision that will ultimately decide its fate in the province.

Quebec’s secularism laws are – in theory – protected from legal challenges because the CAQ pre-emptively invoked the constitutional notwithstanding clause when it passed them .

Protestors gathered in Chelsea, Que., in 2021 after teacher Fatehem Anvari lost her job for refusing to remove her hijab. Anvari says secularism is the top issue for her in this election campaign. (Alexandre Behne/CBC)

The Supreme Court is currently weighing whether the clause can actually be used that way , and a decision is likely in the next few months.

That decision will directly affect how the next government deals with secularism laws.

Some groups want more secularism measures

People such as Anvari and Chelbi, who’ve experienced major consequences of secularism laws, don’t want the next government to wait for the Supreme Court decision to act. They're calling for the laws to be repealed as soon as possible.

Meanwhile, some groups that support the province's secularism laws want to know they'll be protected.

“Evidently, we’re not talking enough about it. It’s Quebec's autonomy that’s at stake,” said Daniel Baril, president of the group Mouvement laïque québécois, a provincial secularism group.

He wants the ban on wearing religious symbols at school expanded to include not just teachers and staff but students as well.

“It’s a method used to engage in religious proselytism in schools, and it creates tensions and conflicts,” he said.

Nadia El-Mabrouk, president of another pro-secularism group, the Rassemblement pour la laïcité, told CBC the group wrote to all the political parties at the start of the campaign proposing more secularism measures, but has yet to hear back.

Her group is pushing for a national secularism day, stricter enforcement of existing laws, and an end to religious tax breaks and livestock slaughter exemptions.

“Unfortunately, we are seeing a backlash, so we need political parties that stand firm,” she said.

CBC reached out to all the parties and asked whether they would strengthen secularism laws, weaken them, or maintain the status quo. Here's what they said:

CAQ would further measures if 'necessary'

The CAQ, which passed the existing secularism laws, is promising to maintain them, and to continue to use the notwithstanding clause to protect them from legal challenges.

“These are all necessary laws to affirm and preserve the secular nature of the state, which is so dear to Quebecers,” the party said in an email.

The CAQ under leader Christine Fréchette says it may introduce further unspecified measures tightening secularism laws 'if necessary.' (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

The CAQ was also the only party that hinted at strengthening the laws.

“We have no intention of backing down from our commitment to secularism, and should further measures prove necessary, we will not hesitate to implement them,” the party said.

PQ, Conservatives would maintain and protect laws

The PQ and the Conservative Party of Quebec also both promised to maintain current secularism laws and to use the notwithstanding clause to protect them, although neither party mentioned any further measures.

The Parti Québécois under leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says it would use the notwithsanding clause to protect secularism laws and any other laws it deems necessary as long as Quebec remains within Canada. (Radio-Canada)

Still, both suggested the notwithstanding clause would be a big part of their plans even beyond secularism laws.

“As long as Quebec remains part of Canada, the Parti Québécois reserves the right to invoke the notwithstanding clause for any law it deems legitimate,” the PQ said in a statement.

The Conservatives went further.

“We will systematically invoke the notwithstanding clause in every law we pass in order to protect the choices of the National Assembly,” the party said.

Like the CAQ and the PQ, the Conservative Party of Quebec under leader Éric Duhaime would maintain Quebec's current secularism laws. The party says it would also systematically invoke the notwithstanding clause for every law it passes. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

Liberals would maintain, but not protect laws

Somewhere in the middle is the Quebec Liberal Party (PLQ).

“The PLQ is in favour of state secularism, but does not plan to adopt new measures regarding current prohibitions,” the party said in a statement.

The Quebec Liberal Party under leader Charles Milliard says it wouldn't introduce any new secularism measures or repeal the existing laws, but it would not renew the notwithstanding clause protecting those laws from legal challenges. The clause protecting Bill 21 is set to expire in 2029. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

The party says it favours a milder version of state secularism first proposed by the Bouchard-Taylor commission in 2008, which would limit the ban on wearing religious symbols at work to people in positions of authority – judges, prosecutors and police – but not teachers or any other civil servants.

The party didn't commit to changing or repealing any of the secularism laws, but it did say it would not renew the notwithstanding clause protecting Bill 21 when it expires in 2029, which would leave the law open to being struck down in a court challenge.

Québec Solidaire would repeal laws

The party with the strongest stance against secularism laws is Québec Solidaire.

“Québec Solidaire believes that the freedom-curbing measures of bills 21, 94 and 9 do not strengthen the secular nature of the state in any way, and that is why we are committed to repealing them,” the party said in a statement.

Québec Solidaire under co-leaders Ruba Ghazal, centre, and Sol Zanetti, right, pictured with candidate Étienne Grandmont, would repeal Quebec's current secularism laws, arguing they curb freedom and do nothing to reinforce state secularism. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

It also said it would regulate the use of the notwithstanding clause to protect rights and freedoms of Quebecers.

Québec Solidaire said there are better ways to strengthen state secularism, such as ending public funding for religious schools.

World.title: Mass shooting at house party in South Africa leaves 11 dead, 3 wounded: police
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Three shooters killed at least 11 people, including a woman who was believed to be pregnant, in an attack at a house party in South Africa, police said Wednesday.

Three others were wounded in the mass shooting late Tuesday night in KwaMakhutha township, about 30 kilometres south of the city of Durban on the country's east coast.

The people had gathered at the house for a party when the suspects entered and opened fire, police said. Ten people, including the pregnant woman, died at the scene and an 11th was declared dead at the hospital.

Authorities did not immediately give out details on the condition of the three people wounded.

Police said they were searching for the attackers and no arrests had been made.

The motive for the shooting was not known, police said, but added that some of the people at the house were known to police as part of investigations into criminal activity. Police said they couldn't give out any more information on those investigations.

"Although the motive of the shooting cannot be confirmed yet, [a] feud between rival groupings cannot be ruled out," police said.

The bodies of some of the victims were laid out on the ground and covered with white sheets outside the small house where the shooting took place. Police cordoned off the larger neighbourhood with yellow tape while forensic investigators worked through the scene.

Police were also investigating if the torching of a car near the house was connected to the shooting.

Killings 'really disturbing,' says premier

Thami Ntuli, the premier of KwaZulu-Natal province, told reporters at the scene that the killings were "really disturbing." He said that there were known problems with drug dealing and illegal firearms in the community.

It's the latest in a series of mass shootings in South Africa in recent years, including one in June when multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighbourhood in Johannesburg. Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December killed 21 people.

South Africa has extremely high rates of violent crime, with official police statistics recording 5,427 homicides in the latest three-month period between April and June, at an average of nearly 60 homicides a day.

Shootings are the most common form of homicide in South Africa, and police and crime experts have long said that one of the biggest problems is a high number of illegal firearms in circulation.

World.title: 'Nuclear' threat or market boom? Either way, AI race looms over Trump-Xi talks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington with a full state arrival ceremony, the leaders are facing intense global pressure to establish safety guardrails over an increasingly volatile artificial intelligence race.

The meeting comes as tech executives from some of the biggest firms have called for meaningful regulation and oversight as the U.S. and China race at breakneck speed to advance the frontier of AI systems and policymakers struggle to keep up.

In fact, some analysts are calling for "nuclear-style" safeguards, likening the AI race to the competition between the two countries during the Cold War.

Calls for a slowdown

The urgency is underscored in recent warnings, including in early September, when a researcher at AI firm Anthropic quit his job, then warned there is more than a 10 per cent chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade .

In the days that followed, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a co-ordinated slowdown, outlining a framework to manage risks. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, CEO of the recently-merged SpaceXAI, endorsed it.

These cautions are accompanied by real-life examples of models going rogue . And considering the competition is narrowing, Chinese companies like DeepSeek have AI models comparable to the U.S. firms and could pose similar risks .

That competition for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has made it increasingly clear to some executives and analysts Beijing and Washington must work together to rein in the technology, despite it also posing the "toughest dilemma," said Amodei in a Sept. 13 interview with CBS's Face the ⁠Nation .

WATCH | Why the U.S. and China may have to co-operate on AI guardrails: Why U.S. and China may have to co-operate on AI guardrails | Duration closed caption 2:42 Chinese and U.S. economic officials have begun talks ahead of a meeting between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping, where AI safety is expected to be a top issue.

"The incentives to pull ahead and ⁠the ⁠military advantage that you get from that ​are so large, that the ability to check that the other side isn't cheating has to be ironclad," he said.

For Amodei, a win coming out of the Trump-Xi summit would be if they could agree to not develop biological weapons or release AI models bioterrorists could use to develop weapons.

Hongying Wang, a political science professor at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, says she hopes AI does top the agenda and that the leaders recognize the very real dangers it poses globally.

She says this period of time reminds her of the "Cold War period, the height of nuclear competition, and the kind of existential threat that posed for the world."

"If they're not part of any kind of agreement, everybody else can do nothing," she said.

AI competition

However, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Sept. 14 called the CEOs' warnings "fearmongering" and a way to contain China's advancements.

Trump also publicly poo-pooed the fears, calling them a "hoax " and claimed the U.S. is "leading China in AI … and whoever wins AI wins ." Despite that, he and Xi agreed to restart the discussion on AI governance when the U.S. president visited Beijing in May and recently said it would be on the agenda for this upcoming visit.

Considering this rhetoric, whether the two can make progress is debatable.

Ho-fung Hung, a professor of political economy at Johns Hopkins University in Washington, D.C., told CBC News Trump's priority is the stock market.

U.S. President Donald Trump, second from left, first lady Melania Trump, left, Chinese President Xi Jinping, second right, and his wife Peng Liyuan, right, stand together as they tour the Forbidden City, Wednesday, Nov. 8, 2017, in Beijing. (Andrew Harnik/Associated Press)

"Trump doesn't want to pour more cold water on this kind of AI-driven financial … boom," he said, and he does not want to be outcompeted by China.

However, he said Trump's interests will be somewhere in between balancing the markets while listening to his advisors about the risks.

Same for Xi, says Hung.

"The most rational thing is to talk."

In China, there's skepticism, too, given the intense competition, and the fact Washington could value the quest for dominance over anything else.

"I don't think the two sides have any space for co-operation or co-ordination," said Tu Xinquan, a professor who leads an institute studying the World Trade Organization at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing.

These takes are unsurprising as the relationship is steeped in mistrust and rivalry. The U.S. has tried to restrict the flow of advanced semiconductor chips to China . China has leveraged its monopoly on rare earths.

Now, AI is the new frontier.

"The U.S. has put a lot of weight on AI … as an all-in kind of strategy," said Tu.

Political and social stability

China's leadership has also recognized the power and risks of the technology, although for different reasons.

"Beijing is concerned, first and foremost, with political stability," said Kyle Chan, a fellow with D.C.-based Brookings Institute whose research focuses on China and AI. The U.S. is more focused on existential threats.

Chan said China's earliest AI regulations centred around controlling content similar to social media.

"The last thing Chinese policy makers want is for deep fakes or sensitive political topics to be produced by these Chinese AI models," he said.

Despite the ideological differences in their approach, there are likely issues both countries will want to get ahead of, like national and global security.

While there are other looming issues to sort, including the expiry of the trade truce struck in Busan, South Korea, in November, and the war in Iran raging on, both leaders will want to announce some wins. Further co-operation on AI could be a timely one.

The details don't necessarily need to be worked out, either.

There are still two other opportunities to do that this year, says Sourabh Gupta, senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies in Washington.

In November, Shenzhen will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) and the G20 Leaders' Summit will take place in Miami, Fla., the following month.

"The opportunity exists to deepen that conversation and actually have outcomes perhaps later this year or even next year," he said.

The question may be whether they can make progress fast enough to keep up with the technology.

World.title: Robert Pattinson's Primetime hates Chris Hansen
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's 9 p.m. on a Wednesday. Do you know where your children are?

If you're the fictionalized version of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen portrayed by Robert Pattinson in A24's Primetime, you're convinced you do — at least, you've convinced your network you know where everybody else's are.

This Hansen explains, drink in hand, to his airplane seatmate: it's what got his show greenlit in the first place. As he tells his executives, children aren't off roaming the streets or falling down wells. They're alone in their rooms. But outside, Hansen says, is a man standing on the porch, genitalia in hand. And in movie-Hansen's shockingly vulgar description that we're not going to fully quote here: he's about to charge up to that bedroom.

But if his audience just watches To Catch a Predator tonight on NBC, Hansen pitches, he'll tell them how to stop him.

WATCH | Primetime trailer:

The value of that advice he's offering is obvious to anyone familiar with what happened on that 2004 show. The Dateline series had Hansen pop out of closets and bedrooms to confront alleged child predators his team had lured there — and that infamously led to failed prosecutions, dangerous copycats and at least one death.

But Primetime is anything but a strait-laced critique. What spins out from the movie charting this fraught history is a whirligig of obscenity and oddity. It's a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy. And one so off-putting (it is produced by The Strange Thing About the Johnsons' Ari Aster, after all) you're not even shocked when it pairs that offhand humour with stomach-churning horror.

We see Tony Revolori (Spider-Man: Homecoming) making bug-eyed, intentionally ridiculous faces at the camera along with images of butchered children's bodies abandoned in a nameless jungle. We see Pattinson's Hansen inexplicably projectile-spitting mouthwash into a sink — while standing in a bent-arms, leaned-forward pose that looks less like a journalist, and more like an attacking goose.

And then, later, we see that same goose-man chasing down an actual monster, a personification of what is supposedly lurking outside of society. But as he keeps looking for that evil outside of himself, and stares into the face of evil, we stare right back into his.

There's a high-wire act of unself-conscious commitment-to-the-bit that Pattinson so often brings to his roles: a seeming incapability to feel embarrassment that allows him to dive completely into accents, impersonations and general absurdity.

Here, that's a campy, elevated, Spirit Halloween version of Chris Hansen: one that drawls "Why don't you take a seat" with a gravelly self-seriousness that, in anyone else's hands, would just read as ridiculous.

The absurd, chaotic depiction of Chris Hansen in Primetime says something new, and odd, about the To Catch a Predator host. (Elevation Pictures)

As director Lance Oppenheim and writer Ajon Singh would have us believe, all those over-the-top affectations are really meant to expose a deep rot at the centre of the real man. Because based as it is on the blistering article "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die," about a shocking outcome to one of his stings, Primetime is not exactly a fan of Hansen's Dateline series. Echoing criticism — and even court rulings — against the ensuing "Creep Catcher" groups that would copy To Catch a Predator 's modus operandi , this screenplay offers deep and obvious condemnations.

Which makes it evident as to why the real Chris Hansen hasn't exactly made himself a friend to the project.

Instead, he says he bought his own trailers ahead of the movie , to say the story you're about to see is completely fabricated. Like the Church of Latter-day Saints did in the Playbill for The Book of Mormon , he'll point audiences toward his own tome of content where, he says, the true story lies.

The true-crime streaming network he's since built continues to release content around sexual offences. An unending slew of new shows follow the format of, and capitalize on audiences' insatiable appetite for , the public-shaming vigilantism of To Catch a Predator.

The critical read of Primetime's funhouse-mirror interpretation is right there. Instead of giving Predator's seemingly righteous goals even a tiny bit of credit, Oppenheim makes it his rhetorical aim to deliberately deconstruct Hansen's assumed self-interest while unreservedly humanizing his targets.

Throughout Hansen's interactions with a harried and hapless producer (Merritt Wever), a clearly traumatized and exploited "decoy" actor used for luring these alleged criminals (Skyler Gisondo) and the empathetically depicted subjects themselves, Primetime's message is clear.

Glassy-eyed, preening and frantic Hansen does not run Predator as some sacred calling, the film says. He does not manipulate local police forces into bypassing laws around search and seizure, wake up his barely grade-school sons in the middle of the night to watch his latest catch or stare hatefully at NBC reporter Stone Phillips reporting on "real" news because he's performing some sacred calling.

In the eyes of Primetime, he's doing it because he wants just that: to be on prime time.

Robert Pattinson, right, appears with actor Tony Revolori in a scene from Primetime. (Elevation Pictures)

That alone wouldn't be enough. The idea that respectability died first on the airwaves is obvious to the point of insulting; it wasn't enough to float the sci-fi commentary on capitalism The Running Man last year, and it's not enough to float the Rupert Murdoch/Larry Lamb biopic Ink that showed at this year's TIFF.

Neither is it enough to merely acknowledge the existential fear around stranger danger that has fuelled political campaigns and platforms of the past 50 years. From the genuinely moving, loosely inspired adaptation of six-year-old Etan Patz's disappearance in Without a Trace to the abysmally exploitative child-trafficking film Sound of Freedom, the blinding fear around the vulnerability of children already clearly motivates us.

What Primetime gets at is more probative, and more unsettling. A question not necessarily about self-delusion, but about how a lack of humanity seems justified, even encouraged, when dealing with Hansen's subjects.

It's a topic raised by that same airplane seatmate, who asks Hansen whether he ever wants to skip the justice system and just "bleed" the men he catches.

And it's a proposition Hansen considers, then says that just maybe, what he's doing is worse. And then he smiles.

World.title: Hurricane Polo in the Pacific Ocean considered 'one of the strongest storms ever'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hurricane Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades and was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a Category 5 storm.

Polo was an "extremely dangerous" storm, with maximum sustained winds of 265 km/h, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said Tuesday night.

Polo was nearly stationary early Wednesday, about 300 kilometres south of Zihuatanejo in Guerrero state and 540 kilometres southeast of Manzanillo, moving north at four kilometres per hour with maximum sustained winds of 255 km/h, the centre reported.

It was forecast to turn sharply to the northwest during the day and then move in west-northwest over the next several days.

U.S. National Hurricane Center data shows Polo's winds reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which had winds that reached 346 km/h in 2015.

"This is one of the strongest storms ever in the [Pacific] Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's department of atmospheric and environmental sciences.

I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in the past 24 hours.

Phil Klotzbach, research scientist in the department of atmospheric science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fuelled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region.

In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.

"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.

Warnings of life-threatening flooding

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated that the hurricane was not likely to touch land. Still, hurricane-force winds extend up to 65 kilometres from the storm's centre and tropical storm-force winds up to 169 kilometres from the eye, the U.S. centre said.

Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About eight to 15 centimetres of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states.

Mexican National Guard members on Tuesday warned beachgoers and tourists in Acapulco, Mexico, of the potential dangerous effects from Polo. (Javier Verdin/Reuters)

The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities.

"Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions — intensified by storms — may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement.

Tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states Wednesday into Thursday.

The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by a number of powerful cyclones in recent years. Beaches emptied and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas.

Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care.

Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city, Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build.

"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."

Meanwhile, Odalys strengthened to a Category 1 hurricane early Wednesday and was about 2,085 kilometres off the southern tip of Baja California in Mexico, with maximum sustained winds of 120 km/h, the hurricane centre said.

LISTEN | Experts discuss what could transpire in months ahead: What on Earth? 25:02 Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

Pacific-Atlantic contrast

Polo is the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 253 kilometres per hour.

In the U.S., California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday declared a state of emergency in order to marshal state resources over the potential impacts of El Niño ahead of the winter season. The order directs stage agencies to prepare roads and critical infrastructure for the risk of floods and landslides in vulnerable communities.

A partially submerged boat is seen in Acapulco Bay as strong waves and winds caused by Hurricane Polo were evident in Acapulco, Mexico, on Tuesday. (Francisco Robles/AFB/Getty Images)

The developments in the Pacific come as a new research report released Wednesday by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says El Niño, combined with the record global heat it is driving, could lead to tens of thousands of more heat-related deaths over the next six months.

The heaviest toll, the lab said, is expected in poorer countries, particularly in the Southern Hemisphere.

In contrast to the Pacific, no hurricanes have formed yet this year in the Atlantic Ocean. The effects of El Niño have so far crushed storms before they develop.

World.title: Why Russia has Europe on edge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | FRONT BURNER: Front Burner 26:05 Why Russia has Europe on edge

Earlier this week, Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party won a record number of seats in the country's parliamentary elections. Putin is expected to frame the result as an endorsement of his war with Ukraine. And, according to Ukrainian intelligence, he may mobilize hundreds of thousands more Russian troops before the end of the year.

All of this has Europe on edge. Because Russia hasn't just been targeting Ukraine – but Ukraine’s allies too. In the last few weeks, a Russian ship fired flares at a Danish military helicopter, NATO jets shot down a drone over Lithuania, and Germany thwarted a suspected Russian drone attack at one of their airports.

Many observers think Russia is intentionally trying to provoke NATO. But why? And what happens if NATO decides to fight back?

Victor Jack, POLITICO’s NATO reporter, joins us from NATO’s headquarters in Brussels.
