What bringing your pet to Costa Rica actually requires

You need an International Veterinary Certificate from the official veterinary service of the country of origin. It must be numbered, and every page signed and stamped with the official stamp. Electronic certificates are accepted where the issuing authority runs an online system to verify them.

It must be in Spanish or English, or carry an official certified translation into Spanish. It must state the animal’s breed, sex, colour and date of birth, and its microchip number if it has one. It must also name the exporter, the consignee, the means of transport, the official veterinarian, the authority’s stamp and the date.

Two things are explicitly not required, and both sheets say so. You do not need a notary public’s seal, and you do not need any stamp from a Costa Rican consulate. People are still paying for both. SENASA also warns that requirements can change without notice, so download the sheet again shortly before you fly.

The two timing windows, and the vaccines

Only two clocks matter, and both run backwards from your departure date. The clinical examination must fall within two weeks, meaning 14 days, of departure. The vet certifies the animal is healthy, with no tumours, no fresh wounds and no wounds in the process of healing, and free of external parasites.

The second clock is treatment against internal and external parasites, within 15 days of export, with approved drugs and ensuring freedom from ticks. The certificate must record the date, the brand name, the lot number and the active ingredient.

Dogs need distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus and leptospirosis. Cats need feline viral rhinotracheitis, calicivirus and panleukopenia. Bordetella and parainfluenza are not on the list, whatever a shipping company may tell you.

Rabies is the one people get wrong. Dogs and cats over three months old must be vaccinated, and the vaccine must be valid on the day the animal enters. There is no waiting period in the SENASA text, neither 21 days nor 30. Puppies and kittens under three months must not be given a rabies shot; the age-appropriate plan is certified instead.

The titre test is not Costa Rica’s requirement

Costa Rica does not require a rabies antibody titration test to import a dog or a cat. The single mention of one applies to pets from the European Union, the United Kingdom and EFTA states that will return home. Those must carry a valid result of 0.5 international units per millilitre or higher.

That line exists because Europe demands the test on re-entry. So a European moving permanently needs no titre test, while one coming for a season should do it before departure. An American needs it in neither direction.

Permits, fees and the arrival inspection

This is where most guides overcharge you. If the pet travels in the cabin, or as checked baggage with its owner, the sheets require only the health certificate at the border inspection post. No import permit. No customs broker. No prior application.

If the animal travels as cargo, or arrives without its owner, the importer must hire a Costa Rican customs broker. The broker applies for the import permit before the animal arrives, and SENASA resolves it within 24 working hours.

The permit is line C.01 in SENASA’s 2026 tariff, which runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 January 2027. It costs ¢10,653 (about US$23.67) and is exempt from value-added tax. Blogs quote US$35, US$50 or nothing. The broker’s fee is separate and not set by SENASA.

Neither sheet imposes routine quarantine on dogs or cats. A healthy, compliant, accompanied animal clears and goes home with you. The only stated grounds for refusal at the port are tumours, fresh or healing wounds, and external parasites. One line in the tariff is unexplained. Supervised home quarantine for imported animals costs ¢100,750 (about US$223.89) per shipment, and what triggers it for a dog or cat could not be confirmed.

From the United States, and from Europe

For American owners the certificate must be issued by an accredited veterinarian and then endorsed by a federal Veterinary Services vet. That digital endorsement is mandatory. The endorsed certificate prints from the federal system and must travel with the animal, so allow several business days.

The agency’s Costa Rica page, updated on 6 February 2026, repeats that a permit is required for unaccompanied pets. Europe has no equivalent portal. There the state or national veterinary authority issues and stamps the certificate, not your local practice.

The airline is the real obstacle, and the cost

Copa Airlines, the hub carrier via Panama City, allows a pet plus carrier of up to 10 kilos in the cabin. The soft carrier may be no larger than 18 by 11 by 11 inches. Minimum age is 16 weeks and the international fee is US$125. Copa does not accept animals as checked baggage at all.

Copa cargo runs Monday to Thursday only. It bans pit bulls, American Staffordshire terriers, dogos argentinos, fila brasileiros, cane corsos and English bulldogs outright, and requires larger crates for French bulldogs, Boston terriers, boxers and pugs. American Airlines Cargo prohibits all snub-nosed breeds.

Both refuse pets when the temperature at any airport on the route is above 85°F (29°C) or below 45°F (7°C). San José sits at roughly 900 metres and rarely breaches the ceiling, so your departure airport is the problem.

A cat or small dog in the cabin from the United States comes to roughly US$400 to US$800. That is the US$125 fee, US$150 to US$400 for the vet and certificate, and US$50 to US$150 for a carrier. The federal endorsement fee is charged separately and could not be confirmed. Full service is quoted at US$2,495 to US$6,495. No credible published range exists for Europe.

Costa Rica has no breed-specific ban. SENASA said so directly in 2023: no law here defines any breed as dangerous. Liability sits with the owner under the companion animal regulation. The restrictions you will actually hit are the airlines’.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Costa Rica require a rabies titre test? No, not for entry. The only titre requirement in the SENASA sheet applies to pets from the European Union, the United Kingdom and EFTA states that will return home, because Europe demands it on re-entry. An American owner needs no titre test in either direction. Do I need an import permit for my dog? Only if the animal travels as cargo or arrives without you, in which case a Costa Rican customs broker must apply for it beforehand. The permit costs ¢10,653 (about US$23.67) under the 2026 tariff. A pet flying in the cabin or as checked baggage with its owner needs only the health certificate. How close to the flight must the paperwork be done? The clinical examination must fall within 14 days of the departure date, and the parasite treatment within 15 days of export. The ten-day certificate window quoted by some shipping companies does not appear in the SENASA text. Rabies vaccine simply has to be valid on the day of arrival. Can I bring a pet bird, ferret or reptile? Probably not without a case-by-case decision. SENASA publishes species sheets only for a narrow list, including canaries from Spain and snakes from Germany, and none for pet birds or reptiles from other countries. Call the animal quarantine directorate on +506 2587-1600 before you book anything.

World.title: Starting a Company in Costa Rica: S.A. or S.R.L. for Foreigners
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. Its company law sits in one statute, the Código de Comercio, Ley 3284.

— Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. Its company law sits in one statute, the Código de Comercio, Ley 3284. The system — two forms cover almost every case. The sociedad anónima, or S.A., divides capital into shares and needs a board of three plus a supervisory officer. The sociedad de responsabilidad limitada, or S.R.L., divides capital into quotas and is run by one or more managers.

The sociedad de responsabilidad limitada, or S.R.L., divides capital into quotas and is run by one or more managers. What matters now — Ley 10840, published on 6 March 2026, abolished the carta poder as a way of being represented at a shareholders’ meeting. Absent owners now need a notarised power of attorney instead.

The annual legal entity tax runs from ¢69,330 (about US$154) for an inactive company to ¢231,100 (about US$514) for the largest, and the education stamp from ¢5,000 (about US$11). What it means for you — a dormant holding company still costs money every year. Three consecutive years of unpaid legal entity tax dissolve it by operation of law.

— a dormant holding company still costs money every year. Three consecutive years of unpaid legal entity tax dissolve it by operation of law. Still open — the widely quoted registry charge of 0.5% of declared capital comes from a law firm’s cost page, not from the tariff statute. Check the Registro Nacional arancel before you budget.

Two company forms, no minimum capital, no nationality bar — and a set of annual charges that quietly dissolve the companies whose owners stop paying attention.

Starting a company in Costa Rica is quick, cheap by regional standards and open to foreigners without restriction. The decisions that matter come early. Which of the two forms you use, how much capital you declare, and who can act for you while you are abroad. The annual bill is small, but ignoring it has a legal consequence.

Every Costa Rican company is created by public deed before a Costa Rican notary.

Starting a company in Costa Rica: the two forms

Company law sits in the Código de Comercio, Ley 3284. Two forms cover almost every case: the sociedad anónima, the S.A., and the sociedad de responsabilidad limitada, the S.R.L. In both, owners are liable only for what they contribute.

Neither has a minimum capital. Founders set the figure themselves. There is a practical catch, though. The capital you declare drives the registry charges and the annual education and culture stamp, so a high nominal figure costs money for no benefit.

Colon amounts here use the Banco Central reference rate for 22 September 2026, ¢450 (about US$1) to the dollar.

Where the two forms differ

An S.A. divides capital into shares, under Article 102, and those shares transfer freely. It needs a board of at least three people under Articles 181 onward: president, secretary and treasurer. It also needs a supervisory officer, the fiscal.

An S.R.L. divides capital into quotas, under Article 78. Quotas can never be transferred by endorsement, and moving one requires the other quotaholders’ consent. The company is run by one or more gerentes, or managers, with no board and no fiscal.

Article 104 asks an S.A. for at least two shareholders at the deed stage, each subscribing at least one share. Of shares paid for in cash, 25% of the value must be paid in at incorporation. Of shares paid in kind, the full value must be delivered then.

After incorporation one person may hold every share without affecting the company. So the two-founder rule is a formality at the deed, not a lasting constraint. In practice the S.R.L. suits property holding and closely held ventures, the S.A. larger operations and outside investors.

Can a foreigner own all of it?

Yes. There is no nationality restriction on holding shares or quotas, or on serving as a director or manager. The obstacles are documentary rather than legal.

Foreign shareholders and officers need a Costa Rican tax identification. Anyone without a cédula or DIMEX obtains a NITE, a special tax number issued against a passport. Sectoral rules sit outside company law, for example in maritime zone concessions and broadcasting.

Owning a company is not a work permit. A foreign owner who personally works in the business in Costa Rica still needs immigration authorisation for that activity, and the legal representative role does not supply it.

One 2026 change matters for absent owners. Ley 10840, published on 6 March 2026 and in force that day, reformed Articles 98 and 146 of the Código de Comercio. It abolished the carta poder for representation at shareholders’ meetings. Representation now requires a notarised power: generalísimo, general or special. A narrow exception covers small firms and farmers registered with MEIC or MAG, and powers granted earlier remain valid.

The notary and the road to a cédula jurídica

Incorporation is by public deed before a Costa Rican notary, and a foreign notary cannot do it. Under the Código Notarial the profession is limited to lawyers of at least two years’ standing in the Colegio de Abogados, with fixed residence and an office here.

The sequence is short. Agree the structure with the notary, execute the deed, then pay the registry fees and stamps. Registration at the Registro de Personas Jurídicas produces the cédula jurídica, the company identity number. Register the official email address, then register as a taxpayer through TRIBU-CR.

Two filings follow: the beneficial ownership register, and Caja registration as an employer if you hire. The bank account comes last and takes longest, with close scrutiny of foreign beneficial owners.

Practitioners quote one to three weeks to a registered company with complete papers, or five to 15 business days for the deed and registration stage. Allow a few more weeks for the bank.

What it costs to set up

Ranges reported by Costa Rican practitioners in 2026 run as follows. Notary and legal fees of ¢150,000 (about US$333) to ¢400,000 (about US$889). Registry stamps and rights of ¢30,000 (about US$67) to ¢80,000 (about US$178). For an S.A., publication in La Gaceta at ¢15,000 (about US$33) to ¢40,000 (about US$89).

That puts a typical total at ¢225,000 (about US$500) to ¢510,000 (about US$1,135) and upward. One firm describes the registry charge as roughly 0.5% of declared capital plus fixed stamps. That formula comes from a law firm’s page rather than the tariff statute, so treat it as indicative.

What it costs every year

Three obligations follow every company, trading or not. The legal entity tax under Ley 9428 is a percentage of the salario base, which for 2026 is ¢462,200 (about US$1,027) and has not moved since 2021.

An inactive company pays 15%, or ¢69,330 (about US$154). An active company with gross income under 120 salarios base pays 25%, or ¢115,550 (about US$257). The middle band pays 30%, ¢138,660 (about US$308), and the top band 50%, ¢231,100 (about US$514). The deadline is 31 January.

Non-payment bites. Legal representatives become personally liable, the Registro marks the company’s documents defective from 1 February, and the debt becomes a lien over registered assets. After three consecutive years of non-payment the company is dissolved by operation of law.

The education and culture stamp under Ley 5923 is due by 31 March, from every company including inactive ones. It runs from ¢5,000 (about US$11) where net capital is up to ¢500,000 (about US$1,111), to ¢18,000 (about US$40) above ¢4,000,000 (about US$8,889).

The beneficial ownership register, known as the RTBF, is filed with the Banco Central by 30 April. Only the legal representative with a digital signature may file, or an attorney holding a registered general power. Special powers are now excluded. The sanction is 2% of gross income, with a minimum of ¢1,386,600 (about US$3,081).

Add an accountant, and a dormant holding company still costs roughly US$200 to US$500 a year before professional fees are counted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which suits a foreigner better, an S.A. or an S.R.L.? It depends on who else is involved. The S.R.L. is simpler, with quotas, one or more managers, no board and no fiscal, and quotas cannot move without the other holders’ consent. The S.A. suits outside investors, because shares transfer freely, but it needs a three-person board and a fiscal. Can a foreigner own 100% of a Costa Rican company? Yes. There is no nationality restriction on shareholders, quotaholders, directors or managers. You will need a Costa Rican tax identification, which is a NITE if you hold no cédula or DIMEX. Does owning a company let me work in Costa Rica? No. Neither share ownership nor the legal representative role is a work permit. A foreigner who personally performs the work here needs immigration authorisation for that activity. What does a dormant company cost each year? Budget roughly US$200 to US$500 before professional fees. That covers the legal entity tax of ¢69,330 (about US$154), the education and culture stamp from ¢5,000 (about US$11), and the annual beneficial ownership filing.

World.title: Costa Rica Permanent Residency and Citizenship: The 2026 Rules
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. Citizenship is handled not by a ministry but by the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones, the body that also runs elections.

— Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. Citizenship is handled not by a ministry but by the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones, the body that also runs elections. The rule — Article 78 of the immigration law, Ley 8764, opens permanent residency to anyone who has held temporary residency for three consecutive years, and to first-degree blood relatives of a Costa Rican. Every temporary subcategory waits the same three years.

— Article 78 of the immigration law, Ley 8764, opens permanent residency to anyone who has held temporary residency for three consecutive years, and to first-degree blood relatives of a Costa Rican. Every temporary subcategory waits the same three years. What matters now — the incentive window in Ley 9996 closed on 14 July 2026, five years after the law was published, and the investor threshold it set is now disputed.

— the incentive window in Ley 9996 closed on 14 July 2026, five years after the law was published, and the investor threshold it set is now disputed. What happened — this guide records, as of September 2026, the routes to permanent residency, the social security condition behind every renewal, and what naturalisation really demands.

— this guide records, as of September 2026, the routes to permanent residency, the social security condition behind every renewal, and what naturalisation really demands. The numbers — a pensionado needs a foreign pension of US$1,000 a month, a rentista US$2,500 a month. Naturalisation itself is free: the only official charges are timbres of ¢20 (about US$0.04) or ¢200 (about US$0.44), and the published resolution period is 285 business days.

— a pensionado needs a foreign pension of US$1,000 a month, a rentista US$2,500 a month. Naturalisation itself is free: the only official charges are timbres of ¢20 (about US$0.04) or ¢200 (about US$0.44), and the published resolution period is 285 business days. What it means for you — unbroken affiliation to the Caja, the public social insurance fund, is the condition that decides renewals at every stage. A lapse puts your card at risk.

— unbroken affiliation to the Caja, the public social insurance fund, is the condition that decides renewals at every stage. A lapse puts your card at risk. Still open — whether the investor route now requires US$150,000 or US$200,000 is unresolved in Costa Rican law. Get a written ruling from the immigration authority before committing capital.

Three years, then three more documents than you expected, and one social security payment that quietly decides whether any of it holds together.

Costa Rica permanent residency is reached by waiting, not by buying. Three consecutive years of temporary residency is the standard path, and the shortcuts you have read about are mostly misreadings of the statute. Citizenship is a second, longer stage with two school exams attached. Here is what the law actually says, and where it leaves questions open.

Permanent residency is decided by the immigration directorate, naturalisation by the electoral tribunal. Photo: "Casa Presidencial Costa Rica 2014" by MadriCR, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The three-year rule for Costa Rica permanent residency

Article 78 of Ley 8764 lists who may apply. The main route is three consecutive years of temporary residency, and it covers the foreigner, the spouse and first-degree blood relatives who have held that status.

Three years is the figure for every temporary subcategory in Article 79. Pensionado, rentista, inversionista, specialised employee, religious worker, scientist, athlete, journalist and dependants all wait the same time. No category runs faster.

A third route covers people granted the status by the Comisión de Visas Restringidas y Refugio.

Marriage, children and the direct route

Article 78(2) is the route with no waiting period, and it is narrower than it looks. It covers first-degree consanguinity with a Costa Rican: parents, minor children, adult children with a disability, and minor siblings or adult siblings with a disability.

A spouse is not a blood relative and is not on that list. Several widely read English-language guides state that marrying a Costa Rican leads straight to permanent residency. The statute says otherwise.

Marriage is governed by Article 73. The foreign spouse receives a status that is conditional and temporary, for one year at a time. It is renewed annually on proof that the couple still live together, and the marriage must be registered in the Costa Rican Registro Civil. After three consecutive years, that record gives access to permanent residency.

Article 73 bis, added by Ley 8781 of 11 November 2009, extends the same route to a recognised unión de hecho, on production of the judicial recognition. Having a Costa Rican child gives the direct route. Marrying a Costa Rican does not.

The Caja condition behind every renewal

The social insurance requirement is written into the statute twice over. The final paragraph of Article 78 says permanent residents must prove affiliation to the Caja, from the moment residency was granted and without interruption, to renew their cédula de extranjería.

The final paragraph of Article 80 says the same for temporary residents. Article 86 makes an extension conditional on still meeting the requirements and on being insured. Article 83 repeats the point for executives and technical staff.

Read together the message is blunt. Unbroken enrolment decides renewals at every stage, and a lapse puts the card at risk.

Pensionado, rentista and the investor question

The statute sets the income thresholds for the routes that lead there. Article 81 asks a pensionado for a monthly, permanent and stable pension from abroad of at least US$1,000. Article 82 asks a rentista for at least US$2,500 a month, from abroad or from the national banking system, covering the applicant, spouse and children under 25.

The investor figure is unsettled. Ley 9996, published on 14 July 2021, offered incentives to investors, rentistas and pensionados. Its Article 12 gave applicants five years to opt in, so the window closed on 14 July 2026.

Those incentives are shut to new applicants. They covered a one-off exemption on household goods and duty-free import of up to two vehicles. They also gave a 20% cut in the real estate transfer tax, and exemption from income tax on the sums declared to qualify. People already granted them keep them for ten years. These article numbers come from Costa Rican firms’ analysis rather than the statute text.

Here is the gap. Article 8 of Ley 9996 set the investor threshold at US$150,000, while the immigration regulation, Decreto 37112-GOB, has US$200,000. The sunset clause names only the incentives, not the investment figure. In early September 2026 the immigration checklist still showed US$150,000, and no official statement has settled the point. Ask for a written ruling before you commit capital.

Naturalisation: five years or seven

Citizenship rules sit in the Constitution, at Articles 13 to 17. Article 14, as reformed by Ley 7879 of 27 May 1999, sets two periods of official residence.

Five years applies to nationals of other Central American countries, to Spaniards, and to Ibero-Americans by birth. Seven years applies to everyone else, including people who hold one of those nationalities other than by birth.

Article 15 adds the substance: good conduct, competence in Spanish, knowledge of the country’s history, and an oath to respect the constitutional order. The Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones runs the procedure under Ley 1155.

The exams, the cost and the wait

Two written exams stand in the way, set by the education ministry, the MEP: Español and Estudios Sociales. Studies completed and passed in Costa Rica can be recognised instead. Older adults are exempt, as are people with a certified permanent health or cognitive impediment.

The file is strict. You need a certified copy of your DIMEX, the foreigner identity card, or another immigration or foreign ministry document. A passport is not accepted. Add an apostilled birth certificate with official translation, two witnesses who have known you for the statutory period, and proof of your means of living.

The police certificate must come from a federal or national authority in your country of origin or last country of foreign residence. State, county and consular certificates are refused, and it must be presented within three months of issue. After filing you publish a notice in La Gaceta, and missing that deadline means outright rejection.

The Tribunal states that the service is free. Colon amounts here use the Banco Central reference rate for 22 September 2026, ¢450 (about US$1) to the dollar. The only official charges are timbres fiscales of ¢20 (about US$0.04) for Central American citizens and ¢200 (about US$0.44) for other nationalities. You still pay for apostilles, translations and the Gaceta notice, whose price the sheet does not state.

The published resolution period is 285 business days, roughly 13 to 14 months once the file is complete. Add the time to gather apostilled papers and pass the exams. Two years is a fair expectation.

Dual nationality is allowed. Article 16 of the Constitution, reformed in 1995, says Costa Rican nationality is neither lost nor renounceable. Nothing obliges a new citizen to give up their first nationality, though that is decided by the other country’s law. Citizenship also brings compulsory voting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does marrying a Costa Rican give immediate permanent residency? No. Article 73 of Ley 8764 gives the foreign spouse a conditional, temporary status for one year at a time, renewed on proof of living together. Permanent residency follows after three consecutive years, and the marriage must be registered in the Costa Rican Registro Civil. How long must I hold temporary residency first? Three consecutive years, under Article 78 of Ley 8764. That period is the same for pensionado, rentista, inversionista and every other temporary subcategory, and for dependants who hold status through the main applicant. Is the investor threshold US$150,000 or US$200,000? It is genuinely unresolved. Ley 9996 set US$150,000 while the immigration regulation has US$200,000, and the five-year window in the law closed on 14 July 2026 without settling the question. Ask the immigration authority for a written ruling before committing money. What does naturalisation cost? The Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones states that the service is free. The only official charges on its requirements sheet are timbres of ¢20 (about US$0.04) or ¢200 (about US$0.44) depending on nationality, and you pay separately for apostilles, translations and the La Gaceta notice.

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. President Laura Fernández Delgado took office on 8 May 2026.

— Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and a services-led economy. President Laura Fernández Delgado took office on 8 May 2026. The system — taxation is territorial. Article 1 of the income tax law, Ley 7092 of 21 April 1988, reaches income from a Costa Rican source, which it defines as services rendered, goods located or capital used in the national territory. Nothing else is caught.

— taxation is territorial. Article 1 of the income tax law, Ley 7092 of 21 April 1988, reaches income from a Costa Rican source, which it defines as services rendered, goods located or capital used in the national territory. Nothing else is caught. What matters now — the 183-day test lives in the regulation rather than the statute, at Article 10 of Decreto 43198-H, and the statute itself delegates the point. Becoming tax resident changes very little for someone whose income is all foreign.

Becoming tax resident changes very little for someone whose income is all foreign. What happened — this guide sets out, as of September 2026, how fiscal residency is determined, what falls inside and outside the tax, and what is only proposed.

— this guide sets out, as of September 2026, how fiscal residency is determined, what falls inside and outside the tax, and what is only proposed. The numbers — more than 183 days in the fiscal period makes you resident, with absences under 30 consecutive days still counted. Costa Rican capital income is taxed at 15%, with a one-off 2.25% option on assets held since before July 2019.

— more than 183 days in the fiscal period makes you resident, with absences under 30 consecutive days still counted. Costa Rican capital income is taxed at 15%, with a one-off 2.25% option on assets held since before July 2019. What it means for you — a foreign pension, a foreign salary for work done abroad and foreign dividends are outside Costa Rican income tax. Your home country may still tax them, and there is no double taxation treaty with the United States.

— a foreign pension, a foreign salary for work done abroad and foreign dividends are outside Costa Rican income tax. Your home country may still tax them, and there is no double taxation treaty with the United States. Still open — a bill filed on 20 August 2026, expediente 25.734, would tax foreign passive income linked to Costa Rican elements. It is awaiting committee assignment and is not law.

Costa Rica taxes what happens inside Costa Rica. That one idea answers most of the questions foreigners ask about their tax bill here, and most guides get it wrong.

Costa Rica tax residency sounds like the decisive question, and for most new arrivals it is not. The country taxes income by its source, not by the taxpayer’s passport or address. Crossing the 183-day line makes you a fiscal resident; it does not pull your foreign pension, foreign salary or foreign dividends into the Costa Rican tax net. What follows is where the rules actually live.

Fiscal residency is certified by the Dirección General de Tributación. Photo: Emabcr, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Where Costa Rica tax residency is actually defined

Article 1 of Ley 7092, the income tax law of 21 April 1988, reaches Costa Rican source income received or accrued by people and companies domiciled in the country. Then it does something unusual. It delegates the meaning of domicile to the regulation.

So the famous 183-day test is not in the statute at all. It sits in the Reglamento. The concept was rewritten to match the international fiscal residency standard by Decreto Ejecutivo 41274-H, published on 24 October 2018.

Under the current Reglamento, Decreto 43198-H, the rule is at Article 10, numeral 1(a). You are fiscally resident if you stay in the country for more than 183 days in the fiscal period, continuously or not, counting the days of entry and exit.

Counting the days, and getting the certificate

Two refinements decide most real cases. A sporadic absence of fewer than 30 consecutive calendar days still counts toward your 183 days. A long weekend in Panama resets nothing.

An absence of more than 30 continuous days does not count, unless you can prove fiscal residency somewhere else. For taxes whose period is not annual, the authority examines the 12 months before the tax fell due.

The certificate of fiscal residency is issued by the Dirección General de Tributación under Resolución DGT-R-65-2018, as later amended. You will need it whenever another country asks where you are resident.

What is taxed, and what is not

Article 1 defines Costa Rican source income in three geographic limbs: services rendered, goods located, or capital used in the national territory. Article 2 makes nationality, domicile and place of incorporation irrelevant to who pays. Only the source counts.

Taxed: a salary for work performed in Costa Rica. Also profits of a business operating here, rent from Costa Rican property, and interest on capital lent and used here. Gains on the sale of Costa Rican assets are caught as well. Note one trap. A freelancer’s fees for services physically performed in Costa Rica are Costa Rican source, even when the client sits abroad.

Not taxed: a foreign salary for work performed abroad. Nor dividends from a foreign company, interest on a foreign bank account, or rent from a house in Florida. Gains on foreign shares and a foreign pension, state or private, stay outside the tax.

Costa Rican capital income has had its own rates since 1 July 2019, under Ley 9635. The general rate is 15%, covering capital gains, rental income, dividends and most movable capital. On rent it falls on 85% of the gross after a fixed 15% expense deduction, an effective 12.75%. Real-estate funds deduct 20% instead, an effective 12%. A one-off option of 2.25% applies to the first sale of an asset acquired before July 2019. A non-resident selling property to a resident taxpayer faces a 2.5% withholding.

The EU list, and what Ley 10381 really changed

On 14 February 2023 the Council of the European Union placed Costa Rica on Annex I, its list of non-cooperative jurisdictions. The stated reason was a commitment the country had not fulfilled on the harmful aspects of its foreign source income exemption regime.

Costa Rica answered with Ley 10381, published in La Gaceta 180 on 2 October 2023. The Council moved the country off Annex I on 17 October 2023 and onto Annex II, the grey list. It left Annex II on 18 February 2025, and in 2026 appears on neither list.

The politics were close. Then-president Chaves vetoed the law, preferring a rule that taxed foreign income where an economic link to Costa Rica existed. The Assembly overrode the veto by 38 votes to 15.

What the law did is narrower than most guides suggest. It did not introduce worldwide taxation. It made foreign source passive income — dividends, interest, royalties and capital gains — taxable only for an entidad no calificada. That means a member of a multinational group that cannot show real substance here: premises, qualified staff and decisions taken in the country. An ordinary resident individual and a purely domestic company stay outside it.

The bill that would change the rules

On 20 August 2026 the Frente Amplio filed bill 25.734. It would amend the income tax law to tax foreign passive income: dividends, interest, royalties and capital gains. The tax would bite where that income derives from services, goods or capital used in Costa Rica.

It would also reach later income generated from those same elements, earned inside the country or outside it. Colon figures here use the Banco Central reference rate for 22 September 2026, ¢450 (about US$1) to the dollar. The bill’s justification cites 36 administrative determinations on extraterritorial income, with Delfino reporting some ¢36,943.6 million (about US$82 million) of tax at stake.

That figure is reported rather than official, and its phrasing is ambiguous, so treat the magnitude with care. The status matters more. The bill is awaiting committee assignment. It is not law, and none of it applies today.

What a retiree on a foreign pension owes

On the pension itself, no Costa Rican income tax. A pension paid from abroad, for work done abroad, has no Costa Rican source under Article 1 of Ley 7092. Becoming a fiscal resident does not change that.

The real bill is the Caja, the public social insurance fund, and it is not a tax. Unbroken affiliation is a condition of renewing a residency card under Articles 78 and 80 of the immigration law, Ley 8764. A retiree with no local income joins as a voluntary insured person. Figures commonly cited for a couple are around US$115 a month combined, which is indicative rather than official.

Then come the local items. Income tax applies to anything generated here, including 15% on rent from a Costa Rican property. The 15% is charged on 85% of the gross rent after the fixed expense allowance, an effective 12.75%. Property tax runs at 0.25% of registered value, with a separate solidarity tax on high-value homes. Value added tax of 13% sits on what you buy.

Finally, your own country. The United States taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, and Costa Rica has no double taxation treaty with it. The Costa Rican treaty network is thin, with Spain and Germany the main partners, though the full current list was not verified for this guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does becoming tax resident mean my foreign income is taxed here? No. Costa Rica taxes income from Costa Rican sources, defined in Article 1 of Ley 7092 as services rendered, goods located or capital used in the territory. Fiscal residency changes very little for a person whose income is entirely foreign. How are the 183 days counted? They need not be consecutive, and the days of entry and exit both count. An absence of fewer than 30 consecutive days still counts toward the total, while a longer absence drops out unless you can prove fiscal residency in another country. Did Ley 10381 end the territorial system? No. It created a narrow regime for foreign source passive income earned by entities in multinational groups that cannot show real substance in Costa Rica. Individuals and purely domestic companies remain outside it, and the source test in Article 1 is unchanged. Is Costa Rica still on an EU tax list? No. It was added to Annex I in February 2023, moved to Annex II that October, and removed from Annex II on 18 February 2025. In 2026 it appears on neither list.

World.title: Costa Rica Work Visa 2026: The Employer-Sponsored Route Explained
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and an economy led by services, tourism, medical devices and agriculture. Every lawful job here runs through the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social, the public social insurance fund.

— Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and an economy led by services, tourism, medical devices and agriculture. Every lawful job here runs through the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social, the public social insurance fund. How work is authorised — there is no single document called a work permit. Article 80 of the immigration law, Ley 8764, lets a temporary resident carry out only the paid activities the immigration authority, the DGME, has authorised, so each foreign hire is cleared for one job with one employer.

— there is no single document called a work permit. Article 80 of the immigration law, Ley 8764, lets a temporary resident carry out only the paid activities the immigration authority, the DGME, has authorised, so each foreign hire is cleared for one job with one employer. What matters now — the rule that an employer must keep 90% Costa Rican staff and pay them 85% of the wage bill has not existed since 29 January 1999. The Sala Constitucional annulled Article 13 of the Labour Code that day in vote 616-99.

— the rule that an employer must keep 90% Costa Rican staff and pay them 85% of the wage bill has not existed since 29 January 1999. The Sala Constitucional annulled Article 13 of the Labour Code that day in vote 616-99. What happened — this guide records, as of September 2026, which categories exist, what the employer files, what the government charges and what happens when the job ends.

— this guide records, as of September 2026, which categories exist, what the employer files, what the government charges and what happens when the job ends. The numbers — the 2026 salario base, the unit used for fines, is ¢462,200 (about US$1,027). Hiring a foreigner who is not authorised for the work costs two to twelve of them, ¢924,400 (about US$2,054) to ¢5,546,400 (about US$12,325). A change of migratory category costs US$200.

— the 2026 salario base, the unit used for fines, is ¢462,200 (about US$1,027). Hiring a foreigner who is not authorised for the work costs two to twelve of them, ¢924,400 (about US$2,054) to ¢5,546,400 (about US$12,325). A change of migratory category costs US$200. What it means for you — your permit names your employer, so resigning removes its basis. There is a change-of-employer procedure at the DGME, and no extra government charge for it.

— your permit names your employer, so resigning removes its basis. There is a change-of-employer procedure at the DGME, and no extra government charge for it. Still open — the DGME website could not be opened during the research for this guide. The current fee sheet, the price of the DIMEX card, the employer guarantee deposit and today’s processing times should be confirmed directly with the authority.

Costa Rica does not issue a general licence to work. It authorises one person, for one job, with one employer, and everything else follows from that.

A Costa Rica work visa is not a document you carry from job to job. It is a permission attached to a named post at a named company, and most of the file is your employer’s to assemble, not yours. That single fact explains the paperwork, the salary floor, the waiting time and what happens on the day you resign.

The employer assembles most of the file, not the worker. Photo: "San Jose Costa Rica Skyline, December 2023" by Spicypepper999, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

How a Costa Rica work visa is actually granted

There is no single document called a permiso de trabajo. Work authorisation is spread across categories in the immigration law, Ley 8764, and each one is granted for a named job.

Article 80 is the reason. A temporary resident may carry out only the paid activities that the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería, the DGME, authorises. The authorisation is the permit. Change the job and you change what was authorised.

Colon amounts in this guide use the Banco Central reference rate for 22 September 2026, ¢450 (about US$1) to the dollar.

The categories, and the one most people use

Article 79(3) covers executives, representatives, managers and technical staff of companies established in the country, plus specialised employees the DGME considers necessary. Spouses and children are included. The grant runs for more than 90 days and up to two years, renewable for equal periods.

Article 79(5) covers scientists, professionals, interns and specialised technicians. Article 100 creates the trabajador de ocupación específica, the workhorse category for ordinary employment, used where the labour ministry, the MTSS, recommends the occupation. It also covers transfers within a corporate group and after-sales staff.

Article 99 covers temporary and seasonal work, limited to the terms, zones and employers the DGME authorises. The MTSS fixes quotas by activity, called contingentes, on the basis of technical studies. Cross-border workers from neighbouring states have separate rules from Article 102 onward.

Companies that hire foreign staff regularly may register with the DGME under Decreto 36576-G-COMEX, which streamlines the handling of their personnel files.

What your employer has to prove

Expect a company registration certificate, the personería jurídica, issued no more than a month earlier. Add proof of being current on taxes and municipal charges, and proof of registration and payment with the Caja.

There must be a formal job offer stating the position, functions, hours and salary. Article 83 sets a floor for the Article 79(3) group. Executives, representatives, managers and technical staff must be paid at least the legal minimum wage for that post, increased by 25%.

In practice the DGME also wants to see why a Costa Rican could not fill the role. Under Articles 99 and 100 the MTSS opinion is the gate through which the file passes.

The duties do not stop at hiring. Article 175 bars giving work to a foreigner who is irregular, or who is legally in the country but not authorised for that activity. Article 176 requires the employer to check status and demand the document. Article 177 punishes the breach with two to twelve salarios base, from ¢924,400 (about US$2,054) to ¢5,546,400 (about US$12,325). Article 178 adds that paying the fine cancels neither wages owed nor social security duties.

The 90% payroll rule that no longer exists

Almost every English-language guide repeats it: an employer must keep 90% Costa Rican staff and pay them 85% of the wage bill. That rule was Article 13 of the Labour Code, Ley 2 of 1943. The Sala Constitucional annulled it in vote 616-99 on 29 January 1999.

The labour ministry’s own consolidated text of the code now carries a single line at Article 13, recording the annulment. The court held that the right to work belongs to everyone, and that a numerical nationality quota had no objective basis in capacity or aptitude. The ruling left the immigration rules untouched.

What survives is Article 68 of the Constitution: in equal conditions, the Costa Rican worker is preferred. That is a soft preference, not a ratio anyone can calculate. The real constraint is migratory and applies post by post.

One curiosity. Article 41 of the Labour Code is alive and bars contracting Costa Rican workers for services abroad without MTSS permission. It is the mirror image of the annulled rule, and the two are often confused.

Which jobs are closed to foreigners

There is no consolidated official list, and the lists circulating in expat guides are not sourced to law. Treat any such list with suspicion until you have checked the relevant professional body yourself.

The clearest verified restriction is the notarial profession. Under the Código Notarial, Ley 7764, a notary must have belonged to the Colegio de Abogados de Costa Rica for at least two years. They must also hold fixed residence here, keep an office open to the public and write correct Spanish. Foreigners who meet those conditions may practise only where their own country grants Costa Rican notaries the same benefit.

For most regulated fields the practical barrier is different. It is incorporation into a colegio profesional, which requires recognition of foreign degrees and, for some bodies, residency. Public and elected office are reserved to citizens.

Fees, timing and leaving the job

Ley 8764 sets the government charges itself. Article 33 requires US$25 to the migration social fund on the grant of status and on each renewal, plus US$5 a year for non-resident and special categories. An irregular stay costs US$100 for every month.

A change of category costs US$200 under Articles 89, 95 and 125, and a tourist extension costs US$100. Procedural charges are minor: ¢125 (about US$0.28) plus ¢2.50 (about US$0.01) per page in especies fiscales. The DGME states that the service itself is free.

Three to six months is the range commonly quoted for work files, and backlogs stretch it. Renewal requires unbroken Caja affiliation from the moment residency was granted, under the final paragraph of Article 80.

Resigning ends the basis of the permit, because Article 101 ties the authorisation to the employer named in it. The change-of-employer procedure asks for a written request, an authenticated job offer and the new employer’s solvency and corporate papers. No extra government charge applies. If nothing is arranged within the validity of your category, you must change category or leave the country.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a quota on foreign workers in Costa Rica? No. The 90% staff and 85% payroll rule was Article 13 of the Labour Code, and the Sala Constitucional annulled it in January 1999. What remains is the constitutional preference for the Costa Rican worker in equal conditions, plus authorisation granted post by post. How long does a work permit take? Three to six months is the range commonly quoted for work files, and backlogs make it longer. The temporary residence itself is granted for more than 90 days and up to two years, renewable for equal periods. What happens if I quit or lose the job? The authorisation names your employer, so the job and the permit stand or fall together. The DGME runs a change-of-employer procedure with no additional government charge, but if nothing is arranged within the validity of your category you must change category or leave. Can my employer be fined over my papers? Yes, under Article 177 of Ley 8764. Giving work to a foreigner who is not authorised for it, or for work other than the work authorised, carries a fine of two to twelve salarios base. At the 2026 figure that is ¢924,400 (about US$2,054) to ¢5,546,400 (about US$12,325).

World.title: Freelancing in Costa Rica: What Foreigners May Legally Do in 2026
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and an economy built on services, tourism and exports. Almost everyone who earns money here pays into one public social insurance fund, the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social.

— Costa Rica is a Central American democracy of about five million people, with no army and an economy built on services, tourism and exports. Almost everyone who earns money here pays into one public social insurance fund, the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social. The rule behind everything — Article 80 of the immigration law, Ley 8764 of 19 August 2009, says temporary residents may carry out only the paid activities that the immigration authority, the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería or DGME, expressly authorises. That covers own-account work and salaried work alike.

— Article 80 of the immigration law, Ley 8764 of 19 August 2009, says temporary residents may carry out only the paid activities that the immigration authority, the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería or DGME, expressly authorises. That covers own-account work and salaried work alike. What matters now — electronic invoicing in version 4.4 has been compulsory since 1 September 2025, and tax registration has moved to the TRIBU-CR platform. An unregistered freelancer is easier for the tax authority to spot than at any point before.

— electronic invoicing in version 4.4 has been compulsory since 1 September 2025, and tax registration has moved to the TRIBU-CR platform. An unregistered freelancer is easier for the tax authority to spot than at any point before. What happened — this guide sets out, as of September 2026, who may lawfully freelance here, what you register, what you pay, and what the remote-worker permit does not allow.

— this guide sets out, as of September 2026, who may lawfully freelance here, what you register, what you pay, and what the remote-worker permit does not allow. The numbers — the 2026 salario base, the reference unit used for tax fines, is ¢462,200 (about US$1,027). Failing to register with Tributación, the tax administration, costs half of that per month: ¢231,100 (about US$514), capped at ¢1,386,600 (about US$3,081).

— the 2026 salario base, the reference unit used for tax fines, is ¢462,200 (about US$1,027). Failing to register with Tributación, the tax administration, costs half of that per month: ¢231,100 (about US$514), capped at ¢1,386,600 (about US$3,081). What it means for you — check your migratory category before you take a single client. If the DGME has not authorised own-account work, no amount of tax and Caja compliance makes that work lawful.

— check your migratory category before you take a single client. If the DGME has not authorised own-account work, no amount of tax and Caja compliance makes that work lawful. Still open — the 2026 contribution bands used here, 7.05% to 19.11%, come from Costa Rican tax practitioners. No CCSS publication of the January 2026 scale could be located for this guide, and the last full Caja table is dated January 2025.

The paperwork is the easy part. The question that decides whether you may freelance here at all is written into one paragraph of the immigration law.

Freelancing in Costa Rica is not one decision. It is two, and most guides answer only the second. The first question is migratory: does your residency category let you work on your own account at all? The second is administrative: how you register, invoice and pay. Get the order wrong and you can be perfectly tax-compliant and still working illegally.

The tax authority and the Caja both sit in San José, and both must be registered with. Photo: "San José Costa Rica aerea" by IgnacioAFQ, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.

What Article 80 means for freelancing in Costa Rica

The controlling rule is Article 80 of the Ley General de Migración y Extranjería, Ley 8764. Temporary residents may carry out only the remunerated or profit-making activities that the DGME authorises. The article names both kinds in the same breath: work on your own account, and work for an employer.

Read that twice, because it is narrow. A residence permit is not general permission to earn. It authorises named activities, and the DGME decides, after advisory opinions from the labour ministry, the MTSS.

So a pensionado permit, granted because you draw a foreign pension, authorises you to receive that pension. It does not by itself let you invoice Costa Rican clients. The same holds for the rentista and inversionista categories. This is the single most common error in English-language guides.

Who may work on their own account

Permanent residents and Costa Rican citizens may freelance freely. Permanent residency is libre de condición, meaning it carries no restriction on the kind of work you do. Articles 77 and 78 of Ley 8764 set out that category.

Temporary residents need the activity authorised. There is a specific door for this. The second paragraph of Article 100 creates a class called trabajadores de ocupación específica. It expressly includes own-account workers, a status the DGME grants on the basis of national labour needs. It is discretionary, not automatic.

Tourists may not freelance for Costa Rican clients. Article 100 also defines the visitante de negocios, a business visitor limited to buying and selling goods or services, negotiating contracts and attending business activities. Even that visitor must comply with Costa Rican tax law on the activity.

Registering with the Caja as a trabajador independiente

If you may work on your own account, the Caja comes next. Its Reglamento del Trabajador Independiente defines the status in Article 1: a person who habitually, personally and directly runs an economic activity for profit, with no employment contract.

Affiliation is compulsory under Article 1, which rests on article 3 of the Ley Constitutiva de la CCSS. It covers health cover, known as SEM, and the pension scheme, known as IVM. Holding a salaried job does not exempt you. Someone who is employed and also freelances contributes in both capacities. Article 4 gives you eight business days from starting the activity to register.

Article 10 sets your contribution base on net income, meaning gross income less the necessary and reasonable costs of the activity. Where you cannot document that figure, the Caja builds a base presunta from your tax return, minimum wages and other evidence. Article 8 is something else: the requirements for de-registration. In your first year the Caja uses a reference salary fixed by its board. You may revise the base by declaring real income, but no more often than quarterly. Article 6 exempts the self-employed from the employer quota, and Article 12 allows appeals to the Tribunal Fiscal Administrativo.

How much? The last scale the Caja published in full is dated January 2025, and on it the top band is 10.69% for health plus 8.26% for pensions. A 2026 scale is in force from 1 January, with bands of 7.05%, 9.98%, 13.77%, 16% and 19.11% of assessed net income. Those 2026 percentages are as set out by Costa Rican tax practitioners, not from a CCSS document located for this guide. The Caja has not lodged the table in SINALEVI, where the most recent full table dates from 2018. Ask the Caja for your own band.

Tax registration, invoices and IVA

Tax registration is separate from the Caja. You enter the Registro Único Tributario through TRIBU-CR, the online platform that replaced the old ATV system. The form is still styled D-140. You have 10 business days from starting the activity.

You need a Costa Rican tax identity to do it. Residents use their DIMEX, the foreigner identity card issued by the DGME. Anyone without a cédula or DIMEX needs a NITE, a special tax identification number issued against a passport.

Electronic invoicing is compulsory for every taxpayer in the general regime, freelancers included. Version 4.4 has been mandatory since 1 September 2025, under resolution MH-DGT-RES-0027-2024. Not issuing invoices costs two salarios base, ¢924,400 (about US$2,054), and repeat offences can close your premises for five business days.

Professional and freelance services carry value added tax, IVA, at 13%. You declare it monthly on the D-104 return, also filed in TRIBU-CR.

What you pay in income tax

The 2026 rates come from Decreto Ejecutivo 45333-H, published in La Gaceta 229 on 5 December 2025. The fiscal year is now the calendar year. Brackets were trimmed by 0.38% to track consumer prices, so they fell slightly.

Colon amounts here use the Banco Central reference rate for 22 September 2026, ¢450 (about US$1) to the dollar. Self-employed people pay nothing on the first ¢6,244,000 (about US$13,876) of annual net income. Above that the rate is 10%, then 15% from ¢8,329,000 (about US$18,509), then 20% from ¢10,414,000 (about US$23,142), and 25% above ¢20,872,000 (about US$46,382).

Family credits are small: ¢20,520 (about US$46) a year per child and ¢31,080 (about US$69) per spouse. One warning on sources. PwC’s worldwide tax summary page for Costa Rica, reviewed in June 2026, still shows older brackets that are not the 2026 figures.

The remote-worker permit is not a freelance licence

Ley 10008 created a remote-worker stay in 2021, with a regulation published on 8 July 2022. It grants one year, extendable by one more, to people earning at least US$3,000 a month, or US$4,000 where dependants are included. The income must originate abroad.

The status exempts that foreign income from Costa Rican income tax and allows duty-free import of basic telework equipment. Renewal asks for at least 80 days of physical presence in the first period, and fees of US$90 cover the stay document, certification and the social fund contribution. Private medical cover is required, because there is no Caja affiliation on this status.

What it does not do matters more. It is an estancia, a special stay, not residency. You may not work for a Costa Rican employer or sell services into the local market, and the time does not count toward permanent residency or naturalisation. You may not register as a trabajador independiente for Costa Rican clients on this permit alone.

A local client who pays you anyway is exposed. Article 177 of Ley 8764 fines anyone who gives work to a foreigner not authorised for it. The range is two to twelve salarios base: ¢924,400 (about US$2,054) to ¢5,546,400 (about US$12,325).

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I freelance on a pensionado or rentista permit? Not automatically. Those categories authorise you to receive the qualifying foreign income, and Article 80 of Ley 8764 limits a temporary resident to the paid activities the DGME has authorised. Ask the DGME to authorise own-account work before you invoice anyone. Do I pay the Caja if I already have a salaried job here? Yes. Article 1 of the Reglamento del Trabajador Independiente makes affiliation compulsory for the self-employed. Being a salaried employee does not exempt you, so a person who is both employed and freelancing contributes in both capacities. How fast do I have to register after starting work? Two clocks run at once. The Caja allows eight business days from the start of the activity, and Tributación allows 10 business days for the Registro Único Tributario. Missing the tax deadline costs ¢231,100 (about US$514) a month, capped at ¢1,386,600 (about US$3,081). Can a digital nomad take on Costa Rican clients? No. The Ley 10008 status covers services provided to people and companies located abroad. Selling into the Costa Rican market is a different activity that needs a different migratory category, and the local payer risks a fine under Article 177.

World.title: Shopping and Daily Life in Costa Rica: Ferias, IVA and SINPE
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica is a Central American republic of about five million people with a formal, well-stocked retail sector. Almost everything is available somewhere, and almost everything imported costs more than it did at home.

— Costa Rica is a Central American republic of about five million people with a formal, well-stocked retail sector. Almost everything is available somewhere, and almost everything imported costs more than it did at home. The system — three things govern daily spending here. A supermarket ladder that runs from bare warehouse discounters to one premium chain, a network of farmers’ markets regulated by law, and a 13 percent value-added tax called IVA that is already inside every shelf price.

— three things govern daily spending here. A supermarket ladder that runs from bare warehouse discounters to one premium chain, a network of farmers’ markets regulated by law, and a 13 percent value-added tax called IVA that is already inside every shelf price. What matters now — the central bank capped text-message payments on SINPE Móvil, the national phone-number transfer system, at ¢100,000 (about US$222) a day in August 2025. App transfers keep the higher bank limits.

— the central bank capped text-message payments on SINPE Móvil, the national phone-number transfer system, at ¢100,000 (about US$222) a day in August 2025. App transfers keep the higher bank limits. What happened — this guide sets out prices, store counts and payment rules as they stood in September 2026.

— this guide sets out prices, store counts and payment rules as they stood in September 2026. The numbers — Walmart ran 347 stores in March 2026, Megasuper 85, Auto Mercado 24 and PriceSmart 10. A plate lunch costs about ¢5,500 (about US$12.22). Average household income was ¢1,209,825 (about US$2,689) a month in the 2025 household survey.

— Walmart ran 347 stores in March 2026, Megasuper 85, Auto Mercado 24 and PriceSmart 10. A plate lunch costs about ¢5,500 (about US$12.22). Average household income was ¢1,209,825 (about US$2,689) a month in the 2025 household survey. What it means for you — buy local and fresh and you do well. Buy imported and processed and the gap widens every year. Local bananas cost ¢732 (about US$1.63) a kilo, imported apples ¢2,332 (about US$5.18).

— buy local and fresh and you do well. Buy imported and processed and the gap widens every year. Local bananas cost ¢732 (about US$1.63) a kilo, imported apples ¢2,332 (about US$5.18). Still open — no current official supermarket basket comparison could be retrieved, the statutory split of the reduced IVA rates could not be checked, and no specific import duty on consumer electronics could be found.

The cheapest thing in the shop is grown here. The most expensive thing was flown here. Everything else follows from that.

Shopping and daily life in Costa Rica run on three rails. There is a supermarket ladder with a real spread top to bottom, a farmers’ market on Saturday morning, and a phone-number payment system most newcomers cannot use yet. Learn all three and your monthly spend drops. Colón figures here convert at ¢450 (about US$1), the Banco Central reference rate on 22 September 2026.

Ferias del agricultor run between Thursday and Sunday, with Saturday the main day.

What shopping and daily life in Costa Rica costs each week

The best current figures are crowdsourced rather than official, and should be read as indicative. Numbeo’s San José page was updated on 11 September 2026, from 546 entries by 38 contributors. It puts a litre of milk at ¢1,080 (about US$2.40) and a dozen eggs at ¢1,595 (about US$3.54). A kilo of rice is ¢1,122 (about US$2.49) and a kilo of chicken breast ¢4,744 (about US$10.54).

Two rows tell the whole story. Local bananas cost ¢732 (about US$1.63) a kilo. Imported apples cost ¢2,332 (about US$5.18). A casado, the standard plate lunch of rice, beans, salad and a protein, runs about ¢5,500 (about US$12.22). Basic utilities for an 85 square metre flat come to ¢43,183 (about US$95.96) a month.

Read that against local earnings, not against a salary at home. The statistics institute put average monthly household income at ¢1,209,825 (about US$2,689) in its 2025 household survey. Food inflation has been the pressure point: food and soft drinks rose 14.6 percent between December 2020 and September 2025, against general inflation of 8.2 percent. Coffee rose 91.7 percent over five years, while leafy greens and citrus fell.

The supermarket ladder, cheapest to dearest

Two naming corrections first: Auto Mercado and Automercado are the same chain, and Megasuper is one word. Now the ladder. Maxi Palí, Walmart’s warehouse discounter, is the cheapest formal option with 61 stores. Palí, the small hard-discount format, is the most numerous shop in the country with 233 branches.

Above them sit the Walmart supercentres, dearer per item but far broader in catalogue, and Más x Menos, the urban mid-market banner. Walmart Costa Rica counted 347 stores on 15 March 2026 under a US$600 million investment plan. Megasuper, independently owned, had 85 stores across all seven provinces in May 2026 and is often the best option outside the Central Valley.

Auto Mercado is the premium end, with 24 stores, the best fresh produce and the deepest imported range. PriceSmart is a membership warehouse club with 10 clubs as of August 2026 and an eleventh being built. Membership is roughly ¢20,500 (about US$45) a year and compulsory to enter, though that figure comes from a price-comparison app rather than from PriceSmart itself.

The official price tool is MimejorcompraCR, run by the economy ministry, and it works interactively only. Ignore the two basket comparisons that dominate search results. One is from 2012 and the other from 2022.

Ferias del agricultor, and the directory that died

The feria del agricultor is the farmers’ market, and there were 80 registered nationally as of 2023. They run between Thursday and Sunday, with Saturday morning the main day in most towns. Go early. The good produce is gone by mid-morning, and the last hour brings discounts on what is left.

The model is what makes it cheap. Only small and medium producers may sell, cutting out the middleman, which is why the feria beats the supermarket on anything grown locally. The system dates from the late 1970s and is governed by Ley 8533, which also bans unauthorised use of the name.

One warning. The national directory at deferia.cr, launched in October 2024 to list all 80 markets with hours and prices, no longer works. It now redirects to an unrelated foreign site, yet expat guides still name it as the way to find your feria. Use your municipality’s website instead, or ask a neighbour.

SINPE Móvil, and why you may not get it yet

SINPE Móvil is run by the Banco Central de Costa Rica and sends money to a phone number. It is how Costa Ricans pay market vendors, taxi drivers, gardeners, hairdressers and small shops. Many businesses display a phone number where you would expect a card terminal.

On 6 August 2025 the central bank board capped transfers started by text message. The ceiling is now ¢100,000 (about US$222) a day, down from as much as ¢500,000 (about US$1,111) at some banks. The reason was fraud, since text messages lack strong authentication. Transfers made in a bank app or through online banking keep the higher limits. Use the app, not SMS.

The real friction is getting in at all. SINPE Móvil needs a Costa Rican bank account, and at most banks that needs a DIMEX, the identity card issued to legal residents. A newcomer on a tourist entry is locked out of the country’s default payment rail for months and will be reaching for cash.

Bills work three ways: through your bank app under pago de servicios, in cash at a supermarket till, or by direct debit. The electricity company also offers a virtual agency, an app and email invoicing. The marchamo, the annual vehicle circulation tax, is paid the same way.

The 13 percent IVA, and what is genuinely expensive

IVA is the value-added tax. The general rate is 13 percent, with reduced rates of 4, 2 and 1 percent for things like private healthcare, medicines and the basic food basket. It replaced the old sales tax on 1 July 2019. Shelf prices already include it, so what you see is what you pay.

Restaurants are the exception. They add 13 percent IVA and a legally required 10 percent service charge, so a ¢5,500 (about US$12.22) menu price lands at roughly ¢6,765 (about US$15.03) on the bill. The 10 percent is the tip, and anything further is optional. One caveat: the statutory split of the reduced rates could not be checked against the law itself, because the government legal database refused access.

Now the correction most guides get wrong. Imported goods are not expensive here because of punitive tariffs. Under the CAFTA-DR trade agreement, all United States consumer and industrial goods have entered duty-free since 1 January 2015. What you pay above the home price is freight, the 13 percent IVA and retail margin.

Cars are the genuine exception. Selective consumption tax on vehicles runs 30 to 50 percent on top, which is why Costa Ricans keep cars running for twenty years. The composite used-car figures circulating online could not be confirmed from any government source, so price a specific vehicle through the treasury’s AutoValor tool. No specific electronics duty was found either.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which supermarket is cheapest in Costa Rica? Maxi Palí wins most direct price comparisons, and Palí is the small-format version of the same discount model. Auto Mercado sits at the other end with the best produce and the highest prices. No current official basket comparison could be retrieved to confirm the ranking. Can I use SINPE Móvil as a tourist? In practice no. SINPE Móvil requires a Costa Rican bank account, and most banks require a DIMEX residency card to open one. Plan on cash and cards until your residency comes through. When are the farmers markets held? Ferias run between Thursday and Sunday, and Saturday morning is the main day in most towns. Go early for quality and late for discounts. The national online directory no longer works, so check your municipality’s website. Is there a tip on top of the bill in restaurants? A 10 percent service charge is legally required and already appears on the bill, alongside 13 percent IVA. That service charge is the tip. Anything extra is entirely optional.

World.title: Expat Communities in Costa Rica: Where They Are and How to Join
World.content:
Guides · Costa Rica

Key Facts The country — Costa Rica had 5,044,197 people in the national statistics institute’s 2022 estimate. Foreigners are not spread evenly across it. They concentrate in perhaps twenty towns, and in several of those they are a visible share of the population.

— Costa Rica had 5,044,197 people in the national statistics institute’s 2022 estimate. Foreigners are not spread evenly across it. They concentrate in perhaps twenty towns, and in several of those they are a visible share of the population. The background — there is no current official count of United States, Canadian or European residents. The 2022 census was replaced by a population estimate that carries no country-of-birth breakdown, so the last full nativity data is the 2011 census.

— there is no current official count of United States, Canadian or European residents. The 2022 census was replaced by a population estimate that carries no country-of-birth breakdown, so the last full nativity data is the 2011 census. What matters now — the national conversation about foreigners is contested. Delfino reported in January 2025 that nearly nine in ten Costa Ricans believe foreigners are gentrifying the coastal zones, and the coverage since has been sharper still.

— the national conversation about foreigners is contested. Delfino reported in January 2025 that nearly nine in ten Costa Ricans believe foreigners are gentrifying the coastal zones, and the coverage since has been sharper still. What happened — this guide records the clusters, the organised groups and their published fees as they stood in September 2026.

— this guide records the clusters, the organised groups and their published fees as they stood in September 2026. The numbers — ARCR, the residents’ association, charges US$75 a year plus 13 percent value-added tax. AmCham, the American chamber of commerce, charges individuals ¢274,215 (about US$609) a year plus a one-off ¢88,375 (about US$196) joining fee.

— ARCR, the residents’ association, charges US$75 a year plus 13 percent value-added tax. AmCham, the American chamber of commerce, charges individuals ¢274,215 (about US$609) a year plus a one-off ¢88,375 (about US$196) joining fee. What it means for you — the organised foreign circuit will solve your first month and will not give you Costa Rican friends. Those come from Spanish, from where you choose to live, and from paying local people properly.

— the organised foreign circuit will solve your first month and will not give you Costa Rican friends. Those come from Spanish, from where you choose to live, and from paying local people properly. Still open — no Facebook group member count could be verified, several clubs are known only from a listing published in 2018, and the Women’s Club publishes neither a fee nor a meeting schedule.

Nobody can tell you how many Americans live in Costa Rica. Everybody can tell you which towns they live in.

Expat communities in Costa Rica are far easier to join than to measure. No official body knows how many Americans, Canadians or Europeans live here, because the last usable count is fifteen years old. What does exist is a reliable map of the towns where foreigners gather. There is also a short list of clubs with published fees, and an honest account of what none of it buys you.

Puerto Viejo draws a younger and more European crowd than the Pacific beach towns.
