World.title: Loneliness and social isolation cost you up to six years of healthy life
World.content:
Social isolation refers to limited contact and participation with others, while loneliness is a subjective experience of feeling disconnected from the world around them. While the two are not the same, a new study published in the journal Nature Communications has found that both are associated with fewer healthy years of life.

 

On average, loneliness and social isolation cost people around six disease-free years, taking a toll on both physical and mental health, researchers found after analysing data from over 270,000 adults between the ages of 40 and 69.

“Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy,” said lead author Lu Qi, professor at Tulane University.

The study found the associations were stronger for the loss of years free of mental disorders — depression and anxiety — than for years free of physical diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory disease, neurodegenerative disease, and cancer.

The good news is that maintaining a healthy lifestyle can mitigate the negative impact of social isolation. The bad news — it does not appear to compensate for the damage caused by loneliness.

At age 50, individuals experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived fewer years free of major chronic diseases compared with those experiencing neither.

How are men and women impacted differently?

Men and women do not suffer from loneliness and social isolation in the same way, and that is also reflected in the impact those have on their health. Because women may prioritise emotional connection, their mental health struggles are more strongly linked to loneliness, while men’s mental health shows a stronger association with social isolation.

Among women, loneliness and social isolation meant 2.4 years spent in worse physical health and 3.7 years in worse mental health, while for men it meant 1.7 years of physical disease-free life lost and 5.8 years of mental disorder-free life lost.

Males were more likely to experience both loneliness and social isolation, had a lack of social, material, and economic resources, and had a lower healthy lifestyle score.

The authors noted that this gender gap may be explained by differences in how men and women obtain support and achieve psychological well-being, with men tending to rely more on physical presence and frequent social interactions and women more on emotional support.

World.title: Qatar's emir urges talks with Iran as regional leaders demand stronger action against Israel at UN
World.content:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani told the United Nations General Assembly that the Gulf was going through "one of the most dangerous phases" in its recent history and that the Iran war was the result of cumulative years of postponing diplomatic solutions.

 

In his speech at the UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday, Sheikh Tamim called for a “regional system of collective security” based on national sovereignty, non-interference and the peaceful resolution of disputes.

Such a system could have prevented the current Iran war and without it, he warned, vital facilities could be attacked and important waterways closed.

Any lasting agreement with Tehran should protect the whole region, including Iran, Sheikh Tamim said.

“The opportunity for a peaceful diplomatic solution, which we believe is both possible and realistic, must not be missed," he added.

Underlining that Qatar is "a trusted mediator," Sheikh Tamim called for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened and warned that Gulf countries were being drawn into a war that was not theirs.

“We remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war,” the Qatari emir said.

Qatar was doing “everything in our power to address the conflict in the region through diplomatic means," he added.

On Gaza, Sheikh Tamim stated that what had happened there was “genocide in every sense of the word."

“There can be no talk of a just international order as long as Palestine remains in its plight," he said, adding that the scale of the destruction had not been matched by the international response.

He called on Israel to fully implement the ceasefire by ending military operations, withdrawing from Gaza, lifting the blockade and allowing humanitarian aid to enter without conditions.

The emir also criticised Israeli actions in Syria and Lebanon, adding that the international response would show whether international law was being applied equally.

Turkey warns against wider war

In his speech at the General Assembly, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called for freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz to be maintained and said Turkey was working with other countries to end the fighting in the Gulf.

He added that letting the war spread to neighbouring countries would help no one.

On Gaza, Erdoğan described the territory as the “most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time” and urged UN members to increase pressure on Israel.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

He also called on countries that have not recognised Palestine to reconsider their position.

During his fiery speech, the Israeli delegation left the hall.

The Turkish president also criticised Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas's absence from the General Assembly. Abbas could not attend after the US denied him a visa for the second consecutive year.

Erdoğan renewed his demand for UN Security Council reform, arguing that decisions affecting more than 190 countries should not depend on its five permanent members.

He repeated his long-standing slogan that the “world is bigger than five” and said international law should not be applied differently to strong and weak countries.

Jordan says international inaction is a choice

Jordan's King Abdullah contrasted the international response to Israel with the sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes and diplomatic isolation used in other conflicts.

When it came to Israel, he said, resolutions had repeatedly remained on paper.

He called the failure to act a political “choice” and said the problem was not a lack of available tools.

Jordan’s King Abdullah II addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura

The Hashemite kingdom's monarch accused Israel of seizing land, expanding settlements and allowing settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, and said that forced displacement constitutes a war crime.

He described Gaza and the occupied West Bank as two parts of an effort to make a viable Palestinian state impossible.

King Abdullah said decades of managing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict instead of tackling its causes had allowed temporary measures to become permanent policy.

He also warned that Israeli actions in southern Syria, including territorial expansion around water resources, posed a direct threat to Jordan’s northern border and water security.

On Iran, King Abdullah said the war was hurting trade and investment and raising energy and food bills worldwide.

World.title: Russia pounds Kyiv with drones, killing two and wounding 23 hours before Zelenskyy's UN address
World.content:
Russia hammered Ukraine's capital Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday, hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was due to address world leaders at the UN General Assembly.

 

Two people were killed and 23 were wounded in Kyiv, and palls of black smoke floated above the city following the latest in what have been daily Russian attacks that torment Ukrainian civilians.

The drones set off fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight, authorities said.

Ukrainian Railways chief Oleksandr Pertsovsky said Kyiv's rail network was "under fire" and urged "maximum" vigilance from passengers using the city's central station.

In Zaporizhzhia, in southeastern Ukraine, two men aged 37 and 39 were wounded by a strike that started a large fire at a shopping mall.

Emergency services said the fire spread across about 6,000 square meters before coming under control.

Firefighters extinguish a fire at a burning building following a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, 23 September, 2026 AP Photo

In Ukraine's southern Black Sea port of Odesa, the captain of a cargo ship was killed in a Russian attack, part of a wave of strikes from both sides on commercial vessels designed to hit export revenues.

The head of the Odesa region, Oleg Kiper, said the Ukrainian captain was in charge of the vessel, which was sailing on the Black Sea under the flag of Antigua and Barbuda.

At least 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been hit on the Black Sea since the start of the conflict, Turkey's IMEAK chamber of shipping said.

Around 70% of those attacks took place in the first eight months of this year.

Turkey, whose vessels are increasingly in the firing line, has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end strikes on civilian ships but the two foes have failed to act on it.

"The recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea are unacceptable, regardless of who is responsible," Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

International support

Zelenskyy is in New York for the annual UN gathering as part of his diplomatic effort to shore up and recruit further international support for his country’s gruelling fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump on Tuesday, who has shown impatience with the lack of progress in talks aimed at ending the war and the escalating aerial attacks by both sides this year.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, who is accused by NATO officials and European governments of sabotage, espionage and other hybrid attacks, is not scheduled to attend the General Assembly this year.

Ukraine has hit back at Russia by damaging oil refineries that are a vital pillar of the country's economy.

US President Donald Trump meets with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during the United Nations General Assembly, 22 September, 2026 AP Photo

Zelenskyy said at the start of his US visit that he had proposals to make about possible de-escalation in the war.

Urgent issues for Kyiv are halting devastating Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and ensuring Ukrainian grain can be shipped to world markets through the Black Sea despite the war.

Ukraine also needs more US-made Patriot air defence systems as a shield against Russian ballistic missiles, but Patriots are in short supply after the war in Iran began.

The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces struck Ukraine’s military-industrial and energy sector facilities, logistics centres and sea vessels overnight.

The ministry said its air defences intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

World.title: UK to review Chagos deal after Trump tells Burnham it is 'terrible'
World.content:
Britain will go back to the drawing board on its agreement to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said on Wednesday. The move comes a day after US President Donald Trump attacked the deal during his first meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

 

The two leaders met on Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. With Burnham sitting beside him, Trump said he expected the British leader to reconsider the "terrible deal". Burnham nodded and replied "yep".

Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, later told broadcasters that Britain would "work hard" to resolve the issue and that he was "confident we can find it working with our US partners".

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting said Trump's objections were "not news to us". But he said the president's latest remarks "provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing".

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it," he said.

Streeting also confirmed that Britain would not "at this stage" make the annual payments of at least £120 million (€139 million) it had agreed to pay Mauritius to lease back the military base on Diego Garcia.

Months of US opposition

The agreement, reached last year between Starmer and the Mauritian government, would hand the Indian Ocean archipelago back to Britain's former colony. Britain would then lease the strategic US-UK base on Diego Garcia for 99 years, with the option to extend. Britain announced in April that the plans were on hold.

Trump first backed the pact but later turned against it, calling it "an act of great stupidity", and it has caused friction with his administration for months.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham met US President Donald Trump for the first time in person on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. 22 September, 2026. AP Photo

Starmer defended the agreement by arguing that international legal rulings had cast doubt on Britain's claim to the islands, and that only a deal with Mauritius could secure continued US and UK use of the base.

Britain held on to the Chagos Islands when Mauritius became independent in the 1960s. It removed thousands of islanders, who have since brought a series of compensation claims in British courts. In 2019, the International Court of Justice concluded that Britain unlawfully separated Chagos from Mauritius when ending colonial rule..

'Ostrich strategy'

James Cartlidge, defence spokesman for the opposition Conservatives, said the agreement "should be binned entirely".

Streeting rejected that approach. He told Times Radio: "The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away ... is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world."

Jack Pannell, a senior researcher at the British Foreign Policy Group think-tank, told AFP that Burnham's focus with Trump would be on "the big international issues", such as AI regulation, Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Success for Burnham means avoiding this issue becoming a millstone around his neck while he pursues his other foreign policy priorities and focuses on his domestic agenda," Pannell said. "The chances of a breakthrough on this issue are slim, and that may suit the prime minister just fine."

Also on Tuesday, Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that will allow the US to build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.

World.title: Tigray rebels seize airport and clash with federal forces as fighting in Ethiopia reignites
World.content:
Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of a key airport and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring region of Afar on Wednesday, as long-standing tensions spilt into open battle.

 

Fighting escalated "since last night in Abala and Erebti (in Afar) between TPLF and federal forces," an NGO source in the region said, requesting anonymity.

"We are expecting it to expand. We just sent a truck with food to help the people displaced," they added.

Abala lies in the mountain ranges that mark the border with Tigray. Erebti lies around 100 kilometres further into Afar.

Another humanitarian source confirmed clashes in the two locations, as did a foreign security source in Ethiopia.

A former TPLF senior official said the rebels were in control of Berhale, Erebti, Abala, Megale, Dalul and Konoba in Afar.

The federal forces are "fast-retreating", he added.

Meanwhile, local and security sources said Tigrayan forces were in control of the airport in the regional capital Mekelle.

Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to three airports in Tigray — Mekelle, Axum and Shire — "due to the current situation".

"While we were on our way to the airport for work, our supervisor called the driver and told him that the airport had been taken over by Tigray forces. Since there were no flights, he told us to return home," an employee at Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle said.

A foreign security source based in Ethiopia confirmed the information.

A small number of federal police guard the airport and their situation was unknown.

Between 2020 and 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fought a devastating war with the federal government that resulted in the deaths of some 600,000 people, according to African Union estimates.

Sporadic clashes in recent months have raised fears of a return to war.

Abiy under fire

Ethiopia faces multiple insurgencies, including in its most populous regions, Oromia and Amhara.

On Sunday, the TPLF announced it had joined a seven-group military alliance dubbed Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival aiming to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and install a transitional administration.

The alliance also includes Amhara nationalist Fano militias — who fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the last war — and the Oromo Liberation Army, an active insurgency in Ethiopia's most populous region, along with four groups from three other regions, making up half of the country's 12 regional states.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, which eventually triggered the war in 2020.

The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the war and maintained an uneasy calm until late 2025, when clashes resumed.

The federal government has since launched drone strikes in Tigray and massed troops at the regional border.

Rights groups have accused the TPLF of a campaign of forced recruitment this year as it prepares for renewed fighting.

The region has not recovered from the last war, with around 1 million people still displaced and many parts of the peace deal unfulfilled.

Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 partly for brokering a peace agreement with neighbouring Eritrea.

Good friends and neighbours

The federal government has a significant military advantage, having ramped up production of military drones since the last war.

Yet the TPLF's Tigray Defence Forces retain a significant inherited arsenal from their years at the helm of Ethiopia's military before 2018, including tanks, artillery, long-range guided rockets and ballistic missiles documented by open-source military analysts during the 2020-2022 war.

Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos said in June that TPLF hardliners had been "actively accumulating and acquiring new arms" in violation of the Pretoria Agreement.

Neighbouring countries have also been implicated in backing the rebels.

ACLED conflict monitoring group assessed earlier this year that Eritrean forces had moved troops toward western Tigray in coordination with the TDF and that Eritrea was providing weapons and hosting Tigrayan fighters.

Ethiopia's government formally accused Sudan's armed forces in May of providing "arms and financial support" to TPLF-linked forces and described Sudan as "a hub of anti-Ethiopian forces". Sudan denied the allegation.

Locked in a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, Egypt is assessed by analysts at the Soufan Center as providing diplomatic cover and logistical support to Ethiopian opposition factions, although no direct weapons transfers to the TPLF have been documented.

World.title: AI and ski to cruises and Gen Z: dnata’s CEO on the trends driving travel in the UAE and beyond
World.content:
Travel in the Middle East is evolving rapidly, with shifts in technology and consumer behaviour transforming both the industry and how people explore the region and beyond.

 

Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing how holidays are planned and sold, while ski trips, cruises and experiences are gaining popularity among Middle Eastern travellers, according to the new Group Chief Executive Officer of global aviation and travel services company dnata.

Nabil Sultan Al Murr, who took over the role in June 2026, told Euronews Travel that these changing preferences are pushing companies to adapt more quickly, while technology is influencing everything from inspiration and booking to the airport experience.

Part of the Emirates Group, Dubai-based dnata operates across several divisions in aviation and tourism, including ground handling, cargo, travel services, catering and retail.

Overseeing its businesses across 162 cities in 37 countries, Sultan says the company has been assessing opportunities in emerging markets, including the Middle East, Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Eastern Europe. But it is technology and changing traveller behaviour that could have some of the biggest impacts on how people plan and experience their holidays.

How could AI change the travel experience?

AI has quickly become one of the biggest talking points in tourism, with travellers increasingly using tools to research destinations and plan their next trip. Sultan believes new technologies also have the potential to improve the passenger experience by allowing travel companies to process information and get relevant offers in front of customers much more quickly.

“I honestly think that AI and technology will bring in huge advantages in terms of improving the whole passenger experience and being able to put out the best offers and products,” he told Euronews at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai.

One example is the thousands of hotel contracts handled by dnata. Sultan says information from these contracts was previously processed manually, meaning getting deals into the system could take months.

“Now with AI we've adapted the whole thing and of course everything happens in almost real time,” he said. “That just shows the importance of how AI actually brings in that agility and speed and improvement in the whole work process.”

Ski holidays and winter travel grow in popularity

Technology isn't the only thing changing. Where – and how – people want to holiday is evolving too. One of the most noticeable shifts dnata is seeing in the UAE is growing demand for winter travel. “People going out for skiing, which was never the trend almost four to five years ago, is becoming such a huge trend,” Sultan says.

Responding to that interest, dnata has launched a winter programme featuring around 10 ski destinations. The company is also looking beyond conventional ski holidays towards other winter experiences. Sultan gives the example of Finland and seeing the Northern Lights as the types of trips attracting interest.

“These are all new kinds of features and experiences that we're trying to bring to the traveller and actually meet their emerging demand that we continue to see,” he said.

Cruises are gaining momentum in the Middle East and Gulf Alla Rome/Unsplash

How cruises, Gen Z and food will drive the next era

Sultan expects traveller preferences to continue changing quickly over the next five years. Cruising is one area already gaining momentum in the Middle East and Gulf, he says, despite historically being a less established form of holiday in the region.

“I think the tourism and travel industry has been so dynamic and has been changing so rapidly and we've been seeing that,” Sultan said. “I think the key thing, of course, is to keep up with all of these changes and continue to introduce new elements in the whole entire experience.

“We see cruising now is becoming a huge trend. And you know that was never the case in this part of the world.”

The next major shift could come from younger travellers and how the industry adapts to their preferences. “Five years from now there's probably going to be a whole new trend, especially with the Generation Z, who probably look at different sorts of priorities in their travel experience,” he said.

Sultan points to food tourism as one example of how those priorities could change. “Food and healthy food is becoming a real trend,” he said. “So how do we bring that element into travel? It is a revolution and we're staying very close to the customer to really understand how we position our product offering.”

World.title: Norwegian diplomat behind Oslo Accords to apologise for Epstein ties in documentary
World.content:
A prominent former Norwegian diplomat, one of the architects of the Oslo Accords, will apologise for his dealings with late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in a documentary to be broadcast on Wednesday evening.

 

Terje Rod-Larsen and his wife, fellow diplomat Mona Juul, are currently under investigation in Norway. Juul for "aggravated corruption" and Rod-Larsen for "complicity in aggravated corruption."

They are both known for having played key roles in the secret Israeli-Palestinian negotiations that led to the Oslo Accords of the early 1990s.

In particular, police are investigating a loan given by Epstein, his involvement in the couple's purchase of a flat in Oslo at below market price, a trip to the American financier's island in 2011, and the payment of home help services for Rod-Larsen.

The couple deny having committed any offence.

Epstein had also in his will left $10 million (€8.7 million) to their two children. One of them took his own life in April aged 25.

The Norwegian Ambassador to Britain Mona Juul and her husband Terje Rod-Larsen during the annual Norwegian Christmas tree lighting ceremony in London, 6 December, 2018 AP Photo

"I deeply regret today the relationship I had with Epstein," Rod-Larsen told public broadcaster NRK in a documentary premiering on Wednesday evening.

"I should have cut all ties with him earlier," he said.

Documents released at the end of January by the US Department of Justice revealed sustained, long-lasting contacts with Epstein up until 2019, the year he died while in jail awaiting trial for sex trafficking.

In 2008, Epstein had already been convicted of recruiting a minor for prostitution.

Now in poor health after two strokes, Rod-Larsen justified his dealings with Epstein by the intermediary and donor roles he played. At the time, between 2005-2020, Rod-Larsen was heading the International Peace Institute (IPI) think tank in New York.

The Epstein affair has implicated several other prominent Norwegian personalities, including Queen Mette-Marit and former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland, who later chaired the committee that selects Nobel Peace Prize winners.

Norway's parliament has launched a parliamentary scrutiny procedure and set up an independent commission.

Next week, the parliament's committee on constitutional affairs will question foreign minister Espen Barth Eide and all his predecessors since 2005, including Jonas Gahr Støre, who has since become prime minister.

World.title: Ethiopia: Fighting resumes in Tigray
World.content:
Rebels in northern Ethiopia have seized regional airports and engaged government troops in Afar and Amhara. Observers fear deadly clashes could expand after rebels announced a new anti-government alliance.

Rebels from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) have reportedly taken control of regional airports in Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, and further clashed with government forces in the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions.

Wednesday's clashes are the latest of several in recent months and have sparked fears of renewed intense fighting in the war-ravaged region.

The African Union (AU) estimates that some 600,000 people were killed in fighting between the TPLF and Ethiopian forces during a 2020-2022 civil war and that more than 1 million people remain displaced.

On Wednesday, state-owned Ethiopian Airlines announced that it had canceled service at Mekelle, Tigray's capital, as well as Axum and Shire regional airports "due to the current situation."

Local witnesses reported that TPLF rebels armed with light weapons had taken Mekelle Airport — which is normally controlled by government forces — without a fight.

Renewed fighting comes just days after the TPLF announced that it had entered an "Alliance for Survival" with other groups aimed at removing Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his government from power.

Abiy and his Prosperity Party won reelection in June, though the vote was boycotted by Ethiopia's main opposition groups.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 until 2018, when it was replaced by Abiy, whose election sparked the country's civil war.

The Pretoria Peace Agreement brought an end to the conflict, but peace has remained elusive, with government troops resuming drone strikes in 2025 as TPLF rebels began amassing troops at regional borders.

Ethiopia has accused the TPLF of allying with neighboring Eritrea and other armed groups.

An advisor to Prime Minister Abiy called Wednesday's development "heartbreaking," saying rebels had launched offensives against government forces in Afar and Amhara as well as taking control of airports in Tigray.

However, the Tigray army "has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion launched against us, and has entered into a defensive battle," the Tigray government said in a statement on Facebook.

World.title: ICC convicts CAR ex-rebel leader of crimes against humanity
World.content:
The International Criminal Court has found Mahamat Said Abdel Kani guilty of overseeing torture and other crimes. He headed a feared prison unit that held political prisoners.

The International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted a former Central African Republic rebel commander on four counts of crimes against humanity committed while he was in charge of a detention center in 2013.

The court found that Mahamat Said Abdel Kani, 56, oversaw beatings and maltreatment as the country was gripped by sectarian violence.

Said also faced three counts of war crimes but was acquitted of them. During his trial, he pleaded not guilty to all charges for the crimes, which were carried out between April and August 2013.

A sentence, which could be life imprisonment, is to be handed down at a later date.

The presiding judge at the trial was Miatta Maria Samba (third from L) Image: Remko De Waal/REUTERS

What was Said charged with?

Said was a top commander of the mainly Muslim Seleka rebel group that ousted President Francois Bozize in 2013 amid a civil war.

He was put in charge of the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry (OCRB), a prison unit in the capital, Bangui.

Prosecutors allege that prisoners at the facility, who were suspected supporters of Bozize, were subjected to various forms of torture, including whippings and body mutilation.

According to the court, inmates were also denied food or water, with some drinking their own urine out of desperation.

One cell, dubbed "the hole," where prisoners were held in dire conditions, was said by the court to be directly under Said's office.

Said stood accused of overseeing this maltreatment and personally participating in the beating of at least one prisoner, the court found.

Said (R) had pleaded not guilty to all charges Image: Remko De Waal/REUTERS

First trial of a Seleka member

Said was extradited to the ICC by Central African authorities in 2021, with his trial beginning in September 2022.

It is the first time that a member of the Seleka group has stood trial at the ICC.

The ICC, established in The Hague in 2022, is the world's only independent tribunal capable of prosecuting those accused of the world's worst crimes.

World.title: As the EU advances free trade with Southeast Asia, why is there no ASEAN-wide deal?
World.content:
After years of arduous negotiations, the EU is closing on a string of bilateral trade deals with countries in Southeast Asia. And yet, a bloc-to-bloc agreement between the EU and ASEAN remains a distant prospect.

The EU and several Southeast Asian nations are nearing the finish line on bilateral trade deals, and if the current deadlines hold, the European bloc will have agreements in place with six out of 11 ASEAN states by the middle of next year.

Free trade agreements with Singapore and Vietnam are already in force. Negotiations with Indonesia have concluded, and Jakarta aims to sign the agreement in October, with implementation targeted for early 2027.

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Talks with Thailand, relaunched in 2023, have reached nine negotiating rounds, while Malaysia resumed negotiations in early 2025 after a 13-year pause. Both are expected to be finalized by the end of the year or early 2027.

Earlier this week, the EU and the Philippines announced that they had reached "substantial agreement" on their free trade agreement, putting it on course for formal conclusion in the coming months.

Trade up by more than half in single decade

Speaking to DW, Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, described EU engagement with ASEAN on trade and investment issues as "at an all-time high."

EU-Southeast Asia goods trade reached €274.9 billion ($313.7 billion) last year, up around 6% from the previous year and more than 50% from the €177.9 billion recorded in 2016, according to EU data.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is now the EU's third-largest goods trading partner outside Europe, behind only the United States and China.

The Philippines is chair of ASEAN — these are its goals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This week, Manila hosted both the ASEAN–EU Business Summit and the 22nd meeting of ASEAN economic ministers and the EU's trade commissioner. The two blocs pledged greater cooperation to protect themselves from rising geopolitical tensions, including unilateral trade actions and regional conflicts, that "collectively threaten the rules-based international order."

Why is Southeast Asia so important for Europe?

Brussels is expanding its network of trade agreements globally as it looks to expand to new markets and form more resilient supply chains. Southeast Asia, in turn, sits at the center of supply chains for semiconductors, electronics, electric vehicles and batteries, with investment pouring into data centers, renewable energy and digital services.

EU-Mercosur free trade deal: Who gains the most? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An article published this month by the International Monetary Fund said ASEAN's 11 economies already form a $4.5 trillion bloc, growing at more than 4.5% a year.

Such economic expansion, combined with multinational firms' efforts to diversify production beyond China, has made access to Southeast Asian markets more attractive for European companies.

Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW that geopolitical and geo-economic changes are also accelerating cooperation between the two regions.

US President Donald Trump's "protectionist and erratic trade policies" have acted as a crucial catalyst, he said, while the EU's strategy of "de-risking from China" and diversifying supply chains boosted Southeast Asia's strategic importance.

A stronger partnership with European nations also plays in favor of Southeast Asia governments, who have long tried to maintain broad economic relationships with competing powers rather than becoming excessively dependent on China, the United States or any other single partner.

EU companies push for an ASEAN-wide deal

The EU-ASEAN Business Council, said Humphrey, is calling for a region-to-region economic framework with a clear pathway to an eventual region-to-region free trade deal, "something European business has consistently called for."

"This would adopt a modular approach, perhaps starting with a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and an Investment Protection Agreement," Humphrey told DW.

The idea is not exactly new — the EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-to-region agreement in 2007, but the talks bogged down over enormous differences between ASEAN economies and disagreements over the agreement's scope.

The talks were put on ice by mutual agreement in 2009, after which Brussels switched to negotiating bilateral deals with individual ASEAN members.

The main difficulty preservers to this day, as ASEAN includes Singapore, one of the world's wealthiest economies, alongside developing and least-developed members, making it difficult to agree on common commitments acceptable to Brussels.

"In addition, meeting the EU's high social, labor and environmental standards is difficult for the less-developed ASEAN members," said Gerstl.

Is the Commission ready to up the stakes?

Yet, even without an immediate prospect of a full region-to-region agreement, completing the current bilateral deals would give the EU preferential trade arrangements with most of ASEAN's largest economies and demonstrate that Southeast Asia has moved higher up Brussels' trade agenda.

For Humphrey, however, that should be the starting point rather than the endpoint. The concern, he said, is the European Commission might not be willing to move towards region-to-region agreements.

"With 2027 marking the 50th Anniversary of EU-ASEAN relations, we remain hopeful that the Commission will take this milestone seriously and ramp up work on a region-to-region economic architecture," he told DW.

"Failing to do so will only make ASEAN think that the EU does not take the region seriously."

World.title: Munich, Berlin, Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr – Germany's three Olympic candidates
World.content:
Munich, Berlin, or the Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr region? Germany aims to host the Olympic Games again. Three candidates are in the running, with one city considered the slight favorite.

Germany is hoping to win the right to host the Olympic Games in 2036, 2040 or 2044. On Saturday, the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) is to meet to vote on which of three bids (Munich, Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr, Berlin) to throw its support behind.

Munich: Political and public support

The motto of Munich's Olympic bid is "For Games with heart and soul." The concept focuses on sustainability, with the 1972 Olympic Park serving as the centerpiece. According to documents published by the bid committee, around 90% of the competition venues are located less than 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) from the Olympic Village. Most of the venues that would be used already exist, with only a few temporary facilities to be constructed.

In addition to existing infrastructure, other advantages include Munich's experience in hosting major sporting events and its Olympic legacy from 1972. The organizers aim to offer an alternative model to the pricey Olympic projects of the past.

Munich's bid would lean heavily on already existing venues Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

Political support for the Munich bid is strong: "In Munich, we have the perfect conditions to host the Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games," Munich Mayor Dominik Krause is quoted as saying on the city website, "muenchen.de."

"Hosting the Olympic Games in Munich would be an investment in the future — not only because of the immense social value but also due to the resulting acceleration of key urban development and infrastructure projects. Munich is ready for the Olympics!"

Munich residents also appear to support the bid. In a city referendum held last October, just over 305,000 residents cast their votes, with 66.4% voting in favor of an Olympic bid.

Berlin: Political opposition and a the weight of history

The situation is different in Germany's capital. The Left Party (Die Linke) won the most votes in Sunday's election in Berlin, meaning Elif Eralp, its chairperson, could become the city-state's new governing mayor. She is on the record as opposing the idea of bringing the Games to the capital, describing the bid as a "waste of taxpayer money." The Green Party, a potential coalition partner for Eralp, also opposes an Olympic bid.

Berlin's Olympic Stadium is at the heart of the capital's bid to host a future Summer Games Image: Andreas Gora/dpa/picture alliance

The prospect of hosting the Games in 2036 has sparked further debate. Critics point to the 1936 Berlin Olympics, which were exploited by Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime as a propaganda tool. Proponents, however, argue that the 2036 Games could showcase the values ​​of a democratic and cosmopolitan Germany.

Berlin's bid also envisages mainly using existing sports facilities for the Games.

"Ninety-seven percent of the required sports facilities already exist. Apart from one privately financed arena, we do not need to build any new venues," said Kaweh Niroomand, Berlin's Olympic commissioner, told the "Die Welt" newspaper.

"The Games should fit Berlin — not Berlin the Games."

Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr: Sustainability and public support

Unlike Munich and Berlin, this third bid encompasses an entire region, featuring numerous venues that are widely dispersed. Cologne would serve as the "lead city" in the bid that features 15 municipalities in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Cologne would host the Olympic Village and a temporary athletics stadium.

Organizers highlight the fact that all of the venues either already exist or would be temporary and to the fact that 66% of those who voted in lasts April's referenda in the affected municipalities voted in favor of the bid.

Schalke's football stadium would be temporarily transformed into swimming venue with a capacity of 60,000 Image: Marcus Hirnschal/osnapix/picture alliance

Apart from sustainability, the Rhine-Ruhr region's dense sports infrastructure is considered a key strength. A potential drawback is the location of competitions across many cities in Germany's most densely populated region. Traffic jams are a daily occurrence and many trains run late or are cancelled altogether.

Munich with a slight edge

A total of 144 votes are up for grabs in Saturday's vote. Eligible to vote are Germany's 42 Olympic sports federations — including those for winter sports — along with the 10-member DOSB Executive Board and eight individual DOSB members. The individual sports federations each hold three votes.

If none of the three bids wins an absolute majority in the first round of voting, the last-placed bid drops out for the second round – meaning a decision will come after no more than two rounds of voting.

The final report by a DOSB evaluation commission makes Munich's bid the slight favorite, with 87.03 out of a possible 100 points, ahead of Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr (85.02) and Berlin (74.64).

This is just the next step in a long process of deciding who will host the next three Olympic Summer Games. The International Olympic Committee isn't to decide on who will host the 2036 Olympics until 2029.

This article was adapted from German.

World.title: Rome's Colosseum closes after worker falls to his death
World.content:
The man had been working on a new lighting installation in the iconic Roman amphitheater. Italian authorities said they were working on determining the circumstances of the accident.

The Colosseum in Rome was closed on Wednesday after a worker fell to his death overnight.

Andrea Moretti, 22, died after falling while working on a new lighting installation.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she hoped that the cause of the accident would be clarified as soon as possible.

"We are deeply shocked and saddened by the news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, a skilled worker who lost his life last night following an accident at the Colosseum," she said. "For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable and even more so when it happens in the workplace."

Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli described the incident as a "tragic event that has left us shocked and stunned."

The Culture Ministry said "the second-tier section where the accident occurred" would be closed

Authorities were working on determining the circumstances of the accident, according to the statement.

The ministry said the site would be fully closed to the public for the day after all visitors leave.

The part of the site where the accident occurred had already been closed early on Wednesday.

What is Rome's Colosseum?

The ancient Colosseum is the world's largest amphitheater.

It was built in the first century under the Roman Empire. It was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts.

It is one of Rome's most iconic sites and gets up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

World.title: Hungary: EU Commission wants to unblock €4.2b in funding
World.content:
The Commission's president has argued that Budapest is strengthening the rule of law with Viktor Orban finally out of office. Funds had been blocked over corruption allegations under Hungary's former government.

The European Commission on Wednesday proposed unlocking some €4.2 billion ($4.8 billion) in frozen funds to be paid out to Hungary.

The cash had been blocked over allegations of corruption tied to Hungary's former government, led by Viktor Orban and his Fidesz party.

"Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the [European] Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.

A Commission press release said reforms implemented after Hungary elected Peter Magyar prime minister had addressed "shortcomings in areas such as public procurement, the anti-corruption framework, risks of conflicts of interest and the effectiveness of prosecutorial action."

Orban, a feverent critic of the EU, was often at odds with the bloc over accusations that he and his cronies had undermined rule of law and democracy in the country and that he had engaged in self-dealing and corruption — all charges that he vehemently denied.

The Commission said that steps taken by the new Magyar government to rectify prior problems should result in funds being partially unfrozen and the country once again being allowed to participate in European academic exchange and research programs.

In May, the Commission said it was prepared to unfreeze a total of €16.4 billion in earmarked funds should Budapest make good on its promises to implement all proposed reforms.

EU member states must now approve the Commission's plan.

World.title: OECD says growth 'resilient' in 2026 despite Middle East war
World.content:
The OECD group of industrialized nations put its 2026 growth forecast at 2.9%. It said investment in AI was helping drive growth, while the war in the Middle East was fueling inflation.

The OECD group of industrialized countries on Wednesday lifted its global growth forecast for 2026 despite the war in the Middle East.

It put the figure at 2.9%, an increase of 0.1 percentage points over June's estimates.

The 38-member Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) is a Paris-based forum for industrialized nations.

The OECD said that 'broader financial conditions remain supportive' Image: John Angelillo/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

What did the OECD say about 2026 growth?

The OECD said growth remained "resilient" in 2026, and that "broader financial conditions remain supportive."

It added that the impact of the Middle East war was being softened by other factors.

"Sizeable oil inventories, additional supply from outside the Gulf economies and discretionary government support measures all helped to cushion the impact on the global economy," the group said.

It said investments in artificial intelligence could result in "stronger growth than projected," but warned that growth could still slow if investments do not pay off as expected.

Growth still threatened

However, global growth has dropped from last year's 3.4%, and the OECD has also dropped its 2027 forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3%.

Governments around the world have begun raising interest rates to cushion inflationary pressures sparked by rising oil and gas prices.

The OECD stressed that the outlook depends on whether a lasting resolution to the conflict is found, as continued fighting would likely lead to higher inflation.

The United States and Israel's war with Iran has sent oil and gas prices soaring Image: Matthew Hoen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

The crisis has also led to an increase in government bond yields.

"Rising bond yields underline more than ever the need for enhanced efforts to contain and reallocate government spending, improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen revenues to ensure longer-term debt sustainability and maintain the ability of governments to react to significant shocks," the OECD said.

It said that other threats include weather-related risks like the El Nino pattern, which could cause supply bottlenecks and high food costs.

World.title: Campus Project 2026: Georgia Takes Center Stage
World.content:
The Beethovenfest exchange project brings German and Georgian musical traditions together. And the reasons go beyond music.

Last June, a group of around 20 young German musicians — members of the Federal Youth Orchestra and Federal Youth Choir — arrived in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. They were immediately captivated by the Caucasus metropolis and its overwhelming atmosphere of relaxed freedom.

But that freedom can be deceptive. Everyone was aware of Georgia's tense political and social situation and had seen images of the pro-European protests in Tbilisi.

Hand in hand: German and Georgian musicians rehearsing in Tbilisi Image: DW

The next morning, the German musicians gathered in a simple room in central Tbilisi with an equally sized group of young Georgian musicians from the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra as well as singers from the independent music scene.

Finding a Shared Sound

The young musicians from Georgia and members of the Federal Youth Orchestra first met in June in Tbilisi to rehearse for the joint "Campus Concert" at the Beethovenfest in Bonn .

But before that, they had to find a shared sound and develop a program that would bring together two major musical traditions from the two countries.

"We Georgians are known as hot-blooded Southerners with a lot of raw emotion," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili, conductor and artistic director of the project. "Sometimes the intensity of our emotions is higher than in German music. But once you listen to German music, you understand that people are full of emotions there, too, but there's different approaches to how we express them. In music, I couldn't see any differences."

Conductor Mirian Khukhunaishvili and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze Image: Jasper Techel/Beethovenfest

After final rehearsals in Bonn, joint concerts will take place on Sept. 23 and 24: first at the Beethovenfest in Bonn and the following day in Berlin. DW will broadcast the concert live on the DW Classical Music YouTube channel .

A Political Message Behind the Music

The Campus project is about more than an exciting musical experiment — and not just for the Georgian participants.

"One goal is to bring the classical repertoire of Georgian music closer to an international audience," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili. "And then we want to send a message. We couldn't simply play and sing without reflecting the reality around us."

For Kokhunaishvili, the music itself is the strongest message: "Our concert is about the geopolitical reality we live in. We want to express our hope for Europe — not just the hope of joining something somewhere, but that this is our shared home. We are fighting to belong there. The core message is that in Georgia, we share Western European values of human rights."

A highlight of the program is a new synthesis arranged by Georgian composer Mika Mdinaradze. The composition combines Beethoven's choral piece "Europa steht!" ("Europe Stands!") from the cantata "The Glorious Moment" with traditional Georgian songs.

"Beethoven naturally remains unmistakable, while the Georgian polyphonic structures preserve their own identity," Mdinaradze explains in an interview with DW. "Together, they create a sonic model of Europe — a dialogue instead of forced unity — a musical declaration of where Georgia belongs."

Making a Statement Through Campus

Since 2001, the Beethovenfest Bonn has organized the Campus project, a platform for exchange among young musicians, with a focus on countries experiencing historic transformation.

"Previous projects have included Ukraine, Afghanistan, Iran and now, for the second time, Georgia — after first participating in 2003," says Thomas Scheider, who leads the Campus project team at the Beethovenfest. "These are places where culture is not simply a side effect of history, but becomes a central field where history is understood, negotiated and questioned."

Standing ovations: Mirian Kukhunaishvili conducted the German National Youth Orchestra in Tbilisi, August 2026 Image: Dato Shalikashvili

For the Federal Youth Orchestra (BJO), which has been a partner in shaping the Campus project for 10 years, the encounter also went far beyond music. "Although music is naturally at the center, the exchange showed so much more: personal connections, cultural richness, significant history, impressive nature and also the challenging current political situation," says Sönke Lentz, orchestra director of the BJO and one of the project organizers. "Pro-European artists and what is likely the vast majority of the population need our solidarity and support."

The Federal Youth Orchestra also incorporated the Campus project into this year's international tour, performing three concerts in Georgia under the direction of Mirian Khukhunaishvili and featuring soloist Giorgi Gigashvili. "Sold-out venues in Tbilisi and Kutaisi, with standing ovations, impressed us and showed us the importance of a project like this," says Sönke Lentz.

Tsotne Zedginidze: Georgian Prodigy and Campus Composer

"The new Mozart" — that is how none other than conductor Daniel Barenboim described Georgian pianist and composer Tsotne Zedginidze when he was just 16 years old.

Zedginidze has just turned 17, making him the project's youngest commissioned composer in the project's history. He composed "Chmebi: Georgian Fantasia" for piano and chamber orchestra. The Georgian word "chmebi" means "voices." The young composer himself will play piano at at the world premiere in Bonn and the subsequent performance in Berlin. "Beethoven would be completely shocked, but it would inspire him," Tsotne says with a smile about his work and the project as a whole.



In his score, Zedginidze draws on ancient, complex Georgian folk traditions for the first time, combining them with unconventional harmonies and fiery folk dance elements. "About my Georgian Fantasia, I tried not to be artificial. It resembles as much as possible Georgian music — all Genres and styles. But at the same time, it's my individual understanding, my own interpretation of Georgian music," he tells DW

Supporting talent: Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili with pianist and composer Tsotne Zedginidze Image: DW

Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili is eagerly awaiting the premiere of Tsotne's work. Through her foundation ((name of the foundation?)), the musician, who moved from Georgia to Germany at age 12, supports young artists in her home country. Tsotne is among the foundation's scholarship recipients.

"Over the past 20 years, I have been able to witness how the friendship between Germany and Georgia has grown and how openly and with such interest people here have approached my home country," says Batiashvili. "It is especially beautiful to see young musicians from both countries making music together, learning from each other and inspiring one another." And perhaps, Batiashvili says, something greater than music can emerge from this: a vision of a shared future.

World.title: Zapatero asegura al juez que las joyas son un “obsequio” que el rey de Arabia Saudí le hizo en 2007
World.content:
El expresidente pide a la Audiencia Nacional que reclame cooperación a la monarquía saudí para acreditar su relato

José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero ha aclarado este miércoles el origen de las joyas tasadas en 1,3 millones de euros que la Policía le incautó: se trata de un “obsequio” personal que Arabia Saudí le hizo en 2007 cuando estaba en La Moncloa. El expresidente del Gobierno, en un escrito dirigido al juez, que le mantiene investigado en el caso Plus Ultra, y que ha avanzado EL PAÍS, asegura que el origen de una docena de piezas valiosas halladas durante el registro en su despacho el pasado mes de mayo fue un regalo del monarca saudí Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud (fallecido en 2015). Pide a la Audiencia Nacional que solicite la cooperación del país para acreditar su relato.

“Se trató de una atención estrictamente personal, aceptada por deferencia y como muestra de agradecimiento y respeto de mi representado hacia el monarca saudı́“, ha expresado el abogado del expresidente, Víctor Moreno Catena, en el documento de seis páginas entregado este miércoles. Las alhajas ”se guardaron y permanecieron guardadas durante todo este tiempo, junto a las de origen familiar y otros regalos de amigos, sin uso ni destino alguno, y sin conciencia de su valor material", ha puntualizado.

El que fuera líder de los socialistas da este paso después de que el juez José Luis Calama le diera un plazo de tres días para entregar toda la documentación que tuviese en su poder y esclarecer los dos delitos relacionados con las joyas por los que se le investiga: un delito fiscal y otro de contrabando. El instructor reclamó esta información después de que Zapatero rechazara durante su declaración del pasado junio responder preguntas sobre ese asunto y se comprometiera a aportar toda la información en el plazo de una semana o diez días. Tres meses después no había ocurrido porque fuentes del entorno del mandatario aseguran que se han tenido diversas “conversaciones diplomáticas” para poder certificar los extremos.

El valor de las joyas

El escrito detalla que las 12 piezas de más valor encontradas en la caja fuerte fueron tres conjuntos de collares, pulseras, sortijas y pendientes. Se trata de rubíes integrados por cuatro piezas, “todas ellas realizadas en oro blanco de 18 quilates con rubíes y diamantes talla brillante”; un juego de esmeraldas, conformado por “cuatro piezas realizadas en oro blanco de 18 quilates, con esmeraldas de origen Zambia y diamantes talla brillante”; y un juego de zafiros integrado por “cuatro piezas realizadas en oro blanco de 18 quilates con zafiros y diamantes talla brillante”. Estas componían el regalo, mientras que las demás estaban relacionadas con piezas familiares o de herencias.

Según la tasación realizada por orden judicial, solo las 12 joyas están valoradas en 1,2 millones de euros, casi el monto total de lo analizado. El letrado de Zapatero, sin embargo, defiende en su escrito que dicha valoración “es indudablemente muy superior al valor real de las piezas”. “Esta parte no acepta ni hace propia la valoración realizada por Ansorena”, subraya. En su relato expone que el valor que se atribuye es el del mercado de 2026, con los impuestos incluidos, y que esta estimación no puede aproximarse a lo que valía el regalo 19 años antes.

En esta línea de investigación, el juez ha solicitado a la joyería Yanes un nuevo informe pericial gemológico y joyero de las alhajas incautadas para profundizar en los materiales y el origen, por lo que en las próximas semanas se podrán concretar algunos detalles de interés.

Carta a la monarquía saudí

El expresidente ha estado meses ultimando la justificación del origen de las joyas, con la que busca zanjar un asunto capital no solo para él como investigado, sino para el corazón de los valores socialistas que él representa desde hace décadas.

En el escrito, el abogado explica que Zapatero, un día antes de declarar ante el juez el pasado junio, envió ―a través de la Embajada de Arabia Saudí en Madrid― una carta al jefe de protocolo de la Corte Real de Arabia Saudí para “obtener” la “corroboración” de que las joyas fueron un regalo de Abdalá bin Abdelaziz. “Como posiblemente recordará”, decía la misiva, “la Corte, con motivo del viaje oficial de su alteza real saudí, el custodio de las dos sagradas mezquitas, su majestad el rey Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud, los días 18 y 19 de junio de 2007, y en el marco de las relaciones entre nuestros dos países, entregó sus muestras de consideración de las que fuimos objeto”.

La carta insistía en que el regalo que recibió Zapatero era “estrictamente personal” y rogaba a la monarquía saudí, “con la única pretensión de honrar la verdad de lo acontecido”, que confirmara “la veracidad de los hechos referidos en la forma que estime más oportuno”.

El pasado 12 de agosto, el abogado del expresidente envió una nueva carta “por el mismo conducto” informando a la embajada de que pedirían en la Audiencia Nacional una “solicitud de cooperación judicial internacional”. Por eso, solicita al juez que inste a las autoridades competentes en Arabia Saudí a confirmar dos extremos: por un lado, si efectivamente en ese viaje de Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud se hizo el regalo a Zapatero; y, por otro, si este regalo eran efectivamente los collares, pendientes, anillos y pulseras que están bajo el foco por su grandísimo valor.

La prescripción

La certificación de que las joyas están en poder del expresidente desde hace casi 20 años, en principio, supondría la prescripción de los delitos concretos de esa pieza separada y, por tanto, la intención es que el tema de las joyas quede zanjado. De un lado, los delitos fiscales prescriben a los cinco años en España y a los 10 en casos agravados, es decir, si la cuota defraudada superara los 600.000 euros. En ambos escenarios, el tipo delictivo se habría extinguido. Y de otro, el delito de contrabando se disiparía al haber sido el monarca saudí el que introdujera las joyas en territorio nacional.

El expresidente, sin embargo, no entregó esas joyas a Patrimonio Nacional al salir del Ejecutivo, como sí hizo, por ejemplo, con dos relojes con esmeraldas que le había regalado el rey saudí en las mismas fechas. Zapatero entregó 531 regalos a Patrimonio tras casi ocho años en el Palacio de La Moncloa, pero no esos. Fuentes jurídicas explican que la Fiscalía Anticorrupción y el juez Calama pueden solicitar más diligencias encaminadas a verificar todos los extremos de este relato.

El que fuera líder socialista había confesado a su entorno que sabía que la justificación de las joyas es nuclear para la investigación, pero sobre todo para su propia imagen y la del Partido Socialista, formación de la que él es un símbolo político. Por ello, reconocía en privado que no podía errar ni dar un paso en falso y a eso, explican, obedece el tiempo que ha tardado en dar una explicación.

El juez Calama abrió una rama de la investigación para esclarecer la posibilidad de que Zapatero no hubiera pagado los impuestos correspondientes por las joyas y que, además, no hubiera declarado las joyas a Hacienda si fueron adquiridas en otro país y traídas a España. El entorno del expresidente en un inicio transmitió el mensaje de que eran regalos y herencias familiares de la esposa del presidente del Gobierno y que en total valían entre 30.000 y 50.000 euros.

La tasación encargada por el magistrado a la joyería Ansorena, en la que también participó el Instituto Gemológico Español, terminó confirmando que la cifra de mercado de las alhajas era concretamente 1.323.915 euros.

El expresidente declaró durante tres horas ante Calama el 18 de junio, pero rechazó comentar nada sobre las joyas y se comprometió con el togado a que lo haría cuando pudiera centrar y acreditar sus explicaciones. Desde entonces, el expresidente públicamente, durante la única entrevista que ha dado en el programa Mañaneros 360 de TVE, incidió en la misma línea, en que se trató de un regalo de “cortesía personal”.

El entorno del expresidente ya había deslizado la idea de que estas joyas fueran un regalo del rey de Arabia Saudí Abdala bin Abdelaziz en su visita a España en el año 2007, cuando en un viaje oficial visitó al entonces rey Juan Carlos I, quien le concedió el toisón de oro, y se reunió también con Zapatero en La Moncloa. El rey de Riad falleció en 2015, cuatro años después de que Zapatero saliera de la presidencia, pero su sucesor pertenece a la misma dinastía.

World.title: Estas son las 12 joyas que Zapatero señala como un regalo del Rey saudí en 2007
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

La defensa del expresidente sostiene que las piezas no están valoradas en 1,2 millones de euros, como apuntaba la casa de subastas Ansorena

La defensa del expresidente José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero ha argumentado ante el juez que lo investiga que 12 de las más de 60 joyas encontradas en la caja fuerte de su despacho —las más valiosas— fueron un regalo, con ocasión de una visita oficial en 2007, del por entonces rey de Arabia Saudí Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud. La docena de joyas señalada por Zapatero constituye un lote que la casa de subastas Ansorena valoró en más de 1.233.000 euros. O, lo que es lo mismo, el 93,2% del valor de todas las piezas incautadas en el registro de su despacho.

En el escrito, avanzado por EL PAÍS, el letrado del antiguo dirigente socialista hace un repaso pormenorizado de estas joyas, y las clasifica en tres lotes de cuatro piezas cada una: un juego de rubíes, otro de esmeraldas y otro de zafiros.

Juego de rubíes

El juego de rubíes consta de cuatro piezas, “todas ellas realizadas en oro blanco de 18 quilates, con rubíes y diamantes talla brillante”. Estos, agrupados en tres paquetes por el informe policial, tienen un valor total de 313.000, según Ansonera. En el lote figura una de las piezas más valiosas, según la casa de subastas, de todas las encontradas en la caja fuerte del expresidente: un collar de oro blanco con cinco rubíes naturales que tiene un valor de 155.000 euros. A él se suma una pulsera con dos rubíes y una montura con diamantes (72.000 euros), una sortija con un rubí (26.500) y una pareja de pendientes (60.000 euros).

Juego de esmeraldas

El de esmeraldas cuenta también con cuatro piezas “realizadas en oro blanco de 18 quilates, con esmeraldas de origen de Zambia y diamantes talla brillante”. Este juego tiene, según la casa de subastas, un valor de 538.000 euros. A él pertenece la pieza más valiosa de las más de 60 halladas en la caja fuerte: un collar con dos esmeraldas naturales y una cadena “tipo ‘rivière’ en U” cuajada de diamantes, que tiene un valor de 278.000 euros. Le acompañan una pulsera de 95.000 euros, una sortija “tipo cocktail” (85.000 euros) y una pareja de pendientes (80.000 euros).

El último juego que reconoce Zapatero está formado por otras cuatro piezas en oro blanco de 18 quilates, “con zafiros y diamantes talla brillante”. Este lote tiene un valor, según el único informe que se ha presentado de momento ante el juez, el de Ansorena, de 382.000 euros. Se compone de un collar con trece zafiros con origen en Tailandia (según la casa de subastas) acompañado de diamantes y que tiene un valor de 220.000 euros; una pulsera de oro blanco, esta con siete zafiros, que Ansorena valora en 80.000 euros, una sortija con un zafiro rodeado de diamantes (12.000 euros) y una nueva pareja de pendientes, con ocho zafiros (70.000 euros).
