World.title: La buena cara de la industria cosmética española
World.content:
El sector del cuidado personal y la belleza, que aporta el 1% del PIB y emplea a 50.000 personas, se alza paulatinamente como una industria puntera en España y en el mundo. Sin embargo, su futuro pasa por superar tres grandes desafíos: hacer productos más sostenibles, combatir las falsificaciones y mantener las exportaciones en un clima internacional adverso

LICO Cosmetics Estefanía Ferrer Fundadora y directora ejecutiva Laboratorio de ingeniería cosmética nacido en Sevilla y concebido como una compañía nativa digital. Cantabria Labs Juan Matji Presidente Laboratorio farmacéutico español especializado en productos para el cuidado de la salud de la piel

La industria de la cosmética no tiene que maquillar sus cifras para demostrar su éxito. Así lo cree Óscar Mateo, director de Conocimiento y Estudios de Mercado de la Asociación Nacional de Perfumería y Cosmética (Stanpa). El informe más reciente de la asociación, que integra a más del 90% del sector, en torno a 300 empresas, asegura que en los últimos cinco años, el negocio ha crecido un 44% y ha duplicado sus exportaciones. Este es un ámbito económico amplio que aglutina la fabricación de productos para la higiene personal, el cuidado de la piel y el cabello, el maquillaje y hasta los perfumes. Precisamente estos últimos constituyen, en palabras de Mateo, el buque insignia del sector, gracias al peso de compañías españolas como Puig, cuya presencia trasciende nuestras fronteras.

El otro pilar es el cuidado de la piel, para el que la industria ha adoptado el nombre en inglés: skincare. Debe su crecimiento al interés cada vez mayor por mantener una piel sana y con buen aspecto. Lo dice Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, una compañía farmacéutica que fabrica productos, tanto cosméticos como medicamentos, para el cuidado de la piel. “Antiguamente las cremas eran para un cierto grupo de mujeres que contaban con recursos económicos, hoy se ha democratizado”, explica el empresario en un nuevo capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen, de Banco Sabadell.

El auge del sector también obliga a afrontar una nueva lista de desafíos que aparecen por el camino como poros abiertos. Entre ellos, destacan la búsqueda de fórmulas más sostenibles sin perder eficacia, la protección frente a las falsificaciones y la lucha contra la llamada quimicofobia, término con el que Estefanía Ferrer, ingeniera química y fundadora de LICO Cosmetics, describe la desconfianza que ciertos ingredientes generan en la población. Ferrer, cuya marca nació en el entorno digital, comparte conversación con Matji en este episodio del pódcast. La charla entre ambos empresarios sirve para conocer mejor sus historias y desgranar un negocio que enfrenta un futuro fresco y radiante.

“El ‘skincare’ está aquí para quedarse. Antiguamente era para un cierto grupo de mujeres con recursos económicos, pero hoy se ha democratizado” Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, sobre el ‘boom’ de la cosmética en España

Las fortalezas Una industria que avanza con paso firme y se expande por el mundo

Una industria en expansión. El sector de la cosmética y el cuidado personal avanza a un ritmo moderado, pero sostenido. Ha pasado de representar el 0,9% del PIB español al 1,03% en los últimos cuatro años. Entre las razones de su consolidación se encuentran el desarrollo de una cultura del cuidado de la piel y el cabello y el bienestar personal, con una mención especial a los cosméticos para el rostro y la fotoprotección solar, que empieza a consumirse de manera notable fuera del verano.

Potencia exportadora. España vende cada año más productos al extranjero y ya supera a manufacturas emblemáticas como el aceite de oliva, el vino y el calzado. Además, España es el segundo exportador mundial de perfumes, solo por detrás de Francia.

Con buena reputación. La industria española produce bajo uno de los marcos regulatorios más exigentes del mundo: el europeo. Además, trabaja constantemente para crear formulaciones más seguras. Para ello invierte de media el 3,4% en I+D+i. La media general de las empresas españolas de toda la economía es el 0,9%, de acuerdo con el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE). Esto permite adaptarse mejor a los cambios en el mercado. En los dos últimos años se ha reformulado uno de cada tres productos, de acuerdo con Stanpa.

Distribuida por el territorio. Aunque Cataluña, Madrid y la Comunidad Valenciana concentran gran parte de la producción, Stanpa destaca que existe bastante descentralización, como demuestran las empresas protagonistas del vídeo, con sede en Sevilla y Cantabria.

“España compite bien internacionalmente con el ‘skincare’. No tenemos nada que envidiar a los coreanos, que están tan de moda ahora” Juan Matji, presidente de Cantabria Labs, acerca del buen estado de salud de la industria española

Los desafios Un sector que se esfuerza por garantizar la seguridad de sus productos y por reducir su impacto ambiental

Adaptarse a una regulación cada vez más compleja. Los productos y los procesos tienen que responder a nuevas exigencias europeas sobre ingredientes, seguridad, información al consumidor y trazabilidad.

El reto continuo de mejorar en sostenibilidad. Las empresas se enfrentan a varios desafíos para reducir su impacto en el medio ambiente.

Limitar el uso del plástico y mejorar las posibilidades de reciclaje de sus envases

Reducir el consumo del agua en la fabricación de sus productos, así como desarrollar metodologías para medir y reducir su huella hídrica

Encontrar ingredientes biodegradables que no impacten en la naturaleza, sin perder la eficacia

Mantener la competitividad internacional. Permanecer como el segundo exportador mundial de perfumes se transforma en un desafío en un escenario internacional complejo por las tensiones comerciales, los conflictos políticos y el aumento de los aranceles. En 2025, las exportaciones a Estados Unidos cayeron un 13% por el impacto de los aranceles, de acuerdo con Stanpa.

Combatir las falsificaciones. La compra de buena parte de los productos, como los perfumes o la cosmética de alta gama, resulta aspiracional y se enmarca en el lujo accesible. Por eso, son uno de los principales objetivos de los falsificadores. Y estas copias pueden no cumplir los requisitos europeos de seguridad y etiquetado.

Luchar contra la desinformación. El consumidor cada vez está más formado, aun así, se ha extendido a través de internet la idea de que cuantos menos productos químicos tenga una crema o un perfume, mejor será para la salud, un fenómeno que se conoce como quimiofobia, ya que se da por supuesto que los ingredientes químicos pueden ser perjudiciales para la salud. Pero hay que tener cuidado con esa información, resalta la fundadora de LICO Cosmetics. Los materiales que componen un cosmético siempre son químicos, tanto si proceden de una planta como si se sintetizan en un laboratorio. Y deben ser seguros para el consumo humano, algo que se encarga de garantizar el Comité Científico de Seguridad de los Consumidores (CCSC, por sus siglas en inglés).

World.title: Escribir el futuro desde España: “Podemos ser una gran potencia tecnológica europea”
World.content:
Ruth Díaz, directora para España y Portugal de Amazon recalca el grado de digitalización del país en la última década y media y el papel que, gracias a las energías renovables, a la presencia de centros de datos y a agentes como AWS, puede jugar en los próximos años

Habla

Las vistas despejadas desde la undécima planta de este rascacielos madrileño casan a la perfección con la claridad con que discurre y se expresa Ruth Díaz, directora general de Amazon para España y Portugal: “Esta es una empresa plenamente española. Con 30.000 trabajadores, más de mil de ellos ingenieros, somos uno de los diez máximos empleadores del país. Aquí se han puesto en marcha iniciativas piloto que ahora se aplican por todo el mundo. Ya se han invertido 25.000 millones desde 2010, y se van a invertir otros 33.700 para expandir los centros de datos en Aragón en la próxima década, con los que se prevé que se generen 6.000 empleos más. No se puede arrancar a esta empresa de España”.

Cuenta Díaz en esta entrevista del espacio Hablan las marcas, con motivo del 50º aniversario de EL PAÍS, que el potencial de crecimiento es enorme: porque España es un gran productor de energías limpias y, gracias a ello, Amazon podrá cumplir su objetivo de cero emisiones netas para 2040, porque el comercio digital representa aquí todavía solo un 8% y, sin embargo, el último año ya han conseguido entregar más de 190 millones de paquetes antes de 24 horas, y hay mucho margen todavía para flexibilizar y personalizar esas recepciones; porque la implementación de herramientas tecnológicas como la IA en la empresa española está siete puntos por encima de la media europea, porque, según defiende, ella ha sido testigo de “cómo lo extraordinario se volvía cotidiano” en estos últimos 15 años, y eso es justamente lo que espera que siga ocurriendo: “Limitaremos el tiempo que las personas pierden en otras tareas para que puedan dedicárselo a sus familiares, amigos y seres queridos”.

World.title: Soy mayor de 65 años y voy a vender mi vivienda habitual. ¿Podría hacer una segunda venta más adelante y estaría exenta de tributación?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Tengo 66 años y voy a vender mi vivienda habitual, que tiene mayor valor que la que compro. Sé que puedo optar por varios modos de exención del incremento patrimonial. En el caso de que pasado unos años quisiera vender la casa, ¿podría volver a eximir plusvalías, siendo vivienda habitual y mayor de 65 años, pero siendo una segunda venta? A. Gómez

Respuesta. Está exenta de tributación en el IRPF la ganancia patrimonial obtenida por una persona mayor de 65 años como consecuencia de la transmisión de su vivienda habitual, sin que sea necesario reinvertir el importe obtenido en la adquisición de otra vivienda ni en ningún otro producto.

A estos efectos, se considera vivienda habitual aquella de la que el contribuyente sea pleno propietario y en la que haya residido de forma efectiva y continuada durante un plazo mínimo de tres años.

Por tanto, si se cumple este requisito, cualquier ganancia patrimonial obtenida con la venta de la vivienda habitual, con independencia de su importe, estará exenta de tributación en el IRPF, aunque no se reinvierta total o parcialmente el importe obtenido en otra vivienda habitual.

Asimismo, un mismo contribuyente mayor de 65 años puede beneficiarse de esta exención en más de una ocasión, siempre que cada una de las viviendas transmitidas tenga la consideración de vivienda habitual en el momento de la venta. Para ello, será necesario que haya residido en la nueva vivienda de manera efectiva y continuada durante un período mínimo de tres años.

En consecuencia, también podría aplicarse la exención a la ganancia patrimonial generada por la venta de una nueva vivienda habitual adquirida con posterioridad, aunque se trate de una segunda transmisión de vivienda habitual realizada por una persona mayor de 65 años.

No obstante, esta exención se refiere exclusivamente a la ganancia patrimonial en el IRPF. Es decir, no está exento del Impuesto sobre el Incremento de Valor de los Terrenos de Naturaleza Urbana (plusvalía municipal), que también se devenga con motivo de la venta y debe liquidarse ante el ayuntamiento correspondiente, aunque se trate de la vivienda habitual de una persona mayor de 65 años.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: 10 experiencias en el Matarraña para sacarle todo el jugo a la comarca aragonesa en septiembre
World.content:
Pedalear por la vía verde de la Val de Zafán, caminar por el Solo Sculpture Trail, dormir en un antiguo molino de papel y más pistas en esta zona de la provincia de Teruel que es tierra de cañones y, sobre todo, de buitres

Wikipedia dice, todo el mundo repite —incluida la IA—, y será verdad mientras no se demuestre lo contrario, que el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del planeta es el Matarraña. Este afluente del Ebro, de casi 100 kilómetros de longitud, ha dado nombre a la comarca en la que Teruel se funde y confunde con Tarragona y Castellón, y ha labrado las rocas calizas de los Puertos de Beceite, donde nace, como si en vez de agua pura llevara carburo de silicio verde, abrasivo y cortante a más no poder. Aparte de fabulosos cañones y de pozas que piden a gritos bañarse hasta bien entrado el otoño, este rincón del noreste de la provincia de Teruel tiene muchas otras cosas que sorprenden al viajero.

La primera es que aquí no hablan como los demás turolenses, sino chapurriau, una variedad aragonesa del catalán cantarina y cadenciosa que, a los forasteros, salvo que sean de las provincias de al lado, les suena a valenciano. Matarraña —o Matarranya, como lo escriben también— es un no parar de sorpresas. Tomen nota de estas 10.

Más información 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa

Penetrar en la comarca siguiendo a un tren loco

Por Matarraña pasó un tren hoy difícil de explicar, que iba de La Puebla de Híjar a Tortosa, del norte de Teruel al Bajo Ebro, y que pretendía llegar algún día hasta la orilla del mar. Un loco sueño ferroviario que duró 30 años (de 1941 a 1971) y que dejó este abrupto y solitario rincón del mapa aragonés lleno de puentes inútiles y de estaciones en mitad de ninguna parte.

Se esfumó el tren, pero su itinerario y su espíritu insensatos permanecen en la vía verde de la Val de Zafán. Una buena manera de hincarle el diente a la comarca es echarse a pedalear desde la que fue la estación de Valjunquera con las bicis y los guías de Senda. Salvo en un par de túneles, que no se ve nada, se va descubriendo un paisaje cada vez más ordenado de olivos y almendros y una luz cada vez más mediterránea. Hay una parada obligada en el alto viaducto que hay a 9,5 kilómetros del inicio, para saludar al río Matarraña. Al otro lado, en otra antigua estación, se halla el muy recomendable hotel La Parada del Compte.

Comer lo que comió Picasso

Pedaleando por una vía verde llana no es que se haga mucho ejercicio, pero hambre sí que se hace. Para calmarla, no hay mejor opción en toda la comarca que Fonda Alcalá. Ubicado en Calaceite, miembro de la Asociación Los Pueblos Más Bonitos de España, por esta casa de comidas algo más que centenaria —data de 1922— han pasado García Márquez, Álvaro Cunqueiro, Francesc Català Roca, Paco de Lucía, Serrat… No en este orden, lógicamente. El que no pasó, pero sí comió lo que aquí se hace, fue Picasso. Les perdius de Picasso, las perdices que le guisaron en esta casa y le llevaron enlatadas a Francia en 1967, y las judías blancas de Beceite con sardinas de cubo son dos platos legendarios, fundamentales. Pero el chef Ignacio Alcalá se inventa todos los días otros más excitantes y divertidos, que es lo que aprendió a hacer en las cocinas de Neichel y Can Roca.

Hacer senderismo en una galería de arte

He aquí sin duda lo más flipante de la comarca, naturaleza aparte: Solo Houses, una hermosa finca campestre de 200 hectáreas en el municipio de Cretas, donde llevan 13 años materializándose como naves alienígenas casas alucinantes de arquitectos de vanguardia que se pueden alquilar desde 850 euros por noche y donde pronto lo hará un hotel de habitaciones circulares exentas, con vistas al bosque diseñado por Smiljan Radić, Premio Pritzker 2026. Obviamente, alojarse aquí es solo para amantes de la arquitectura y gente con pasta.

Una mujer pasea entre esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, en la localidad de Cretas. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

El resto debe contentarse con ver los ovnis de lejos, paseando entre las vides de la bodega Venta D’Aubert y las esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, un circuito creado por los propietarios de todo esto, los galeristas Christian Bourdais y Eva Albarrán, para exponer al aire libre y vender obras que tampoco parecen de este mundo. Se tarda hora y media en ver las 20 esculturas y solo cuesta cinco euros. También se puede visitar la bodega y catar cinco de sus vinos por 25.

La bodega Venta D’Aubert. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Asomarse a la vecina Tarragona por un desfiladero

Si pasear por un sendero de pago entre esculturas carísimas parece algo pijo y rebuscado, en el pueblo de al lado, en Arnes, podemos hacerlo en un lugar verdaderamente salvaje, el desfiladero de Els Estrets, y bañarnos en las aguas inmaculadas del río que lo atraviesa —un afluente del río Algás, que a su vez lo es del Matarraña—, sin pagar un euro. Al llegar al aparcamiento donde arranca la senda, descubriremos estupefactos Les Gronses, unas formidables moles anaranjadas donde pululan escaladores, cabras monteses y buitres leonados.

El desfiladero de Els Estrets, en la vecina Terra Alta de Tarragona. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Y nada más echarnos a andar, un cartel que dice: “Parc Natural dels Ports”. Estamos en Cataluña, concretamente en la Terra Alta de Tarragona. Otro cartel advierte que el baño solo está permitido en el Toll Blau (el charco azul). Allí veremos dos o tres humanos y, más adelante, si es que se dejan ver, alguna nutria y la libélula Macromia splendens, en peligro de extinción. Mucho más fácil de observar, libando en las lavandas, es la mariposa Cleopatra. El desfiladero se recorre, yendo y volviendo por camino evidente, en un par de horas.

Dormir en un antiguo molino de papel

Vistas desde el hotel La Fábrica de Solfa, en Beceite. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Beceite, además de un bonito pueblo, con muchas de sus casas colgadas sobre el encañonado río Matarraña, es el campo base ideal para explorar la comarca, porque está cerca de su paraje más deseado —el Parrizal, donde nace aquél— y porque hay un hotelito familiar que es un hotelazo. La Fábrica de Solfa, que así se llama, fue un molino de papel: con la fuerza del río se trituraba ropa vieja y se obtenía la pasta necesaria. Ahora es una fábrica de actividades: todas las que se cuentan en este reportaje y algunas más. De amorosos cuidados que prodigan Javier y Alberto Moragrega a los que llegan exhaustos después de hacerlas. Y de ricos platos: el recapte de fesols de Beceite, el ternasco de Aragón, las texturas de té de roca y todo lo que se sirve en el restaurante Marca al Agua. Tampoco se desayuna mal, viendo a las nutrias jugar en el río saltarín. Lo único malo es que aparecen al rayar el sol, así que hay que madrugar.

Darse un baño de multitudes y otro en un ‘fish spa’ natural

A solo tres kilómetros de Beceite se encuentra el Parrizal (o Parrissal), el desfiladero que nadie que visita esta comarca deja de admirar y recorrer, a tal punto que hay que reservar online para evitar mayores aglomeraciones de las que ya se forman sobre las tablas de dos palmos de ancho que hay instaladas en las paredes verticales del cañón, a buena altura sobre las aguas impolutas del recién nacido Matarraña. Avanzar nadando por el propio río, que sería lo deseable para librarse del sudor propio y de los atascos, está prohibido.

Pasarelas en la senda del Parrizal. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Donde sí está permitido mojarse y remojarse es en La Pesquera, en las pozas que forma el río Ulldemó, afluente del Matarraña, a tres kilómetros también de Beceite. Comparadas con las de otros ríos de montaña, estas aguas de hipnótico color verde jade son hasta cálidas. Y mucho más relajantes: metes los pies y acuden docenas de diminutos barbos y madrillas a limpiar tus células muertas. Esto es ictioterapia y La Pesquera, un fish spa natural, sin kimonos ni musiquillas new age.

Remar con el último sol en el pantano de Pena

Kayak al atardecer en el pantano de Pena. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

A la misma distancia de Beceite que el Parrizal y La Pesquera, está el pantano de Pena, uno de los más antiguos de Teruel (de 1930) y el único de la cuenca del Matarraña. Si hubiera muchos pantanos, no sería el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del mundo. Ir allí a navegar en kayak al atardecer es una de las actividades que recomienda y organiza La Fábrica de Solfa. Desde el hotel se llega con una bici eléctrica en un cuarto de hora y, después de rodear el embalse en media más, se embarca y se rema hasta el centro para admirar cómo el penúltimo sol se duplica en la cabecera y el agua se vuelve de oro. Girando luego el kayak en redondo y apuntando con la proa hacia el noreste, se ve cómo los últimos rayos iluminan la Caixa, una cumbre que a los matarrañeses les parece que tiene forma de caja de caudales y por eso la llaman así. Si remando y girando se vuelca accidentalmente, o adrede para refrescarse, no pasa nada: aquí está permitido el baño.

Asistir al banquete de 500 aves carroñeras

José Ramón Moragrega entre buitres en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

En la sierra de Arca, donde está la Caixa, anidan multitud de buitres leonados. No es solo que allí hay cortados rocosos idóneos para ellos. Es que al pie de la montaña, en una masía de Valderrobres, vive José Ramón Moragrega, que lleva más de 30 años alimentándolos. Todos los días, Buitreman —así le llaman— sale a las 9.15 con una carretilla llena de pulmones de cerdo y la vuelca ante una muchedumbre expectante de estas enormes carroñeras. Hasta 500 de ellas se reúnen para compartir de muy malos modos este desayuno, formando una monumental tremolina de polvo, chillidos e iracundos aleteos. Todo puede verse y fotografiarse en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol, una masía que es también un formidable hide, con grandes ventanales orientados a los cuatro vientos para no perderse nada, desde el momento en que Buitreman vuelca la carretilla y se aparta a toda velocidad de sus pequeños de picos afilados como cuchillos —por eso va con casco, porque más de una vez ha salido descalabrado—, hasta cuando aparecen los alimoches para disputarse las migajas de la tragantona.

Al despedirse de los visitantes, Moragrega les confía casi entre lágrimas su delicado estado de salud y que sus niños pueden quedarse pronto sin desayuno si alguna entidad pública o privada no asume la gestión del observatorio, que es también alojamiento rural. Es un negocio rentable, asegura.

Vuelta a las rocas huesudas del Masmut

Muchos buitres leonados que desayunan en Mas de Bunyol pasan el resto del día haciendo la digestión en las Rocas del Masmut, en Peñarroya de Tastavins, donde hay una importante colonia de ellos. El PR TE-157, uno de los Senderos Turísticos de Aragón, bien mantenido y señalizado, invita a rodear este manojo de peñas anaranjadas de más de 100 metros de altura, similares a los Mallos de Riglos, cuyo nombre se cree que viene de los masmuda, una tribu bereber que quizá estuviera asentada aquí cuando España era musulmana.

Es una ruta circular de poco más de tres horas, cuatro si el senderista se desvía a los tres kilómetros para subir al mirador del Masmut. Situado a 500 metros de las rocas y a similar altura, es un buen lugar para verlas como las ven los buitres, asomando como las falanges de un gigante muerto y enterrado bajo la costra caliza del Matarraña.

Un pícnic regenerativo para despedirse del Matarraña

La última sorpresa de esta ruta llena de ellas la puede dar Tel·lúric, una masía centenaria del municipio de Ráfels cuyos nuevos propietarios no es que respeten la tradición agrícola de los masos, de estas catedrales civiles del campo matarrañés, es que van un paso más allá. O un paso más acá, porque trabajan la tierra con tal cuidado que no solo no se agota, sino que se regenera. Los olivos, los almendros y las viñas que atiende Sorin Dragoman no son soldados invasores de ejércitos cuadriculados, sino pacíficos hermanos de los pinos, las carrascas, el tomillo, el romero, el té de roca y el poleo.

Con todo lo que aquí se produce (vinos, aceite y almendras con certificación ecológica y de agricultura regenerativa) dispuesto sobre un mantel a cuadros, y también con las carnes a la brasa que salen sin parar de la cocina, se organizan unos pícnics delante de la masía que son una manera estupenda de despedirse del Matarraña. El águila culebrera sobrevuela los cultivos de Tel·lúric sin sospechar que son cosa de humanos.

World.title: Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

When the residents of the Brabant town of Oisterwijk smelled the pungent odor of gas on Wednesday, they called their local fire department, who turned out to be the culprits.

Fire fighters spent the morning searching for a gas leak to no avail. Together with gas provider Enexis, they tested levels throughout the town but could not find a source, only the smell.

Meanwhile, back at the fire station, staff discovered a canister of THT was missing. The chemical is added to gas, which is naturally odorless, to so that people can smell any leak immediately.

The cannister had been accidently thrown out and had spent the morning in the back of a garbage truck, which was making its rounds.

“We were able to have a laugh about it for a moment,” firefighter Ronald Blokpoel told Omroep Brabant.

Residents may continue to smell gas for a time while the chemical dissipates. The fire depart warns there is no danger to public health.

World.title: Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
World.content:
Around 150 people joined a funeral procession on Wednesday for a man who died while being detained by police who stopped him while searching for a stolen fatbike.

The body of 51-year-old Alfredo Goeloe was carried in a white coffin in a carriage drawn by two white horses to the Zuiderbegraafplaats in Rotterdam, 10 days after he collapsed while being pinned to the ground and handcuffed.

Friends and relatives who followed the coffin carried banners with slogans including “samen tegen onrecht omdat we om elkaar geven” (united against injustice because we care for each other).

One of the mourners, Yenci Vargas, told Nieuwsuur: “He was murdered. I’m not talking about racism, but he was murdered by the negligence and stupidity of the police.”

Another, Marsha Mabosa, said: “Last month we were out in a café and he asked me to dance the bachata. He was a very good dancer. And now we have to miss him in a way that is very unjust.”

Stolen fatbike

Goeloe was stopped by police while riding a fatbike through Rotterdam on the evening of Saturday, September 12.

Police initially said he was suspected of stealing the bike, but later changed their story to say he had been stopped because he was riding too fast. Just before Goeloe’s arrest a fatbike had been reported stolen by a couple aged around 40.

Goeloe tried to run from police when they tried to arrest him for not carrying ID. His family said he had borrowed his sister’s bike to go out to get medication for his diabetes.

He was chased down and passed out while he was being restrained on his belly. Video footage showed he cried out that he had diabetes and was in pain as he lay on the ground.

Official complaint

Goeloe’s family have filed a criminal complaint against four police officers. Lawyer Gerard Roethof said they viewed it as “a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”

Jan Schalkwijk, a lawyer with Control Alt Delete, an organisation that monitors racial profiling in the Netherlands, said the use of force by police was excessive.

“The officers were far superior in number, according to reports he was unarmed, and he could have been approached with less force,” Schalkwijk argued.

Restraint guidelines

But Jaap Timmer, a political scientist at the VU university in Amsterdam who specialises in police use of force, said there was no indication from the film footage that the police had failed to follow protocol.

He said police guidelines said people should be pressed against the ground for as short a time as possible when under arrest, but it was unsafe to let them stand up before they had been handcuffed.

“I understand the police were looking for a fatbike and this man was riding too fast. That could be a reason to ask his identity,” he said.

“He then ran away fast and resisted his arrest. That has nothing to do with ethnic profiling, but with the man’s behaviour.”

World.title: Road safety institute weighing up zero alcohol limit for drivers
World.content:
The Dutch Road Safety Research Institute has released a new study on reducing the drug and alcohol limit for drivers to zero, finding it would probably decrease road accidents but would increase pressure on the police.

SWOV looked at the policy in eight countries with limits lower than the Netherlands, which is of blood alcohol level of 0.05% or 0.02% for those who have been driving for less than 5 years.

The risk of accidents is already elevated at the 0.05% level, the report says. Other countries, including Norway and Sweden, set the level at 0.02% for all drivers.

“An absolute zero limit is considered to be a simple and unambiguous standard that leaves less room for interpretation of what is still permissible and what is not,” the report says, and would improve road safety.

However, lowering the limit will lead to more work for police but also testing facilities. It can be difficult, especially with cannabis, to properly detect the levels, especially with saliva tests.

“Particularly for THC and cocaine, concentrations or metabolites can remain detectable long after the immediate effects have disappeared,” the institute wrote, which would create legal problems for criminal prosecutions.

World.title: Water used to put out waste plant fire contaminated with PFAS
World.content:
Firefighters used water contaminated with PFAS chemicals to put out a blaze at a waste processing plant in Gelderland that was operating illegally.

Aalden municipal council said the water would have to be pumped out of the sewage network to prevent it polluting drinking water supplies, because the purification system is not able to filter it out.

The blaze in Dinxperlo, a village on the German border, burned for several hours on Monday night after a large pile of wood chippings caught fire, covering an area of 20m by 30m at its height.

Firefighters pumped water from Het Blauwe Meer, a nearby recreational lake that has been closed to swimmers since 2024 because of high levels of PFAS. Most of the water subsequently drained away into the sewage system.

The council said it was investigating the impact, but there was no reason to avoid drinking tap water. “At the moment there are no consequences for the use of the sewage network by residents,” a spokesman said.

Police are also investigating the fire. The waste processing plant was shut down in November 2025 on the orders of the council for “serious breaches of environmental regulations.”

No permits

The operators burned large quantities of waste that they did not have permits for and mixed different types of waste that should have been separated, the council found.

Recent studies found that high levels of PFAS are present in Dutch drinking water supplies, particularly in western areas where the water is taken from rivers that have been contaminated by agricultural use.

PFAS chemicals are widely used in pesticides, packaging and products ranging from waterproof clothing to non-stick cooking pans.

They are known as “forever chemicals” because of their high durability, but have also been linked to illnesses such as cancer, diseases of the immune system and complications in unborn babies.

The public health agency RIVM has called for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides by the EU, a move also supported in Germany and the Scandinavian nations.

World.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Workshops and presentations

The fair will also feature over 20 free workshops to help expats with job hunting, finding housing, immigration and settling advice, as well as tips on local leisure and health services, and more. The workshops have limited capacity and are filling up fast, so make sure to book seats as soon as possible — you can sign up here.

Careers and partners

The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and offers additional advice and services for the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “Because of this small but mighty community, we are bringing the Fair back to Eindhoven to support internationals and their families looking to to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools, Dutch classes, and more.”

Families and newcomers

New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti Nutrition.

Every stage covered

Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals may initially come to the Fair looking for Dutch language classes or career opportunities, but later in life, they come to the Fair for different needs, such as preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

World.title: Support for refugees should prioritise finding skilled work: SER
World.content:
The government needs to do more to help settled asylum seekers find work that matches their skills as part of their integration into society, a new report by the socio-economic council (SER) advises.

Municipalities should have a legal obligation to support newcomers find suitable work, with financial input from The Hague, rather than leaving asylum seekers to search for jobs on their own.

The report said the current requirements were unclear and had contradictory aims, with the obligation on new migrants to learn the language and learn citizenship making it harder for them to work.

“At the moment people often have language lessons, with travel time as well. In practice that is often hard to combine with working,” a spokesman told NOS. “We say people should able to work or train and the question is how to organise language and citizenship around that.”

The cabinet has said it wants asylum seekers to be able to start looking for work after three months, rather than the current waiting period of six, but the plan still has to go through parliament.

Currently only 57% of refugees with settled status are working eight years after they are given permission to stay, compared to 81% of the entire working-age population.

Not just numbers

Work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen has set a target of getting 75,000 newcomers into work, but the SER said the numbers should not be the only issue.

The report said there was a risk of skilled migrants being locked in to jobs that did not reflect their talents. “Settled refugees and displaced Ukrainians are often employed in basic agency work that doesn’t reflect their education, experience and ambitions. For them, basic work is not a stepping-stone to a better job.”

A report by the national auditor this year concluded that the Netherlands was missing opportunities to address skills shortages by employing settled refugees in sectors with vacancies.

The SER also said financial support for language lessons should be restored for Ukrainian refugees so they had the same right as other asylum seekers. Settled refugees receive financial support up to B2 level, but this has been stopped for Ukrainians.

Yana Shcherbak, who worked as a doctor in Ukraine for 15 years before the Russian invasion, said she was held back when she first arrived in Amsterdam by the confusing and disjointed rules. “I didn’t know there were language lessons for a year,” she said.

She now works as a dental and psychiatric assistant, but hopes to retrain at Amsterdam’s OVLG hospital. “I often dream that I’m working in the hospital again, in a white coat,” she told the SER. “Then I wake up and realise where I am.”

World.title: The pen is mightier than the scrub: hospitals warn of ink stains
World.content:
Utrecht University Medical Centre is warning its doctors and nurses to check their pockets before putting their scrubs in the wash, as ink stains have become a spot of problem for the laundry.

According to RTL, hundreds of uniforms are thrown away in Dutch hospitals because markets and ballpoint pens end up in the washing machine.

A spokesperson for laundry company CleanLease, which manages the laundry for the Utrecht hospital, says scrubs and other laundry items are sent through an X-ray before getting wet. “We detect 99 percent of the items. But pens and markers are a persistent problem,” they told RTL.

A single pen can cause an entire load of uniforms to be rejected. For UMC Utrecht, this amounts to 50 uniforms per week.

“In healthcare, we already have a shortage of materials, staff, and costs. That is why we must return to common sense and look at the simplest solution: just check your jacket and trouser pockets and take that pen out,” Celina Kroon, sustainability manager at UMC Utrecht, said.

World.title: Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in the second quarter of 2026, more than the national statistic agency CBS’s initial assessment.

The CBS said higher export volumes and stronger household spending were the main reasons for the revision. The second, more detailed assessment is published around 85 days after the end of the quarter.

Over the 12-month period GDP grew by 1.6%, its fastest rate since the first quarter of 2025. That figure was also revised upwards from an initial 1.3%.

The labour market improved, with an additional 15,000 employees and registered freelancers in the second quarter. The initial assessment said the total number of jobs had dropped by 8,000.

World.title: Senior Polish presidential official detained amid probe into misspending of funds
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Agents from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) have detained a senior official from opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s chancellery as part of a probe into alleged misspending of funds under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. An employee of a major right-wing broadcaster, Republika, was also taken into custody as part of the same investigation, which relates to the activities of the Polish National Foundation (PFN), a body created under the PiS government to promote Poland abroad but which was also used to further the party’s political interests. Dzisiaj rano w Warszawie na polecenie Prokuratury Regionalnej w Rzeszowie agenci @CBAgovPL zatrzymali Piotra M. i Annę P. ▶️ Zatrzymane osoby przewożone są do @Prok_Regio_RZE, która prowadzi śledztwo dotyczące nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej. ▶️ Na tym etapie… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) September 23, 2026 On Tuesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, announced that two individuals, named only as Piotr M. and Anna P. under Polish privacy law, had been detained by the CBA at the request of prosecutors investigating irregularities in the PFN. Both suspects previously worked in the chancellery of Prime Minister Beata Szydło, who was head of the PiS government from 2015 to 2017. Piotr M. was head of the Government Information Centre (CIR) and Anna P. led the media services department. Anna P. now works for Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. She is director of the Presidential Events Office, which organises the president’s schedule. Piotr M. currently works as a commentator for Republika, a station generally supportive of Nawrocki and PiS. Agenci CBA zatrzymali w Warszawie Piotra M. i Annę P. Sprawa dotyczy nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej! pic.twitter.com/e3jw3ekdOA — Iwona Hartwich (@iwonahartwich) September 23, 2026 In 2017, while still working in Szydło’s chancellery, Piotr M. and Anna P. founded a PR company called Solvere. Later that same year, the company was hired to run a prominent and controversial campaign for the PFN called “Fair Courts”, receiving a reported 1.2 million zloty (€275,000) for the project. The PFN had been set up the previous year under Szydło’s government with funding from 17 state-owned companies. Its publicly declared and statutory mission was to promote Poland abroad. However, the “Fair Courts” campaign, which cost around 8.4 million zloty, was run in Poland itself, with material in Polish, and aimed to show the alleged failings of the justice system in Poland in order to justify why controversial reforms being implemented by PiS were necessary. Echoing PiS rhetoric, the campaign suggested that judges saw themselves as a “special caste” and highlighted cases of alleged wrongdoing by individual judges, including one who had been caught stealing a sausage. (The judge in question had not ruled on a case since that incident in 2006 and had died in 2015.) In 2018, a Warsaw court ruled that the “Fair Courts” campaign was inconsistent with the PFN’s statutory goals, saying that not only did the adverts fail to enhance Poland’s image abroad, “on the contrary, they significantly weakened it, creating a negative image of the judiciary based on individual cases”. In February 2025, just over a year after PiS lost power, a newly appointed PFN board accused its predecessors of criminal negligence that caused damages of over 30 million zloty to the foundation’s finances. They notified prosecutors of potential crimes. In July this year, two men who had served as PFN board members at the time of the campaign were detained as part of an investigation into the misspending of the foundation’s funds. At that time, the CBA also announced that it had searched the homes of Anna P. and Piotr M. A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Today’s detentions of Anna P. and Piotr M. were welcomed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. He told Polsat News that the “Fair Courts” campaign was a “double scandal” because it was “not only an abuse of public funds, but also for the very clearly malicious purpose” of “attacking the independent judiciary”. Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, told the media that the authorities intended to find out “who stood behind” the actions of Anna P. and Piotr M., because “it’s hard to believe this was their initiative”. However, Jarosław Olechowski, a senior executive at Republika, condemned the detentions, calling them an act of “political revenge by the Donald Tusk regime for an information campaign exposing pathologies in Polish courts”. At the time of writing, the presidential chancellery had not commented on the detention of Anna P., the head of its events office. Earlier this year, Nawrocki’s deputy chief of staff was charged with ordering the falsification of documents, an accusation he denies. ❗️❗️❗️❗️❗️ Funkcjonariusze @CBAgovPL zatrzymali @Matczuk_ publicystę @RepublikaTV Przewożą go do prokuratury w Rzeszowie. Powodem zatrzymania jest zemsta polityczna reżimu @donaldtusk za kampanię informacyjną pokazującą patologie w polskich sądach — Jarek Olechowski (@OlechowskiJarek) September 23, 2026 The “Fair Courts” campaign was just one of a number of controversial initiatives launched by the PFN under the PiS government. The foundation was regularly accused of spending money to support PiS’s political goals or on seemingly wasteful projects. One of its most famous initiatives involved the purchase of a yacht for almost €1 million, which was renamed “I Love Poland” and sent on an around-the-world cruise to mark the centenary of Poland’s independence in 2018 (though it suffered damage and spent weeks stuck in a port, accruing further costs). In 2021, the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) accused the PFN of violating the law by refusing to provide documents required for an audit. World.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”. Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president. Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000. President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO — Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026 The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”. On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage. “The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.” Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland. Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president. However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy. On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location. Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican. 💬Kiedy poznamy ostateczną decyzję w sprawie stałej bazy amerykańskiej w Polsce? 💬Jestem przekonany, że pan prezydent @realDonaldTrump będzie chciał zrobić wszystko, aby tak decyzja zachęcająca Polaków do głosowania na Republikanów mogła zapaść przed wyborami – Stanisław… pic.twitter.com/uPWkmdGQod — RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026 The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”. In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis. The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level. When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”. 💬Ilu w tej chwili w Polsce jest żołnierzy amerykańskich? Ilu będzie docelowo rotacyjnych żołnierzy i w stałej bazie? Odpowiada Stanisław Wziątek @MON_GOV_PL w #RozmowaRMF o 7:00 w @Radio_RMF24@RMF24pl @Radio_RMF24 pic.twitter.com/1Zl66upkp8 — RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026 The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. In 2023, under President Joe Biden, it established its first permanent military garrison in Poland at Camp Kościuszko in the city of Poznań. The following year, a US missile defence base opened in Redzikowo on Poland’s northern Baltic coast. This week, the mayor of Poznań, Jacek Jaśkowiak, told newspaper Fakt that his city was one of two locations being considered for the planned new US base. Recent Polish media reports have also identified the provinces of Lower Silesia and West Pomerania as potential locations. While the Trump administration has chastised many NATO member states for failing to meet the alliance’s defence spending targets, it has hailed Poland, whose defence budget is one of NATO’s highest in relation to GDP, as a “model ally”. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has begun paying state benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, has confirmed. Poland was recently ordered to start recognising such marriages by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). Dziemianowicz-Bąk says there are indications that Polish same-sex couples are now travelling abroad to marry so as to gain rights in Poland, where domestic law still does not allow them to form recognised unions. Wiedzieliście, że ZUS wypłaca już pierwsze zasiłki "małżeństwom jednopłciowym" po transkrypcji aktów wydanych za granicą❓❓❓ To już wiecie 👇 pic.twitter.com/W99ymV3T31 — ɐllǝnuɐɯı (@szef_dywizji) September 18, 2026 In November 2025, the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states, finding that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life. In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry. In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May. At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation. All Polish registry offices can now recognise foreign same-sex marriages, after a new regulation went into force. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality warned local authorities they will be breaking the law if they do not comply with the new rules https://t.co/EWGkuvm7EE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships. However, speaking to news service Wirtualna Polska on Friday, Dziemianowicz-Bąk confirmed that “the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) is already paying the first care allowances to same-sex couples”. Such allowances are paid to someone who is required to provide care for a spouse. The level of the allowance is set at 80% of the recipient’s average salary from the last 12 months, and it is available for up to 14 days per calendar year. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Dziemianowicz-Bąk welcomed the fact that “ZUS, one of the most important institutions, knows and understands that love is love, marriage is marriage, and these rights will be respected”. She is from The Left (Lewica), a junior partner in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and the most enthusiastic supporter of LGBT+ rights. The minister confirmed that her colleague from The Left, Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s plenipotentiary for equality, is “in dialogue with the finance ministry and National Revenue Administration (KAS)” to ensure that same-sex couples who married abroad receive the tax benefits available to other married couples. Dziemianowicz-Bąk also argued that the right-wing opposition and conservative President Karol Nawrocki are unintentionally encouraging Polish same-sex couples to marry by preventing the government from introducing a domestic law on recognising same-sex relationships. In July, Nawrocki vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to obtain certain rights available to married couples, including relating to taxation, property, and access to medical information. However, it would not have allowed same-sex couples to marry or even form civil partnerships. Instead, they would have signed a contract before a notary, formalising their relationship. Yet this step was still too far for Nawrocki, who said that it threatened the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed government bills granting certain rights to unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, for the first time in Poland. He argued that the proposal would have threatened the institution of marriage https://t.co/UXdrNfGfup — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Last week, the ruling coalition attempted to overrule the president’s veto in parliament, which requires the support of a three-fifths majority. However, the vote fell short of that figure after the right-wing opposition voted to uphold the veto. Dziemianowicz-Bąk said that the government’s opponents were “essentially encouraging marriage equality” because they left same-sex couples with only one option to have their relationships recognised: getting married abroad and then having the certificate transcribed into the Polish registry. She told Wirtualna Polska that “we’ve heard indications” that this is precisely what such couples are now doing. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. Over 62% are now in favour, up from 52% last year and just 25% in 2011, when the question was first asked https://t.co/Y9ydpbwsoU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 However, opposition figures have argued that recognition of same-sex marriages violates Poland’s constitution, article 18 of which says: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” In July, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which has a majority of judges appointed by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, ruled that the government’s regulation allowing the transcription of foreign same-sex marriages is unconstitutional. But the government regards the TK as illegitimate since it contains judges unlawfully appointed under PiS. It therefore ignores the tribunal’s rulings. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Dziemianowicz-Bąk’s announcement that ZUS has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples, Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said that it showed how “the left is ready to trample every law, including the constitution, just to get their way”. “What drives them and what they believe in is ideology, and what guides them is the instinct for domination,” added Bosak, who is also a deputy speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. World.title: Poland’s Catholic church recruits priests from Africa and Asia to stave off vocations crisis
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Marcin Choduń (published in cooperation with Tygodnik Powszechny) With the number of Poles training to be priests falling steadily, Catholic parishes are increasingly looking beyond Europe to fill the gaps. Father Fransiskus Laka will never forget his first day in Poland. When he stepped out of the arrivals hall at Warsaw’s Okęcie (now Chopin) airport in October 1999, he thought he would not last long. Why? The bitter chill in the air. “It was only seven degrees,” he laughs. It is not surprising that the young man from Indonesia was having second thoughts. At home, a cool day meant 25°C. Now, though, having spent 27 years in Poland, no weather fazes him. In the middle of winter, he will sometimes even go out in just a T-shirt to shovel snow or bring wood for the stove. Father Fransiskus has settled in the village of Brzegi, near Zakopane in southern Poland, where he has been parish priest for the last two years. And the mountainous Podhale region it is part of still has long, cold and snowy winters. Father Fransiskus, a Verbite, is not the only foreign Roman Catholic priest working in Poland, where around 70% of the population is Catholic. Their numbers are growing every year in response to the rising shortage of Polish priests. Polish dioceses are increasingly keen to invite young foreigners to study at their seminaries. Poland’s shortage of priests Most of those invited are from Africa. In Kielce, for example, there are currently two seminarians from the Central African Republic and seven from Angola. The Tarnów seminary also trained a priest from the Central African Republic in recent years (ordained as a deacon in the nearby village of Szynwałd in 2024). In the diocese of Ełk, Bishop Jerzy Mazur announced in a letter read out in churches in 2023 that he would be combating the shortage of priests by inviting clergy from Africa to the diocesan seminary. In return for receiving training in Poland, the newly ordained priests were to spend at least a few years working in the region. Previously, the support of retired priests had been sufficient. But, as the shortage grew, the curia even considered reducing the number of services or merging parishes. That was when the idea of seeking help from abroad came about. Just one new priest was ordained in Łódź, Poland's fourth largest city, this year – the lowest figure ever recorded One church figure admits there has been a “dramatic decline” in interest in the priesthood while the head of a seminary calls it a “crisis” https://t.co/QuwKsoPSg3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2023 “Priests from Poland increasingly work for as long as their health permits,” says Andrzej Kobyliński, a priest and ethicist from Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University in Warsaw. “However, that doesn’t change the fact that, in a few years’ time, we’ll have a staffing shortfall, because Polish seminaries are more and more deserted.” In recent years, a lack of recruits has led to several seminaries merging or closing down. The Wrocław, Legnica and Świdnica seminaries have been combined into one institution – which in reality means the two smaller schools being transferred to the big city. Clerical students in Kalisz have met a similar fate, having to go to Częstochowa to study, while seminarians from Elbląg have been sent to Olsztyn. The seminaries in Łowicz and Bydgoszcz have closed, and education in Drohiczyn and Sandomierz has been suspended. “The changes are happening at such an alarming rate that at present over a dozen seminaries will need to be closed,” says Kobyliński. “Let’s take the Płock diocese. You could say that the students in the seminary there are being put through a mental ordeal.” “Since there are currently 13 seminarians studying in seven year groups, that means that some years are empty or only have one or two people. That causes terrible loneliness. Because how can you survive seven years on your own?” For Kobyliński, the Ełk diocese is a symbol of the changes that are coming. This year, it only ordained one deacon – from Togo, West Africa. A new home in Poland The deacon’s name is Roger and he arrived in Poland a few years ago, along with another prospective priest from Togo who decided to return home for personal reasons. “There are currently seven people studying in our seminary, three of them from Africa. Apart from Roger, we have two more, from Ghana,” says Marcin Maczan, chancellor of the Ełk curia. According to him, however, the presence of African seminarians in Ełk is not only a response to the shortage of priests. “Bishop Jerzy Mazur, who himself spent several years working in Ghana and in the past was the head of the missions committee of the Polish Episcopal Conference, is familiar with the realities of mission dioceses. He knows very well that they can always use help in training priests.” “So these two ideas were combined: training a priest for his home diocese in Africa and his ministry in Poland for eight to ten years after ordination. All in line with the terms of the agreements that the bishop of Ełk made with bishops in Africa,” Maczan says. These agreements vary. Some priests return to their home dioceses shortly after ordination – seminarians from Kielce, for instance. Others remain for many years, such as Father Fransiskus Laka, whose stay in Poland is prolonged by the congregation’s provincial superior every three years. Poland was not his first choice. Shortly before being ordained, each of the clerical students in Fransiskus’s seminary, the Divine Word Missionaries in Pieniężno, northeastern Poland, was supposed to name three countries where they wished to serve. He chose Ecuador, Nicaragua and, in last place, Poland. Usually, one of the first two options is selected, but the provincial superior suggested otherwise. A surprised Fransiskus agreed, and he has never regretted his decision. After spending the first four years in the parish in Pieniężno, he returned to the seminary to become a prefect, responsible for keeping order. In this period, he travelled the length and breadth of Poland to lead retreats in parishes. He then spent seven years as a curate in Chludów, near Poznań, before in 2024 becoming the priest of the parish of St Anthony in Brzegi in the Podhale region. “I arrived on 8 December – so almost immediately I had Christmas pastoral visits to make to parishioners’ homes,” says Father Fransiskus. “They really welcomed me very warmly. They often help me – show me how to light the stove, or leave food outside my door. I learn hard work, humility, patience and faith from them. The mountains are tough terrain – you really need grit to survive.” Poland became home. Fransiskus feels safe here – despite growing hostility towards foreigners, which is particularly visible in the public and online space (foreign ministry statistics confirm that in 2024-2025 the total number of hate crimes reported in Poland increased by more than 50% – from 760 to almost 1,200 cases). “I’ve never yet encountered any hostile behaviour towards me,” says Fransiskus. Although he regularly visits his home island of Lembata, there are many things in Indonesia that he can no longer accept. The organisation of mass, for example: if it is supposed to begin, say, at 7 a.m., worshippers turn up just before 9. They don’t understand why Fransiskus sees this as a problem. Or a bus journey – when the driver passes his house, he’ll usually take a break to have lunch and play with his children. “The passengers wait patiently and no one thinks anything of it,” laughs Fransiskus. The Togolese footballing priest Father Romuald Mawakina Tchilabalo Mozou, from Togo (pictured top), is a newer arrival in Poland. His stay in the country is on the same basis as Fransiskus – an interdiocesan agreement extended every three years. Romuald has only been here seven years, but already speaks impeccable Polish, with barely a trace of a foreign accent. Upon arriving in Poland, he learned the language intensively – for seven months, from Monday to Saturday, seven hours a day. “I knew from the outset that if I couldn’t communicate well with the faithful, I wouldn’t build any relationship with them,” he says. Romuald was born in the village of Kaza, near Sotouboua. His father was a French teacher in the local primary school. And so his first language was French – he only learned Kabije, the ethnic language in northern Togo, in later years. His family is Catholic. And their neighbours? A mixture, just like everywhere else in Togo: the majority are Muslims, but there are also some Catholics and followers of traditional faiths. The proportion of people in Poland who are religious non-believers has risen to a record 14% while those who attend Sunday mass have fallen to a low of 34%. But a large majority of Poles still identify as believers and Catholics https://t.co/2yqrLePAsw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 23, 2024 The Mozou family are very religious. As a young boy, Romuald and his family would pray together daily, and this was what first brought him into indirect contact with Poland: every evening, along with his parents, two sisters and two brothers, he recited Saint Faustina Kowalska’s Chaplet of the Divine Mercy. He also associated Poland with John Paul II – to date the only pope to have visited Togo. Romuald’s great passion has always been football. His dream of a professional career led him to neglect his studies, until his father made things clear: first school, then football. While at high school, however, Romuald started to consider the priesthood. After taking his exams, he began studying in a seminary in Lomé, the Togolese capital. Three years in, the bishop proposed that he go to Poland to study at the seminary in Opole. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 As a dean, Father Romuald gained hands-on experience in Krapkowice. After his ordination in May 2024, he became a curate in Opole (and from August this year he will be based in nearby Ujazd). I ask him how the new parishioners responded to him. “Well, to be honest, they were a little surprised at first,” he laughed. “But that’s hardly surprising – after all, I’m the first priest from Africa to serve in the Opole diocese. They gave me a very warm welcome, though – I’ve never encountered any unfriendly gestures or words from them.” In Poland, Romuald’s childhood passion has been rekindled: he’s playing football again. First for Maciowakrze, a club playing in Klasa B (the eighth tier of the Polish league system), then in Żywocice, in Klasa A. He now plays as a striker for GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory. “I don’t know if I’ll return to my homeland – everything is possible,” Romuald says. “I feel good in both Poland and Togo.” Polish dioceses recruiting in Africa In 2026, 196 priests are to be ordained in Poland – 12 fewer than last year and some 205 down on the figure from 2013. The number of dioceses in which no ordinations took place because of a lack of candidates is growing – seven this year, compared to six in 2025. “We actually have a vocations crisis everywhere in Europe, so we will be looking for priests in other parts of the world,” says Andrzej Kobyliński. “Essentially, we have two areas where we can recruit candidates for the priesthood. Mainly Africa, and possibly India, but the experiences of German and Italian dioceses show that priests from India find it harder to settle in Europe.” “Latin America is not an option, as the Catholic church there is facing its own crisis of a mass exodus to Pentecostal churches,” he adds. “So in the future we will definitely be working intensively with African dioceses. This is an enormous historical change, because it was once Poland and Europe that sent missionaries to Africa.” One of the lads Przywory, a village near Opole, the GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory home pitch. Seven p.m. Training has started. Father Romuald Mozou is a little late, so he rushes into the dressing room. “Romek, you’re doing push-ups as punishment,” laugh his teammates when he appears on the pitch. Everyone calls him by this Polish diminutive – Romek. The team’s coach, Marcin Chudala, admits that the players like to have a laugh at the footballing priest’s expense. “Sometimes we joke when he’s sitting on the bench staring at his phone: ‘What are you doing, Romek – confessing?’ The banter can be cruel,” says the coach. But he also admits that Romek’s presence has left its mark on the team. Less swearing, for example. Even if there is nothing to suggest that Romek is a priest. “We treat him just like one of the lads from the playground,” Chudala says. The original version of this interview can be seen here. Translated by Ben Koschalka. Marcin Choduń is a journalist and translator of German and English. He publishes his articles mainly in Tygodnik Powszechny and Duży Format, a supplement of Gazeta Wyborcza. In 2012, he was nominated for the Grand Press Award in the reportage category for his article “The Blood of a Skinhead, the Blood of a Jew”. World.title: Poland to expand warning siren network along Ukraine border amid Russian attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland plans to have more than 1,000 warning sirens in the eastern Lublin province by the end of the year in response to increased Russian attacks in Ukraine near the Polish border, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński has announced. The Polish government is also working on an application that would use Cell Broadcast technology to turn mobile phones into warning devices, allowing them to function like sirens in a crisis, the minister added. Minister @MKierwinski w Lublinie:💬Budujemy system ochrony ludności niemal od podstaw. W województwie lubelskim na początku 2024 roku było około 30 syren, które można było uruchomić zdalnie. Dziś jest ich prawie 350, a do końca tego roku będzie ich ponad tysiąc. To pokazuje, jak… pic.twitter.com/6uWAgcNrJh — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 19, 2026 Speaking in Lublin on Saturday, Kierwiński said that the region now has almost 350 automatic sirens, compared to just 30 at the start of 2024. The number is expected to triple to over 1,000 by the end of this year. “Jet-powered drones and missiles are increasingly flying near the Polish border” and Poland is therefore “turning to tools designed to counter the associated threats,” Kierwiński said, quoted by news website OKO Press, adding that the government had to build Poland’s civil protection system “almost from scratch”. As part of these efforts, Poland’s fire service, working with the Lublin governor, is now rolling out a project to identify and mark the province’s nearly 3,500 shelters. Last year, Poland launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in the case of an emergency. By the end of the year, Poland also wants to introduce an application that would allow it to “take over” residents’ phones “to function like a siren”, Kierwiński added, without providing any further details. Residents in areas close to the Ukrainian border have heard warning sirens during Russian attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks and received alerts through the state warning system. The opposition has criticised the alerts for not giving residents clear instructions on what to do when the sirens sound. In response, the ministry has stepped up its public information campaign, including a television and social media campaign on emergency preparedness. Additionally, more than 500 fire stations in the eastern Lublin and Subcarpathian provinces held training over the weekend on how to respond to emergency alerts. The sessions were part of a wider campaign that has already involved 630,000 people across Poland. Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats https://t.co/MS0APufAmq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Poland has stepped up preparations along its eastern border following a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation follows a number of incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski described the attacks in the border area as “another escalation” by Russia, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. During his visit to Ukraine last week, Tusk announced that Poland had joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries working together to develop an integrated air defence system for the continent. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
