World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019041/Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.title: Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019041/Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.content:
An incident at a Shanghai stand-up show in which customers who bought tickets through unofficial channels were denied entry because of the venue’s ticket identity-verification requirements has sparked public debate over China’s ticket scalping market.

The topic has surged to Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 57 million views as of Friday. Many argued that making exceptions for scalped-ticket holders is unfair to legitimate buyers and could further fuel the practice.

The show, held Sept. 11 at the city’s Majestic Theatre, was headlined by Fu Hang, a comedian known for his high-energy performances and distinctive delivery. To combat ticket scalping, show organizer Standby had implemented a system requiring attendees to present their ID cards and undergo real-name checks upon entry.

The scene quickly became chaotic, as ticketholders whose ID cards did not match the identity information provided at the time of purchase were not allowed entry. Videos of the incident circulating online showed a large crowd gathered outside the theater, demanding entry, and delaying the show’s start time. Because of the disorder, all ticket holders were eventually allowed in, and Fu extended his performance for 20 minutes to make up for the delay.

Chinese law prohibits ticket scalping for profit, which can result in administrative penalties, including detention and fees. In 2023, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism and the Ministry of Public Security jointly issued a notice requiring shows with a capacity over 5,000 to adopt real-name ticket purchases and admission.

Ulala Li, a Shanghai resident and comedy fan who bought her ticket through an official channel, told Sixth Tone she felt overlooked by Standby. “Shouldn’t the audience members who entered the venue properly and were left waiting for 20 minutes have received an apology and compensation?” she said.

“I think there’s a legitimate place for a secondary market. But when there are too many professional scalpers, they can seriously disrupt the healthy functioning of the market,” she added.

Tickets for Fu’s show were priced between 280 and 580 yuan ($42 to $86). According to domestic media, one attendee told Fu that he had paid 3,500 yuan for a scalped ticket — roughly seven times its original price.

Event organizer Standby said on Sept. 12 that it would cover documented losses caused by the delayed performance, including cancellation, train and flight ticket change fees, and additional accommodation expenses.

A day later, Shanghai police announced that three scalpers who bought 104 tickets to the show and resold them at higher prices had been placed under criminal coercive measures. The three reportedly made more than 18,000 yuan in illegal profits.

Three others also received administrative penalties for reselling eight tickets they had purchased through official channels, making more than 570 yuan in profit, the police added.

An audience member was also punished for starting a widely spread rumor online that “80% of the show’s tickets were sold through scalpers.”

Internet celebrity and stand-up comedy commentator Luo Yonghao criticized Standby’s actions in a popular Weibo post on Saturday, saying that “ticket scalpers can never be completely eliminated.” He suggested introducing regulated secondary ticketing platforms to legalize ticket resales and called for legislation on the issue.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: A Villar split: Why is Mark Villar breaking ranks with sister Camille?
World.content:
Unlike his sister, Senator-judge Mark Villar does not boycott the voting for the lowering of the conviction threshold in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial

Two roads diverged in the Senate on Wednesday, September 23 — and the Villar siblings took different ones.

Senator-judge Mark Villar broke ranks with his sister, Senator-judge Camille Villar, and the Senate minority bloc in a surprise vote on two key motions during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court heard oral arguments from the defense and prosecution panels on the September 8 appeal of Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo seeking to overturn the July 6 ruling of impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, which set the voting threshold for Duterte’s conviction to 16.

Tulfo also wanted the court to revisit the denominator for the voting threshold amid the absence of Senator-judges Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta, and Jinggoy Estrada.

Legarda remains on extended medical leave abroad, while Dela Rosa is in hiding due to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court over alleged crimes against humanity stemming from the Duterte administration’s drug war.

Marcoleta and Estrada are detained over separate plunder charges.

But before the court proceeded with the voting, Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano — who also serves as the Senate minority leader — made a last-minute bid to defer the vote, arguing that the impeachment court had no authority to interpret the Constitution.

Members of the Senate minority bloc, including Camille, voted in favor of Cayetano, except Mark, who abstained. Thirteen senator-judges then moved to junk the appeal, paving the way for the subsequent voting on Tulfo’s motion.

Mark voted to approve Tulfo’s motion. He was also the sole member of the Senate minority bloc present during the voting. Other minority senators opted to boycott it and not participate in the afternoon proceedings.

Why was Mark voting differently?

For Senator-judge Imee Marcos, the older Villar’s recent graft complaints might be related to the voting decisions.

Play Video

“Well, we are aware of what he is experiencing. So, let us see his decisions,” Marcos told reporters.

Pressed for details, she added: “We know what’s happening with the minority senators. We are all being attacked.”

The Office of the Ombudsman previously said graft complaints were now pending against members of the Villar family due to allegations related to their PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation. This includes the senator-siblings, their parents and former senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, and businessman Paolo Villar.

Mark’s divergence from the bloc came as other minority members face their own legal or political troubles. Apart from the four absentee senators, Padilla was issued a subpoena in relation to the obstruction of justice complaint filed against him over his alleged involvement in Dela Rosa’s escape from Senate premises in May.

Litigator and Free Legal Assistance Group member Raffy Aquino said in a Rappler interview that the Villar siblings’ votes could point to one of two things: they either “demonstrated how it is to vote according to one’s conscience,” or it was a strategy to have a foot on either side of the door. – Rappler.com

World.title: PH leads ASEAN, partner navies in West Philippine Sea drills
World.content:
ADMM-PLUS DRILLS. Ten navy vessels from eight different countries sail behind the BRP Jose Rizal on September 23, 2026, during a joint cooperative activity in waters off the coast of Zambales.

A Chinese Navy vessel is seen close to where eight countries are sailing for the drills, but it does not respond to challenges from the Philippine Navy

ABOARD THE BRP JOSE RIZAL – In waters off the coast of Zambales on the morning of Wednesday, September 23, the domineering figure of the helicopter destroyer JS Ise inched closer and closer to the Navy’s flagship, the BRP Jose Rizal.

It was a welcome sight — a signal that a joint activity under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) would soon commence.

Dotting the waters around Rizal was an impressive array of gray ships — the Philippine Navy’s own BRP Tarlac, two from India, two from New Zealand, and one each from Singapore, Brunei, Australia, the United States, and Japan. All eleven ships from eight countries were in these waters for the sea phase of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security (EWG-MS).

ADMM-Plus is the premier platform for the region’s defense ministers to take up a long list of issues. For the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, the focus was on maritime security and environmental resilience in the face of climate change.

On Wednesday, the Rizal was the lead ship for formation drills and a medical evacuation, while the Japanese forces led search and rescue efforts. The BRP Tarlac, meanwhile, practiced aiding a grounded oil tanker and cross-deck landing drills.

China did not participate in the sea phase of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, although they could have. Representatives from China were present at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS in Zambales on Monday, September 21.

Reporters embarked on the Rizal, including a team from Rappler, saw at least one People’s Liberation Army Navy or Chinese military warship close to the area where the vessels were sailing together. The Rizal issued radio challenges to the Chinese vessel but did not get a response.

Regional cooperation

The sea phase and even the meetings on land aren’t just for showing off new and old assets.

They’re meant to test and practice interoperability, or the ability of different navies and units to work with each other. On a more human level, it’s about establishing familiarity and trust between the armed forces of the bloc and its partners.

Aside from chairing ASEAN, Manila is also chair of the ADMM. The Philippines, with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. as host, is expected to host ministers of the ADMM-Plus before 2026 ends.

“Our collaboration and cooperation not merely in response but in early prepositioning, working together, and in detection becomes more critical,” said Teodoro on Monday, at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EGW-MS.

Alongside the joint cooperative activity is a Future Leaders Program or FLP, which brings junior officers of different navies together to “engage their counterparts on climate change, maritime security, and key topics, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and Critical Underwater Infrastructure security.”

In the region — and in ASEAN especially — maritime security is a major concern. The South China Sea, where up to a third of global trade passes through, encompasses several ASEAN countries. It is also the flashpoint for regional tensions, mostly between Southeast Asian claimant nations and superpower China, which is part of the ADMM-Plus and is an ASEAN dialogue partner.

Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and the Philippines are all claimants to various areas and features of the South China Sea.

Wednesday’s drills were within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, an area where Manila should have sovereign rights or the exclusive rights to exploit and responsibility to protect marine resources. Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, including the Philippine EEZ, which is part of the West Philippine Sea.

China has also refused to recognize the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award.

Tensions between Manila and Beijing have meant confrontations in the West Philippine Sea for the Philippines’ maritime frontliners. China has had tense confrontations, including skirmishes, with other ASEAN claimants in the past.

ASEAN, with Manila as chair, has aspirations of concluding a Code of Conduct on the South China Sea with China before 2026 ends. Teodoro has publicly cast doubt over Beijing’s trustworthiness. – Rappler.com

World.title: In the Public Square: Making sense of the BARMM elections
World.content:
LIVE

What happened during the regional elections? What do the results tell us? And what happens now?

The country passed through a historic moment only a few days ago — but how many Filipinos were even aware of it? The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao held its first parliamentary elections, with 80 seats in the regional parliament and the future of peace and development at stake.

World.title: Carlos, Eldrew Yulo anchor PH to sixth in Asian Games team event
World.content:
SQUAD. Carlos Yulo, Eldrew Yulo, Justine Ace de Leon, Juancho Miguel Besana, and Zachary Nunez of the Philippine men's artistic gymnastics team with their coaches in the 2026 Asian Games.

Set to compete in the floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars finals, Carlos Yulo flashes medal-winning potential, with an Asian Games gold also well within reach

MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo anchored the Philippines to a sixth-place finish in the team all-around event of the men’s artistic gymnastics in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as he and his teammates got some practice in before the apparatus finals in the coming days.

The team, composed of Carlos, his younger brother Eldrew, Juancho Miguel Besana, Justine Ace de Leon, and Zachary Nunez, totaled 227.359 points across the six apparatuses in the eight-team final.

China topped the event for the third consecutive edition, registering 255.095 points to edge reigning Olympic champion Japan for the gold.

Despite being led by Olympic individual all-around gold medalists Daiki Hashimoto and Shinnosuke Oka, Japan settled for silver with 253.826 points.

Chinese Taipei finished a distant third with 239.896 points for the bronze, while Kazakhstan (237.596) and South Korea (236.359) placed fourth and fifth, respectively, ahead of the Philippines.

Set to compete in the floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars finals, Carlos showed medal-winning potential, with a gold also well within reach.

Carlos posted the highest mark in floor exercise with 14.266 points, netted the fourth-best score in vault with 14.566, and tied for the fifth-highest mark in parallel bars with 14.166.

Meanwhile, Eldrew recorded 13.966 points in vault, 13.166 in horizontal bar, 13.0 in floor exercise, 12.233 in rings, 11.933 in parallel bars, and 11.366 in pommel horse — the only one in the team to see action in all apparatuses.

In the team event, only three of the five gymnasts compete in each apparatus, with their scores combined to determine the total.

De Leon contributed 13.833 points in vault, 12.533 in rings, and 10.933 in floor exercise, Nunez added 12.333 in pommel horse and 12.066 in horizontal bar, while Besana chipped in 11.933 points in pommel horse, 11.733 in horizontal bar, and 10.0 in parallel bars as the Philippines came in ahead of Vietnam (214.428) and Singapore (200.928).

Aside from Carlos, Eldrew vies for a medal in floor exercise and horizontal bar, while Besana shoots for a podium finish in vault.

The floor exercise final is scheduled on Thursday, September 24, while the vault, parallel bars, and horizontal bars finals are set on Friday, September 25. – Rappler.com

World.title: MEDAL TALLY: 2026 Asian Games
World.content:
Bannered by champions Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, Nesthy Petecio, and Annie Ramirez, the Philippines eyes an eight-gold haul at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan

MANILA, Philippines – Team Philippines seeks to pull off what it has not done in the Asian Games for decades.

Bannered by champions Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, Nesthy Petecio, and Annie Ramirez, the country eyes an eight-gold haul in the 20th edition of the continental showpiece in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

The Philippines has not surpassed four gold medals in a single Asian Games since 1962, with the country matching that tally in the past two editions in Indonesia in 2018 and China in 2023.

But with the collection of talent the Philippines has at its disposal, sports officials believe that is an achievable goal.

China remains the standard, having won the overall title in each of the last 11 editions since 1982, while host Japan and South Korea stand as the other perennial powers in the field.

World.title: [DECODED] When regulation lags, how do organizations protect their truth?
World.content:
The more advertisers invest in truth, the more trust they build — not just for their respective organizations, but even for our information ecosystem

In case you missed it, the Ad Standards Council (ASC) released last week its guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence in advertising. ASC’s Circular No. 2026-014 mandates that:

Advertisers utilize appropriate human oversight, maintaining full responsibility for all claims and depictions in their respective ads.

Ads created, generated, or materially enhanced using AI include a disclosure.

Disclosures must be clear and reasonably conspicuous, including use of words like “AI-generated,” “AI-assisted,” “Created with AI,” or “Contains AI-generated content.”

Hello, I am Iris B. Gonzales. I started my career in advertising back in 2018. Today, I am a Senior Brand Strategist at The Nerve and am also enrolled at the FEU Institute of Law. I chose both paths because of a growing unease about influence operations and how they affect our information landscape and, ultimately, the democratic systems we seek to uphold.

We at The Nerve have studied how influence operations in the Philippines can mislead audiences, manipulate narratives, and damage organizations’ reputations at scale. These operations now involve synthetic, AI-generated content — and the preliminary report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, co-chaired by The Nerve’s Head of Global Strategy Maria Ressa, points out that such content slowly erodes our ability to distinguish authentic from generated content.

That’s a slippery slope toward distrust of media that could otherwise be truthful, termed the “liar’s dividend” in the UN report.

READ: [DECODED] How crises and disinformation impact brands and reputations

This is why I welcome the ASC’s move to require advertisers to disclose AI use in their content. To be clear, ASC stated that the use of AI by itself doesn’t render an ad misleading or deceptive. The circular merely aims to promote transparency in AI use and compliance with existing laws.

An added benefit, in my view, is that these labels will allow us as consumers to better recognize the tell-tale signs of AI-generated content, and hopefully apply the same discipline to the other content that we consume.

But that discipline only works if the labels are honest in the first place. Advertisers play a crucial role in preserving this authenticity. The more advertisers invest in truth, the more trust they build — not just for their respective organizations, but even for our information ecosystem.

This ASC circular is just one of many discussions we should be having now that AI is developing faster than our ability to measure or govern it. When regulation lags, brands and organizations are often left to police themselves, leaving them vulnerable to reputational risks. For those navigating this shift, the question now becomes: are you ready when that risk hits your organization?

If you’re looking to protect your organization’s reputation in the age of AI, join us in our Crisis Management Masterclass on Friday, October 9. You may also join more of these discussions exploring human values during this year’s Social Good Summit. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kayla Sanchez skips event to get better shot at Asian Games medal
World.content:
STAR. Swimmer Kayla Sanchez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Kayla Sanchez turns her focus on the women's 50m freestyle as she looks to deliver the Philippines its first swimming medal in the Asian Games since 1998

MANILA, Philippines – Kayla Sanchez carries the Philippines’ best hope of ending its 28-year drought for a swimming medal in the Asian Games.

And so, national coaches opted to preserve the 25-year-old star for the women’s 50m freestyle on Thursday, September 24, at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre in Japan as she skipped the women’s 100m backstroke event on Wednesday, September 23.

“There are things we cannot control, there are things we can. Let’s focus on what we can control. So, if we can rest Kayla and prepare her better for tomorrow’s 50-meter event, where she has a very, very good chance of winning a gold, we gave her a rest,” said national coach Ryan Arabejo, a former Olympian and multi-time Southeast Asian Games champion.

Sanchez came oh-so close to becoming the first Filipino swimmer to win a medal in the Asian Games since Raymond Papa bagged a pair of bronzes in the 1998 edition as she finished fourth in the women’s 100m freestyle on Tuesday, September 22.

The Filipina-Canadian clocked 53.65 seconds, just .18 seconds behind China’s Cheng Yujie, who bagged the bronze with a time of 53.47 seconds. Hong Kong’s Siobhan Haughey (52.45) and China’s Yu Yiting (53.21) captured the gold and silver, respectively.

Freestyle is one of Sanchez’s strongest suits.

Back when she still represented Canada, Sanchez was part of the women’s 4x100m freestyle team that scored a silver in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics.

Sanchez also won the women’s 100m freestyle gold and 50m freestyle silver in the 2025 SEA Games in Bangkok, Thailand.

“Anything goes in the 50 meters. It’s anybody’s game, especially in a short-distance event,” said Arabejo.

Sanchez is expected to sit out the women’s 4x200m freestyle relay set on Thursday as well. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan’s New People’s Council Holds First Session, Elects Koshanov As Chair
World.content:
ASTANA – Yerlan Koshanov has been elected Chair of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council), a new consultative body established to strengthen dialogue between citizens and the state, following a proposal by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

Speaking at a Sept. 23 first session, Tokayev proposed Koshanov’s candidacy, highlighting his extensive experience in public service and previous work as Chair of the Mazhilis, the lower house of Parliament.

“This is an authoritative position with constitutional status. Therefore, I believe it should be held by a person well known to society, capable of ensuring effective dialogue between citizens and the authorities,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev also described Koshanov as a responsible professional with extensive public service experience and said his work in the Mazhilis had contributed to implementing large-scale reforms.

“I am confident that as Chair of the Khalyk Kenesi, he will work productively and make a significant contribution to strengthening social harmony,” he said.

Tokayev highlights responsibility of council members

Tokayev also noted that the new consultative body includes highly qualified specialists and citizens who enjoy public trust and are known for their commitment to the country. According to him, the council brings together prominent public and state figures, entrepreneurs, activists and representatives of various professional fields.

“Honest service to the interests of the country is a great honor and a sacred duty. Each member of the Khalyk Kenesi bears a special responsibility,” Tokayev said.

He added that council members are expected to help strengthen unity and social harmony through their active participation. President Tokayev is expected to elaborate on the tasks and priorities of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi at the Sept. 24 session of its inaugural term.

Council brings together 126 members

The Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi consists of 126 members, each serving four-year terms. The composition was formed according to three equal categories, with 42 members representing each: ethnocultural associations, major public associations and other non-governmental organizations, and public councils.

The council represents all regions of Kazakhstan. Twenty members were selected from among maslikhat (local administrative body) deputies, including five who chair maslikhats in two cities of national significance and three regions. Some of the members also hold senior positions in hospitals, libraries, a metallurgical plant, sports organizations and regional business councils. Another 22 members represent regional and city public councils, including four council chairs.

Sixteen Khalyk Kenesi members have previous parliamentary experience. Thirteen previously served in the Mazhilis, four in the Senate, while one served in both chambers. Most of those with parliamentary experience come from the previous convocation.

The council includes 40 women and 86 men, with women accounting for 31.7% of its membership. Representatives of various ethnic groups account for 46 members, or 36.5%. The membership includes academics, including three members of the National Academy of Sciences, as well as teachers, doctors, journalists, writers, lawyers, trade union leaders and entrepreneurs. The council also includes an Olympic champion, an Olympic silver medalist and heads of sports federations, as well as two former ministers.

World.title: Kazakhstan Brings Broader Agenda to UN General Assembly
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is heading into this year’s United Nations General Assembly debate with an expanding agenda that stretches from nuclear disarmament and peacekeeping to water security, artificial intelligence and sustainable development, as the country’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi leads the country’s delegation in New York.

Foreign Minister Tileuberdi is representing Kazakhstan at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, whose annual general debate opened Sept. 22 amid wars, geopolitical tensions and mounting pressure on the international system. He is expected to deliver Kazakhstan’s national statement during the debate.

The delegation is also expected to meet with UN leadership and heads of UN agencies, representatives of the OSCE and the International Committee of the Red Cross, among others.

Bilateral meetings are scheduled with foreign ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Hungary, Jordan, Canada, Cyprus, Kuwait, Moldova, Poland, Russia, Slovenia, Ukraine, Switzerland, and El Salvador, among other countries.

Deepening engagement with UN

The high-level week comes as Kazakhstan seeks to build on more than three decades of engagement with the UN while broadening its traditional focus on nuclear nonproliferation into newer areas including digital cooperation, climate policy and regional water security.

Kazakhstan joined the UN on March 2, 1992, and opened its first UN representation in Almaty the following year. It later served as a non-permanent member of the Security Council in 2017-2018, becoming the first Central Asian country to hold a seat on the council.

Kazakhstan has also sought a broader institutional role within the UN system, serving on bodies including the Security Council, Human Rights Council and Economic and Social Council and securing seats on several UN commissions.

One of Kazakhstan’s most significant recent UN initiatives has been the creation of a regional UN center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty. Kazakhstan has presented the center as part of a broader effort to give the region a stronger institutional role within the UN development system.

Kazakhstan has also expanded its role in UN peacekeeping. According to the Foreign Ministry, 167 Kazakh personnel currently serve in UN peacekeeping operations, including a 139-member national contingent in the Golan Heights.

Kazakhstan’s priorities are increasingly reflected in its cooperation with the UN under a new 2026-2030 cooperation framework. The country’s Foreign Ministry identifies nuclear disarmament, sustainable development, peacekeeping, AI, volunteering, environmental initiatives and water as major areas of Kazakhstan’s UN activity.

Water security is emerging as another major component of Kazakhstan’s multilateral diplomacy. Astana has proposed establishing an international water organization within the UN system, reflecting growing concern over water scarcity and cross-border water management in Central Asia.

Reshaping of international system

That engagement is unfolding as the international system itself is being reshaped. Opening the General Assembly’s General Debate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said power was shifting in three fundamental ways: among states, from governments toward powerful private corporations and individuals, and increasingly from humans to machines through artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons.

“Yet our institutions and systems of global governance continue to reflect the power realities and interests of a largely bygone age. That is the defining challenge before us,” he said.

The shift toward a multipolar world was irreversible, said Guterres, but there were two ways along this path.

One could be a “world of fragmentation and transactionalism,” which reflects the current realities. The other path, however, is towards what Guterres described as “networked multipolarity,” in which multiple centers of influence operate within common rules and international law.

“The greatest power is not the power to dominate. It is the power to build a future that works for everyone,” he said.

On climate change, Guterres described the crisis as a stark imbalance between generations and warned that the world is close to exceeding the 1.5-degree Celsius limit.

Speaking about artificial intelligence, Guterres warned that influence is becoming increasingly concentrated among those controlling data, computing power and algorithms

“The danger is not technology,” he said. “The danger is technology without accountability.”

Trump stresses power and technological competition

United States President Donald Trump offered a different emphasis, portraying artificial intelligence as a field of geopolitical competition. In his 37-minute address, he said the technology should instead be called “superintelligence” and stressed that leadership in the field would be central to future economic and strategic power.

Trump also referred directly to Kazakhstan while discussing the Gaza peace plan, thanking it among countries contributing to relief and reconstruction efforts. He later named Kazakhstan among states supporting the stabilization of Gaza through troops, police or training.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the Board of Peace charter on Jan. 22 in Davos, Switzerland, alongside leaders and representatives from 18 countries.

The debate also underscored the immediate geopolitical pressures confronting the UN system. In his address, Trump defended recent U.S. military action against Iran and called for continued economic pressure on Tehran, while warning that Washington could take further action if diplomacy failed.

Trump said the U.S. would not “allow” Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon and urged other countries to support what he called the country’s “complete economic isolation.” At the same time, he said he believed an agreement with Tehran could eventually be reached.

Central Asia’s voice becomes stronger

During the General Debate, regional leaders also pressed for changes in the international system. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov pointed to his country’s election to the UN Security Council for 2027-2028, saying support from 142 member states demonstrated Central Asia’s growing role in international affairs.

Kazakhstan became the first Central Asian state to serve on the Security Council in 2017-2018. Nearly a decade later, election of the Kyrgyz Republic for the 2027-2028 term extends the region’s representation on the council.

In his remarks, Zhaparov also called for reform of the UN and Security Council to better reflect current realities, while highlighting climate pressures facing mountain countries and the growing role of Central Asia in multilateral diplomacy.

Zhaparov also backed an expansion of Security Council membership and proposed a permanent public registry within the General Assembly to track countries’ implementation of UN resolutions and obligations.

“I believe that when cases of systematic non-implementation of United Nations’ decisions are considered, the permanent members of the Security Council should voluntarily refrain from using the veto,” said Zhaparov.

“If a mechanism designed to ensure the implementation of the organization’s decisions is systematically blocked by permanent members through the use of the veto, such practice would no longer be consistent with the spirit of the UN Charter and the principle of equal responsibility of member states,” he said.

The opening days of the General Debate have brought together several overlapping questions confronting the UN system. The issues at stake include how institutions should adapt to a more multipolar world, how states should respond to ongoing conflicts and how emerging technologies should be governed.

For Kazakhstan, those debates intersect directly with an agenda that increasingly combines its longstanding focus on nuclear security with peacekeeping, sustainable development, water cooperation and artificial intelligence.

World.title: Kazakhstan Shines at FIDE Chess Olympiad as Women Reach Second, Coaches Aid Six Teams
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s women’s chess team moved into second place at the 46th Chess Olympiad after securing its sixth consecutive victory, defeating Azerbaijan 2.5–1.5 in the sixth round.

Alua Nurman delivered the decisive point for Kazakhstan, defeating Gunay Mammadzada 1–0. Bibisara Assaubayeva, Meruert Kamalidenova and Zarina Nurgaliyeva drew their respective games. Kazakhstan now has 12 team points, level with leaders China. The two teams will meet in the seventh round on Sept. 23.

“The last two rounds have been tense. Yesterday, I had a losing position but managed to hold on. Meruert also won on the third board, and thanks to that we secured the victory. This is an Olympiad, so nothing comes easily. We will keep trying,” said Kazakhstan team member Yelnaz Kaliakhmet.

Kazakhstan’s men’s team also secured a convincing victory in the sixth round, defeating Colombia 3.5–0.5. Denis Makhnyov, Sauat Nurgaliyev and Daniyal Sapennov won their games, while Zhandos Agmanov drew. The result moved Kazakhstan to 25th place in the standings, up from its starting position of 35th.

“The Olympiad has been interesting. The guys are trying hard. My tournament is not going exactly as I would like so far, but the team supports me. Overall, we are doing well. We have a strong team. Our girls are performing very well – they have won every match, and we are supporting them,” said Kazakhstan team member Aldiyar Ansat.

Uzbekistan, the host nation, currently leads the men’s standings. Kazakhstan will face Serbia in the seventh round. The Olympiad had a rest day on Sept. 22, with the seventh round scheduled for Sept. 23. The 46th Chess Olympiad consists of 11 rounds.

Kazakh coaches prepare six foreign teams

Kazakh chess coaches have also contributed to the preparation of six foreign national teams competing at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, reported the Kazakh Chess Federation’s press service.

Under the FACI programme, teams from Jordan, Cambodia, the Kyrgyz Republic, Nepal, Pakistan and Turkmenistan prepared for the Olympiad with Kazakh coaches during the current season. Turkmenistan held a two-week training camp in May–June at the Chess House in Kokshetau under Grandmaster Alexander Rakhmanov. The team continued training online during the summer before returning to Kazakhstan for another two-week camp ahead of the Olympiad.

The preparation produced immediate results, with both Turkmenistan’s men’s and women’s teams winning their opening-round matches 4–0. The men defeated Timor-Leste, while the women beat Liechtenstein.

Other Kazakh coaches working with foreign teams include Grandmaster Petr Kostenko, who leads the Kyrgyz Republic’s men’s team; International Master Rustam Kaiyrbekov, who coaches Cambodia’s men’s team; and International Master Kirill Kuderinov, who works with Nepal’s men’s team. Kazakh coaches also worked with players from Jordan and Pakistan shortly before the Olympiad.

Kazakh specialists have previously worked with foreign teams at international competitions. At the 45th Chess Olympiad in Budapest, Dmitry Stativkin served as captain of Oman’s team, Bakhtiyar Askarov worked with Cambodia, and Zhanibek Amanov with Sri Lanka. Grandmaster Evgeny Vladimirov also coached Tajikistan’s team remotely.

World.title: Seven Years of Tokayev: Economy Rebuilt Through Resilience, Investment and Reform
World.content:
ASTANA – Seven years into Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s presidency, Kazakhstan’s economic record is increasingly defined not by a single indicator, but by the breadth of change across investment, manufacturing, infrastructure, small and medium-sized enterprises and the social sector.

The period since 2019 has also been unusually demanding. The economy has gone through the pandemic, global inflation, disrupted supply chains and a sharply altered geopolitical environment. Amid all this, the central economic question is no longer simply whether Kazakhstan has grown. It is whether growth has become more resilient and can generate greater value inside the country. The available indicators point to substantial progress, while also showing where the next phase of economic policy will be more demanding.

Growth with a broader base

Kazakhstan’s GDP per capita rose from $9,813 in 2019 to $15,006.4 in 2025, a 52.9% increase. Real GDP growth reached 6.5% in 2025, according to the updated national statistics. Transport and warehousing grew 19.4%, construction 17.5%, industry 7.7% and information and communications 6.4%.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov noted that the significance of the recent performance is less about one year’s growth than about the economy’s ability to absorb repeated external shocks.

“Over seven years, Kazakhstan has essentially passed several stress tests in a row. The pandemic, broken logistics chains, global inflation, a sharp change in the geopolitical situation and sanctions risks around Russia. Each time, the Kazakh economy adapted relatively quickly,” Sultanov said.

The 2025 figures support that argument. Growth was spread across sectors rather than concentrated exclusively in oil. Manufacturing expanded 6.4% on preliminary production data, while construction and transport posted particularly strong gains. Together, they suggest domestic investment, infrastructure development, and trade are playing a larger role in the growth mix.

At the same time, resilience should not be confused with insulation.

“But it is important to understand that dependence on external conditions has not disappeared. Oil prices, export routes, the state of the Russian and Chinese economies and global interest rates still matter greatly to us. There is also continued dependence of the budget on oil revenues,” Sultanov said.

That distinction is central to Kazakhstan’s economic trajectory: the country has become better able to absorb shocks, but the longer-term goal is to reduce the structural dependence that makes external shocks so consequential in the first place.

This has also been a recurring theme in Tokayev’s economic agenda. In his 2023 state-of-the-nation address, he called for a transition to a new economic model combining political reform with deep social and economic transformation, and identified a strong industrial foundation and greater economic self-sufficiency as key priorities.

The structural shift in industry

One of the clearest indicators of that ambition is the gradual change in the composition of GDP. In 2019, manufacturing accounted for around 11.4% of GDP, while mining accounted for 14.5%. By 2025, manufacturing had risen to around 13%, and mining had declined to around 12%, according to preliminary figures cited by Sultanov.

The shift is accompanied by a wider industrial footprint. From 2019 to 2025, 625 new industrial enterprises were established, creating 61,300 jobs. Over the same period, Kazakhstan attracted $155.8 billion in gross foreign direct investment.

“The changes are there. I would simply not hurry to declare diversification complete. The economy does not diversify faster just because we use the word. The work is permanent,” Sultanov said.

The distinction between industrial expansion and industrial competitiveness is important. Manufacturing growth becomes more meaningful when it brings technology, skilled jobs, supply chains and export capacity rather than simply assembling or processing imported inputs.

“Therefore, the next stage for Kazakhstan is not simply to increase manufacturing’s share of GDP. It is to increase the added value created inside the country,” Sultanov said.

Investment, infrastructure and connectivity

Kazakhstan’s investment proposition has also become more multidimensional.

“Kazakhstan is gradually developing a more interesting combination. There are resources. There is territory between China and Europe. There is growing transit potential. There is an industrial base. There is sufficiently developed digital infrastructure and a financial system. There is the Astana International Financial Centre. And there is an ability to work simultaneously with several major economic centers,” Sultanov said.

The country’s geography has long been described as an advantage. Under Tokayev, however, the emphasis has increasingly shifted from geography itself to the economic value that can be built around it.

In August 2025, addressing transport sector workers, Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s transport system was a driving force of the economy and that the country’s vast geography and transit potential placed transport at the core of economic growth and regional integration. The expansion of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, along with rail links and other logistics infrastructure, reflects this approach: geography is being turned into connectivity, and connectivity into an economic opportunity.

The scale of infrastructure development under President Tokayev is visible beyond transport corridors. Over seven years, 118.3 million square meters of housing were commissioned, 14,200 kilometers of roads were repaired, and construction and repair works covered 21,000 kilometers on the local road network. These investments are not only about construction volumes. Their longer-term economic value lies in whether they improve connectivity, reduce logistical costs, raise productivity and expand access to markets.

For foreign investors, Sultanov said, infrastructure is only one part of the calculation.

“Resources can bring an investor to the country. But institutions keep capital. Here we are doing substantial work, and there is still much to be done,” he said.

That makes predictability an increasingly important component of Kazakhstan’s investment model. Large industrial projects are measured in decades, not election cycles, and investors therefore pay attention to the stability of taxation, regulation, tariffs and market access.

A wider business base

The country’s economic transformation is also visible in the expansion of small and medium-sized enterprises (SME). As of the beginning of 2026, 2.36 million SMEs were registered in Kazakhstan, with 4.53 million people employed in the sector. SME employment increased by 31.6% over seven years.

The figures should be read in the context of the pandemic, which caused a temporary decline in SME employment and business activity. The subsequent recovery was particularly strong in 2022, when SME employment increased 18.3%, and the number of registered SMEs rose 19.6%.

Taken together, the data point to a broader business base than at the start of Tokayev’s current presidential term. The next economic question is how much of that base can move from domestic consumption toward productivity, investment and exports.

Growth and the household economy

The economic transformation has also brought improvements in several social indicators.

Average monthly nominal wages reached 443,300 tenge (US$990) in 2025, 2.4 times the 2019 level. Over seven years, more than 3.6 million jobs were created, and life expectancy reached 75.97 years.

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s growth has unfolded against a difficult inflationary backdrop. Consumer prices rose 12.3% in 2025, with food prices up 13.5% and paid services 12%. These figures add an important dimension to the broader growth story. The next stage of economic policy will increasingly be judged not only by headline GDP or nominal incomes, but by productivity, purchasing power and the quality of life they support.

Tokayev has repeatedly made that connection himself. In a January 2025 interview, he said that all economic development measures and reforms were ultimately aimed at improving citizens’ quality of life, calling this the government’s top priority.

The social and infrastructure footprint is significant. Over seven years, the government allocated 34 trillion tenge (US$76 million) to the social sphere. Kazakhstan built 761 schools, 345 kindergartens and 696 hospitals and polyclinics, while completing 536 new sports facilities.

The scale of these investments illustrates Tokayev’s increasingly expansive approach to economic development: infrastructure and social policy are being treated not as separate tracks, but as part of the country’s productive capacity and quality of life.

Institutional reform and the economic environment

The economic trajectory has also unfolded alongside institutional reforms. Banu Segizbayeva, an expert at the Kazakhstan Institute for Public Development, traces the first institutional steps of the current reform agenda to 2019-2021, including changes to laws on peaceful assemblies and political parties and the introduction of elections for rural akims (governors).

The reform process acquired a more systemic character in 2022, she said, when constitutional amendments were approved by referendum, the Constitutional Court was restored, a single seven-year presidential term was introduced, and the electoral system was updated.

“Modernization rests on constitutional norms and new institutions. Just Kazakhstan became the framework into which new political and economic mechanisms were consistently built. Today, the main question concerns the durability of these institutions in practice, and that work is continuing,” Segizbayeva said.

For the economy, that institutional dimension matters because investment decisions ultimately depend on predictable rules. Tokayev has increasingly linked institutional modernization with economic performance, noting that reforms should strengthen the quality of governance while creating a more predictable environment for business and investment. The broader reform trajectory has therefore increasingly connected institutional change with economic modernization.

The next stage

The seven-year record gives Kazakhstan a larger economic base, deeper infrastructure and a wider set of growth drivers than it had in 2019. GDP per capita has increased by more than half, the industrial base has expanded, SME participation has grown, and investment has remained substantial. But the next stage will require a different kind of progress.

Sultanov identifies the main test as the ability to sustain growth with a gradually smaller dependence on state stimulus. The transition, he notes, should lead toward greater private investment, stronger export performance, higher productivity, deeper processing and a stronger domestic pool of engineers and specialists.

This is also where the scale of Tokayev’s current development agenda becomes significant. The emphasis on infrastructure, industrial capacity, transport connectivity and social construction can create the physical foundations for the next growth cycle. The challenge will be to translate those assets into sustained productivity and competitive businesses.

Seven years of economic policy have produced a broader and more diversified set of capabilities, but the transformation remains a work in progress.

The direction outlined by President Tokayev in recent years points to a next phase that goes beyond maintaining headline growth: toward greater industrial capacity, deeper value creation, stronger private investment, modern infrastructure and higher productivity. His recent remarks have consistently emphasized a new investment cycle, economic diversification, infrastructure development and the improvement of citizens’ well-being.

For Kazakhstan, the central economic task is therefore increasingly clear: not simply to grow faster, but to make growth more resilient, more productive and more deeply rooted in the domestic economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan Strengthens Global AI Ties As NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Plans Visit for AI Month Event
World.content:
ASTANA – NVIDIA Founder and CEO Jensen Huang will visit Kazakhstan for the first time as a special guest of AI Month, a national program bringing together artificial intelligence specialists, developers, startups, researchers and technology companies.

Huang will visit Kazakhstan at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev. His visit is scheduled for Oct. 23, when AI Month will conclude with a special event at the International Center for Artificial Intelligence alem.ai, reported the ministry’s press service.

Huang and Madiyev will hold a fireside chat covering global AI development, major technology trends, the preparation of a new generation of AI specialists and Central Asia’s prospects on the global technology map.

“Today, countries’ competitiveness is determined not only by access to technology, but also by the ability to create their own solutions and develop world-class teams,” Madiyev said.

“We seek to make Kazakhstan a hub for AI talent across Central Eurasia – a place where a strong idea can gain access to expertise, partnerships and an opportunity to reach the global market,” he added.

AI Month opens Sept. 23 with HackAlem AI, described by organisers as one of the world’s largest AI hackathons. Participants will have access to NVIDIA technology resources to develop and test their own AI solutions.

The program will also feature a meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence on Oct. 1, with NVIDIA Vice President Rev Lebaredian taking part. Huang’s participation will bring one of the technology industry’s most prominent executives to Kazakhstan as the country seeks to strengthen international partnerships and develop its domestic AI ecosystem.

Kazakhstan builds links with global AI industry

Kazakhstan’s growing ties with the global AI industry extend beyond AI Month. One example is Higgsfield, an AI-powered video and image generation platform valued at $5.4 billion. The company is an Astana Hub participant and uses NVIDIA computing infrastructure and AI software. According to the provided information, its platform supports more than six million video and image generations daily.

Higgsfield also maintains ties with Kazakhstan and Astana’s technology community and cooperates with Astana Hub to support the regional technology ecosystem.

“Kazakhstan has an exceptional opportunity to become an important centre for AI innovation and talent attraction,” said Higgsfield Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Yerzat Dulat.

“Higgsfield shows what becomes possible when outstanding talent from the region receives support from a strong local technology ecosystem and world-class partners such as NVIDIA,” he added.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UK Discuss International Expertise for Caspian Green Energy Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Kingdom discussed opportunities to draw on international expertise and investment potential for the development of the Caspian Green Energy Corridor during a meeting in Astana on Sept. 21.

Representatives of Kazakhstan’s national electricity grid operator KEGOC met with John Alderdice, the United Kingdom’s Trade Envoy to Azerbaijan and Central Asia and a member of the House of Lords. The meeting was also attended by representatives of the British Embassy in Kazakhstan, led by Ambassador Sally Axworthy.

KEGOC Deputy Chairman Bakytkhan Zhazykabayev told the British delegation about preparations for the project, its technical concept and the next stages of development.

According to KEGOC, the sides discussed current aspects of the project’s implementation, as well as opportunities to attract international experience and expertise. The British delegation presented its capabilities and investment potential in interconnection infrastructure and clean energy.

Project to connect green energy systems across the Caspian

The Caspian Green Energy Corridor envisages the development of infrastructure to transmit renewable electricity across the Caspian Sea and subsequently connect it to European markets.

The project is considering the construction of converter substations in Aktau and Baku, along with a 350–400-kilometer high-voltage direct-current cable under the Caspian Sea. The initiative also involves strengthening the national electricity grids of the participating countries.

Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan have established the Green Corridor Alliance joint venture to develop and implement the project. The system operators of the three countries hold equal stakes in the venture.

Feasibility study underway

Preparatory work is currently underway on a preliminary feasibility study for the corridor. The study is being carried out by Italian engineering company CESI. The assessment is expected to determine the project’s main technical solutions, preliminary cost and parameters for its further implementation.

The involvement of international expertise is intended to support the technical development of the cross-border energy infrastructure as Kazakhstan and its partners explore new opportunities for renewable electricity transmission toward European markets.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s AI Month to Bring Hackathons, Investment Summits and Tech Forums Across Country
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s AI MONTH 2026 program opens Sept. 23 with a $1.1 million HackAlem AI hackathon, launching a month-long series of events focused on artificial intelligence, digital technologies, investment, cybersecurity, robotics and technological entrepreneurship across the country.

Held as part of Kazakhstan’s Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, AI MONTH brings together the technology community, businesses, educational institutions, startups, international experts and regional technology hubs. The program will culminate in the international AI & Digital Bridge 2026 technology forum, which will take place in Astana from Oct. 1 to 3.

HackAlem AI powered by OpenAI will launch AI MONTH on Sept. 23. The organisers describe it as one of the world’s largest hackathons focused on developing AI solutions. Teams of up to three participants will develop agentic AI solutions for 10 key sectors of Kazakhstan’s economy, with the mandatory use of OpenAI Codex and API.

The total value of the hackathon’s prizes and technological resources will reach $1.1 million, including a cash prize pool, API tokens and OpenAI technology resources for developing and launching AI solutions. The winners will be recognised on the main stage of AI & Digital Bridge 2026. The hackathon will bring together developers, students, young professionals, startups and IT enthusiasts, giving participants an opportunity to move from an idea to a working AI solution within a short period.

AI MONTH expands beyond Astana

In 2026, Kazakhstan has expanded its previous AI Week format into AI MONTH, reflecting the growing number of initiatives in artificial intelligence and the expansion of the country’s technology agenda across industries and regions.

The program includes KazHackStan, an international cybersecurity conference scheduled for Sept. 29–30 in Astana. More than 100 regional and international speakers will discuss DevSecOps, open-source intelligence, data protection, malware analysis and emerging cybersecurity threats associated with AI development.

A C5+1 platform dedicated to cooperation between Central Asian countries and the United States in AI will also take place during the period. Participants from governments, international organisations and the technology community will discuss AI regulation, infrastructure development, talent training and international technology cooperation.

AI expands into healthcare and robotics

AI and MedTech Day will focus on the application of artificial intelligence in healthcare, bringing together experts, doctors, developers and startups to discuss AI-powered diagnostics, healthcare management and new MedTech solutions.

The program will also feature a humanoid robotics hackathon organised around Unitree robots. Teams will program Unitree G1 humanoid robots provided by the organisers and solve practical tasks without using simulators.

From Oct. 1 to 3, Astana will also host the Astana AI Film Festival, dedicated to the use of artificial intelligence in filmmaking. The festival will feature AI-generated films, public screenings, professional discussions and workshops examining how AI is changing directing, visual styles, storytelling, character creation, special effects and voice production.

The program will additionally include international FIRST Tech Challenge and FIRST LEGO League robotics competitions, as well as a UNICEF foresight session examining the impact of AI on the future of children and young people.

Regional technology ecosystem

AI MONTH will extend beyond the capital, with events taking place at technology hubs across Kazakhstan throughout the month. The regional program will include workshops, boot camps, hackathons, career meetings, pitch sessions and startup battles. Schoolchildren, students, teachers, developers, entrepreneurs, startup teams and other people interested in learning and applying AI will be able to participate.

The program is designed to give participants from different regions opportunities to develop new skills, create their own solutions and present projects to the professional community. The month-long program will conclude with the Grand Final of the alem.ai Battle, organised by Astana Hub. Teams and young technology talents from Kazakhstan and Central Asia will compete in four categories.

AI MONTH is designed to bring together different stages of Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem in a single program, from education and talent development to AI product creation, technological entrepreneurship, investment and international cooperation. The central event, AI & Digital Bridge 2026, will serve as the main platform for these discussions from Oct. 1 to 3 in Astana.

The open program on Oct. 2–3 is available through the official AI & Digital Bridge website. Regional events and registration details are available through the Astana Hub platform.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Banks Dominate First Fintech Wave, But Infrastructure is Driving Next
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s largest banks have come to dominate one of Central Asia’s most digital consumer finance markets, leaving less room for independent fintech startups and pushing the sector’s next phase of growth toward open banking, embedded finance and shared financial infrastructure, according to a new industry report.

Fintech in Kazakhstan 2026 was presented at the Central Asia Fintech Summit in Almaty. The report was developed by RISE Research & Advisory, in partnership with Tarlan Payments, BCC Hub, and Fintech Center, with the support of the National Bank of Kazakhstan. This is the third annual national study of Kazakhstan’s fintech market.

According to the report, Kazakhstan’s fintech market has become increasingly concentrated around its largest banks, with five banks accounting for 69% of sector assets. Three super-apps have also emerged as the main platforms for everyday financial services.

Their apps now integrate payments, lending, e-commerce, travel, transport, government services and other everyday functions into a single ecosystem. Banks are extending the same model to small businesses, where, according to the report, they address 16 of 19 core needs, spanning from company registration and account opening to payments, credit, payroll and accounting.

Experts said that dominance has left limited space for independent consumer-facing fintech firms, pushing startups toward open banking, embedded finance and other infrastructure-driven business models.

Kazakhstan’s fintech startups raised around $72 million in venture capital between 2021 and 2025, but funding has fallen sharply since its peak at $32 million in 2023.

Investment dropped to $19 million in 2024 and just $8 million last year, with most deals still concentrated at the pre-seed and seed stages. Capital is also shifting away from consumer-facing models towards B2B and financial infrastructure businesses.

Changing market architecture

The report also highlights substantial changes in how the market is regulated. Kazakhstan is reshaping the architecture of its financial market, combining regulatory reforms with shared digital infrastructure designed to connect banks, fintech firms and consumers more closely.

A unified QR payment system, phone-number transfers, the digital tenge, Digital ID and the National Anti-Fraud Center are creating new opportunities for the sector.

According to the experts, the changes could lower barriers to market entry for fintech companies, while also bringing them under stricter compliance and regulatory requirements.

“Over the past year, Kazakhstan has undertaken its most sweeping overhaul of financial regulation in three decades. The changes include a new banking law, a Digital Code and an artificial intelligence law, alongside the rollout of a unified interbank QR payment system, transfers by phone number, the full circulation of the digital tenge, and a nationwide regulatory framework for digital assets operating alongside the jurisdiction of the Astana International Financial Centre,” said National Bank Deputy Governor Binur Zhalenov.

“Kazakhstan has become the only jurisdiction in the region to operate a full stack of digital financial infrastructure, including a central bank digital currency, instant payments, open banking and a regulated digital asset market, within a single regulatory framework,” said Zhalenov.

The shift is also visible in consumer behavior. Kazakhstan has become a predominantly cashless payments market, with non-cash transactions accounting for 88% of payments in 2026, up from 67% in 2019. Within that market, QR payments are gaining ground rapidly. Their share of cashless transactions doubled from 14% in 2023 to 28% in 2025, while QR turnover reached around $17 billion in the first five months of 2026.

On July 19, unified interbank QR and phone-number transfer systems came into effect across retail banks.

Kazakhstan is also building open-API infrastructure to allow banks and technology companies to exchange data more easily. According to the study, this will change the basis of competition. With payment rails becoming more standardized, proprietary payment systems offer less differentiation, putting greater emphasis on product quality, customer experience, data capabilities and value-added services.

“The ability to interact seamlessly between systems should not be a competitive advantage. Customers should be able to transfer money and pay for purchases regardless of which bank they use. Financial institutions, meanwhile, should compete where value is actually created: in customer experience, products, pricing and innovation,” said National Payment Corporation CEO Zhanar Samayeva.

“The same principle applies to trust. As financial services become instantaneous, increasingly data-driven and interconnected, security issues can no longer be addressed only at the level of individual institutions. Fraud prevention, digital identification, cybersecurity and operational resilience should increasingly operate at the level of the entire ecosystem,” she explained.

Banking-as-a-Service

The study points to Banking-as-a-Service as a distinct segment of Kazakhstan’s fintech market. Banking-as-a-Service, or BaaS, allows fintech companies and other businesses to offer financial products using the licensed infrastructure of a partner bank, rather than building a banking operation from scratch.

At least four banks now give external companies access to licensed banking infrastructure, processing and related services, allowing fintech firms and non-financial platforms to launch financial products through a partner bank.

“One of the more visible trends in recent years has been the growth of digital neobanks built on Banking-as-a-Service. Three years ago, such services were offered by perhaps one bank. Today, there are four or five banks providing their licence, processing and infrastructure, allowing fintech companies to create their own digital products, including niche banks,” said Assem Bolatzhan, CEO of Women in Tech Kazakhstan.

“This model is becoming increasingly popular. It works well at scale, for example in Southeast Asia and Korea. Kazakhstan’s market is smaller, but the direction remains promising,” she added.

Dynamic digital assets market

Kazakhstan’s digital asset market is also moving from regulatory experimentation toward a more established part of the financial system. Platforms licensed by the Astana International Financial Centre processed $10.6 billion in digital asset transactions in 2025, while the number of regulated providers has surpassed 50.

As national rules develop alongside the AIFC regime, stablecoins, tokenized real-world assets and crypto payments are beginning to move beyond regulatory sandboxes into commercial use. The next major area of growth could be tokenization, which may give Kazakh assets access to broader pools of global capital.

At a Sept. 15 meeting, the Kazakh government adopted a 65-measure plan to expand Kazakhstan’s regulated digital asset market and announced first tokenization projects.

World.title: Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Race time is set, but getting home is anyone’s guess
World.content:
Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Sports journalist Anar Khanlarov left his home in Sumgayit half an hour earlier than usual on 21 September to make it to Baku in time for a TV programme. But even that was not enough.

He planned to take the metro from 20 January station to Nizami, then a bus to 28 May, followed by bus No 5 towards State Flag Square. As the İdman TV studio was undergoing renovation, filming was taking place at the Rowing Federation building on the boulevard.

His bus became stuck in traffic near Winter Park. Khanlarov continued on foot towards the Puppet Theatre, hoping to catch another bus from there or, failing that, take a taxi. When he reached the theatre at 20:40, he found that the road towards Bayil was closed. The programme began at 21:00, but Khanlarov did not reach the filming location until 21:25, alternating between walking and running. By then he was sweating heavily, and the production team decided he was not in a suitable condition to appear on air. As a result, Khanlarov did not take part in the programme at all that day.

The main events of the Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix will take place on 24–26 September. But even before the racing begins, road closures and changes to bus routes have brought life in the city to a standstill.

26 bus routes changed, leaving passengers with no real alternative

According to a plan by the Azerbaijan Land Transport Agency (AYNA), 26 bus routes have been changed between 21 and 26 September.

Route No 5, which Khanlarov had planned to take, is among those affected. On one section, the bus runs between Nariman Narimanov metro station and Suleyman Rahimov Street, while on another it runs along a route covering the Salyan Highway, Bibi-Heybat Mosque and the Baku Funicular. Under the new arrangements, it is no longer possible to use the bus to travel from the city centre to Bayil via the usual route. Some stops on this and other routes are inside the restricted race zone. There is no alternative public transport available.

The changes have also affected people travelling into the city from the suburbs. Buses No 149 and 149E from the settlement of Sahil and No 195E from Alat now run only as far as the Lokbatan transport hub near the Bina shopping centre. Passengers travelling to the city centre have to change to another form of transport. Bus No 125 reaches the centre via the ring road through Badamdar.

The transit corridors announced by the organisers are also not an alternative for bus passengers. On 21–22 September, they are open from 07:00 to 09:00 and from 18:00 to 20:00. However, these arrangements do not apply to public transport. Except in emergencies, picking up and dropping off passengers is also prohibited within the transit corridors. By the time Khanlarov reached the Puppet Theatre at 20:40, he says, the evening transit window had already closed.

‘We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes’

Former transport officials have also complained about the traffic jams. Mais Aghayev, former head of the Baku Transport Agency’s press service, wrote on Facebook:

“We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes on the stretch from the Mikayil Aliyev roundabout towards Heydar Aliyev Avenue.”

The congestion has also been acknowledged by the authorities. On the evening of 22 September, the Intelligent Transport Management Centre reported traffic jams on 28 May Street, as well as on the section of Shamsi Badalbeyli Street running from Winter Park towards the Central Bank. These streets are also part of the routes affected by AYNA’s changes to bus services.

Seven schools and universities switch to remote learning

Measures related to the race are not limited to changes to transport. According to the Baku City Education Department, seven schools are holding classes online from 22 to 26 September: Public Schools No 6, 7, 8 and 23, Classical Gymnasium No 160, Lyceum No 132–134 and the Ilyas Efendiyev Elite Gymnasium.

Under an order issued by the Ministry of Science and Education, universities in Baku have also switched to remote learning from 23 to 25 September. The ministry says the measure is intended to ensure continuity of the education process.

The move may reduce the number of daily journeys to schools and universities. However, remote learning creates additional difficulties for working parents: who will look after younger children, and how will families ensure they have the devices and internet access needed for online classes? The switch to remote learning does not mean parents no longer have to go to work. So while it may ease pressure on the transport system, it does not necessarily ease the everyday burden on families.

No indication of how much longer journeys will take

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative party, linked the problem to Baku’s fragmented system of governance in a Facebook post on 14 September. In his view, the key factors are the availability of public transport and journey times. He also argues that any changes to working hours should take into account the school schedules of employees’ children.

Economist Akif Nasirli told Radio Azadliq that the race should be held outside the city centre. In his view, the economic benefits of the event should not be used to justify restrictions on residents’ freedom of movement:

“People have the right to move freely in their own country, in their own capital.”

AYNA’s traffic management plan for the race, published on 19 September, lists alternative streets that drivers can use. However, it provides no information on actual bus frequencies along the altered routes, how much additional time journeys will take, or how much time passengers may lose when changing between separate sections of disrupted routes.

For residents, it is not enough simply to know which street a bus will take. They need to know when to leave home, where they will have to change and whether they can get to work on time. Without this information, the burden of adapting to the route changes — and the consequences of any resulting delays — falls on passengers themselves.

World.title: Why Georgia closed 10 schools days into new academic year
World.content:
School closure in Georgia

Ten state schools in Georgia were closed during the first three days of the new academic year. Some of the buildings are due to be demolished and rebuilt, while others will undergo repairs.

The decision followed assessments by the National Forensics Bureau, which found that the school buildings were in a state of disrepair and unsafe for use.

One of the schools is in Tbilisi, while the others are located in different regions across the country.

For the first week after the closures, the schools switched to remote learning. During this period, the Education Ministry and school administrations are expected to urgently find alternative premises.

All 10 schools are likely to be temporarily accommodated in neighbouring schools, with classes held in two or three shifts and lesson times shortened. If any of the alternative schools are too far away, school buses will be provided.

More than 4,000 pupils and around 400 teachers are now waiting for the ministry to decide where they will be relocated and which shifts they will study and work in.

his is not unprecedented. In recent years, thousands of pupils across Georgia have been studying in temporary, “borrowed” premises, while schools that were demolished have yet to be rebuilt.

How events unfolded and what the decisions were based on

The closure of all 10 schools followed the same pattern. The start of the new academic year on 15 September was celebrated as usual, with balloons, flags and flowers in school courtyards and classrooms.

Three days later, on the evening of 17 September, parents received messages informing them that the schools were being closed.

Number of pupils and teachers at the closed schools. Source: JAMnews, based on data from the official schools portal.

In all 10 cases, the decisions to close the schools were based on assessments by the National Forensics Bureau dated 10 September 2026. The education minister says the ministry did not receive the documents until 17 September, explaining why the closures were announced at such short notice.

Some parents do not believe that the school buildings are unsafe. They suspect that some of the decisions may be linked to corrupt deals and investors’ interests.

JAMnews examined publicly available documents relating to all 10 schools, including decisions by the Authorisation Council, expert assessments, public procurement records, renovation plans and municipal reports.

We sought answers to several questions: Why were these schools allowed to begin the academic year as normal on 15 September if their buildings had to be vacated just days later? When did the responsible authorities learn about the condition of the schools? And if the buildings were already destined for demolition, why was money allocated for their renovation year after year?

Renovating schools only to abandon them

The documents examined by JAMnews show that concerns about the poor condition of some of the schools had been known for years. In other cases, however, there had previously appeared to be no need even for repairs, let alone demolition.

Some of the schools underwent minor renovation work in recent years, with substantial sums spent on the projects.

For example, according to public procurement records, Public School No 16 in Kutaisi underwent various repairs in 2015, 2017 and 2022. The largest amount was spent in 2015 — around 190,000 lari [about $70,300].

The Kutaisi school made its most recent purchase just three weeks before the start of the current academic year. On 24 August, the administration signed a 2,500-lari [about $925] contract for maintenance of the school grounds, including mowing and removing grass.

Public School No 16 in Kutaisi. The start of the academic year was celebrated with invited entertainers. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

The public school in the village of Misaktsieli underwent major renovations in 2008, while its heating system was completely upgraded last winter.

This is also confirmed by the Mtskheta municipality’s 2025 budget. According to the document, several schools were due to undergo renovation work funded through a targeted transfer from the state budget. The school in Misaktsieli was among them.

The Misaktsieli school continued to spend money on various works and services in 2026. Its most recent contract, signed on 4 September, was worth 12,515 lari [about $4,635] and covered the removal of flooring, plumbing work and the subsequent installation of granite flooring.

The school in the village of Abranlo, in the Kvemo Kartli region, is the smallest of the schools closed in recent days, with around 80 pupils. It too has undergone renovation work in recent years.

Mariko Tsikoridze, a project co-ordinator for CENN in Kvemo Kartli, says three sanitation and hygiene projects were carried out at the school before 2019. Toilets were built, washbasins renovated, and an illegal rubbish dump created by local residents in the school grounds was cleared.

“We brought in six truckloads of soil and built a sports ground. The local authorities were also actively involved at the time,” Tsikoridze says.

The school is now due to be demolished. Its headteacher, Mikheil Jakeli, wrote on social media that, according to the National Forensics Bureau’s assessment, constructing a new building would be preferable to repairing the existing one, prompting the ministry to decide on demolition.

Problems left unaddressed

For some of the schools, JAMnews was unable to find any relevant records in the public procurement system. However, municipal reports and local media articles show that concerns about the condition of these schools had been raised for years.

For example, parents of pupils at Public School No 5 in Khashuri were calling for repairs as early as January 2023, complaining about damaged walls, floors and doors, as well as loose stair railings.

First day of the new academic year at Public School No 5 in Khashuri. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

In municipal reports from the Imereti region, Public School No 2 in Tskaltubo had for years been listed as a building in need of renovation.
