Available records for 2022-2026 contain no evidence of major renovation work at the school. However, according to Info Imereti, minor repairs were carried out, including in the summer of 2026.

“There is an assessment stating that the building is not cost-effective to repair. It would therefore be better to construct a new one rather than renovate it,” Mamuka Chkhetiani, head of the Tskaltubo education resource centre, told Kutaisi Post.

Officials knew as early as 2022-2023 that Public School No 3 in Senaki was in a state of disrepair. In 2022, the school’s headteacher, Marine Naneishvili, told Etaloni that the building was due to be demolished.

The Finance Ministry’s 2023 review of investment projects listed the “Construction of Public School No 3 in Senaki”as a separate project, with 12.696m lari [about $4.7m] allocated for it. It is unclear what became of the project.

Public School No 3 in Senaki. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

Reaction at schools

Members of the school communities at two of the 10 schools — in Tbilisi and Misaktsieli — responded to the authorities’ decision with protests, which are still continuing. At the other schools, discontent has largely been confined to social media, where parents have complained about the disruption to both their children’s plans and their own.

“We are in shock” is the most common reaction beneath posts announcing each new school closure.

Two of the three schools closed in the Kakheti region — Public School No 3 in Gurjaani and the school in the village of Velistsikhe — are in Gurjaani municipality. More than 500 children attend the Velistsikhe school, while School No 3 has 148 pupils.

“Congratulations to the school community of Velistsikhe Public School — pupils, parents, teachers and everyone interested in improving our school,” headteacher Nona Menabdishvili wrote on social media alongside the news of its closure.

The post attracted numerous comments, many of them essentially asking: “What is there to celebrate?” Others shared stories of schools elsewhere that have remained closed for years.

Unlike Menabdishvili, Mikheil Jakeli, headteacher of the school in Abranlo, expressed no enthusiasm about the Education Ministry’s decision.

He has appealed to the ministry to allow pupils to complete the current academic year in the old building, subject to appropriate safety measures, “to avoid moving the children elsewhere just days after the start of classes and causing them unnecessary stress”.

‘From positive assessment to demolition’ – story of School No 21

The largest of the 10 schools to be closed is Public School No 21 in Tbilisi, formerly Gymnasium No 6. News of its closure was also the first to emerge.

It is one of the capital’s most prestigious schools. Because of its emphasis on German-language teaching, it is often referred to as the “German school”.

According to a National Forensics Bureau assessment dated 10 September 2026, several problems were identified in the school building, including a risk of plaster falling from the façade, a faulty drainage system, cracks in some areas and damage to reinforced concrete blocks.

The assessment also identified seismic vulnerability as a separate problem, citing the absence of an earthquake-resistant reinforcement belt on the roof parapet and other failures to comply with current seismic standards.

Protest outside Public School No 21 on 18 September 2026. “Don’t demolish the Sixth,” reads an improvised protest banner.

However, the same school had previously received a very different assessment from the same National Forensics Bureau on 15 November 2023, when it underwent authorisation. The assessment said the building required repairs, but gave it an overall “positive” evaluation, and the school was authorised to operate until 2032.

In April 2026, the Authorisation Council carried out scheduled monitoring of the school and, citing the positive assessment, said the building required repairs and gave the school until 2028 to address the problems.

In other words, as recently as spring 2026, official documents still listed School No 21 as requiring repairs rather than demolition.

However, by the time the Authorisation Council made that assessment, a new examination of the school building was already under way.

The Municipal Development Fund had requested the examination on 16 September 2025. An expert inspected the building on 10 December, and nine months later, on 10 September 2026, issued a new assessment.

The building was initially classified as Category III based on the extent of the damage. However, following Georgian government decree No 161 of 22 April 2026, which sets out criteria for assessing whether buildings are fit for use, the damage was subsequently classified as Category IV because of seismic safety concerns.

How could the school have deteriorated so severely in three years that it now needs to be demolished? This is the question being asked by parents. Many suspect corruption. The school is located in a prestigious tourist area, prompting speculation that a private investor may be interested in the site.

Parents fear that the school will be demolished and never rebuilt. They are demanding an independent assessment and say they will not allow the building to be torn down. They also oppose both online learning and the relocation of pupils to other schools.

If we don’t act now, we will lose our school’ – story of Misaktsieli village school

Protest outside the school in Misaktsieli, 18 September 2026.

Irine Kalandadze’s child started first grade this year. He had barely had time to settle into school when his parents were told it was closing:

“He had only been at school for three days and was eagerly looking forward to the next one — he liked it so much. Then suddenly we were told the school was closing. I can’t explain this to my child, and it is very painful for me too. This is precisely the stage when children need to develop a love of school, and now we don’t even know where or how he will study.”

The school in Misaktsieli serves five villages in Mtskheta municipality and has more than 500 pupils.

Parents say lessons will be held online for the first week after the closure, after which the children will be transferred to the school in the village of Tsilkani. But that school has capacity for only 300 pupils, meaning classes will have to be held in several shifts.

Parents do not know for certain whether the Misaktsieli school is due to be demolished or is being closed for repairs. On 18 September, residents gathered in the school grounds and demanded an explanation from the headteacher, who told them that he had not yet seen the expert assessment himself.

Villagers fear there may also be business interests behind the decision: the school is in a popular tourist area, occupies a large site and is surrounded by numerous commercial properties.

“We all want our children to study in a modern school. It’s just that we have seen many examples of how school renovation projects have ended,” Irine says.

Parents are demanding that, if the school needs repairs, the work be postponed until spring. If the building is to be demolished, they want construction of a new school to begin simultaneously on vacant land nearby, with the existing building demolished only once its replacement is ready.

“If we don’t act now, we will lose our school,” Irine says.

The protest is continuing, and parents say they have no intention of backing down.

Not an exception, but a wider trend

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, there are 2,086 state schools in the country.

In 2022, the Education Ministry launched a large-scale reconstruction programme that was intended to cover 800 schools.

Since then, hundreds of schools have closed across Georgia. Two years ago, in 2024, the fact-checking platform FactCheck reported that 21,203 pupils had been relocated to alternative premises.

Based on publicly available data, the number is likely still in the tens of thousands. The Municipal Development Fund, which oversees school reconstruction, regularly publishes updates on the completion or launch of work at schools across Georgia.

For example, in August 2026, the fund announced tenders for the reconstruction of 11 schools. None of the 10 schools closed in recent days appears on that list, suggesting that the overall number of schools currently not operating in their own buildings is considerably higher.

On 18 September, as thousands of teachers, pupils and parents were reeling from the news that their schools were being closed, government officials were holding a high-profile ceremony to reopen the renovated Public Schools No 4 and No 5 in Batumi.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze and other senior officials at the opening of two schools in Batumi. Photo: Municipal Development Fund.

What is actually happening?

Education experts say the situation illustrates systemic problems and a lack of a consistent strategy and long-term vision in the education system.

Education expert Revaz Abkhazava lists the problems created by what he describes as a poorly planned intervention — the reconstruction of schools:

It has disrupted the education process;

It has upended established routines for parents and children, including attendance at after-school clubs and additional classes;

It has shown a complete disregard for teachers’ needs, with low salaries forcing many to work at several schools at the same time;

It has imposed additional costs on the state for transporting pupils to other schools.

“The education system is extremely complex. It consists of many interconnected components. If you fail to see it as a whole, you get what we are seeing now. A single decision does not simply create one problem — it can push the entire system to the brink of collapse.”

Abkhazava says such decisions are the result of experienced and qualified professionals with institutional knowledge being pushed out of the education system.

“School reconstruction is a technical task. It does not require any special expertise. Education management professionals could have resolved this issue very easily.”

The expert also points to problems in communication between state institutions. The process, he says, was not managed in a way that would have ensured the assessments were ready at least a month before the start of the academic year.

Revaz Abkhazava believes the root of these problems lies in the politicisation of Georgia’s education system. He says education should not serve any political party and that safeguards are needed to ensure this, including an education council and teachers’ associations. He also argues that the ministry’s strategy should not change every time a new minister takes office.

“The education system should be as decentralised as possible. The ministry should employ professionals with knowledge and experience in education management and education policy.

“The ministry should focus on evaluation, analysis and research, and make decisions based on them. It should support educational institutions, while those institutions should have the autonomy to make decisions on matters that concern them,” the expert concludes.

World.title: Armenian orphanage worker brutally assaults disabled resident
World.content:
Armenian orphanage worker assaults disabled child

A care worker at the Kharberd specialised orphanage in Armenia brutally assaulted a disabled child who is unable to walk or speak.

The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, which oversees the institution, confirmed the incident and said it had taken place several weeks ago. The care worker was immediately dismissed and is now under house arrest.

“A disabled child was beaten with a mop in a place where they were supposed to receive care and support. In reality, this is the kind of care the child needs to be protected from,” said Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda.

Rights activist questions purpose of such institutions

“If we do not want violence, these institutions should not exist at all. Family-based upbringing and alternative forms of care are possible for all children if the state makes the necessary effort and allocates the necessary resources. The state’s obligations do not begin after a disabled child has been beaten, nor do they end with the dismissal of the alleged abuser or their placement under house arrest,” Hovsepyan said.

Until such institutions cease to exist, however, he says the state is obliged to establish a system that:

“prevents violence and identifies signs of it in a timely manner;

provides safe mechanisms enabling all children to report abuse;

guarantees a proper investigation and the child’s swift recovery.”

Details of the incident

Local media have established further details about what happened at the orphanage. The incident is now known to have taken place on 13 August.

The child who was assaulted has cerebral palsy and is unable to walk independently or speak.

The care worker who assaulted the child had worked at the orphanage since September 2012.

“In room D-1 of the orphanage, the care worker initially struck the resident, F.M., several times. After he fell to the floor, she picked up a floor mop and continued striking him on his lower back, spine and left shoulder blade. As a result, F.M. suffered severe physical pain and emotional distress,” journalists reported.

Child’s condition described as satisfactory

Nver Kostanyan, spokesman for the minister of labour and social affairs, wrote on social media that the orphanage administration had “identified the incident” and immediately reported it to law enforcement:

“The care worker has been dismissed, while it is for law enforcement agencies to determine whether criminal charges are warranted. The child is in good health and continues to receive care at the specialised orphanage.”

Kostanyan said such incidents were a “red line” for the ministry:

“Any instance of violence is unacceptable and will be subject to an appropriate criminal-law assessment.”

Expert opinion

Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda, warns that disabled children often avoid speaking about abuse they have experienced.

“There are many reasons. Among other things, they think they will not be believed, because what they say is often called into question,” he wrote on Facebook.

Hovsepyan stressed that the public only learnt about the abuse at the orphanage after it was reported by the media. The rights activist believes such cases should be closely scrutinised by state bodies, particularly now that there is no mechanism for public oversight.

A group of civil society experts previously operated at the initiative of the Labour Ministry, carrying out regular monitoring of care centres for children and elderly people.

“The monitoring group was disbanded about three years ago. Easily. But its work is not being resumed with the same ease,” Hovsepyan said.

Hovsepyan himself was a member of the group. He recalls that in 2021 it visited the Kharberd specialised orphanage and documented a case of discrimination against a minor in its care:

“At the same orphanage, staff wore gloves when touching a teenager living with HIV who had recently been transferred there. Separate dishes were used for him. His clothes were washed separately. Other children were told to stay away from him. And yet the world has long known that HIV is not transmitted through this kind of contact.”

The orphanage staff themselves told the experts about this because they believed they were ‘doing everything right’.

Following the recent violent assault, Hovsepyan says he is not convinced that conditions at the specialised institution have improved:

“I am also not sure whether all new employees receive the necessary training before they start working with children. Nor am I sure that the state is taking steps to ensure that children are in safe hands.”

World.title: A pair of porcupines, Khrashuna and Khramuna, at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Tbilisi Zoo is home to two Indian porcupines, a female and a male named Khrashuna and Khramuna. Their keepers chose the names for a reason: the porcupines make funny “crunching” sounds when they eat. Khrashuna is the bolder of the two, while Khramuna is more cautious.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: ALL VIDEO

______________________________________________________________________________

Contrary to popular belief, porcupines have nothing in common with either badgers or hedgehogs. Badgers are carnivores, hedgehogs are insectivores, while porcupines are rodents.

Their most distinctive feature is their long, thick quills, which they mainly use for defence. When threatened, their first response is to flee rather than attack. And no, porcupines do not shoot their quills — that is simply a myth. When they sense danger, they

Alongside their varied diet, Khrashuna and Khramuna always have branches in their enclosure. They gnaw on the wood, which helps keep their teeth strong.

Porcupines are nocturnal animals. During the day, especially in summer, they prefer to stay in their shelter. They become active in the evening and start looking for food. That is why visitors who come to their enclosure during the day may see nothing more than a nose or head poking out of the burrow.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Porcupines at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: European Court of Human Rights to review case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze
World.content:
The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has accepted the case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze. The case concerns freedom of expression online and administrative proceedings brought against the activist.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) asked the court to refer Miladze’s case to the Grand Chamber in August 2026.

According to GYLA chair Tamar Oniani, this means that until the Grand Chamber delivers its judgment, Georgia’s city and appeals courts cannot cite the case as a precedent when restricting freedom of expression on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

In 2022, authorities fined activist Irakli Miladze for using profanity in a video in which he criticised Tbilisi’s transport policy. He directed some of the offensive language at the city mayor, municipal officials and police officers.

Authorities brought the case under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which covers petty hooliganism, including the use of obscene language in public places. Tbilisi City Court ordered Miladze to pay 2,000 lari [~$740], but the Court of Appeal reduced the fine to 500 lari [~$185].

On 19 May 2026, the ECHR’s Fourth Section ruled on the case and found that the authorities had not violated Miladze’s freedom of expression, which Article 10 of the Convention protects.

Irakli Miladze

The court found that Miladze’s statements did not form part of a public debate and therefore did not warrant the same level of protection for freedom of expression as statements on matters of political or public interest.

The court also considered the size of the fine and its consequences, noting that the sanction did not prevent Miladze from continuing his civic and political activities. At the same time, the court confirmed that the concept of a “public space” also covers online platforms when they are widely accessible to the public.

The case will now be reconsidered, but this does not mean that the Grand Chamber has already found that Miladze’s rights were violated. In its final judgment, it may uphold the previous ruling or take a different position.

The key question will be whether Miladze’s statements on TikTok were protected by freedom of expression and whether imposing an administrative fine on him was justified.

According to GYLA, the significance of referring the case to the Grand Chamber is further underscored by the fact that, after the May 2026 ruling, the Interior Ministry established a so-called “censorship department”. GYLA says its activities are linked to administrative cases brought against citizens over opinions they post on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

World.title: ‘One cashbox’ for two parties: Transparency International Georgia study
World.content:
According to a study by Transparency International Georgia (TI), a significant share of the funding for the pro-government and anti-Western People’s Power party comes from people who have previously funded, or continue to fund, the ruling Georgian Dream party.

The study found that, as of August 2026, 28 people had donated a total of 861,750 lari [~$320,000] to People’s Power, which split from Georgian Dream in 2022. Of these, 21 had previously donated 1,969,169 lari [~$730,000] to Georgian Dream. Another three continue to fund both parties.

TI says these financial links indicate that People’s Power is not independent of the political and business circles surrounding Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili.

The study highlights a group of businesspeople and companies linked to Ivanishvili’s circle. According to the organisation, members of this group donated a total of 381,000 lari [~$141,000] to People’s Power between 2024 and 2026.

One of them is Archil Mamatashvili, CEO of JSC Cartu Insurance Company and a member of the supervisory board of Ivanishvili-linked Artu Holding. In 2025–2026, Mamatashvili donated 70,000 lari [~$26,000] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 55,600 lari [~$20,600] to Georgian Dream.

According to the study, Cartu Insurance Company received government and municipal procurement contracts worth around 3.5 million lari [~$1.3 million]. Other company representatives — Alla Kakhniаuri, Kakha Kobiashvili, Zaza Verdzеuli, Givi Lebanidze and Zurab Chachkhiani — donated a total of around 1 million lari [~$370,000] to Georgian Dream.

Another major donor to People’s Power is Giorgi Damenia, a business partner of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s brother, Alexander Ivanishvili, in the company Tornado+. In 2025–2026, he donated 120,000 lari [~$44,400] to the party. Damenia had previously donated 170,000 lari [~$63,000] to Georgian Dream, while Tornado+ itself donated 85,000 lari [~$31,500] to Ivanishvili’s party between 2016 and 2018.

Another member of Ivanishvili’s business circle is Irakli Bekaури, CEO of Bolero & Company, owned by Vakhtang Karichashvili. Karichashvili, who holds Georgian and Russian citizenship, has been described as a business partner of Ivanishvili’s cousin, Ucha Mamatshvili. According to the study, his companies rank among Georgia’s largest wine exporters to Russia. Between 2014 and 2024, his companies received 56 million lari [~$20.7 million] in subsidies from Georgia’s Agriculture Ministry.

In 2026, Bekauri donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 327,000 lari [~$121,000] to Georgian Dream.

Among people linked to Bekauri and Karichashvili is Levan Getsadze. Public Registry records list him at various times as a representative of companies linked to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business partners. Getsadze donated 13,000 lari [~$4,800] to People’s Power, which the study says was his first political donation.

For many years, Getsadze owned Trezor, a company founded in 2019 that operated a medical laboratory in Tbilisi. Soon after its establishment, the company began taking part in public procurement and has since received contracts worth around 3.2 million lari [~$1.19 million]. The laboratory is now owned by the US company Quest Biosciences LLC.

The study also links another major People’s Power donor, David Balanchivadze, to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business circle. In 2016–2017, the investigative journalism studio Monitor linked Balanchivadze’s appointment as executive director of RMG GOLD to Mamatshvili’s interests.

Balanchivadze began making political donations to Georgian Dream in 2016. According to the study, he donated a total of 532,000 lari [~$197,000] to the party. In 2026, he donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power.

Among the donors to People’s Power is Giorgi Meskhi, who served as director of the state-owned company Sakspetstrans from 2017 to 2020. In 2024, he donated 58,000 lari [~$21,500] to the party.

While running the state-owned company, Meskhi founded the construction company Hiteco Group with his business partner Giorgi Khujadze. Meskhi now owns 100% of the company and serves as its director. Hiteco Group is building a multi-storey hotel in Tbilisi. Meskhi also owns a 33% stake in Gonio Group.

Another People’s Power donor, Guram Tetrashvili, is director of Georgian-Israeli Business Group LLC. The company is owned by Besik Papismedov, who is involved in several construction projects in Tbilisi. Tetrashvili donated 10,000 lari [~$3,700] to the party. According to the study, this was also his first political donation.

According to Transparency International Georgia, three of the 28 donors — Aleksandre Tushuri, Mamuka Gogrchiani and Givi Gabunia — fund both People’s Power and Georgian Dream.

All three donated a total of 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power on 11 December 2025. Three months later, on 18 February 2026, the same people donated another 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to Georgian Dream.

People’s Power was founded in August 2022 by three MPs who left Georgian Dream: Sozar Subari, Dimitri Khundadze and Mikheil Kavelashvili. It initially operated as a civic movement and registered as a political party in March 2024. Sozar Subari is the party’s chairman.

When they launched the movement, its founders said their goal was to provide the public with more information about developments in Georgian politics and defend the country’s national interests. People’s Power has been particularly vocal in criticising the influence of Western political forces and non-governmental organisations. The party initiated the draft law on the “Transparency of Foreign Influence”.

From 2022 to 2024, People’s Power formed part of the Georgian Dream parliamentary majority. In the 2024 parliamentary election, the party ran jointly with Georgian Dream. Today, People’s Power has its own parliamentary political group.

Transparency International Georgia study

World.title: “The ritual is complete”: Why the Kremlin needs elections to the State Duma
World.content:
Russia State Duma elections

Based on a report by Novaya Gazeta Europe

Russia’s first State Duma elections since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine have brought few surprises. According to preliminary official results, the ruling United Russia party has retained its constitutional majority.

Political observers say there is now little genuine political competition left in the country.

But if the vote does little to determine either the composition of the real centers of power or the direction of the Kremlin’s policies, why does the Kremlin continue to hold elections? And what significance do they still have for the authorities and for Russian society?

To explore those questions, Novaya Gazeta Europe spoke with political scientists, a sociologist, a political strategist and an electoral expert.

Yabloko disrupted the script of a quiet campaign

According to an electoral expert who asked not to be identified for security reasons, the authorities had initially planned a campaign that would be as uneventful and tightly controlled as possible.

“Overall, all the candidates and parties that made it onto the ballot tried to run their campaigns as inconspicuously as possible, so as not to give the authorities grounds to target them. Everyone except Yabloko played by the system’s current rules. Yabloko, by contrast, played by the rules the system had five years ago,” he said.

The situation surrounding Yabloko became the campaign’s main development to break from the prescribed script. According to the expert, the party’s position had not changed, but after years of war, the authorities had come to view it as radical.

The federal list of Yabloko was barred from the election by a decision of the Supreme Court. The Central Election Commission removed information about the party from the federal ballot.

“In the end, the authorities chose the coercive route: they removed Yabloko, barred all the more or less prominent candidates, and eliminated the regional lists — with the exception of Novgorod Region. This really became the central story of the election campaign,” the expert said.

Sociologist Igor Eidman said that Yabloko’s attempt to take part in the election at least demonstrated that opponents of the war still exist in Russia. But it produced no meaningful electoral result.



Political analyst Ivan Preobrazhensky does not consider the campaign a genuine election at all. In his view, it was closer to a “performance” or a “special electoral operation,” resembling the Soviet-era plebiscitary votes in which voters were offered no real alternative.

Eidman likewise argues that voters had little meaningful influence over the distribution of political power.

“This was pure political farce — a staged performance, a fake imitation of a political process that does not exist in Russia. The script was written long ago, and all the figures were determined in advance,” he said.

Yet the predetermined outcome does not make the elections meaningless for the Kremlin.

State Duma elections as a political ritual

Political strategist Stanislav Belkovsky describes the elections as a political ritual.

“The event is meaningless in terms of the actual political process, but it is an integral part of the rituals of power. In that sense, it can be compared with the Victory Day parade on Red Square or the Kremlin reception held to mark June 12.”

In his view, Vladimir Putin regards adherence to such rituals as part of maintaining the stability of his own rule.

Alexei Nechaev, chairman of the New People party, left, at the party’s campaign headquarters during a meeting to discuss preliminary results of the State Duma elections. Moscow, Sept. 20, 2026. Photo: Pavel Seleznev / TASS / ZUMA Press / Scanpix / LETA

Belkovsky says the Kremlin is also interested in preserving a liberal façade in the form of the New People party. In his view, its presence allows the authorities to project an image of Russia as a country where legal liberal political forces still exist.

At the same time, he argues that on fundamental issues, the party does not differ from the other established political forces.

There was also uncertainty surrounding A Just Russia, which was hovering near the 5 percent electoral threshold. According to preliminary official results, the party cleared the threshold.

Preobrazhensky argues that even if the party disappeared from Parliament, it would not fundamentally change Russia’s domestic politics.

“There is not a single genuine political party that would be allowed to take part in Russian elections today,” he said.

Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov casts his ballot at a polling station. St. Petersburg, Sept. 20, 2026. Photo: Olga Maltseva / AFP / Scanpix / LETA

Was there any point in voting?

Preobrazhensky believes that taking part in the election may have had a primarily psychological significance. For some people, simply going to the polls, deliberately spoiling a ballot or taking part in the “Noon for Peace” protest became a way to engage in at least a symbolic political act.

Eidman takes a different view. He argues that mass participation helps the authorities maintain the appearance of a normal electoral process.

He points to the 2024 presidential election as an example. At the time, large lines of Putin opponents formed outside polling stations abroad. Yet the official election results remained unchanged.

An independent electoral expert disagrees.

“The greatest joy for anyone rigging an election is absenteeism — people staying away from the polls. It makes their job much easier. High natural turnout is always a problem for those who manipulate elections,” he said.

What happened with election fraud

According to the anonymous expert, opportunities for independent election monitoring have sharply diminished in these elections. As a result, it has become far more difficult to compare the official results with what actually happened at polling stations.

“In my view, even the information that is available is enough to conclude that, in the overwhelming majority of regions, the official results do not correspond to how people actually voted,” he said.

That is the assessment of the newspaper’s source. Russian authorities, by contrast, said the voting took place without violations capable of affecting the outcome. Independent observers and opposition groups reported violations and restrictions on election monitoring.

The expert believes the nature and scale of possible manipulation may also be changing. In the past, observers focused primarily on precinct-level election commissions. Now, he said, some manipulation may be taking place higher up, at territorial election commissions where results from individual polling stations are consolidated.

As an extreme example, he points to Chechnya, where, according to official figures, Ramzan Kadyrov received 99.85 percent of the vote.

“That would mean that across the entire republic, fewer than 1,000 people supposedly voted against Kadyrov, despite turnout being virtually 100 percent. That is even more extreme than in the Soviet Union,” the expert said.

The source also drew particular attention to Moscow. On the final day of voting, the system for issuing paper ballots experienced a failure there.

The expert stressed that there is no evidence that the disruption was deliberate. But many voters who had deliberately chosen not to vote electronically were planning to go to polling stations precisely on the final day.

Preobrazhensky points to another change. In the past, he said, discussion centered on individual regions with particularly conspicuous electoral anomalies. Now, in his view, the anomalies are becoming regions where the alleged falsifications are less extensive and less obvious.

The question of how to legitimize the results, however, remains. Preobrazhensky argues that it is important for the Kremlin to convince both Russians and audiences abroad that the official figures genuinely reflect public sentiment.

“In the West, there is, in my view, a mistaken argument: ‘Perhaps no one elected Putin, but we know anyway that he is supported by an absolute majority of Russians.’ That is not true, because no one knows that,” the political analyst said.

What will change after the election

Belkovsky believes it would be a mistake to view the State Duma election as a turning point after which the Kremlin should embark on a fundamentally new course.

In his view, the State Duma is not an independent center of key political decision-making.

“The State Duma election in itself is neither a milestone, nor a turning point, nor a ‘barometer’… It is simply part of a ritual, and that ritual has been completed,” he said.

Belkovsky said any decision on a new formal mobilization would likewise not be directly linked to the election results. At the same time, he said, the Kremlin still has ways of replenishing the armed forces through less visible and indirect means.

Eidman believes the official results could serve a different purpose for the authorities — as evidence of a public “mandate” for further decisions.

Preobrazhensky points to another possible consequence of the campaign: a struggle for influence within the Russian government itself.

In his view, the election exposed a conflict between the Federal Security Service, or FSB, and the presidential administration over control of domestic politics.

“The main question that emerged during the election was: Who controls domestic policy? During the so-called election campaign, domestic policy was quite clearly controlled primarily by the FSB,” the expert said.

According to Preobrazhensky, the future direction of Russia’s domestic politics will depend to a significant extent on whether the FSB retains that control.

exchange

World.title: ‘My arrest was political from start to finish’ – Georgia’s ex-PM writes seventh letter from prison
World.content:
Garibashvili writes seventh letter from prison

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili, who is serving a five-year prison sentence, has said in his latest – seventh – letter that the real purpose of his arrest was not the criminal case against him, but to neutralise him politically and prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

According to Garibashvili, the authorities initially changed the terms of a plea deal they had agreed with him. Later, when his imprisonment proved more politically damaging to the ruling team itself, they offered him a deal under which he would admit to a new corruption charge.

‘I was screwed over again’

The former prime minister says that on the day he was detained, he received a message telling him that he had to withdraw from politics. In return, he says, he was promised that he would not go to prison but would instead receive a lengthy suspended sentence and a fine.

“I was screwed over again,” Garibashvili writes.

However, he continues, on 4 January 2026 he was unexpectedly informed that the terms had changed and that he would face five years in prison. By that point, he had already pleaded guilty, been released on bail and was awaiting the formalisation of a plea agreement.

20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili

In one of the key parts of the letter, Garibashvili discusses his longstanding relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party. He says that because of his 20-year political and personal relationship with Ivanishvili, he did not want to enter into a political confrontation with him.

“I silently walked to the political slaughterhouse and went to prison because I did not want to enter into confrontation,”the former prime minister writes.

He says that by making this decision, he sacrificed himself to protect the team and the country.

“I made my sacrifice and also spared the team and the country. In return, I was screwed over for a third time,”Garibashvili says.

‘Authorities suffered more from my arrest than I did’

Garibashvili says that in February he communicated with the authorities through an intermediary. Their main message, he says, was that the ruling team had suffered more from his arrest than Garibashvili himself.

He says this left him with the impression that the authorities were preparing a new provocation because his detention and the campaign against him had failed to produce the result they had expected.

“They failed to discredit me sufficiently in the eyes of the public; they failed to achieve the effect they had expected from my arrest and the accompanying propaganda,” the former prime minister writes.

‘My reputation was not significantly damaged’

Garibashvili says there was no further communication with him until July, when the authorities made a new proposal.

According to Garibashvili, this time the authorities acknowledged that his arrest had damaged the ruling team itself, while the former prime minister’s reputation had not suffered significantly.

Garibashvili writes that public sympathy for him had grown, particularly among some Georgian Dream voters.

He says this was also because other people convicted of offences against the authorities had been released with suspended sentences, making his five-year prison term difficult for the public to understand.

Admitting to new corruption charge

According to the former prime minister, it was after this that the authorities developed a new fear that he would return to politics after his release from prison. Garibashvili says he was asked to admit to a new corruption charge.

He says the aim was twofold: to destroy his reputation once and for all and further prevent any possibility of his return to politics:

“Because of this, they demanded that I admit to a new, dirty corruption charge so that, on the one hand, my name would be completely destroyed and, on the other, they could further guard against the risk of my return to politics.”

‘My imprisonment was political from start to finish’

Garibashvili gives a clear assessment of his own case:

“Based on all this, my imprisonment was political from start to finish, from the very first day, and everything that has been done against me is politically motivated and has nothing to do with a legal process.”

The former prime minister says he believes he is in prison because of “absurd suspicions, fears and envy”.

He describes it as an injustice committed not only against him but also against his family.

Response to state propaganda

The second part of the letter contains direct and strongly worded accusations and criticism of the authorities.

Garibashvili says that “false and dirty propaganda” against him has continued over the past two weeks.

The former prime minister describes statements by government representatives as “hypocritical” and “false”.

“As I see it, you have got rather carried away and really settled into your role. Don’t be hypocrites! First take the log out of your own eye, and then talk about corruption,” Garibashvili writes.

He says the public is well aware that the campaign being waged by the authorities is a “farce”.

Irakli Garibashvili

‘You have made state institutions a laughing stock’

Garibashvili also accuses the authorities of damaging state institutions. He says their actions both at home and abroad have made state institutions “a laughing stock”.

“You have given enemies at home and abroad grounds to talk,” he writes.

He says the ruling team’s policies have plunged the country into “continuous chaos and an endless crisis”.

Garibashvili also says the authorities’ own voters have been left confused by their policies, while a sense of hopelessness, instability and uncertainty about the future has taken hold in society.

Parallel with Saakashvili era

The sharpest part of the letter is Garibashvili’s comparison of the authorities’ actions with the rule of Mikheil Saakashvili.

“You are already following Saakashvili’s path and bringing back the methods of rule used by the United National Movement,” Garibashvili writes.

The former prime minister argues that the authorities’ current policies are ultimately harming both Georgian Dream itself and the country.

“You have caused enormous, irreparable damage to your own state, your government and the ruling party itself,” he says.

The letter ends with a warning:

“You are doing evil. Be careful!”

The case against Garibashvili

Garibashvili was first charged with corruption in October 2025. Investigators accused him of large-scale money laundering.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, Garibashvili provided false information in his asset declarations in an attempt to make illegally obtained income appear legitimate.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

In a second case, the former Georgian prime minister is accused of accepting a particularly large bribe. Prosecutors allege that he received 750,000 lari (approximately $289,000) from a scheme involving classified procurement by the Defence Ministry.

The new case followed statements by Garibashvili in which he accused the authorities of pressuring him and demanding that he admit to a new charge.

The case concerns the procurement of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to prosecutors, the ministry carried out three classified procurements from late 2022. At the time, Juansher Burchuladze was defence minister and Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister. Prosecutors, however, plan to reach a plea agreement with Burchuladze, saying the decision was made in view of the extent of his co-operation with the investigation.

World.title: Uzbekistan's UTK receives first batch of new 40-foot high-cube containers
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Today, Uzbekistan has received its first batch of new 40-foot high-cube containers purchased by JSC Uztemiryulcontainer.

This was reflected in the statement by the UTK.

The company plans to add another 2,000 containers over the next five years, with the new equipment to be used on international routes connecting Uzbekistan with China and Europe, as well as the CASCA+ corridor and other international transport routes.

“The expansion of the container fleet will create additional opportunities to increase export and transit shipments and provide exporters with more convenient logistics solutions,” JSC Uztemiryulcontainer said.

The company said the expansion of its container and railcar fleet will allow it to provide integrated transportation and logistics services, covering the process from preparing exporters’ cargo in the regions for shipment to delivering it to the final destination.

The expanded fleet is also expected to facilitate the direct shipment of export cargo from Uzbekistan’s regions to international markets, reducing the need for exporters to arrange separate logistics services.

Uztemiryulcontainer said it will continue developing container transportation and expanding logistics services designed to provide exporters with more convenient and efficient access to international routes.

JSC Uztemiryulcontainer (UTK), the operator of Uzbekistan’s railway container fleet, provides container transportation and freight-forwarding services for export, import and transit cargo, including multimodal logistics and customs services.

World.title: Changi Airports to participate in construction of new airport in Kazakhstan's Astana
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Singapore’s Changi Airports International (CAI), a subsidiary of Changi Airport Group, will be involved in the construction of a new airport in Astana, according to the Astana akimat.

The Astana akimat, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport and CAI have signed a Framework Cooperation Agreement aimed at developing a long-term strategic partnership in the field of airport infrastructure in the capital.

Under the agreement, the parties reached formal arrangements in two main areas: cooperation on the construction of a new airport in Astana and the development of the existing Astana International Airport.

“The parties agreed to cooperate on the implementation of the project to construct a new airport in Astana. The project is being implemented as part of the fulfillment of President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instruction to create an international aviation hub and develop Astana’s transit potential,” the akimat said.

The parties also agreed to cooperate with CAI on the existing Astana International Airport, including the company’s participation in management, operations and maintenance (O&M), as well as other areas of its further development.

The parties are currently working to agree on the partnership structure, project implementation terms and prepare the necessary documents.

The signing of the Framework Cooperation Agreement formalized the agreements reached during the visit of Changi Airport Group management to Astana and provides a basis for further joint implementation of the new airport construction project, as well as cooperation on the development of the existing Astana International Airport, the akimat said.

The cooperation will combine the long-term vision of the Astana akimat and Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport for the development of the capital’s aviation infrastructure with CAI’s international expertise in airport planning, construction and management.

In August 2026, during talks in Kazakhstan, Changi Airport Group expressed its readiness to provide expertise for the construction of a new airport and the development of Astana as a regional aviation hub.

Following the talks, a Kazakh delegation held a meeting with representatives of Changi Airports International in Singapore, where the parties identified the main areas for further cooperation. The signing of the Framework Cooperation Agreement became the next stage of interaction and formalized the agreements reached, the akimat said.

Changi Airport Group (CAG) is Singapore’s state-owned company responsible for managing and developing the country’s airport infrastructure, including Changi Airport. CAG manages airport operations, passenger and cargo traffic, commercial infrastructure, services and digital solutions. In 2025, Changi Airport handled about 70 million passengers and more than 2 million tons of cargo, connecting Singapore with more than 170 cities worldwide.

CAG also implements international projects through its subsidiary Changi Airports International (CAI), which has experience working with more than 90 airports in more than 35 countries.

World.title: IEA predicts 1/3 share of electricity supply in global energy consumption by 2035
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Electricity could cost-effectively meet 33% of global final energy consumption by 2035, up from the current 23%.

This was reflected in an analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA), prepared at the request of Türkiye and Australia for discussions ahead of COP31.

The report reviews opportunities to accelerate electrification on a global scale and assesses its implications for energy security and climate goals.

According to the document, assuming the use of currently available technologies and energy prices consistent with levels prior to the recent supply shock, electricity could cost-effectively supply 33% of global final energy consumption by 2035, compared to 23% today. This would bring the world closer to the electrification target of 35% currently under discussion.

The document noted that, given current energy prices amid the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, shifting an even larger share of global energy consumption to electricity could become economically viable.

The IEA reports that global electricity consumption has grown faster than economic output in recent years—and at nearly twice the rate of overall energy demand—driven primarily by the use of air conditioning, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and electric vehicles.

According to the agency, under an accelerated electrification scenario, fuel-importing nations could see their energy import costs drop by more than $400 billion by 2035 compared to 2025 levels.

The report emphasized that global oil consumption by 2035 could be 18 million barrels per day lower than it would be if current trends continued. The IEA attributes this effect primarily to the more rapid adoption of electric vehicles.

"Electrification can also help reduce carbon dioxide emissions in transport, buildings, and industry. These three sectors account for more than half of energy-related CO2 emissions.

Under an accelerated electrification scenario, CO2 emissions in these three sectors could fall by 40 percent by 2035. According to the report, this would be sufficient to put total energy-related CO2 emissions on a downward trajectory, regardless of the electricity generation mix.

At the same time, the rapid expansion of domestic low-carbon electricity sources could further enhance the benefits of electrification in terms of energy security and emissions reduction," the agency pointed out.

The IEA highlighted significant potential for cost-effective increases in electrification across all regions, although opportunities and priorities vary by country.

"In emerging and developing economies, this potential is linked, in particular, to switching agricultural water pumps to electric power, expanding the use of electric two- and three-wheelers in densely populated cities, and increasing opportunities for small businesses to use electricity in sectors such as food and textile production.

However, realizing this electrification potential will require additional investment in power generation and electricity grids, as well as the deployment of smarter, more flexible energy systems.

The report also noted the need to address emerging threats to electricity system security, including supply chain concentration for key technologies and critical minerals, cybersecurity risks, natural disasters, and climate-related threats," the IEA said.

The agency stressed that to ensure the benefits of electrification are widely shared, public authorities need to help certain households and businesses manage upfront costs.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Kazburgas commissions drilling rig at Karachaganak field
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Kazakhstan’s Kazburgas company has commissioned the mobile RIG 17 drilling rig at the Karachaganak oil and gas condensate field on September 22, 2026, PetroCouncil, of which Kazburgas is a member, reported.

“The drilling rig was manufactured to the company’s individual order and equipped with modern equipment from international manufacturers, including a BENTEC (Germany) Top Drive system, Güçbir Generator diesel generator sets, automation systems and intelligent video monitoring using artificial intelligence technologies,” the company said.

Specialists from Kazakhstan, Germany, China and Türkiye took part in the construction, installation and commissioning of RIG 17.

As reported, Kazakh specialists underwent training with equipment manufacturers and international experts, gaining practical skills in operating modern drilling systems and receiving relevant certificates.

The project is expected to create new jobs, develop engineering competencies and increase the share of qualified Kazakh personnel in the oilfield services sector. The commissioning of the rig is in line with efforts to develop technology, localize expertise and increase local content, supported by the state, the PSA LLP Authorized Body and KPO b.v.

Kazburgas is one of Kazakhstan’s leading oilfield services companies. The company was established in 1996 following the reorganization and merger of two drilling divisions of JSC Karachaganakgazprom - the Karachaganak Drilling Operations Division and the Aksai Drilling Operations Division.

According to KazMunayGas, the Karachaganak field is one of the world’s largest oil and gas condensate fields. It is located in northwestern Kazakhstan near the city of Aksai and covers an area of more than 280 square kilometers.

The field was discovered in 1979, while first production was obtained in November 1984 through a limited pilot industrial development project implemented during the Soviet period.

World.title: 'Need the world to wake up': AI 'Godfather's' stark warning after Trump's speech
World.content:
Professor Yoshua Bengio, the co-chair of the UN's Scientific Panel on AI, says big tech companies are taking enormous risks with their development of the technology and there needs to be an urgent change of direction.

"Its shouldn't be the decisions of just a few CEOs or a few governments to figure out what's good for humanity," Professor Bengio told 7.30 from New York, where he is set to address the UN Security Council overnight.

The winner of the prestigious Turing Award for his pioneering work on AI said international agreement on safeguards is essential to secure humanity's future.

"Dealing with those risks … should be an urgent mission for humanity, so that humans remain in charge and that we keep human dignity flourishing at the centre of our choices," Professor Bengio said.

His comments came after US President Donald Trump labelled concerns about AI "a hoax" in a speech to the UNGA and rejected a joint statement from 22 countries, including Australia, calling for humans to remain in control of AI.

US President Donald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

The US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now," Mr Trump said.

However, Professor Bengio, one of the 'Godfathers' of AI, said the plea from the 22 countries was important.

"What happened with this group of countries is extraordinary and it is important," he said.

"And we have to continue in that direction. We need more countries. We need the world to wake up so that we can have influence on our future.

"The reason I am able to sleep at night and the reason why a country like Australia can make a difference is that we have agency right now.

"When we form coalitions, when we put our resources together, our minds, our energy, our talent, we can be in the game and we can bring the world into a place that's better aligned with our values, with democracy, and the idea that we should keep our sovereignty in a multilateral world."

'Like a recipe for suicide'

The comments come on the eve of a meeting in New York between Mr Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping where AI is expected to feature prominently.

Donald Trump nd Xi Jinping are set to meet once again, this time on the sidelines of the UNGA. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov/Pool)

Professor Bengio said American AI companies are about six months ahead of their Chinese rivals, but that competition should not get in the way of cooperation between Washington and Beijing.

"It is reason enough to sit at a table with the Chinese because, you know, they're humans too. They want to have a life. They want their children to have a life," he said.

" I think it is in the rational interest, self-interest of both parties to sit down and agree on principles like the ones that the heads of state put forward recently. "

Professor Bengio says the greatest dangers posed by AI come from "recursive self-improvement" being developed by the world's leading tech companies — where artificial intelligence trains the next generation of AI.

"Imagine we have an AI that is smarter than us, so it is able to do that research and engineering all by itself," he said.

"It could design an AI that will be even more powerful than itself and even less controllable and even more malicious.

" That's like a recipe for suicide. "

Professor Bengio will tell world leaders at the UN Security Council that they must act.

"The forces of competition between companies and countries is not healthy," he said.

" It is an international question because those powerful AIs, if we lose control of them, that's going to affect all of us. "

World.title: Colosseum closed after worker dies in 10-metre fall
World.content:
A worker has died after a 10-metre fall at Rome's famed Colosseum, the Italian Ministry of Culture has confirmed.

The 22-year-old technician had been installing a lighting system inside the second level of the ancient amphitheatre at the time of the incident.

"Andrea Moretti, a specialist high-altitude rope access worker … died last night inside the Flavian Amphitheatre following a workplace accident," the ministry said.

Part of the Colosseum, which is one of Rome's main tourist attractions, was closed after the worker's death. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli said the "tragic event" had shocked the country.

"The few words we can express are dedicated to Andrea, his family, and his loved ones," Mr Giuli said.

"We extend to everyone our deepest, most sorrowful condolences at the senseless death of a young man dedicated to his work."

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by the news.

"For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable — and even more so when it happens in the workplace," she said in a statement.

The ministry gave no further details of Mr Moretti's fall, but said police were working to determine the circumstances of the incident.

Up to 20,000 visitors flow through the gates of the Colosseum each day during peak tourism months. (Reuters: Alexandros Avradimis)

The Colosseum Archaeological Park initially said part of the Colosseum near to the area where the accident occurred was closed on Wednesday, local time, as a mark of respect to the worker.

It later said that "once the orderly exit of those currently inside is complete, the Colosseum will be closed to the public".

Built 2,000 years ago, the Colosseum was the biggest amphitheatre in the Roman empire and was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts for crowds of up to 50,000 spectators.

It remains one of the city's main tourist attractions, with up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

Italy's biggest union, CGIL, took issue with the decision to close only part of the landmark, saying the full site should be closed for the day.

"We expect Minister Giuli to shed light on the incident and to order the full closure of the Colosseum," CGIL Rome general secretary Natale di Cola said.

"Humanity comes before tourists."

Reuters

World.title: Council general manager sacked with $272k payout after hat-draw mayor mix-up
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The general manager of a northern New South Wales council has been sacked a week after she declared the wrong winner of a mayoral ballot.

Clarence Valley councillors held an extraordinary meeting today, calling for general manager, Laura Black, to resign or face having her contract terminated.

In confidential papers accidentally published on the council's website, a breakdown in the relationship between Ms Black and the majority of councillors was cited as the reason for asking her to step down.

Some of the Clarence Valley councillors who voted on the general manager's tenure. (Supplied: Clarence Valley Council.)

The motion said it had led to the council becoming "dysfunctional".

Ms Black did not attend the meeting, but in her absence, councillors voted to terminate her contract.

Councillors noted that Ms Black had not been given notice of any dispute, nor had performance related issues raised previously.

The ABC has attempted to contact Ms Black for comment.

Botched mayoral vote

The contract termination comes a week after Ms Black declared the incorrect winner of a mayoral ballot, leaving the council in disarray.

Incumbent mayor Ray Smith and Cr Peter Johnstone were tied after a council vote.

Their names were put in a hat, and Mr Smith's name was drawn, but instead of calling him the winner as the rules stipulated, Ms Black named Mr Johnstone the new mayor.

When the error was discovered, Mr Johnstone resigned as mayor.

Five-year contract

Ms Black was appointed as the Clarence Valley Council general manager on October 7, 2022, on a five-year performance-based contract.

She had previously held the roles of acting general manager and director corporate governance of Clarence Valley Council.

Ms Black was paid a salary of $372,591 in the 2024/25 financial year.

Her contract includes a clause which entitles her to 38 weeks pay, which is approximately $272,000, plus entitlements.

The councillors thanked Ms Black for her service to the Clarence Valley Council and the community.

The director of Environment and Planning, Adam Cameron was appointed as the acting general manager for four weeks.

The council currently has no mayor, and no general manager. Cr Cristie Yager is the deputy and acting mayor.

Councillors were expected to meet next week to discuss the mayoral role.

World.title: 'Yes dear': Mal and Marge's secret to 75 years
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

As they celebrate three-quarters of a century together, Mal and Marge Grimley, at 95 and 93 respectively, have not forgotten their rainy 1951 Sydney wedding day.

"Marge was 18, and I was 20," Mr Grimley says. "And it wasn't a shotgun wedding," Mrs Grimley interjects.

"It was like winning a lottery that we were so young," Mrs Grimley adds.

Decades later, the couple's romantic-comedy meet-cute at the local cinema is still fresh in their minds.

"You pinched my seat," Mrs Grimley says. "No, you pinched my seat," Mr Grimley says.

"At interval we went out and when I came back in, Marge was sitting in my seat … she wouldn't get out.

"So I sat on her lap," Mr Grimley says.

Marge Grimley says being with husband Mal was like winning the lottery. (ABC News: Ruby McIntosh)

And in what Mrs Grimley describes as a different time, the pair waited nine months for their first kiss.

"One night, we had been to the movies; we sat on the front doorstep … I said, 'If you don't kiss me tonight, I will kiss you,'" she remembers.

" So he kissed me. It wouldn't happen like that these days. "

Diamond anniversary

The couple's diamond anniversary was held at the independent living facility where Mrs Grimley still lives, while Mr Grimley has only recently moved into assisted living.

After 75 years together, it is hard to now face the prospect of living apart.

"It's lonely," he says. "It's hard looking at one toothbrush on the sink," she says.

The couple's three-quarters of a century together was celebrated by everyone, from close family members to their cleaner and personal trainer.

The Grimleys celebrated their diamond anniversary with loved ones. (ABC News: Ruby McIntosh)

Their daughter, Dana Whitty, says her parents' philosophy is:

"Treat your partner as you wish to be treated, listen to what they are saying and look at their point of view. "Embrace Indigenous and multicultural customs and people; they have experienced many things that we have not. "And lastly, in a world where you can be anything, be kind."

'Great wife, big softie'

Moving between Woollahra, the NSW coast and then settling in Canberra for the past 27 years, the couple has volunteered for local charities and cheered for local sporting teams.

Their daughter says they are always the first to roll up their sleeves and help out.

Mal and Marge Grimley at their wedding in 1951. (Supplied)

For their anniversary, the couple was showered in flowers, gifts and cards, even from King Charles III and Queen Camilla and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Their next-door neighbour, who was at the celebration, says: "You get what you give, and they gave a lot."

Mrs Grimley did not want to advise any younger couples hoping to make the distance, but she pointed to Mr Grimley's words, which she said made good advice.

"Two words to make a marriage … yes, and dear," he said.

Tearing up when asked what he loved about his wife of 75 years, Mr Grimley wondered what was not to love about her.

"Couldn't be without her … Marge carried all the weight," he said.

"She's been a great wife and a great nurse and cook and everything else … she's carried all the weight."

And Mrs Grimley? Here's what she said when asked what she loves about Mr Grimley: "He's a big softie; that's what I love about him, big softie."

World.title: 'Terrifies me': Victorian Premier makes One Nation admission
World.content:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has declared "One Nation terrifies me" as he escalated the state Labor party's warning about the prospect of the Coalition governing with Pauline Hanson's party after November's state election.

One Nation has recently won seats in by-elections, first in the federal NSW seat of Farrer and in the WA state seat of Secret Harbour.

The rise of Senator Hanson's party has been seen as a warning shot fired across both sides of the political divide as Labor and the Coalition struggle in opinion polls.

Since becoming Victoria's premier in July, Mr Carroll has used the possibility of a Coalition-One Nation government as a central plank of Labor's campaign for re-election, particularly as support for the minor party has surged in the state.

"I will fight every day against the Liberal Party and One Nation coming together, because that is what will happen in November if Labor is not successful," Mr Carroll told 7.30.

" That is why Labor must be successful. Failure is not an option. "

Asked if he was worried about One Nation's rise, Mr Carroll admitted the prospect "terrifies him".

"[The] Liberal Party and One Nation teaming together … they're about attacking working people. I'm about fighting for them."

Pauline Hanson's party has enjoyed a swift rise of late. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Carroll accused of 'fear campaign'

While Mr Carroll was concerned about One Nation, that was not the case for Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson.

"I'm not really interested in the other parties," Ms Wilson told 7.30.

"I am running to win majority government at this election because I know that we have the plan to fix Victoria, and I know the only way to do that is to achieve majority government."

Liberal leader Jess Wilson is not concerned about One Nation's popularity in the polls. (ABC News)

Ms Wilson said she had not spoken to One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering and urged voters to "fix this state" by voting for the Coalition.

7.30 approached One Nation for comment, but they did not respond.

The competing pitches have sharpened the battle lines with just over two months until election day.

Redbridge insights adviser Kristy McSweeney — who is a former political advisor and contested the 2022 federal election as the Liberal candidate for the Western Australian seat of Swan — said Mr Carroll was ramping up his One Nation warnings to specifically target disillusioned Labor voters who were considering switching their vote.

"He's going for a fear campaign due to Labor's very low primary vote and Labor trailing those two parties consistently over polls the last six months, including post his leadership change as the third party among Liberal, Labor and One Nation," Ms McSweeney said.

" He's throwing it at the wall to spark the fear of people from switching from Labor. "

Redbridge insights adviser Kristy McSweeney is a former Liberal candidate for the WA seat of Swan. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Recent Redbridge polling shows the scale of One Nation's rise.

Its latest survey of almost 2,400 Victorian voters conducted earlier this month put the Coalition on 29 per cent, One Nation on 25 per cent and Labor on 24 per cent of the primary vote.

Ms McSweeney said Labor's warnings were particularly aimed at voters in Melbourne's west, where the party's traditional support base was frustrated that infrastructure had failed to keep pace with rapid population growth.

"It is a pitch to them to say, 'If you switch from Labor, you will get a One Nation-Liberal Coalition and that represents a lot of things that you don't like in multicultural communities out there on the peri-urban fringe," she said.

Could 'the red wall' fall?

Melbourne's outer west is traditionally a safe Labor area and known as the 'Red Wall'.

The region includes the seat of Melton — the nation's fastest growing local government area — as well as suburbs like Sunbury and Werribee, where Labor has built a strong base among migrant, working-class and first-home-buying communities.

Melton is held by Labor on a 4.6 per cent margin, but the once-safe seat is showing signs of vulnerability after more than three decades in Labor hands.

It was closely watched at the 2022 Victorian election when it was the only seat in the state to swing against Labor, and is now more vulnerable with long-standing Labor member, Stephen McGhie retiring at this election.

Warren Pickering is the leader of One Nation in Victoria. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

There are other concerns too. There have been delays to some infrastructure builds in the area, including the electrification of the Melton train line.

While Ms McSweeney said that Labor faced challenges, she also said voters were starting to have concerns about One Nation policy.

"A lot of people are saying, 'I'm starting to look at One Nation's policies for Victoria and I can't see what they're going to do for Victoria'," she said.

" They're starting to clock that One Nation hasn't come up with specific local policies, or at least not yet. "
