World.title: Commonwealth to foot bill for maintenance, safety of abandoned WA oil platform
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Taxpayers will foot the immediate bill to keep an abandoned oil rig off Western Australia's Midwest coast in a safe condition.

The Cliff Head oil platform has sat mothballed since the collapse of owners Pilot Energy and Triangle Energy in July, leaving locals in Dongara, 350 kilometres north of Perth, worried about the potential impact on crayfishing grounds nearby.

Describing the rig as mothballed and neglected, local fishermen have demanded clarity on who would oversee the decommissioning of the rig and surrounding pipelines.

In a ministerial instrument signed last week, Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King authorised taxpayer funding to stabilise the rig, with her office maintaining all costs to government would be recovered.

A spokesperson said it would be unacceptable to do nothing while waiting for the insolvency process to be completed.

The Cliff Head platform has operated since 2006, but today it sits abandoned off the Dongara coastline. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"The Government is stepping up to protect the environment because parts of the gas industry have failed to plan for the decommissioning of older facilities," the statement said.

"This is unacceptable.

"And so we are taking action. All costs of government will be recovered and the taxpayer will not foot the bill."

Who pays?

It is not the first time the government has been forced to step in.

Australian law requires the removal of all property and infrastructure when offshore oil and gas operations have ended.

In 2020 it took responsibility for decommissioning and re-mediating the Northern Endeavour, a deteriorating oil production vessel 550 kilometres off Darwin, after its owner went into liquidation.

According to local fishers, the aging, ocean-worn Cliff Head platform is falling into neglect with minimal maintenance work being done. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The work is ongoing, with costs running into the hundreds of millions.

Government says it is recouping those costs through a levy on offshore petroleum producers.

Warning for the future

Conservation Council executive director Matt Roberts said the government's intervention at Cliff Head was another liability that should be borne by individual energy companies.

"We shouldn't be in a situation where yet again we are seeing taxpayer money committed to cleaning up failed industry when it comes to our offshore decommissioning," he said.

"This pattern is something we should be acting on right now so that we don't see this repeated into the future.

" We are looking at the next 50 to 60 years being major decommissioning of a lot of projects off the coast of Western Australia. "

The former offshore oil platform Northern Endeavour in the Timor Sea. (Supplied: Northern Oil and Gas)

Oil and gas decommissioning has been estimated to cost $60 billion over the next 30 to 50 years.

While Ms King's office declined to say how much would be spent maintaining Cliff Head, a 2025 government backed report estimated decommissioning Cliff Head would cost $200 million.

Mr Roberts said the costs should be made public, and stricter obligations should be placed on oil and gas companies to finance decommissioning.

"There needs to be transparency around this," he said.

World.title: Damning report finds no evidence $40m youth program reduces offending
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A damning report has found no evidence that a multi-million-dollar government program established to reduce youth crime in Victoria has led to a reduction in offending.

The Victorian Auditor-General Office's (VAGO) report tabled in state parliament this morning also found that about two thirds of young people engaged in the Youth Crime Prevention Program offended within six months of starting it.

Since 2016 the Victorian government has allocated about $40 million to organisations that provide mentoring and case management services to at-risk young people.

The number of alleged youth offender incidents has continued to climb in Victoria. (ABC News: Kristofor Lawson)

In that time the number of alleged youth offender incidents has climbed to a record level, from 17,115 in 2022 to 23,893 incidents last year.

A statistical analysis indicates that a small group of repeat offenders is driving the increase.

The report also found it was unclear if the program was reaching its intended recipients.

"At least half of program places go to young people who have offended or are alleged to have offended," it said.

"But this varies widely between community organisations [delivering the program], from 18 per cent to 92 per cent.

"We do not know if the remaining participants are 'at-risk' of offending because program criteria are broad and record-keeping is poor."

The VAGO report recommendations accepted by the justice department included the introduction of minimum participant data and record-keeping requirements to support participant eligibility decisions.

Crime has shaped up to be a major issue in Victoria's forthcoming election, and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson seized on the report's findings on Wednesday.

"We've had another auditor-general's report that demonstrates that this Labor government is wasting taxpayer while seeing crime rates skyrocket in this state," she said.

Paul Edbrooke says the VAGO report highlights the changing nature of youth offending. (ABC News: Nathan O'Brien)

Crime Prevention Minister Paul Edbrooke said youth offending rates had been declining in recent times and that a Violence Reduction Unit was established in late 2025.

"VAGO confirms what we already know: the nature of youth offending is changing, which is why we've already given Victoria Police the powers they need to tackle serious and repeat offending," he said.

Andrew Bruun from Youth Support and Advocacy Service, which participates in the Youth Crime Prevention Program, said the organisation had seen promising results.

"For the clients we've currently got engaged in our program, 50 per cent of them have ceased their offending, they've got through their [community corrections] order," he told the ABC.

Mr Bruun said the report's finding that 30 per cent of participants do not offend could be viewed as an improvement in community safety if those people were previously involved in serious, high-volume offending.

Andrew Bruun says it is far more effective to pay for youth support than incarceration. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

He also said investment in this kind of program was a better option than paying to keep young people in custody.

"If you look at the numbers, [it costs] $7,304 per day to keep a young person in custody," Mr Bruun said.

"Our program cost $17,000 to put a young person through about a year of intensive support to get a result."

He said the topic had become a political football in recent years.

"There's a lot of people who don't understand how damn disadvantaged some of these kids are," Mr Bruun said.

The Crime Statistics Agency is scheduled to release data for the 2025-26 financial year on Thursday.

World.title: Alleged $5m 'extortion attempt' labelled a 'lie' at NSW ICAC
World.content:
A $5 million demand at the centre of an alleged "extortion attempt" against fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has been labelled a "lie" amid a NSW corruption watchdog probe.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) heard Mr Nassif claimed he was being extorted by former Toplace contractor Navid Ardestani, who was pursuing him for money he believed he was owed and communicating with other staff about outstanding payments.

Mr Nassif forwarded some of the messages with Mr Ardestani to his associate and former Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran as evidence of an alleged "extortion attempt".

During Mr Maheswaran's third day at ICAC, counsel assisting the commission Peggy Dwyer SC suggested the full exchange instead showed Mr Ardestani trying to secure payment for contractors and organise remediation work at Mr Nassif's defected developments.

"What I'm putting to you puts a lie to your claim that this was an extortion. This is clearly a request for payment so that remediation works can take place on Jean Nassif's building," Dr Dwyer said.

Mr Maheswaran maintained there was a possible extortion attempt, although it was not reported to police at the time.

Mr Ardestani is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Fugitive property developer, Jean Nassif, appears before NSW ICAC on Monday, September 14, 2026 from Beirut in Lebanon via video link. (ABC News)

$5 million dispute over remedial work

In a message read to the commission, Mr Ardestani told Mr Nassif a meeting was intended to arrange for a builder to carry out remediation work requested by then-NSW building commissioner David Chandler.

The commission heard that Mr Ardestani later told Mr Nassif to have a $5 million bank cheque ready for the remedial construction company, as well as $250,000 for painting and rendering work.

He said the construction company's lawyer would attend the meeting and warned that if the money was not ready, the builders would not sit down with them.

When the messages turned to payment for work already completed, Mr Nassif accused Mr Ardestani of playing "illegal games".

Mr Ardestani rejected the accusation and asked Mr Nassif to pay the workers so the dispute could be resolved.

"We don't make threats, and we never did… and also, we don't do anything illegal," Mr Ardestani said.

Peggy Dwyer grilled Mr Maheswaran on the dispute. (Supplied: NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption)

Dr Dwyer put it to Mr Maheswaran that the exchange appeared to show Mr Ardestani was genuinely trying to get paid.

Dr Dwyer: "Mr Maheswaran, you're a lawyer … you have ethical duties to properly assess the evidence before you. "Surely you could see that Mr Navid was genuinely pleading with Mr Nassif to be paid and was refuting any suggestion of corruption?" Mr Maheswaran: "In writing, he appears to be. Yes, and people very rarely put those things in writing."

In a separate exchange between the pair, Mr Nassif said he did not want to work with the contractors and claimed they were already paid.

He accused them of threatening him with the union and the then-building commissioner Mr Chandler.

Mr Ardestani denied doing so.

"I really don't understand your text Jean … Get us paid please and we can finalise friendly," Mr Ardestani said.

Mr Maheswaran maintained that Mr Nassif's messages were evidence that some form of threat had been made, even if that threat was not contained in the messages.

'I'm told you control the government'

Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler pictured. (ABC News: David Hirst, Abubakr Sajid)

ICAC is examining whether prohibited political donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including removing Mr Chandler as building commissioner and stopping him from investigating Mr Nassif's developments.

Phone taps were heard at the inquiry.

In a recorded call between Mr Nassif and Mr Ardestani, Mr Nassif repeatedly accused the contractor of passing a report about his developments to Mr Chandler.

"I didn't know you were so f***ing powerful mate … I'm told you control the government, the commissioner, and the ministers," Mr Nassif said. "Why you sent this report to the commission … Can you tell me why?"

Mr Ardestani did not accept the accusation and pushed for a face-to-face meeting, later denying he knew the building commissioner.

When asked if the recording supported the allegation of extortion, Mr Maheswaran said Mr Ardestani's voice was "slightly menacing".

Extortion allegation potentially fabricated

The commission previously heard an allegation of an "extortion attempt" being raised during a 2021 meeting involving Toplace representatives, including Mr Maraswaran, as Mr Chandler was scrutinising serious defects at Skyview.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Mr Chandler told the inquiry that he was informed of an alleged demand for $5 million and offered to accompany a Toplace representative to police to report it.

The probe heard the alleged payment was linked to a claim that Mr Chandler would lift a prohibition order affecting the development, which Mr Chandler has denied.

Mr Chandler is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Dr Dwyer: "I suggest to you it was a tactic that you had adopted to try and pressure an independent office holder who was appointed to clean up the building industry, that is, Mr Chandler." Mr Maherswaran: "I can't even understand the logic of that suggestion, but I reject it."

Mr Nassif previously denied that he fabricated the extortion allegation to damage Mr Chandler.

World.title: ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval Rob Harris September 23, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose” and warn that Australia must help shape what replaces it as growing strategic competition between the United States and China transforms the Indo-Pacific. In a major foreign policy address in New York, the prime minister will argue that the assumptions underpinning the global system since the end of the Cold War are being tested, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the rules that remain essential. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters in New York City on Wednesday, AEST. Dominic Lorrimer “Since the end of the Cold War, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security; efficiency mattered more than resilience; and international rules would be observed as a matter of course,” Albanese will tell the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen Awards dinner on Wednesday night, where he will be honoured alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali and actor and singer Cynthia Erivo. “Both those expectations are now being tested. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”



His speech carries echoes of the message Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered nine months ago at the World Economic Forum at Davos, Switzerland, where he said the “old order is not coming back” and urged fellow middle powers to unite to find a new way. Albanese will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday (New York time), where the two countries are expected to sign a bilateral security arrangement. As US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping prepare to meet at the White House on Thursday, Albanese sought several leaders of middle power nations, including Britain’s Andy Burnham, Canada’s Mark Carney and France’s Emmanuel Macron, to help build consensus on several issues, including the rise of artificial intelligence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations headquarters in New York City. Dominic Lorrimer But efforts appear to have been fruitless, as Trump very publicly rejected the push from more than 20 leading economies several times in his UN address, saying he was interested only in the economic benefits of winning the technology race, and not regulating AI’s capacity.



Albanese was also at loggerheads with the Trump administration, which has condemned Australia’s plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content. In a submission to the Albanese government, the US embassy described the reforms as “facilitating censorship”. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way,” Albanese told journalists in New York. The prime minister later met Trump at a UN leaders’ reception, posting a picture of the pair on his social media platforms saying it was “always good to catch up” with the president. There is growing discontent within the group of middle powers at the lack of progress towards peace in the Middle East, Trump’s war against Iran, and Russia’s continued aerial bombardment of Ukraine after nearly five years. Several experts, including former prime minister Kevin Rudd, have also warned about the increased risk of conflict in the Indo-Pacific over Taiwan in the coming years. Albanese will use his speech to set out a vision for Australia to help build a new international order rather than simply respond to the changes under way.



“Australia’s response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old,” he will say, while preserving “the rules that matter most” and creating new partnerships and relationships. Related Article Social media Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast The prime minister will identify the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing as the “most consequential factor” shaping the Indo-Pacific, while rejecting the idea that the region should be viewed solely through the prism of the two superpowers. “Our alliance with the United States is the anchor of Australia’s foreign policy,” Albanese will say. But he will also reaffirm his government’s approach to China, Australia’s largest trading partner, saying the country would engage in the national interest. “How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly,” he will say. “But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.”



“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces. Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script.” Albanese will argue that the upheaval of recent years, including war and the pandemic, has exposed the vulnerabilities of supply chains and forced governments to put resilience alongside economic efficiency. “Governments must build the capacity to withstand shocks they did not cause and cannot control,” he will say. That will include strengthening Australia’s sovereign capability while working with partners on economic security, critical supply chains and energy. The Atlantic Council dinner is one of the high-profile events of UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government, business, military, media and civil-society figures expected to attend.



Albanese is being recognised by the Washington-based think tank for his role in strengthening Australia’s alliances and partnerships and promoting security and stability across the Indo-Pacific. Related Article Updated

AI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons His speech places particular emphasis on Australia’s expanding network of partnerships across the Indo-Pacific, including its relationship with ASEAN and a growing web of security agreements with Pacific nations. He will describe the Pacific as “both a home and a family to Australia” and say the region’s priorities, sovereignty and culture must be respected. “For our Pacific neighbours, climate change is the most immediate security threat,” Albanese will say.



The speech will culminate in a concise formulation of the government’s foreign policy. “Building resilience without abandoning openness,” Albanese will say. “Strengthening regional partnerships without abandoning rules.” And Australia would deepen its alliance with the United States and engage its largest trading partner, China, “without allowing either relationship to define who we are”. “In an uncertain world, leadership means showing up for one another, sharing burdens and giving our neighbours greater power to shape their futures,” he will say. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Tanks for the penalties
World.content:
It’s true that we’ve done this before, but with the NFL season come some truly great names. George Zivkovic of Northmead has identified the best of them and asks, “How can the NRL or AFL possibly compete with, let alone surpass, these handles? Kool-Aid McKinstry, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sauce Gardner, Storm Duck, Younghoe Koo, DeMarvion Overshown, Tank Bigsby and Tank Dell. All right, I’ll grant that FuiFui MoiMoi and Steele Sidebottom are pretty good, too.”

The celebrity encounters (C8) continue: “When I was 14, a friend of my father arranged for me to meet Ricky Nelson in the dressing room of the Sydney Stadium,” recalls Janet Scilly of Waterloo. “Of course, my father had to be there. I had a lot to say but was struck dumb on seeing him. My father thought he was a nice young man because he called Dad ‘Sir’ and shook his hand.”

“I’m not sure if I share Alan Phillips’ (C8) view about C8 driving AI mad,” thinks Seppo Ranki of Glenhaven. “As an experiment, I checked out my name and suburb on Google. Part of the AI Overview said: ‘He frequently writes short, witty observations and life stories for The Sydney Morning Herald’s popular Column 8 section. His published items often feature memories of farm life, old vehicles and everyday humorous encounters.’ I suspect AI has a pretty good handle on both C8 and me.”

Mark Berg of Caringbah South writes: “When at high-school German classes (C8) in the late 1970s, we watched German videos and were expected to translate the script. One memorable line was ‘Mit einer Perucke bist du ein anderer Mensch’. It means, ‘with a wig, you are another person’. Very useful indeed.”

“I’m still waiting to inform anyone who’s interested, in my best schoolboy French, that ‘the pen of the gardener’s niece is on the table in the conservatory’,” informs John Clarke (Jean Leclerc to his mates) of Lorn. Interestingly, Rob Phillips of North Epping says he’s waiting to use the rather congruent “‘my aunt’s pen is on the table’. Regrettably, it doesn’t get you much to eat in a French restaurant.”

World.title: ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner Catherine Strohfeldt September 23, 2026 — 8:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The death of a 69-year-old Brisbane woman during medical testing might prompt a rethink of southern Brisbane’s health and hospital system, a coronial report has suggested. Yaqin Han died on October 14, 2022, when she suffered a cardiac arrest during a diagnostic test at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital. Coroner Ainslie Kierkegaard ruled that while the test – which involved having the 69-year-old run on a treadmill – triggered her cardiac arrest, Han’s doctors had acted appropriately throughout the procedure. Brisbane woman Yaqin Han was referred to the Princess Alexandra Hospital, but treated at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital (pictured). Courtney Kruk Kierkegaard said Han’s doctor during the test – cardiologist Reza Reyaldeen – stopped it as soon as the 69-year-old began complaining of symptoms.



By that point, Han’s heartbeat had become erratic before declining into a cardiac arrest, from which she could not be revived. Related Article Mental health Wards were over capacity when patient took her life, inquest told The coroner said it was only “with the benefit of hindsight” that the care team led by Reyaldeen might have stopped the test sooner, as it would have been outside normal practice based on Han’s vital signs, which were being monitored throughout. However, Kierkegaard highlighted that another south Brisbane hospital, the Princess Alexandra, was the area’s “heart valve centre of excellence”. Han was initially referred to the PA Hospital, but was treated through a hub at the QEII Hospital, which was closer to her home.



She had been diagnosed with aortic stenosis – a narrowing of the heart’s aortic valve – having suffered dizziness, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath walking up hills. However, various doctors who treated Han were unclear whether her condition was a moderate or severe case. Experts testifying to the court agreed her symptoms were not enough to determine the severity of her diagnosis. Her care team decided to undertake an exercise stress test, rather than invasive diagnostic procedures, to determine whether she would need surgery. However, Kierkegaard said there were potential warning signs about Han’s condition being more severe than cardiologists at the QEII Hospital suspected, but they were missed because her care was fragmented.



Related Article Healthcare Doctors almost sent Kris home with a migraine. Then her whole face went numb Han was also a Mandarin speaker, requiring a translator for her appointments. The inquest found medical staff, in some instances, had trouble contacting Han, and a period of 10 months had elapsed between the last time she was questioned about her symptoms and the decision to order the stress test. The maximum acceptable limit for the gap between consultation and testing, experts at the inquest testified, was 12 months. In an independent inquiry, which Kierkegaard referenced throughout her inquest, Staff Specialist Interventional Cardiologist Anthony Camuglia provided four reasons for the time lapse.



These included interruption from the COVID-19 pandemic, Han’s multiple GPs, the Metro South Health system, and staff turnover at the QEII Hospital. Kierkegaard agreed COVID-19 restrictions had some effect, but said there was “scope for the health service to re-examine its model of cardiac care”. She pointed to a triage system used in Brisbane’s northern hospital service, where complex cases are referred to the Prince Charles Hospital. World.title: Watch: The colossal hits that set the tone for a new NRL force
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Watch: The colossal hits that set the tone for a new NRL force Nick Wright September 23, 2026 — 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was the hit that did more than rattle Brandon Smith’s rib cage and left him writhing on the ground in pain; it signalled a fledgling NRL juggernaut was getting ready to emerge. When the Dolphins headed into their first game in 2023, fans and pundits across the rugby league landscape were left questioning whether they would ever register a win, given their unsuccessful attempts to lure marquee talent. Inaugural prop Mark Nicholls recalled training in a gym under the Redcliffe stadium grandstand and being left without a video room, adding to their underdog status. Mark Nicholls scored the second try in Dolphins history, in their debut against the Roosters. Getty But that was the position coach Wayne Bennett wanted to be in. And when Felise Kaufusi charged out of the defensive line and laid on one of the hits of the season as Smith went to pass, setting up a shock 28-18 triumph over the Sydney Roosters, the competition was on notice.



“All of a sudden, the crowd was in the game, and when someone in your team can put on a play like that, it turns momentum. It’s inspiring, and on the back of that, we went into the sheds at half-time pretty confident of where we were going,” Nicholls told this masthead. “The club had been criticised for their jerseys, criticised for their recruitment, the squad was too old, there were no star players. But Wayne loves that; to be put in the underdog position by the outsiders is where Wayne does his best work. “From that point on, I sort of knew there was a special thing here. We told the fans what we were about, and the league.” Nicholls would score shortly after that crunching Kaufusi blow – one that followed another devastating hit on Nat Butcher – to level the score at 12-all.



Kaufusi – already an established State of Origin star and premiership-winner from his time at the Melbourne Storm – would replicate his defensive heroics a week later, laying on a similarly ferocious shot on Hudson Young. The Dolphins would emerge victorious against the Canberra Raiders, to truly cement their early reputation as a team that would not take a backwards step. That, according to Nicholls and Kaufusi, was the DNA Bennett had called on them to embed. “He wanted winners around. I was lucky the Bromwich brothers [Jesse and Kenny] came here to create a winning culture, and guys who knew the standard they had to be to win games,” Kaufusi said.



“You can talk as much as you want, but if you don’t show it on the training paddock or out on the field, I don’t think people will follow.” Related Article NRL 2026 A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void? Nicholls added: “[Bennett] talked about not wanting to let the fans down or give up in games – if we were going to lose, we were going to be fighting to the last minute. That sort of attitude the group’s continued.” It is in somewhat ironic circumstances that the Dolphins’ maiden preliminary final will take place against the Roosters on Friday night at Suncorp Stadium. But things are very different than they were four years ago. Once condemned as a squad that was unable to impact the premiership race, they now face a fight to keep the framework of their group together.



While the Dolphins have re-signed Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, Tevita Naufahu (2029) and Brad Schneider (2028), marquee men Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow are among the 12 players who will become free agents from November 1. Dolphins squad movements Losses Jamayne Isaako (Storm), Oryn Keeley (Storm, mid-season), Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers), Ray Stone (retirement), Daniel Saifiti (medical retirement, mid-season) Gains George Williams Key retentions Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (2029), Tevita Naufahu (2029), Brad Schneider (2028), Kurt Donoghoe (2028), Francis Molo (2028) Off contract (at the end of 2027) Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Thomas Flegler, Connelly Lemuelu, Morgan Knowles, Trai Fuller, Felise Kaufusi, LJ Nonu, Sebastian Su’a, Elijah Rasmussen, John Fineanganofo However, with only England halfback George Williams signed on as a 2027 recruit, and the salary cap to rise from 2028 following the unveiling of a $5.3 billion broadcast deal, Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader remained confident the bulk of the squad would remain. And Nicholls believed the talent production coming out of the academy pathways – boom edge forward Brian Pouniu and winger Naufahu the first graduates to impress – would ensure ongoing success, even if some key figures were prised from the club’s clutches. So much so, he admitted he “selfishly” had not wanted to retire at the end of last season.



“I could feel as a player I was getting towards the end of my career, but I felt like there was a good crop of young guys coming through and there was a nucleus of a good team,” Nicholls said. Related Article NRL 2026 How an AFL great has unlocked rugby league’s next great halfback “The spine has been there since day one. There are game breakers all along the backline, a forward pack who are willing to rip in, and guys in there who would do anything to fight over a 50-cent coin. Selfishly, I was keen to play on because I had the feeling the group was going somewhere. “There were all these young guys coming through they needed to keep. I know I made the right decision now, but at the time I was keen to play on because I knew something special was brewing. “You’ve got to back your junior development at some stage, and it may mean you lose two or three of those star players. The club is doing all the right things to make sure that if we do lose a couple of those star players, there are certainly plenty who are ready to fill the spots.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Toxic multitasking’ is breaking your brain. Here’s how to take control
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessMental health ‘Toxic multitasking’ is breaking your brain. Here’s how to take control Jolie Kerr September 23, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In our busy, always-on world, multitasking – performing several tasks or engaging in more than one activity concurrently – has become a default setting. At work and at play, our focus is increasingly given to more than one thing at a time: checking emails during a Zoom meeting, scrolling Instagram while watching television, switching browser tabs or responding to notifications while engaged in deep or focused work. “Toxic multitasking is the illusion of productivity,” says Sandi Chapman, the chief director at the Centre for BrainHealth in the US and a professor of psychology at the University of Texas at Dallas. “Multitasking is often seen as a sign of high productivity. Unfortunately, your brain experiences it as a performance bottleneck. We think we’re getting two complex things done at once, but our brains simply aren’t wired for it.” Picking up your phone while working or watching TV is a perfect example of toxic multitasking. Getty Images Not all forms of multitasking are unhealthy, but multitasking can, and often does, turn into problematic behaviour that can become addictive, and that has a real effect on how our brain and nervous system function. Toxic multitasking is the norm, but that doesn’t make it normal



“Today, more and more people are doing multiple things at the same time, double- and triple-booked on meetings,” says Ashish Kothari, founder and chief executive of Happiness Squad, a consulting group focused on employee engagement. Although it may give the appearance and feeling of productivity, multitasking that is characterised by constant “context switching” is detrimental without breaks. “When you switch between tasks, your brain doesn’t instantly reset,” Chapman says. “It burns through your mental energy. Your brain works harder and produces less.” She compares multitasking to trying to read two books at once. “You don’t absorb twice as much information from reading both at the same time. Instead, you simply keep losing your place in both.” Related Article Sleep Three minutes a day could be all it takes to prevent this common sleep issue This way of working doesn’t stop at work. The urge to multitask continues outside of business hours, permeating our non-work time. “We’re on phones all the time,” Kothari says. “We might be watching TV and doing something else. As a result our sleep is affected and, combined, creates a heavy toxic effect on our holistic well-being, physically, emotionally, mentally and spiritually.” Digital multitasking, such as looking at more than one entertainment device at a time (like watching TV while scrolling on TikTok), has a particularly strong negative effect on our attention – and, ironically, on our ability to multitask. “These types of inputs actually reduce your ability to handle multiple inputs at once,” says neuroscientist Kay Linker.



Linker distinguishes between good multitasking and bad, pointing out that multitasking can be beneficial when used correctly. “Once a task becomes automatic, it is transferred to a different part of the brain, allowing for parallel processing,” she says. Examples of this include listening to a podcast or book while taking a walk or calling a friend while commuting to work, in contrast to what Linker calls “task switching, which drains your control and focus”. Looking at your phone doesn’t give your brain a break, but taking a short walk does. Getty Images The effects of toxic multitasking are real, and so are the drivers There are consequences to all this multitasking, and the effects can be serious, affecting performance at work and creating a high degree of exhaustion, stress and burnout that leads to the inability to think clearly, i.e., brain fog. There are also emotional and interpersonal repercussions, including irritability, a reduced ability to connect with others, a shallow or insincere affect, and a loss in satisfaction at work and life. Chapman says that toxic multitasking is a natural extension of hustle culture. “There’s pressure on us, both professionally and personally, to prioritise output and quantity over quality,” she says. The pressures of expectation, driven by technology, have created a constant hunger for productivity, in which we feel the need to always be on and to give our attention away to social media and smartphones.



“We have become dopamine addicts,” says Kothari, who adds that the pace at which we’re expected to take in and respond to information is “putting us in a constant fight-flight-freeze mode, wanting us to keep taking action and feeling like we can’t stop”. Related Article Mental health ADHD symptoms change as you age. Here’s what to expect Because toxic multitasking has been so normalised, you may not even be aware of how much you’re engaging in it, but there are clear signs that it has become a problem. “Usually, the first symptom of toxic multitasking is emotional strain,” Chapman says. “If a quick question from a co-worker makes you want to snap, that’s often a sign your brain is overwhelmed from constant distractions or overload.” There are other ways to determine whether multitasking is a problem, and Kothari recommends using these assessments to identify an attention problem: Do you know how often you pick up your phone? Counting the number of times you pick up your phone during the day provides a data point to quantify a digital multitasking habit. “Most people pick their phone up over 150 times a day,” Kothari says. “It’s a clear indicator that we have lost our ability to focus.”



Are you addicted to dopamine? To determine whether the problem is a dopamine addiction, set a timer and sit quietly while doing nothing. Doing so will tell you how long you can go without being distracted. Is your wearable telling you to cool it? ”If you wear an Oura ring or another wearable,” Kothari says, “look at the amount of time you spent in a high-stress zone.” How to break a toxic multitasking habit It can be difficult to wrest back control of your time and attention in a world full of distractions, but here are some ways to exert power over technology and the pressure to appear productive: Try meditation. Kothari calls meditation and other mindfulness practices “foundational” to increasing focus and our ability to stay in the moment.



Practice single-tasking. Linker recommends improving your attention span by engaging in a single task such as writing or reading for a sustained period, which she defines as an hour or more. Design your environment for success. Silencing notifications, closing unnecessary browser windows, and keeping your phone out of sight and out of reach will help deepen your focus. “Keeping a scratch pad on your desk lets you quickly log random errands or stray thoughts on paper without interrupting your workflow,” Chapman says. Use technology that cuts off a digital multitasking habit. To address the overuse of smartphones, Kothari recommends the Brick device. “It’s a tile that you can use to turn off all apps or even access to your phone completely.” Recalibrate norms at the office to encourage deep work. In workplaces where multitasking makes it impossible to get things done well, or even at all, Kothari says, “set norms for focused, deep work time where all of your notifications are off and your colleagues commit to not disturbing you.” Take regular brain breaks. Giving your brain a break by taking a short walk, going outside, stretching or simply sitting quietly for a few minutes will restore your mental energy and attention span – and prevent late-afternoon crashes. “A break is not switching from your laptop to your phone,” Chapman says. “A true brain break means stepping away from screens altogether.”



Engage in one form of entertainment at a time. ”Limiting concurrent device usage and social media short-form videos will improve the … assault this type of entertainment has on our ability to focus,” Linker says. Make a deliberate choice. Chapman says that reclaiming our attention spans is entirely in our control but that it requires making the deliberate choice to stop multitasking and start single-tasking. “With this one simple change, many people notice an immediate improvement in their focus, mental energy and productivity,” she says. World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes built more than a century ago
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes built more than a century ago Shona Hendley September 23, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With distinctive details such as ceiling roses and leadlight windows, warm materials including timber flooring and a sense of space created by high ceilings, homes built last century offer unique architectural character and a range of benefits. The craftsmanship and materials also demonstrate these homes’ longevity. Here are five favourite luxury homes for sale right now that were built more than a century ago. 3 Moule Avenue, Brighton VIC A Brighton landmark since 1889, “Narellan” is located in the suburb’s Golden Mile.



The Italianate residence features a striking facade with a wraparound verandah, a corner turret and large arched windows that showcase its period elegance. The interiors – high ceilings, a formal dining room and a billiard room, stained-glass windows and wooden floorboards – continue this. Renovated throughout, the period style blends with modern updates, evident in the kitchen and the wellness space with a sauna and gym. Other features include bay views from the private tower room inside the turret, a self-contained two-bedroom guest wing and a dedicated wine cellar. 2a Barry Street, Clovelly NSW



This c. 1920 seaside residence, “Darby”, has been renovated by the award-winning architects Potter & Wilson. Within walking distance of Clovelly Beach, the three-level home, plus basement, blends modern design with heritage character, using soft curves, arches, Mediterranean architecture and materials such as European oak and jewel-toned quartzite that provide warmth. Preserved original features include ornate ceilings and the front facade. The basement includes a wellness studio/cellar, while a rooftop eyrie offers 180-degree ocean views extending to Botany Bay.



Outside, a barbecue terrace and a heated pool create a resort-style oasis in the landscaped backyard. 121-123 Nelson Road, South Melbourne VIC This c.1920 residence, “Torquay”, has undergone extensive renovation and extension by Statkus Architecture. Located in the St Vincent Gardens Precinct, close to Albert Park village, the double-fronted, freestanding home showcases its Victorian character through a beautiful, ornate open fireplace and facade.



Modern features include polished concrete floors, Venetian plaster walls, a gourmet stone kitchen with a concealed scullery and a custom walk-in robe with full-height storage in the master bedroom suite. A highlight is the curved concrete staircase, while outside are Hamilton Landscapes gardens, a paved al fresco area and a mosaic-tiled infinity-edge pool. 33 Bradleys Head Road, Mosman NSW This Federation home is set on a corner block on approximately 1080 square metres in Clifton Gardens, close to Mosman Village, Bradleys Head and Clifton Gardens Reserve.



Built c.1902, the home features restored sculpted arches, leadlight glazing, pressed-metal ceilings, marble fireplaces, and both formal and informal areas. There are five bedrooms across two levels, plus a home office and harbour views from the upper floor. Outside are landscaped gardens, terraces, a saltwater pool, a gated driveway and a lock-up garage. 4 Holmes Street, Toowong QLD



“Kiarraba” is a c.1900 Victorian gentleman’s residence on approximately 2261 square metres in Toowong, close to shopping and dining and Brisbane schools. Outside, the property features a large swimming pool, easy-care gardens including a herb and veggie patch, wide wraparound verandahs, a private gated entry and a separate visitors’ entry. The interiors are just as indulgent, with a recreation or games room, formal and informal areas, soaring ceilings and wood-burning fireplaces. The home is also practical, with four bedrooms, ample indoor and underfloor storage and a country kitchen with a breakfast bar.

World.title: The world economy is becoming wary of America
World.content:
BusinessMarketsGlobal economy The world economy is becoming wary of America Alan Rappeport September 23, 2026 — 7:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Global investors are balking at US bonds. Talk of the US dollar’s dwindling power is getting louder. Foreign governments are hauling their gold out of American vaults. Almost two years into President Donald Trump’s second term, the world economy is increasingly looking for ways to distance itself from the United States. Concerns about a $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) debt burden, the excessive use of sanctions to solve foreign policy problems and Trump’s penchant for pushing the limits of the rule of law are raising questions about the appeal of the world’s largest economy as a haven for global investment. Top of the world: Almost two years into President Donald Trump’s second term, the global economy is increasingly looking for ways to distance itself from America. Matt Willis Despite pledges by foreign companies and nations to invest in the United States — in many cases to curry favour with the White House — capital is starting to seek alternative destinations. “Geopolitical factors and US weaponisation of the dollar through financial sanctions are causing central banks and other official investors to attempt to diversify away from dollar assets,” said Eswar Prasad, the former head of the International Monetary Fund’s China division.



The United States is not yet an investment pariah. Private investors are still pouring money into American financial markets and stocks, artificial intelligence infrastructure is booming and no rival currency is poised to topple the US dollar imminently. In testimony before Congress last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he remained confident in the credibility of the country’s financial system, arguing that bond auctions continue to operate successfully and that the dollar is still thriving as measured by its share of global transactions. ‘It’s like the countries don’t trust the US. I do think that there is a fear factor.’ Daniel Tannebaum, former Treasury Department and Federal Reserve Bank of New York official “The US is, in fact, the leader, and the leader does not fear competition,” Bessent said. “Competition makes us better.” But cracks in America’s economic dominance are starting to show.



The most glaring example is the bond market. Yields have been soaring as investors, nervous about the mounting national debt demand a higher rate of return for buying Treasury bonds. Earlier this month, the yield on the 10-year Treasury topped 5 per cent, reaching its highest level since 2007. The ominous bond threshold was crossed a week after the US Treasury Department purchased $US5.2 billion of its own debt maturing in the next 10 to 20 years, part of a plan to inject demand into the Treasury market to try to push prices higher and yields lower. Bessent said investors were failing to understand the underlying strength of the economy and dared them to bet against him. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent has been trying to allay the bond market with bigger buybacks, hoping to push down rates. AP “It’s my dream,” Bessent said at Southern Methodist University. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now.” The Federal Reserve’s decision last week to raise rates has somewhat calmed concerns about the central bank’s grip on elevated inflation, fears that injected jitters into bond markets.



Yet with the United States’ long-term fiscal situation looking shaky, some countries are starting to wonder if America is a wise investment. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world, has said it plans to reduce its holdings of US Treasurys as it looks elsewhere for stronger returns. And then there is the future of the greenback. Nearly 90 per cent of global foreign exchange transactions are in US dollars. But the share of dollars being held in central bank reserves has been steadily declining over the past decade, falling to 56 per cent at the end of 2025 from 64 per cent in 2015. Last year, Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, said erratic policymaking in the United States was setting the stage for a “global euro moment.” The United States has taken advantage of the greenback’s special status to use it as a foreign policy tool, imposing stiff sanctions on adversaries such as Iran and Russia. As the United States ramps up its use of sanctions to resolve global conflicts, the permanence of the US dollar as the world’s reserve currency has come into question with greater frequency.



Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist This year, the United States tried to start scaling back its sanctions program amid worries that an overuse of financial warfare was leading other countries to seek alternatives to the dollar. The dollar is used in most cross-border financial transactions, so sanctions can essentially cut off a country’s ability to interact with the Western financial system. Frustrated with how the US uses its economic might, more countries are seeking alternative financial systems that America cannot touch. However, Bessent reversed course in August when he announced Operation Economic Outcast. The initiative aims to strangle Iran’s economy and threatens secondary sanctions on any country that maintains economic ties to Iran. Even the treasury secretary acknowledged that if the United States is forced to make good on that threat, it could “blow up the global financial system.” Although the euro and China’s renminbi do not appear ready to overtake the dollar anytime soon, the emergence of central bank digital currencies, stablecoins and cryptocurrencies gives US adversaries new avenues to circumvent the American financial system when making international transactions. China has been leading the development of a cross-border digital currency platform with Hong Kong, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia that would allow money to move more quickly and with lower fees than what is possible with traditional banking transactions. A similar cross-border payments project led by some Group of 7 major industrialised nations and Western financial institutions is also in development but is not as far along as China’s initiative, which is known as mBridge.



Russia and India said this month they are working on a plan that would let them use central bank digital currencies to settle international trade payments. Such a mechanism would allow the countries to expand their trade relationship and reduce reliance on Western financial institutions that can be targeted by US sanctions. “The story of moving away from the dollar is one of the oldest stories that exists,” said Josh Lipsky, the chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council. “Countries have thought about working around the dollar, and technology is making it a little cheaper and easier to do it than before.” Demand for gold is so high that some countries also want to keep theirs closer to home. Bloomberg While some countries are focused on digital money, others are going for gold as they fret about the stability of the United States. In 2025, world international reserves held in gold surpassed foreign official holdings of US Treasury securities. This year, the price of gold exceeded $US5000 per troy ounce for the first time in history as central banks stocked up on the metal amid intensifying global conflicts and concerns over inflation.





That fear factor is also creating blowback for American companies that are trying to do business abroad. Loading Tannebaum, who is a partner in global management consulting firm Oliver Wyman’s finance and risk practice, said the aggressive use of tariffs and export controls by the United States has made European countries and companies wary of adopting American technology for sensitive industries such as AI. They worry that if they are dependent on the US for such infrastructure, it could be used against them if Washington decides to ban or disable the technology, as it has done during disputes with China and Russia. All of this has contributed to an erosion of the United States’ status as a safe haven. “Governments and companies now have to ask what would happen if the United States turned its economic leverage against them,” Tannebaum said.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval Rob Harris September 23, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose” and warn that Australia must help shape what replaces it as growing strategic competition between the United States and China transforms the Indo-Pacific. In a major foreign policy address in New York, the prime minister will argue that the assumptions underpinning the global system since the end of the Cold War are being tested, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the rules that remain essential. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters in New York City on Wednesday, AEST. Dominic Lorrimer “Since the end of the Cold War, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security; efficiency mattered more than resilience; and international rules would be observed as a matter of course,” Albanese will tell the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen Awards dinner on Wednesday night, where he will be honoured alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali and actor and singer Cynthia Erivo. “Both those expectations are now being tested. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”



His speech carries echoes of the message Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered nine months ago at the World Economic Forum at Davos, Switzerland, where he said the “old order is not coming back” and urged fellow middle powers to unite to find a new way. Albanese will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday (New York time), where the two countries are expected to sign a bilateral security arrangement. As US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping prepare to meet at the White House on Thursday, Albanese sought several leaders of middle power nations, including Britain’s Andy Burnham, Canada’s Mark Carney and France’s Emmanuel Macron, to help build consensus on several issues, including the rise of artificial intelligence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations headquarters in New York City. Dominic Lorrimer But efforts appear to have been fruitless, as Trump very publicly rejected the push from more than 20 leading economies several times in his UN address, saying he was interested only in the economic benefits of winning the technology race, and not regulating AI’s capacity.



Albanese was also at loggerheads with the Trump administration, which has condemned Australia’s plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content. In a submission to the Albanese government, the US embassy described the reforms as “facilitating censorship”. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way,” Albanese told journalists in New York. The prime minister later met Trump at a UN leaders’ reception, posting a picture of the pair on his social media platforms saying it was “always good to catch up” with the president. There is growing discontent within the group of middle powers at the lack of progress towards peace in the Middle East, Trump’s war against Iran, and Russia’s continued aerial bombardment of Ukraine after nearly five years. Several experts, including former prime minister Kevin Rudd, have also warned about the increased risk of conflict in the Indo-Pacific over Taiwan in the coming years. Albanese will use his speech to set out a vision for Australia to help build a new international order rather than simply respond to the changes under way.



“Australia’s response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old,” he will say, while preserving “the rules that matter most” and creating new partnerships and relationships. Related Article Social media Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast The prime minister will identify the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing as the “most consequential factor” shaping the Indo-Pacific, while rejecting the idea that the region should be viewed solely through the prism of the two superpowers. “Our alliance with the United States is the anchor of Australia’s foreign policy,” Albanese will say. But he will also reaffirm his government’s approach to China, Australia’s largest trading partner, saying the country would engage in the national interest. “How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly,” he will say. “But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.”



“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces. Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script.” Albanese will argue that the upheaval of recent years, including war and the pandemic, has exposed the vulnerabilities of supply chains and forced governments to put resilience alongside economic efficiency. “Governments must build the capacity to withstand shocks they did not cause and cannot control,” he will say. That will include strengthening Australia’s sovereign capability while working with partners on economic security, critical supply chains and energy. The Atlantic Council dinner is one of the high-profile events of UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government, business, military, media and civil-society figures expected to attend.



Albanese is being recognised by the Washington-based think tank for his role in strengthening Australia’s alliances and partnerships and promoting security and stability across the Indo-Pacific. Related Article Updated

AI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons His speech places particular emphasis on Australia’s expanding network of partnerships across the Indo-Pacific, including its relationship with ASEAN and a growing web of security agreements with Pacific nations. He will describe the Pacific as “both a home and a family to Australia” and say the region’s priorities, sovereignty and culture must be respected. “For our Pacific neighbours, climate change is the most immediate security threat,” Albanese will say.



The speech will culminate in a concise formulation of the government’s foreign policy. “Building resilience without abandoning openness,” Albanese will say. “Strengthening regional partnerships without abandoning rules.” And Australia would deepen its alliance with the United States and engage its largest trading partner, China, “without allowing either relationship to define who we are”. “In an uncertain world, leadership means showing up for one another, sharing burdens and giving our neighbours greater power to shape their futures,” he will say. It’s true that we’ve done this before, but with the NFL season come some truly great names. Kool-Aid McKinstry, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sauce Gardner, Storm Duck, Younghoe Koo, DeMarvion Overshown, Tank Bigsby and Tank Dell. All right, I’ll grant that FuiFui MoiMoi and Steele Sidebottom are pretty good, too.”

The celebrity encounters (C8) continue: “When I was 14, a friend of my father arranged for me to meet Ricky Nelson in the dressing room of the Sydney Stadium,” recalls Janet Scilly of Waterloo. “Of course, my father had to be there. I had a lot to say but was struck dumb on seeing him. My father thought he was a nice young man because he called Dad ‘Sir’ and shook his hand.”

“I’m not sure if I share Alan Phillips’ (C8) view about C8 driving AI mad,” thinks Seppo Ranki of Glenhaven. “As an experiment, I checked out my name and suburb on Google. Part of the AI Overview said: ‘He frequently writes short, witty observations and life stories for The Sydney Morning Herald’s popular Column 8 section. His published items often feature memories of farm life, old vehicles and everyday humorous encounters.’ I suspect AI has a pretty good handle on both C8 and me.”

Mark Berg of Caringbah South writes: “When at high-school German classes (C8) in the late 1970s, we watched German videos and were expected to translate the script. One memorable line was ‘Mit einer Perucke bist du ein anderer Mensch’. It means, ‘with a wig, you are another person’. Very useful indeed.”

“I’m still waiting to inform anyone who’s interested, in my best schoolboy French, that ‘the pen of the gardener’s niece is on the table in the conservatory’,” informs John Clarke (Jean Leclerc to his mates) of Lorn. Interestingly, Rob Phillips of North Epping says he’s waiting to use the rather congruent “‘my aunt’s pen is on the table’. Regrettably, it doesn’t get you much to eat in a French restaurant.”

World.title: ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner Catherine Strohfeldt September 23, 2026 — 8:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The death of a 69-year-old Brisbane woman during medical testing might prompt a rethink of southern Brisbane’s health and hospital system, a coronial report has suggested. Yaqin Han died on October 14, 2022, when she suffered a cardiac arrest during a diagnostic test at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital. Coroner Ainslie Kierkegaard ruled that while the test – which involved having the 69-year-old run on a treadmill – triggered her cardiac arrest, Han’s doctors had acted appropriately throughout the procedure. Brisbane woman Yaqin Han was referred to the Princess Alexandra Hospital, but treated at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital (pictured). Courtney Kruk Kierkegaard said Han’s doctor during the test – cardiologist Reza Reyaldeen – stopped it as soon as the 69-year-old began complaining of symptoms.



By that point, Han’s heartbeat had become erratic before declining into a cardiac arrest, from which she could not be revived. Related Article Mental health Wards were over capacity when patient took her life, inquest told The coroner said it was only “with the benefit of hindsight” that the care team led by Reyaldeen might have stopped the test sooner, as it would have been outside normal practice based on Han’s vital signs, which were being monitored throughout. However, Kierkegaard highlighted that another south Brisbane hospital, the Princess Alexandra, was the area’s “heart valve centre of excellence”. Han was initially referred to the PA Hospital, but was treated through a hub at the QEII Hospital, which was closer to her home.



She had been diagnosed with aortic stenosis – a narrowing of the heart’s aortic valve – having suffered dizziness, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath walking up hills. However, various doctors who treated Han were unclear whether her condition was a moderate or severe case. Experts testifying to the court agreed her symptoms were not enough to determine the severity of her diagnosis. Her care team decided to undertake an exercise stress test, rather than invasive diagnostic procedures, to determine whether she would need surgery. However, Kierkegaard said there were potential warning signs about Han’s condition being more severe than cardiologists at the QEII Hospital suspected, but they were missed because her care was fragmented.



Related Article Healthcare Doctors almost sent Kris home with a migraine. Then her whole face went numb Han was also a Mandarin speaker, requiring a translator for her appointments. The inquest found medical staff, in some instances, had trouble contacting Han, and a period of 10 months had elapsed between the last time she was questioned about her symptoms and the decision to order the stress test. The maximum acceptable limit for the gap between consultation and testing, experts at the inquest testified, was 12 months. In an independent inquiry, which Kierkegaard referenced throughout her inquest, Staff Specialist Interventional Cardiologist Anthony Camuglia provided four reasons for the time lapse.



These included interruption from the COVID-19 pandemic, Han’s multiple GPs, the Metro South Health system, and staff turnover at the QEII Hospital. Kierkegaard agreed COVID-19 restrictions had some effect, but said there was “scope for the health service to re-examine its model of cardiac care”. She pointed to a triage system used in Brisbane’s northern hospital service, where complex cases are referred to the Prince Charles Hospital.
