World.title: Watch: The colossal hits that set the tone for a new NRL force
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Watch: The colossal hits that set the tone for a new NRL force Nick Wright September 23, 2026 — 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was the hit that did more than rattle Brandon Smith’s rib cage and left him writhing on the ground in pain; it signalled a fledgling NRL juggernaut was getting ready to emerge. When the Dolphins headed into their first game in 2023, fans and pundits across the rugby league landscape were left questioning whether they would ever register a win, given their unsuccessful attempts to lure marquee talent. Inaugural prop Mark Nicholls recalled training in a gym under the Redcliffe stadium grandstand and being left without a video room, adding to their underdog status. Mark Nicholls scored the second try in Dolphins history, in their debut against the Roosters. Getty But that was the position coach Wayne Bennett wanted to be in. And when Felise Kaufusi charged out of the defensive line and laid on one of the hits of the season as Smith went to pass, setting up a shock 28-18 triumph over the Sydney Roosters, the competition was on notice.



“All of a sudden, the crowd was in the game, and when someone in your team can put on a play like that, it turns momentum. It’s inspiring, and on the back of that, we went into the sheds at half-time pretty confident of where we were going,” Nicholls told this masthead. “The club had been criticised for their jerseys, criticised for their recruitment, the squad was too old, there were no star players. But Wayne loves that; to be put in the underdog position by the outsiders is where Wayne does his best work. “From that point on, I sort of knew there was a special thing here. We told the fans what we were about, and the league.” Nicholls would score shortly after that crunching Kaufusi blow – one that followed another devastating hit on Nat Butcher – to level the score at 12-all.



Kaufusi – already an established State of Origin star and premiership-winner from his time at the Melbourne Storm – would replicate his defensive heroics a week later, laying on a similarly ferocious shot on Hudson Young. The Dolphins would emerge victorious against the Canberra Raiders, to truly cement their early reputation as a team that would not take a backwards step. That, according to Nicholls and Kaufusi, was the DNA Bennett had called on them to embed. “He wanted winners around. I was lucky the Bromwich brothers [Jesse and Kenny] came here to create a winning culture, and guys who knew the standard they had to be to win games,” Kaufusi said.



“You can talk as much as you want, but if you don’t show it on the training paddock or out on the field, I don’t think people will follow.” Related Article NRL 2026 A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void? Nicholls added: “[Bennett] talked about not wanting to let the fans down or give up in games – if we were going to lose, we were going to be fighting to the last minute. That sort of attitude the group’s continued.” It is in somewhat ironic circumstances that the Dolphins’ maiden preliminary final will take place against the Roosters on Friday night at Suncorp Stadium. But things are very different than they were four years ago. Once condemned as a squad that was unable to impact the premiership race, they now face a fight to keep the framework of their group together.



While the Dolphins have re-signed Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, Tevita Naufahu (2029) and Brad Schneider (2028), marquee men Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow are among the 12 players who will become free agents from November 1. Dolphins squad movements Losses Jamayne Isaako (Storm), Oryn Keeley (Storm, mid-season), Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers), Ray Stone (retirement), Daniel Saifiti (medical retirement, mid-season) Gains George Williams Key retentions Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (2029), Tevita Naufahu (2029), Brad Schneider (2028), Kurt Donoghoe (2028), Francis Molo (2028) Off contract (at the end of 2027) Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Thomas Flegler, Connelly Lemuelu, Morgan Knowles, Trai Fuller, Felise Kaufusi, LJ Nonu, Sebastian Su’a, Elijah Rasmussen, John Fineanganofo However, with only England halfback George Williams signed on as a 2027 recruit, and the salary cap to rise from 2028 following the unveiling of a $5.3 billion broadcast deal, Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader remained confident the bulk of the squad would remain. And Nicholls believed the talent production coming out of the academy pathways – boom edge forward Brian Pouniu and winger Naufahu the first graduates to impress – would ensure ongoing success, even if some key figures were prised from the club’s clutches. So much so, he admitted he “selfishly” had not wanted to retire at the end of last season.



“I could feel as a player I was getting towards the end of my career, but I felt like there was a good crop of young guys coming through and there was a nucleus of a good team,” Nicholls said. Related Article NRL 2026 How an AFL great has unlocked rugby league’s next great halfback “The spine has been there since day one. There are game breakers all along the backline, a forward pack who are willing to rip in, and guys in there who would do anything to fight over a 50-cent coin. Selfishly, I was keen to play on because I had the feeling the group was going somewhere. “There were all these young guys coming through they needed to keep. I know I made the right decision now, but at the time I was keen to play on because I knew something special was brewing. “You’ve got to back your junior development at some stage, and it may mean you lose two or three of those star players. The club is doing all the right things to make sure that if we do lose a couple of those star players, there are certainly plenty who are ready to fill the spots.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Motorcyclists are being let down by state of the roads
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Motorcyclists are being let down by state of the roads September 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Motorcycles are increasingly hazardous on today’s public roads, not because riders are reckless, but because the infrastructure itself is failing them (″⁣Crash victims part of a growing wave of litigation″⁣, 23/9). Potholes, crumbling surfaces and poorly maintained lanes create traps that cars can absorb but bikes cannot. A minor defect at speed can mean a catastrophic crash.

Riders face an outsized exposure to danger. With no seatbelt, airbag or crumple zone, they meet the road directly. Injuries are severe and rising, turning what should be routine commutes into high-stakes gambles.

If motorcycles were invented today, would regulators permit them on public roads? Given modern safety standards, noise limits and emissions rules, it is doubtful. Yet, we tolerate their risks as inevitable rather than addressable. It is time to ask whether our roads are designed for people, or merely for vehicles.

Angus McLeod, Cremorne Examination of construction needed

The crash victims story highlights the condition of our roads. This reminds me of the number of bird-bath pools of water visible on roads after rain, which instead of draining off the surface seeps through the tar, softening the road foundations leading to potholes. This suggests more attention should be given to the construction of roads including camber, foundations and paving of road surfaces.

Kim Dunstan, Brighton Spend more on maintenance

It is not as if road engineers have forgotten how to build and repair roads. What has changed is the increase in commerce caused by more people and the increase in traffic that is a result.

The problem is worsened by the increase in weight of vehicles. Trucks have been replaced by B-doubles and sedans have been replaced by SUVs, big utes and electric cars and their weighty batteries. We need to spend a lot more on road maintenance, but that can be funded only by higher taxes and road-usage charges.

Welcome to the future.

Peter Hendrickson, East Melbourne



Dodging and weaving in the commute

Re ″⁣Drunk driver weaving all over the road, or pothole dodger?” (Letters, 19/9): On the busy morning commute along Neerim Road between Murrumbeena Road and Kambrook Road, continual pothole dodging and weaving is the norm for drivers, cyclists and motorcyclists. It’s an increasingly hazardous, potholed journey as cars, buses and bicycles dodge and weave around the ever-more numerous, ever-larger, ever-deeper potholes.

On occasion, traffic in both directions must simultaneously zig-zag, while cyclists in bike lanes – mostly children on their way to school – also dodge and weave. With this crowded, pothole-dodging, moving mass of mixed commuters, it’s only a matter of time ...

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East There is a mental health toll

It is traumatic to drive any Victorian road, dodging potholes with anxiety compounded by being on high alert for previous pothole locations, even after they have been filled. What is the mental health impact of lax road and drainage maintenance?

Cherie Forrester, Gembrook Everything is connected

It is easy for people to dismiss the focus on potholes as “insignificant given the challenges of climate change and war-induced economic disaster”. In fact, this issue highlights the factors that underpin the social unrest and political disconnection affecting our communities. These include the harmful effects of privatisation and of elites profiteering at the expense of essential services. Add the failures of the political class to act on the everyday impacts of climate change and we are linked back to potholes. Economics, environment, politics – everything is connected.

As we mourn the loss of activist Gloria Steinem, I’m reminded of her quote: “The future depends entirely on what each of us does every day; a movement is only people moving.”

Philomena Horsley, Carlisle River THE FORUM More than lip service

The Liberals’ updated energy policy includes a core commitment to set up a “technology-neutral” capacity planning mechanism, including nuclear, coal and gas. Priorities will be affordability and reliability.

In addition, you would hope that they would include as a priority the contribution to carbon emissions.

If the Liberal-National parties want to pay more than lip-service to climate action, they must keep carbon emissions reduction as a core part of their energy policy.

John Hughes, Mentone



PM, here’s the mail

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese needs to take off the blinkers, sack his advisers, stop listening to vested interests, read the letters to The Age, and follow the advice given. There’s still time to stop the downward spiral Australia is in because of his timid approach.

Albanese must use his majority and redeem himself and his government.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn The trust dilemma

What matters more for Australia (Comment, 23/9) than public knowledge of government workings is public trust. Unfortunately, increase in public knowledge can result in decrease of public trust, which is why governments fight tooth and nail against more transparency.

Ruth Farr, Blackburn South Shameful echo

“Aborigines are the most primitive people on earth.” The last time I heard that was in grade 4. It’s taken most of my 82 years to learn how wrong, demeaning and ignorant white attitudes were. It was a shock to hear Pauline Hanson say it.

I apologise to Indigenous people for quoting the words.

Anne McNamara, Armadale Irony bypass

Donald Trump criticises Australia for its stance on AI, arguing that it would be an assault on free speech the day after the Washington press pool downs tools in retaliation for Trump banning three networks from press conferences because he doesn’t like their coverage.

Stephen Dinham, Metung Plan out of touch

I read Julian Leeser’s Liberal plan for solving the difficulties faced within schools, and was saddened and disappointed.

As a humanities teacher of 42 years across a range of schools in inner-city and regional settings, I wonder about his understanding of such things as “pride in the Australian flag and Western culture”.

Amazed at the idea of “removal of Indigenous history and culture, Asia and Australia’s engagement with the region and sustainability” because they’re not being taught by people with expertise in those fields. This just sounds like a policy that is so out of touch with the reality of teaching in 2026.

To teach Indigenous history in “discrete, carefully planned topics” reminds me of how we were taught about Indigenous history back in the 1960s.

What does he mean by “our British foundation and multicultural character”, yet not teaching about our Asian region!

The most disturbing aspect of the plan is the encouragement of ex-ADF staff to become teachers after one year because they “have no problem with discipline”.

Kathy Diviny, Coburg



Asleep at the wheel

One wonders how much consultation took place with residents before the construction of these monolith-type buildings housing the AI data centres, or did the authorities say aren’t they lucky to have a data centre located on their doorstep?

All very well for the government to now introduce planning regulations but in a number of cases the gate has been well and truly shut after the horse has bolted. These controls should have been part of the approval process, so one can only surmise the government was asleep at the wheel when applications were considered. Why is it not possible for architects to design buildings that are neighbourhood friendly so that in 10 or 20 years, we can be proud of the structure instead of buildings that make grain silos look positively attractive?

Bruce MacKenzie, South Kingsville AI safeguards

The prime minister is to be commended for seeking greater safeguards on AI development (“PM joins global push for new AI safeguards”, 21/9). Given the threat of AI-developed biological weapons, the government is also to be commended for its efforts to strengthen the Biological Weapons Convention with a board of experts and enhanced verification and compliance measures. However, it could do more to reduce the risks of AI-related harms.

It should significantly increase resourcing to the Australian AI Safety Institute. It should also require mandatory reporting of significant AI-related harms by developers and sellers of AI models, and voluntary reporting for users negatively affected by AI. The government cannot regulate a problem it doesn’t fully understand.

Having a reporting mechanism for significant harms would create an evidence base to inform regulators, provide early warnings of systemic risk, and build public trust in the legitimate use of AI.

Mark Zirnsak, Parkville Children the losers

The Royal Children’s Hospital is begging for funds to staff its new emergency department. The government’s response – “the government was working closely with the hospital to transition services into the expanded emergency department″⁣.

No new staff, just robbing Peter to pay Paul.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South Not the news

Donald Trump’s love for TV, enthusiasm for allowing reporter access, and frequent press conferences are of little democratic value where much of what he says is exaggerated, stripped of context, or simply untrue. The term ″⁣transparent″⁣ implies that Trump’s White House provides the public with access to accurate information about government activities, decisions, and budgets. It doesn’t. Rather, it gluts the media cycle with self-serving distortions. Sheer quantity over quality.

Declan Melia, East Melbourne Justified objections

Carlton residents who object to large crowds drinking on public land near their homes are justified in their objections (″⁣No happy median in clamp on roadway drinking″⁣, 22/9). Many well-known problems arise due to the combination of crowds and alcohol. There are many existing options for alcohol consumption, and making this space an alcohol-free one isn’t making it ″⁣sacrosanct″⁣ at all – it’s simply reinforcing the rights of everyone to enjoy the area safely and without nuisance. Not being permitted to drink there is a reasonable sacrifice to make for community harmony. Abstaining in relaxed outdoor environments seems to be challenging for many, but it is possible.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave



Wrong priorities

The plan by Opposition Leader Jess Wilson (″⁣Coalition pledges new select-entry high schools″⁣, 20/9) to spend millions building more select-entry schools to further advantage students who are already capable will further destroy the public education system and decrease overall educational outcomes in Victoria as public schools lose their role models and mentors. This money could be better used to build state-of-the-art technical schools in the outer suburbs mentioned in the article to provide the builders and tradies we need.

Lauren Basil, Footscray Iran’s long game

For a theological dictatorship, the Islamic Republic of Iran sure knows how American democracy works under Donald Trump. In the words of Paul Keating, they are ″⁣doing (Trump) slowly″⁣ by extending the war for as long as it makes Trump look bad leading up to the mid-term elections in November. Trump’s war-mongering and talk of annihilating Iran is like water off a duck’s back for the Iran leadership. They know US voters will do more damage to Trump than a barrage of drone attacks.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Peace remains elusive

Columnist Rodger Shanahan (Comment, 23/9) states that while Israel’s simultaneous occupation of Syrian, Palestinian and Lebanese territory may give Israel short-term security, wise leaders understand that long-term security comes through a willingness to cede land for peace.

But the reality is that previous Israeli offers and actions to cede land in surrounding territories resulted in the Second Intifada, Hezbollah’s reoccupation of southern Lebanon, and October 7, 2023. Long-term peace has been maintained between Israel and neighbouring Jordan and Egypt, including in the latter case by Israel’s ceding of the Sinai Peninsula.

However, a lasting peace remains elusive with a Palestinian leadership which either seeks Israel’s elimination, in the case of Hamas, or else has a “pay for slay” policy of rewarding terrorism, in the case of the Palestinian Authority.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Putin on the blitz

Vladimir Putin no doubt had pre-election jitters, concerned that the Ukraine war might have had an impact on his electoral appeal (“Putin secures Russian vote”, 23/9) – a war that has resulted in possibly 500,000 Russian fatalities, caused fuel shortages and pushed up food prices.

He must feel relieved and chuffed that his party, despite all of this, was still able to achieve a record number of seats in the Russian parliament.

Dennis Walker, North Melbourne Waning power

Despite his bluff and bluster, the self-proclaimed ″⁣genius″⁣ US President Donald Trump is steadily eroding his power, influence and relevance on the world stage.

Jon Smith, Leongatha



AND ANOTHER THING Trump

President Donald Trump is right – he runs the most transparent White House ever. Everybody, except the willfully “blind”, can see right through him.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Another Trump deal to end the “military conflict” after the midterm elections. Why am I

not convinced?

Graham Fetherstonhaugh, North Fitzroy For Trump, who claims to be master of the deal, a media boycott was always on the cards. Long live the free press.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor I know it’s not a peace prize but will Donald Trump get a participation ribbon for turning up at the UN’s General Assembly and giving a rant?

James Lane, Hampton East



Furthermore

Pauline Hanson needs a more down-to-earth means of transport. Can someone give her a bicycle? (“Questions over One Nation’s missing plane”, 23/9)

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton Brisbane Lions player Lachie Neale’s story is truly painful. As a St Kilda supporter, it resonates deeply with the absence, through suspension, of Carl Ditterich from our only premiership team,

60 years ago in 1966. Time has not healed that anguish.

Mark Cherny, Caulfield North Data centres are not a panacea for economic ills.

Helena Kilingerova, Vermont With regard to the potential for artificial intelligence to escape, did no one learn anything when HAL refused to open the pod bay doors in 2001, A Space Odyssey?

Greg Brown, Tarneit Your correspondent (Letters, 23/9) is correct to write, “if climate change is an intergenerational threat, 37 new fossil-fuel approvals is an odd response”. He could also have written not if, but when.

Lesley Walker, Northcote Finally

Smart glasses can be easily hackable? We’ve all been framed!

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon

World.title: ‘Toxic multitasking’ is breaking your brain. Here’s how to take control
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessMental health ‘Toxic multitasking’ is breaking your brain. Here’s how to take control Jolie Kerr September 23, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In our busy, always-on world, multitasking – performing several tasks or engaging in more than one activity concurrently – has become a default setting. At work and at play, our focus is increasingly given to more than one thing at a time: checking emails during a Zoom meeting, scrolling Instagram while watching television, switching browser tabs or responding to notifications while engaged in deep or focused work. “Toxic multitasking is the illusion of productivity,” says Sandi Chapman, the chief director at the Centre for BrainHealth in the US and a professor of psychology at the University of Texas at Dallas. “Multitasking is often seen as a sign of high productivity. Unfortunately, your brain experiences it as a performance bottleneck. We think we’re getting two complex things done at once, but our brains simply aren’t wired for it.” Picking up your phone while working or watching TV is a perfect example of toxic multitasking. Getty Images Not all forms of multitasking are unhealthy, but multitasking can, and often does, turn into problematic behaviour that can become addictive, and that has a real effect on how our brain and nervous system function. Toxic multitasking is the norm, but that doesn’t make it normal



“Today, more and more people are doing multiple things at the same time, double- and triple-booked on meetings,” says Ashish Kothari, founder and chief executive of Happiness Squad, a consulting group focused on employee engagement. Although it may give the appearance and feeling of productivity, multitasking that is characterised by constant “context switching” is detrimental without breaks. “When you switch between tasks, your brain doesn’t instantly reset,” Chapman says. “It burns through your mental energy. Your brain works harder and produces less.” She compares multitasking to trying to read two books at once. “You don’t absorb twice as much information from reading both at the same time. Instead, you simply keep losing your place in both.” Related Article Sleep Three minutes a day could be all it takes to prevent this common sleep issue This way of working doesn’t stop at work. The urge to multitask continues outside of business hours, permeating our non-work time. “We’re on phones all the time,” Kothari says. “We might be watching TV and doing something else. As a result our sleep is affected and, combined, creates a heavy toxic effect on our holistic well-being, physically, emotionally, mentally and spiritually.” Digital multitasking, such as looking at more than one entertainment device at a time (like watching TV while scrolling on TikTok), has a particularly strong negative effect on our attention – and, ironically, on our ability to multitask. “These types of inputs actually reduce your ability to handle multiple inputs at once,” says neuroscientist Kay Linker.



Linker distinguishes between good multitasking and bad, pointing out that multitasking can be beneficial when used correctly. “Once a task becomes automatic, it is transferred to a different part of the brain, allowing for parallel processing,” she says. Examples of this include listening to a podcast or book while taking a walk or calling a friend while commuting to work, in contrast to what Linker calls “task switching, which drains your control and focus”. Looking at your phone doesn’t give your brain a break, but taking a short walk does. Getty Images The effects of toxic multitasking are real, and so are the drivers There are consequences to all this multitasking, and the effects can be serious, affecting performance at work and creating a high degree of exhaustion, stress and burnout that leads to the inability to think clearly, i.e., brain fog. There are also emotional and interpersonal repercussions, including irritability, a reduced ability to connect with others, a shallow or insincere affect, and a loss in satisfaction at work and life. Chapman says that toxic multitasking is a natural extension of hustle culture. “There’s pressure on us, both professionally and personally, to prioritise output and quantity over quality,” she says. The pressures of expectation, driven by technology, have created a constant hunger for productivity, in which we feel the need to always be on and to give our attention away to social media and smartphones.



“We have become dopamine addicts,” says Kothari, who adds that the pace at which we’re expected to take in and respond to information is “putting us in a constant fight-flight-freeze mode, wanting us to keep taking action and feeling like we can’t stop”. Related Article Mental health ADHD symptoms change as you age. Here’s what to expect Because toxic multitasking has been so normalised, you may not even be aware of how much you’re engaging in it, but there are clear signs that it has become a problem. “Usually, the first symptom of toxic multitasking is emotional strain,” Chapman says. “If a quick question from a co-worker makes you want to snap, that’s often a sign your brain is overwhelmed from constant distractions or overload.” There are other ways to determine whether multitasking is a problem, and Kothari recommends using these assessments to identify an attention problem: Do you know how often you pick up your phone? Counting the number of times you pick up your phone during the day provides a data point to quantify a digital multitasking habit. “Most people pick their phone up over 150 times a day,” Kothari says. “It’s a clear indicator that we have lost our ability to focus.”



Are you addicted to dopamine? To determine whether the problem is a dopamine addiction, set a timer and sit quietly while doing nothing. Doing so will tell you how long you can go without being distracted. Is your wearable telling you to cool it? ”If you wear an Oura ring or another wearable,” Kothari says, “look at the amount of time you spent in a high-stress zone.” How to break a toxic multitasking habit It can be difficult to wrest back control of your time and attention in a world full of distractions, but here are some ways to exert power over technology and the pressure to appear productive: Try meditation. Kothari calls meditation and other mindfulness practices “foundational” to increasing focus and our ability to stay in the moment.



Practice single-tasking. Linker recommends improving your attention span by engaging in a single task such as writing or reading for a sustained period, which she defines as an hour or more. Design your environment for success. Silencing notifications, closing unnecessary browser windows, and keeping your phone out of sight and out of reach will help deepen your focus. “Keeping a scratch pad on your desk lets you quickly log random errands or stray thoughts on paper without interrupting your workflow,” Chapman says. Use technology that cuts off a digital multitasking habit. To address the overuse of smartphones, Kothari recommends the Brick device. “It’s a tile that you can use to turn off all apps or even access to your phone completely.” Recalibrate norms at the office to encourage deep work. In workplaces where multitasking makes it impossible to get things done well, or even at all, Kothari says, “set norms for focused, deep work time where all of your notifications are off and your colleagues commit to not disturbing you.” Take regular brain breaks. Giving your brain a break by taking a short walk, going outside, stretching or simply sitting quietly for a few minutes will restore your mental energy and attention span – and prevent late-afternoon crashes. “A break is not switching from your laptop to your phone,” Chapman says. “A true brain break means stepping away from screens altogether.”



Engage in one form of entertainment at a time. ”Limiting concurrent device usage and social media short-form videos will improve the … assault this type of entertainment has on our ability to focus,” Linker says. Make a deliberate choice. Chapman says that reclaiming our attention spans is entirely in our control but that it requires making the deliberate choice to stop multitasking and start single-tasking. “With this one simple change, many people notice an immediate improvement in their focus, mental energy and productivity,” she says. World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes built more than a century ago
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes built more than a century ago Shona Hendley September 23, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With distinctive details such as ceiling roses and leadlight windows, warm materials including timber flooring and a sense of space created by high ceilings, homes built last century offer unique architectural character and a range of benefits. The craftsmanship and materials also demonstrate these homes’ longevity. Here are five favourite luxury homes for sale right now that were built more than a century ago. 3 Moule Avenue, Brighton VIC A Brighton landmark since 1889, “Narellan” is located in the suburb’s Golden Mile.



The Italianate residence features a striking facade with a wraparound verandah, a corner turret and large arched windows that showcase its period elegance. The interiors – high ceilings, a formal dining room and a billiard room, stained-glass windows and wooden floorboards – continue this. Renovated throughout, the period style blends with modern updates, evident in the kitchen and the wellness space with a sauna and gym. Other features include bay views from the private tower room inside the turret, a self-contained two-bedroom guest wing and a dedicated wine cellar. 2a Barry Street, Clovelly NSW



This c. 1920 seaside residence, “Darby”, has been renovated by the award-winning architects Potter & Wilson. Within walking distance of Clovelly Beach, the three-level home, plus basement, blends modern design with heritage character, using soft curves, arches, Mediterranean architecture and materials such as European oak and jewel-toned quartzite that provide warmth. Preserved original features include ornate ceilings and the front facade. The basement includes a wellness studio/cellar, while a rooftop eyrie offers 180-degree ocean views extending to Botany Bay.



Outside, a barbecue terrace and a heated pool create a resort-style oasis in the landscaped backyard. 121-123 Nelson Road, South Melbourne VIC This c.1920 residence, “Torquay”, has undergone extensive renovation and extension by Statkus Architecture. Located in the St Vincent Gardens Precinct, close to Albert Park village, the double-fronted, freestanding home showcases its Victorian character through a beautiful, ornate open fireplace and facade.



Modern features include polished concrete floors, Venetian plaster walls, a gourmet stone kitchen with a concealed scullery and a custom walk-in robe with full-height storage in the master bedroom suite. A highlight is the curved concrete staircase, while outside are Hamilton Landscapes gardens, a paved al fresco area and a mosaic-tiled infinity-edge pool. 33 Bradleys Head Road, Mosman NSW This Federation home is set on a corner block on approximately 1080 square metres in Clifton Gardens, close to Mosman Village, Bradleys Head and Clifton Gardens Reserve.



Built c.1902, the home features restored sculpted arches, leadlight glazing, pressed-metal ceilings, marble fireplaces, and both formal and informal areas. There are five bedrooms across two levels, plus a home office and harbour views from the upper floor. Outside are landscaped gardens, terraces, a saltwater pool, a gated driveway and a lock-up garage. 4 Holmes Street, Toowong QLD



“Kiarraba” is a c.1900 Victorian gentleman’s residence on approximately 2261 square metres in Toowong, close to shopping and dining and Brisbane schools. Outside, the property features a large swimming pool, easy-care gardens including a herb and veggie patch, wide wraparound verandahs, a private gated entry and a separate visitors’ entry. The interiors are just as indulgent, with a recreation or games room, formal and informal areas, soaring ceilings and wood-burning fireplaces. The home is also practical, with four bedrooms, ample indoor and underfloor storage and a country kitchen with a breakfast bar.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki, police failed 12-year-old - whānau member
World.content:
Tears as whānau member tells inquest 12-year-old was failed

A whānau member of a 12-year-old New Plymouth girl - who died of a suspected suicide in 2017 - has told an inquest that the adults and agencies involved in the girl's life failed her.

There was barely a dry eye as the woman's words were read out by a lawyer while she watched proceedings via a video link at the New Plymouth District Court.

She said problems in the family were well known to social workers and police, but they didn't get the help they required.

Oranga Tamariki "had failed" them, she said.

"There were three children living in neglect and I struggle to understand how this was not recognised as requiring urgent action."

The whānau member remembered the 12-year-old "trying on numerous occasions to seek help in the period before her death" but said her concerns "were not properly heard or acted upon".

She believed that had someone listened to the girl and acted appropriately, she might still be alive today.

Two years after the girl's death, a drug-addicted Taranaki woman was jailed for four years and three months for the physical and psychological abuse of three children.

The whānau member described home circumstances where the children were often "not properly fed" and left to care for themselves in an unsafe environment while "adults drank and used drugs around them".

The mother would "repeatedly choose drugs and alcohol" over the children's well being, she said.

The whānau member acknowledged some of the adults had experienced hardship themselves, but said it didn't excuse the "harm caused" or their "repeated failure" to protect the children.

Schools the children attended were aware of their circumstances and they received school lunches and additional support from teachers, "which demonstrated that concerns had been identified".

But despite regular contact with social workers - at home and at school - the children didn't receive the protection or intervention they needed, the woman said.

Police were also in the firing line.

The whānau member said police were aware of the children's living situation "yet no meaningful action was taken to improve" their safety or well-being.

She recognised the "complexity" of what happened but said she had written the statement to ensure the experience of the 12-year-old was fully acknowledged.

"I hope this inquest leads to change for other families who experience what my family did. However, it is gravely disappointing that it has taken nine years for someone to listen and take action."

Coroner Heather McKenzie thanked the woman for the "courage" and "grace" she had shown in engaging with the inquest, and apologised for its delay.

The whānau member made a heart sign with her hands before logging off the video call.

Earlier the inquest heard from Detective Sergeant Louise Prendergast who had conducted an executive review of the case for the coroner.

Her report addressed the evolution of police reporting systems, family harm policy, inter-agency co-operation, the family harm history of the 12-year-old's whānau and the police response.

Detective Sergeant Prendergast said the girl's whānau had been involved in 27 family harm incidents, five before she was born, 21 during her lifetime and one after her death.

On three occasions the 12-year-old was identified as the victim.

Detective Sergeant Prendergast said an investigation into serious allegation made by the girl in the weeks before her death was dropped because there wasn't enough evidence to pursue it.

Her mother - the first person to be told of the allegation - denied it happened and the child did not give an evidential interview.

The inquest heard a community constable's failure to record the incident correctly would not have changed that outcome.

Detective Sergeant Prendergast was content police had done all they could to help the girl.

"Based on this review, my assessment is that police responded appropriately to each reported event, based on the information available at the time ... omissions would not have materially changed the information available to police or altered the response provided.

"Accordingly, I'm satisfied that the police response was appropriate in the circumstances, and the recording omissions had no material impact on police actions" prior to the 12 year-old's death.

Detective Sergeant Prendergast said there was high level of formalised inter-agency co-operation and sharing of information, but there were occasionally gaps.

She pointed to a 2013 report of neglect involving the children while they were living in Waitara, that wasn't referred to police.

"This would have been investigated at that time ... it's difficult to determine if a prosecution would have resulted from that investigation, but it would have given police an opportunity to begin an investigation and hold an occurrence of this in NIA [the police computer]."

The 2013 report of neglect would later form part of a prosecution.

A senior Oranga Tamariki manager, who can't be named, also gave evidence.

She said the 2013 report of neglect in Waitara, which involved headlice, cleanliness and whānau drug use didn't meet the threshold to inform police.

The manager said it would be normal following such a report for a social worker to help the family with those problems via a support and educational approach.

The inquest has concluded.

World.title: Decision on LNG terminal delayed
World.content:
ACT and New Zealand First have all but confirmed a decision on whether the government should underwrite a new liquefied natural gas terminal has been put off until after the election.

The government had been intending to sign a contract for the LNG terminal before the election, so it could be up and running by mid-2028.

The intent is so the country has back-up to mitigate dry-year risk, but the government has had to back down on introducing levy to pay for the terminal.

The energy minister, Simeon Brown, has previously said the a contract could still be signed during the election campaign.

A Cabinet committee had met on Wednesday morning to discuss the plans.

On Wednesday afternoon, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said no decision had been made.

"The Cabinet position was not to make a decision today, and that's where the matter sits at this point in time, and that's precisely and totally what the decision was. So any other variations and translations are false."

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Peters confirmed that was the collective decision of all three parties at the sub-committee, and that there had been no pushback.

He would not say what his preference was, but it was a "possibility" he would express a view on the campaign trail.

ACT leader and deputy prime minister David Seymour said ACT's position was that the government got the best possible deal, and it would be responsible to keep its options open.

"I don't know that a deal is possible before the election," he said.

It did not mean ACT opposed work continuing on the terminal, however.

RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"There can be progress. I mean, the government is carrying out a tender, and that can continue. But it doesn't mean that you make your decision before the election," Seymour said.

He said signing a contract before the election would be "irresponsible."

Brown would not talk about what was discussed in Cabinet or Cabinet committees, and said he would have more to say when decisions were made.

"Ultimately the process will, to some extent, dictate the timing," he said.

Methanex, which was at times using close to half the country's natural gas supply, is closing its Taranaki plant next year.

Genesis Energy has since announced it has picked up major gas contracts that run from March next year to December 2029.

Brown said that may "provide some relief," but the government would continue to work through the LNG process.

World.title: 'New frontier' as Predator Free Dunedin sets sights on more pests
World.content:
Audio player for " Predator Free Dunedin targeting pests in sanctuary " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/environment/1541308%2Fnew-frontier-as-predator-free-dunedin-sets-sights-on-more-pests

Predator Free Dunedin targeting pests in sanctuary Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

As wildlife flourishes in a fenced Otago ecosanctuary, mahi is ramping up to protect the birds flying the coop.

In July, Predator Free Dunedin received $3.9 million over three years from the Department of Conservation to boost its predator elimination work.

That funding meant they would soon be targeting mustelids, rats, rabbits and feral cats lurking around the Orokonui Ecosanctuary.

Behind a predator fence, the ecosanctuary has become a safe haven for native wildlife.

Comms lead Taylor Davies-Colley said there has been a lot of breeding success.

"For some of these species, like the kakaruia, to some extent, the kākā as well, we're now at a point where we may well be at carrying capacity inside the sanctuary," he said.

"And so the next stage of their expansion, their return into coastal Otago will have to involve areas outside of Orokonui."

Orokonui Ecosanctuary comms lead Taylor Davies-Colley says any work to remove pests from around the fence helps to reduce the risk of a predator breaking in. RNZ/Tess Brunton

They were seeing more kakaruia outside the fence, but they were not witnessing nesting success, he said.

That was where he hoped work to eliminate predators from the surrounding area would make a significant difference.

"Our ultimate goal is never to be the only place with these manu," Davies-Colley said.

"Our work ends when there are so many of these birds across the landscape that we have no need to worry about them anymore, that people are woken up by kākā in their backyard before they come to visit Orokonui. And so for that to happen, they need breeding success outside the fence."

The Halo Project was working on the ground to remove pests for Predator Free Dunedin as its delivery partner.

Its predator free project manager Jonah Kitto-Verhoef said they would be targeting a range of pests.

"That's the new frontier. We're very confident now in our approach to possums and now we're looking to explore, is there synergies and cost savings by doing more species at once?

"Can we clear areas quicker? Because that's really the goal. We can't keep going back to the same areas to tick off yet another species year after year."

Halo Project predator free project manager Jonah Kitto-Verhoef with new scat dog, Pepper. RNZ/Tess Brunton

They would be using a range of techniques, including rabbit shooting, toxins, live capture devices, and AI-assisted trapping.

They were also training up 10-month-old Pepper as another scat detection dog to help them find stoats

In 2024, a pilot using AI to differentiate predators from native birds was rolled out in the area around Orokonui.

Jonah Kitto-Verhoef said they had upgraded their auto trap network of about 100, which could safely identify between curious kākā and possums and rodents.

Predator Free Dunedin project lead Rhys Millar said the funding meant they could target multiple pests at once.

"We're going to remove prey first, so the rabbits and rat populations will be reduced to very low numbers," he said.

"By doing so, the stoats and the feral cats will become increasingly hungry and therefore more vulnerable to our removal techniques."

Supplied/Predator Free Dunedin

The area would cover from Port Chalmers to Orokonui, Aramoana and Blueskin Bay.

"We're also going to be testing PAPP sausage, a new toxin in this environment, which will be a first. So it is a bit of a project of firsts, new techniques, new ways of working on effectively a mainland situation."

The project was off the back of the successful removal of possums from the Otago Peninsula after years of hard mahi.

But Rhys Millar said not having a fence or natural barrier like the peninsula would be challenging.

"One of the key things that we will need to do is to learn how to detect animals quickly because we will be subject to constant reincursions, detecting those animals, the stoats and the feral cats, very quickly and then removing them quickly.

The view from Orokonui Ecosanctuary RNZ/Tess Brunton

Jonah Kitto-Verhoef said the ecosanctuary showed us what predator freedom looked like.

"The opportunity and what Orokonui provides is a really amazing creche for reseeding the whole landscape with a range of vulnerable species," he said.

"t's so exciting to think about the fact we can have all these things that may not have been present on the mainland for sometimes decades, sometimes 150 years or more, and they could again thrive in their natural environment."

World.title: Body found in Waikato River after earlier report of man jumping into water
World.content:
The body of a man has been found in the Waikato River after it was reported he jumped in the early hours of the morning.

Police first received reports of the incident near Swarbrick Landing off River Rd about 1.30am on Wednesday.

Search and Rescue boats and a helicopter were used in the search.

Hamilton Area Commander, Inspector Scott Miller said the body was the man reported missing and he had left his clothes and phone behind.

RNZ / Rachel Moore

The man's body was located near River Oaks Place, approximately 3km from where he was first reported missing from.

"Police extend their deepest condolences to the man's family and loved ones during this very difficult time.

"Police would also like to thank all those involved in the search and the members of public who kept an eye out for items of interest in the area."

A council sign at the river warns of a sudden drop, strong currents and submerged objects and says no diving or jumping is advised.

It was quiet when RNZ visited the scene, apart from police flying the drone.

Picnic tables and a BBQ sit on the landing next to the river pathway in a pull in bay off River Road.

A viewing platform overlooks the river.

World.title: Parliament ends for another term with sneers and cheers
World.content:
Parliament has ended for another term with politicians landing their final pre-election blows in the House.

The adjournment debate was full of sneers and cheers, with party leaders criticising their opposition and crowing about their own successes, and what they bring to the electorate.

It began with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defending the coalition's stability, followed by Labour leader Chris Hipkins suggesting ACT and New Zealand First had run rings around National.

Here's what each party leader had to say.

Christopher Luxon

Christopher Luxon repeated National's "no new taxes" refrain multiple times in the House. File photo. VNP/Phil Smith

Luxon thanked his own MPs, as well as coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First.

"Despite every prediction, we have delivered strong and stable government at the moment New Zealanders needed it most," he said.

"We have shown that three parties can disagree honestly and still work together for New Zealand, and we have found common ground and we have governed in the National interest."

He laid out the government's achievements across the term, comparing them against a country "in trouble" when , before moving on to what National could offer New Zealanders.

"Make no mistake, this is a policy election," he said, proceeding to list National's policies.

Luxon repeated National's "no new taxes" refrain multiple times, with MPs echoing it in chorus around him.

"This election is a very straight choice: a National party growing the economy so Kiwis can get ahead, or a radical, a radical Labour coalition addicted to spending and taxing and borrowing," he said.

Chris Hipkins

Chris Hipkins said government failed to deliver on its promise to fix the cost of living. File photo. VNP / Phil Smith

Hipkins immediately questioned Luxon's claims about the coalition's strength.

"Three years ago, I said that if Christopher Luxon went into government with David Seymour and Winston Peters, they would run circles around them," he said.

"Well, it's just as well they work in a round building, Mr Speaker, because they've run the carpet threadbare."

Hipkins said the government failed to deliver on its promise to fix the cost of living.

"This is a government that's had the wrong priorities, that's been out of touch with New Zealanders, and now they are out of time as well," he said.

He offered three stories which he said illustrated the government's track record: one about a conversation with an emergency department nurse who said their ED was always in crisis, a Wellington business owner whose turnover plummeted following public sector job cuts, and new parents in a supermarket who said they could not make ends meet.

"We cannot afford three more years of this government," he said, adding that Labour would offer New Zealanders real help with the cost of living.

Chlöe Swarbrick

Chlöe Swarbrick said politics was a game to the coalition parties, but it wasn't a game for those sturggling to get by. File photo. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Swarbrick brought along props: print-outs of headlines illustrating what she asserted were the government's failings, on everything from climate change to pay equity changes and benefit sanctions.

She laid into the coalition, saying it was ironic that the prime minister believed Māori ceded sovereignty because Winston Peters is "the most self-sovereign individual this Parliament has ever seen".

Swarbrick also took aim at the government's priorities.

"This parliament has spent hours and hours making English an official language, and the three men in charge of this country have decided to waste all of our time defining what a woman is," she said.

Swarbrick said this term she had realised politics was a game to the coalition parties.

"But politics is not a game when it is the difference between whether your family can eat, whether they have a roof over their head," she said.

"I know that means that we get a reputation for being uptight dorks, I know that it means that we get a reputation for being angry, but Mr Speaker, I make no apologies for caring about this country, because that is the point."

David Seymour

David Seymour claimed ACT was responsible for $14 billion in savings. File photo. VNP/Phil Smith

Seymour thanked Luxon and Peters "for the way we've worked together more successfully than our worst enemies' worst nightmares to put a record amount of legislation through this House, making New Zealand a better place."

He said ACT was responsible for $14 billion in savings from its ministers and policies over the term.

"We worked out that's $57,000 for each person who voted for us.

"Now, when you consider it's free to give your party vote to ACT, it's got to be a good deal."

He also claimed victory for stopping three new taxes during the term.

"We welcome new disciples to the Church of No New Taxes, no matter how recently they may have sinned," he said.

"We know Chris [Luxon] has changed churches before, and we're glad to see him at our one preaching no new taxes."

He said this term ACT started a debate no one else was willing to - over the Treaty of Waitangi principles - and said the party would continue to campaign for "one law for all".

Winston Peters

Winton Peters said he was "coming back real big time". File photo. VNP / Phil Smith

In a typically combative speech, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters railed against other MPs in the House, the previous government's ferry terminals, vaccine mandates, and the "waa-waa-wānanga."

He began by referencing the 56 members bills New Zealand First MPs have submitted throughout the term, saying they represented New Zealand First's values of "social conservatism, patriotism, economic nationalism, and common sense," and that they would be adopted in the next coalition agreement.

Speaking of his own foreign affairs work, Peters noted he had been to all 17 Pacific member states, and China twice.

Peters was frequently heckled during his speech, particularly by the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, to which he responded "we know what a Treaty is. We know what a woman is," to further heckling.

"Oh, bye bye Winston? Stand back sunshine. I've got news for you. I'm coming back real big time. We're coming back with an army."

Rawiri Waititi

Rawiri Waititi said it had been the "most anti-Māori, anti-Tiriti, anti-taiao, anti-worker government in a generation". File photo. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi said while this would be the last speech he delivered this term, "like Arnold Schwarzenegger said, I'll be back".

Waititi went on to describe the government as "the most anti-Māori, anti-Tiriti, anti-taiao, anti-worker government in a generation," and on November 7th the opposition would "issue their move-on orders" from Parliament.

He referenced pay equity, the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori ward reforms, the removal of Section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, and the Treaty Principles Bill.

Waititi thought he had been given 10 minutes, but the Speaker reminded him he had a split call, and so only five.

"I will go to the back page, Mr Speaker," he said.

World.title: Search for missing plane in southern lake ends with no answers
World.content:
Police have finished searching a South Westland lake for a plane that disappeared almost 50 years ago with seven people on board, but say nothing was found that warranted further investigation.

The aircraft - ZK-EBU - went missing in 1978 during a chartered scenic flight from Dunedin through Queenstown, Milford Sound and Preservation Inlet.

Last contact with the plane was made while it was flying through Milford Sound.

The seven people on board included pilot Edward Morrison and passengers David Hogg and Earl, Elizabeth, David, Alec and Rosemary Eliza Stuart.

Navy, police and coastguard crews have scoured Lake Moeraki north of Haast for the past two days, following a possible sighting of the plane.

Senior Sergeant Mark Kirkwood said sonar and divers were used to assess the lake bed, but nothing useful was found.

He said the outcome was disappointing for families after a difficult and emotional few days.

"We know this search has carried great significance for the families of the seven people who disappeared nearly five decades ago."

The missing plane. Supplied

Five members of the Stuart family of Dunedin were on the plane, and a spokesperson today said the family was grateful for the search.

"The Stuart family at the search site would like to give our sincerest gratitude to Gavin Grimmer for all his continued effort in searching for our family. We would also like to thank the various agencies including New Zealand Police, the police national dive squad, the Royal New Zealand Navy and the coast guard whom dedicated their precious time and resources to the search, and for their empathetic and courteous approach towards us during this difficult time.

"The outcome was obviously not what we wanted and it has brought up many raw emotions and memories but it has been a pleasure to be with family and share stories of those lost."

Pete and Steve from Coastguard during the search for Piper Cherokee Six aircraft ZK-EBU. Supplied / NZ Police

Kirkwood said while the outcome may be disappointing for the families keen for answers, the operation had allowed investigators to assess information that warranted examination.

"Whenever new information of this nature comes to light, we have a responsibility to assess it carefully and professionally.

"Although we have not located anything that requires further investigation today, the work carried out means we can confidently account for the areas searched and the information that led us here."

Dive squad getting ready to go underwater. Supplied / NZ Police

Kirkwood also acknowledged the support of Te Rūnanga o Makaawhio, partner agencies, local landowners, and the wider Haast community throughout the operation.

"We are also grateful to the families for the trust they have placed in us and for the dignity they have shown throughout what has been an emotional and significant few days."

He said police did not expect to carry out any further search activity at Lake Moeraki, but data gathered will be analysed over coming days.

World.title: Boil water notice issued for Mangaore after dead rats found in reservoir
World.content:
A boil water notice for the Mangaore community after two dead rats were found in a reservoir supplying drinking water to the area.

The Horowhenua District Council said the rats were found during a routine monitoring using an underwater drone.

It said it carried out monthly inspections of its reservoirs, with the last testing on September 13. There was no indication of how long the two rats had been in the reservoir.

The council said about 30 to 40 properties may be affected.

The affected reservoir has been taken offline and an existing alternative reservoir is now supplying the local network.

Chief executive Monique Davidson said the council acted quickly after the rodents were discovered and is working with Taumata Arowai, the Water Services Authority.

"Our teams today have been flushing the main water network, draining any potentially contaminated water from the network, reducing the risk to having a minimal impact, however, caution still applies and that is why we've issued the boil water notice," she said.

The affected reservoir will be drained, cleaned and disinfected before being refilled.

"We understand this news may be unsettling for our Mangaore residents, and we want to ensure the community are well informed about the status of their drinking water."

The council said thorough water quality testing would be carried out before the reservoir was returned to service.

The work was expected to be completed by tomorrow afternoon.

Until the notice is lifted, residents are advised to boil water for drinking, preparing food, brushing teeth, washing fruit and vegetables, making ice and preparing infant formula.

World.title: Fans throng to Dockers HQ for last home training before grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Thousands of Fremantle Dockers fans have packed out the club's headquarters to watch the team train for the last time in Western Australia before they head to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

It has been 13 years since the Dockers last made a grand final, and the open training session in Cockburn saw so much demand that the team ticketed the event.

All 3,000 tickets were sold.

Long-term supporter Katie said the Dockers' success this year had special significance for her and her son Finlay.

Katie wants the Dockers to win for her son Finlay. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Finlay was just six weeks old when the 2013 grand final was held. Two years later, he developed cancer, and relapsed a year later.

"It's 10 years now since his relapse," Katie said.

"So it's his year and it's the Dockers' year, and all he wants is the Dockers to win on grand final day … that's his celebration."

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox and his teammates at the open training session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Imogen Somerville, who has also supported the Dockers "her entire life", described the event as overwhelming.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It was really cool to be able to get down here," she said.

"It was like five bucks to get in, which was awesome, so couldn't miss out on that."

Doing the right thing

Fans cheered the team on the field, then posed for photographs with their football heroes, who signed jerseys, posters and autographs.

Thousands of fans thronged to the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it was not just the public who were in the stands — past players, the club's chief executive Simon Garlick and Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti also attended the session.

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

Lee Spurr, who played in the 2013 grand final, said he felt "nothing but proud" to see his club back in the running for the flag.

"I was pretty nervous watching the prelim, but now that they're there, I feel like I'm almost playing. My phone's been blowing up," he said.

After experiencing the lead-up to the AFL's biggest week, Spurr said it was important for the players to turn off their phones and stick to preparation.

Former Dockers grand finalist Lee Spurr advises the team to lock in ahead of the game. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"My advice would be don't get caught up in doing too much, " he said.

" This week's about doing the process, doing what's right and preparing. "

Pure excitement

Superstar ruckman Luke Jackson said he loved having the fans participate in the club's biggest week.

Several Dockers said they loved having their fans take part in the session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Just pure excitement. Can't wait to get over there and can't wait to play on Saturday in front of all these fans. It will be good fun," he said.

Jackson was in his second AFL season when he won his first premiership with the Melbourne Demons in 2021 in Perth.

He said he was looking forward to playing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Dockers will face the Brisbane Lions.

Dockers defender Jordan Clark (left) talks to coach Justin Longmuir at Fremantle's open training session in Cockburn. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Defender Jordan Clark was also excited, and grateful, to see the fans.

"They support us through thick and thin, as they have done for the last 30 years," he said.

All the tickets for the training event were sold. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"So they're pretty happy with this moment and they rightly deserve to be, so it's pretty special when we get this support."

With no chance of making the training session, dozens of Dockers fans 1,600 kilometres away flocked to Broome airport today to catch the only direct flight to Melbourne before Saturday.

David Leslie, who goes by Docker Dave, has followed the team since its inception said his faith had been “restored” after their stellar final performances against Swans and Geelong.

The last direct flight to Melbourne from Broome this week was packed with Dockers fans. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"We are going to flog the lions," he said.

World.title: Heeney 'extremely thankful' after addressing entire Swans club on return
World.content:
Sydney Swans forward Isaac Heeney says he is "thankful" for the opportunity to address his teammates and the club for the first time since he and four other players were suspended.

Heeney and his fellow banned teammates arrived at Swans HQ in Moore Park for their exit meetings on Wednesday evening after Sydney's 2026 season came to an end last week.

"It was really nice to address the whole club," Heeney said in a short statement.

"Extremely thankful they could give us their time and understanding … so yeah, it was really good."

Heeney (right) and Warner (centre) were the only banned players to speak to reporters at Swans HQ on Wednesday. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

It is Heeney's first public comment since he and four teammates — Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice — were suspended by the club for a breach of standards last month.

Warner and Bice arrived at Swans HQ first before Heeney, Jordon and Blakey arrived as a group shortly afterwards.

Warner was questioned by reporters on whether he would apologise to his teammates and said: "I don't know, we'll wait and see."

The banned players were met at the door by Swans executive general manager of football, Leon Cameron. Blakey, Jordon and Bice did not speak.

Sydney's season came to an end last week after it was defeated by Fremantle in the preliminary final. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Heeney polled a team-high 26 votes at the Brownlow Medal on Monday evening, well short of medal-winner Nick Daicos's record total of 47.

No decision has been made by Sydney on the playing futures of the five suspended players beyond this season.

Warner and Jordon are contracted through 2027 while Heeney and Bice are contracted through 2028. Blakey's contract with Sydney runs through the 2031 season.

An undermanned Swans side shocked grand finalists Brisbane in a qualifying final earlier this month before being beaten by Fremantle in last week's preliminary final.

World.title: The NRL finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object
World.content:
If we're ever going to solve that old question about unstoppable forces and immovable objects, the best way might be letting Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew run straight into each other.

The Penrith and Newcastle wingers will go head-to-head in Sunday's preliminary final with collisions that promise to rock the foundations of Stadium Australia.

Between them they boast a little over 200kg of prime Samoan beef, forged by pumping ludicrous amounts of steel in one case and fuelled by a truly startling quantity of Coke Zero in the other.

With a grand final berth on the line they will do what they do best: taking the ball and smashing into each other and anything else that gets in their way.

To'o has long been counted as one of the NRL's top wingers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They'll do it returning kicks, they'll do it early in sets, they'll do it close to the line to try and barge in and score and they'll do it over and over again until one of them is grand final bound.

Nobody can do all those things, grand finals included, like To'o, which is why he's the best winger of his time, but having played against Marzhew since the two's junior days he'll readily admit to taking some inspiration from the Knights wrecking machine.

"He's someone I like to base my game on, he's really strong and a big part of their team. I'm honoured to battle it out with my uso Greg," said To'o.

"It's our job to put our body on the front line and get the set started. It doesn't matter if it's one person in front of you, or two or three or four or five, just go as hard as you can."

Marzhew has enjoyed one of the best years of his career in 2026. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Likewise, Marzhew has looked to To'o plenty of times before and this season has the Panthers legend covered for tries (24 to 16), line breaks (27 to 21) and tackle busts (124 to 112), although To'o has him beat for average run metres (194 per game to 188)

Marzhew's form has earned him Newcastle's player's player award and he believes the challenge of taking on players like To'o has brought out the best in him.

"Penrith are one of my favourite teams to play against, they have so many representative players and I'm getting to go up against one of the best wingers to ever do it," said Marzhew

"I pride myself on that kind of stuff [big carries]. I try to excel with it because it's what the boys expect of me, if the crowd gets on top that's the cherry on top."

Fighting against greater numbers and winning is To'o's specialty. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's been doing it for so long now it's hard to imagine a time when To'o didn't relish the contact but he did have to learn to love it.

"When I was a bit younger, I was a bit shorter than I am now, I wouldn't say I was scared but there was that feeling that I might get knocked around," said To'o.

"I don't know if that counts as scared, I guess it pretty much does.

"It wasn't until my old man said, 'You're running it straight and getting knocked down or you're coming off and going home.'

"So I decided I'd run it straight. That was probably under-13s, I just dialled in and decided."

For Marzhew, who's got about 10kg on To'o, the issue was much simpler — there's never been any fear because he has always felt made for this

"Nah, that's the job description [running into people]," said Marzhew.

"That's what I signed up for."

The duo have plenty in common aside from their belief that the best way to solve a rugby league problem is to run right through it.

Both can really put on the dancing shoes — To'o's been hitting a little samba-type number after scoring recently, most notable after wrapping up Penrith's qualifying final over the Roosters with a late intercept try following one of his best games of the season.

"It's a Brazilian dance on TikTok, all the kids in my family, my nieces and nephews are always doing it," said To'o.

"My son does the dance and a Spider-man celebration as well, so I just wanted to honour all the kids.

"Now it's become a thing, I'll see kids down at the shops and they'll ask me to do it.

"But Greg's got me. He's built different. I've seen his moves, he's got the hips for it."

To'o's not kidding — Marzhew was a champion breakdancer in his youth, twice travelling to the United States to represent Australia in the world championships.

He says he's too big to move like he used to but the popping and locking and clean backflip he landed at the NRL's fan fest before the season opener in Las Vegas says otherwise.

But Marzhew needs just one try to equal Dom Young's record for most four-pointers in a season for the Knights and he'll likely have to go over To'o to do it, so the dancing will have to wait.

Marzhew and the Knights will be out to defy the odds yet again. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

"I'll let him take it, my mind is on something else — maybe after the game," said Marzhew.

"No dance, but I'd love to equal the record and share it with my brother, Dom Young, on the other wing."

If Penrith win, it will mark To'o's sixth grand final appearance while Marzhew is after his first.

A crowd of over 50,000 is expected, with a horde of Knights fans expected on hand for the club's first preliminary final since 2013.

The support comes as no shock to Marzhew, who has loved the city ever since arriving from Gold Coast in 2023, and he's ready to run into, over or through anything that gets in the way of Newcastle premiership dream.

"It's not a surprise, I wouldn't expect it but I love it and to play for them in this situation is an honour," said Marzhew.

"It's always a privilege to play in any game for Newcastle. I love playing for this town. It was home right from that first year."

World.title: Umpire felt 'threatened' by player, fan abuse after unruly AFL finale
World.content:
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.

He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.

AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.

The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.

He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.

Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.

Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo

Sicily and Barrass (number 37) were seen having words with Meyer (left) immediately following the final siren. (AFL)

Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.

He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.

"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.

"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.

"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.

"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."

Meyer says Sicily (pictured) is yet to apologise for abusing him on the final siren. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.

"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.

"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'

" That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help. "

Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.

"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.

"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.

"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."

Jarman Impey (left) admitted the umpires had made the right call in penalising him for holding the ball in the final seconds. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.

"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.

"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."

Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

World.title: Neale breaks silence on grand final ban as Lions downplay appeal impact
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Lachie Neale says he will remain in Melbourne to support Brisbane in Saturday's AFL grand final even if he is not successful with his appeals board hearing.

An appeals board hearing is the final avenue available for Neale, who unsuccessfully challenged the ban at a tribunal hearing last night.

The Lions announced this afternoon they would appeal the tribunal's decision.

Neale's dad 'worried for him' if ban keeps him from playing grand final Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale has travelled to Melbourne with the Lions squad. The appeals board hearing will be held tomorrow, beginning at 4pm, AEST.

"Obviously, as you guys will be aware, the club and myself have decided to appeal the decision," Neale told reporters at Melbourne Airport.

"Obviously very hopeful that that's successful, but regardless of the result, I will be here to support the boys and the club this week. It's a big week for the club."

Neale did not take any questions from reporters and departed after giving a brief statement.

Brisbane veteran Dayne Zorko said the lead-up to this year's grand final was "not too dissimilar" to last year', when Neale was under an injury cloud.

There were doubts over Neale's availability in the lead-up to last year's grand final against Geelong due to a calf injury. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"There was a lot of scrutiny last year about whether he'd play or he wouldn't [and] in '24 he had a broken foot, so we're used to it," he said.

"He [Neale] seems to be fine. He wants to play and he's just taking it in his stride.

"You work so hard to get to this position, so he is disappointed, but we'll appeal it and go from there.

"We've had this stuff in the past. It's water under a bridge for us. We just keep going forward with our process and worry about what we can control.

"[Neale has an] impeccable record, you'd like to think that would carry a bit of weight [at the tribunal]. Maybe it doesn't.

"We can't get too carried away about it just being a Lachie Neale team. We're the Brisbane Lions, we've got a lot of players on our list.

"We played a few finals last year without him, as well. We'll just let that run its course. We're not going to get distracted by that, it's not our business to get distracted by it.

"We'd love for him to be out there, we hope he's out there, but if he's not, the next man up mentality is going to come into play."

Brisbane has brought an extended squad down to Melbourne ahead of the grand final.
