Tech.title: A Startup Wants to Power Data Centers With ‘Supercritical’ Carbon Dioxide
Tech.content:
A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide.

American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing.

“We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham.

Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component.

These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants.

The size of some of these plants combined with their inefficiency is a recipe for climate disaster. A massive data-center power plant in Texas that Amazon is building with just simple-cycle turbines, for instance, is permitted to emit more than 33 million tons of greenhouse gases per year—more than the annual total of some small countries.

But all these small, inefficient turbines could be a great match for supercritical CO 2 technology, American Supercritical’s founders say. Carbon dioxide becomes supercritical when it’s pressurized and held at a certain temperature. In this state, it gets the density of liquid but still behaves like a gas, meaning it can move energy more efficiently through much smaller amounts of equipment.

American Supercritical wants to attach its units to small gas turbines and help generate more energy. While the turbines themselves would still use gas, the supercritical CO 2 unit can use the hot exhaust generated from those turbines to create additional electricity. Instead of using that heat to boil water and create steam, the heat is transferred directly by the pressurized CO 2 to generate additional energy with no additional emissions.

“We’re essentially building miniature combined-cycle plants,” says Shuham.

Using supercritical CO 2 also can eliminate or greatly reduce water use in the power generation process—something that’s drawn intense scrutiny when it comes to data centers. Importantly, the CO 2 involved operates in a closed-loop system, meaning that it doesn’t have to be refilled. Cofounder Matthew Carlson, who researched supercritical CO 2 for more than a decade, likens it to refrigeration systems that circulate CO 2 to facilitate cooling.

The company plans to initially sell a 10-megawatt unit—relatively small by gas plant standards. By American Supercritical’s math, adding supercritical CO 2 units could increase turbines’ efficiency by up to 50 percent without adding any more greenhouse gas emissions or water use.

Tech.title: This App Makes Your Laptop Screen Look Like Paper
Tech.content:
Tech is so sterile now—everything lives on the same shiny screens. It's nice, then, when you find an application that exists mostly just to add a little grit to these devices.

That's how I'm interpreting Paperman, which makes everything on your computer screen look like it’s printed on paper. The application, from Finnish developers DoublOne, does this by adding a textural overlay onto everything you see on the screen. I'm typing this on my MacBook, but everything on my screen looks like it's on premium stationery.

Fans of old video games know about CRT filters, which emulate the look of old convex displays. Paperman is like that, but it mimics paper instead of a retro television. Just open the application, choose which kind of paper you want, and your entire display gets overlaid with a pleasing texture.

The goal is to help you focus on your work and to make the screen more pleasing to look at. The developers have collected a bunch of academic research, collected on a page on Paperman’s website, that points to studies showing that matte surfaces and paper texture help with visual fatigue. Can a virtual matte or paper layer on your screen help in the same way?

Courtesy of Justin Pot

Zoé Kilperti, half of the two-person DoublOne studio behind the application, admits she isn't sure. “A lot of that research looks at why reading on physical paper feels so restful,” she tells WIRED. “Its texture breaks up harsh light and softens sharp edges. Modern displays are the opposite: an intensely uniform, razor-sharp grid of backlight.” Paperman's filter is built to break up that uniformity.

The app offers a variety of textures, from Classic Matte to Sunbaked Parchment. I'm partial to Whisper Weave, the recommended texture. You can toggle how much intensity there is to the effect, and I recommend that you do.

I find this application works best when I'm reading, writing, or otherwise working with text. But you should know that everything on the screen is textured, including images, videos, and even some games. You can set Paperman to not apply the texture when certain applications are open, which is useful if you're doing something like graphic design work or browsing photos.

If you use multiple screens, you can also toggle Paperman to apply the texture effect to the content of one display and not the other. There are also customizable keyboard shortcuts, meaning you can toggle the effect on and off on the fly. You're always going to want to have some method of turning the effect off, so it's good there are so many options.

Tech.title: SmartLabels QR Code Organizing System Review (2026): AI Made Sense of My Junk Drawer
Tech.content:
A key ingredient to feeling organized is having a space that’s organized. That logic also helps explain the ubiquity of the junk drawer. It’s simply not realistic to have a dedicated spot for every item you own, so assigning a single destination where you can house all the leftover stuff makes sense. That is, until you can’t find your utility scissors or flashlight or stamps or favorite highlighter or double-sided tape when you need any of those things.

Regular organizing conventions won’t help you keep track of everything in your junk drawer—or any other storage area, for that matter. For example, nicely labeling your boxes is great, but if you lose track of where you put them, you’re toast. Also, that box labeled “kitchen stuff?” You definitely don’t know every item that’s inside. The clever SmartLabels system, which uses a QR code sticker for the outside of a bin, box, drawer, or other location and a companion app to keep a digital inventory of its contents, could help with each of these organizational pitfalls.

The system is simple to use, but its value in functioning as an up-to-date digital inventory of your belongings depends heavily on how often you update the app. The app won’t know, for instance, if you absentmindedly stow away your double-sided tape with your wrapping paper instead of putting it back in the junk drawer where it is cataloged. You’ll also need to remember to add new items to the app as you add them to a bin in question. But if you’re a gold-star user of SmartLabels, they do stand to help you keep track of your treasures.

Photographic Memory

Photograph: Alexis Berger

Each package of SmartLabels includes 48 unique QR-code stickers (four sheets of 12 codes each). After you download the free SmartLabels app (compatible with iOS and Android), fire it up and select the QR code sticker you want to use for the bin in question. The app will prompt you to take a photo of the QR code, then it’ll ask you to photograph the contents that you’re going to store. Every item must be clearly visible, so you can’t simply dump random products in a box and snap a photo. If the camera can’t see an item, the app won’t be able to catalog it. The app is free, but you can opt for a premium subscription ($15 per year) that offers exportable PDFs and spreadsheets of your SmartLabel inventory, among a few other benefits. Businesses might be interested in this capability, but the average home organizer doesn’t need it.

Tech.title: Kate Tolo Says Her Quest to Be ‘the Female Bryan Johnson’ Is ‘for Women’
Tech.content:
Kate Tolo got her first period at 13—an experience she says left her lying prostrate on the floor, debilitated by cramps and breaking out into a full-body sweat.

When she told her dad why she was home from school early, she remembers him saying, “We don’t talk about that female stuff.” Then he walked away.

For most of her teenage years, that was how Tolo thought about her period—as something “you just didn’t talk about.” When she was in her early twenties and experienced extreme pain while defecating, sending her to the emergency room, a doctor suggested Tolo may have endometriosis, a chronic disease believed to affect an estimated 10 percent of women of reproductive age, according to WHO data.

Caused by an overgrowth of endometrium-like tissue (uterine lining), endometriosis is primarily characterized by extremely heavy and painful periods, as well as pelvic floor dysfunction, bowel issues, and dyspareunia (pain during sex). The doctor recommended Tolo have a laparoscopy, an invasive surgical procedure required to get an official diagnosis and remove endometriosis tissue. But she refused: “I wasn’t going to undergo an invasive surgical procedure, or cut myself open,” she says. “That just wasn’t an option for me.”

Then in early 2026, Tolo started developing a concierge health service with her boyfriend Bryan Johnson, the technologist-cum-multimillionaire-cum-biohacker known for his quest to become immortal via rigid self-optimization and wellness protocols. During a clinical intake, she shared her lifelong struggle with suspected endometriosis—and he became obsessed with finding a cure.

Since hard-launching their relationship last December, Johnson has positioned his girlfriend as “the female Bryan Johnson,” with Tolo adopting a rigorous self-tracking protocol to optimize her health. Using $2.6 million in funding from Immortals, the wellness company the two founded, Tolo is tracking more than 1,500 biomarkers from sources such as her blood, urine, and stool over the course of her menstrual cycle, via “an elaborately choreographed four-hour techno ballet of scratching, sniffing, spitting, scanning, stretching, gripping, vibrating, flexing, plucking, poking, pulling, peeing, and pooping,” as one recent Business Insider profile put it.

It’s a relatively new role for the 30-year-old Tolo, who worked in fashion marketing before becoming Johnson’s executive assistant and special projects director for Kernel, his neurotech company, in 2021.

Describing herself as an introvert, she says she was initially uneasy about becoming “the world’s most measured woman,” as Johnson put it in a video from last August. (He’s also declared her vagina’s microbiome to be in the “top 1 percent” of all vaginal ecosystems.) Prone to depression and anxiety, she had a panic attack on week two of the protocol, prompted by her internet going down while she was trying to conduct red-light therapy. “It’s a deeply uncomfortable experience for someone who doesn’t love a routine,” she concedes. “And so all of that pressure just really got to me.”

But to hear her tell it, it all serves a larger purpose.

“Even when every part of me, individually, is screaming ‘Make it stop,’ I can see myself pushing myself to the absolute limit of what is possible, mentally and also physically, in my body. Because I’m doing this for women,” she tells me.

One of Tolo’s primary interests is coming up with reliable diagnostic and treatment methods for endometriosis, a process that the couple has been documenting on their social channels. Though Tolo never underwent surgery and has never been officially diagnosed with endometriosis, so far the two claim they have diagnosed Tolo with the condition over the course of 42 days using noninvasive methods, such as a saliva and blood test and an endo-specific ultrasound. (A transvaginal ultrasound and an initial MRI originally came back clear.) Their next step is creating an organoid using cells from Tolo’s menstrual blood—“essentially, me in a petri dish,” as she explains it—to test various interventions, the results of which she will compare next to a more conventional biopsy.

Tech.title: AT&T Is Automating Away Jobs—and Its Old Telecom Empire
Tech.content:
AT&T, which already shed more than half of its workforce over the past decade, says it's going to continue laying off staff as it gears up for the AI era. The telecommunications giant is also doing away with its old-school landline service and using artificial intelligence to automate some internal processes. All this downsizing is resulting in tangible benefits, including a considerable decrease in electricity usage, AT&T chief technology officer Jeremy Legg tells WIRED.

“We’re not going to have the same headcount in five years as we do today,” Legg says, adding that comparing its staffing levels to that of peers plays a role in its decisionmaking. According to public financial disclosures, AT&T generated less revenue per employee last year than its competitors Verizon and T-Mobile, both of which have let go of workers in recent months.

If AT&T continues cutting jobs at the same pace as last year, when it shed 8,000 people, its workforce could approach 85,000 employees by 2030. A person familiar with the matter, who was not authorized to speak publicly, described that number as the company’s target. AT&T called the figure inaccurate. In the first half of 2026, the telecom giant cut some 2,100 jobs.

By the end of the decade, AT&T wants to be seen as a “dramatically different” company with a “fantastic” fiber internet service and “kickass wireless network,” AT&T CEO John Stankey said at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco earlier this month.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former AT&T employee with more to say? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24.

AT&T’s transition provides a window into how legacy companies are trying to rebuild their operations as artificial intelligence tools become increasingly capable. AT&T has been around for 150 years, and it still plays a major role in the global economy. Legg says it handles about 15 percent of the world’s internet traffic, and the company employed nearly 131,000 people as of June. The question is whether it can drive innovation while also shedding costs and trying to keep up with the likes of Elon Musk.

Tech.title: She’s 28, Loves God and Her Family, and Might Be the Reason You Can’t Have Kids
Tech.content:
Waters loved life in DC: walking 24,000 steps a day, getting coffee with everyone and their mom, hosting dinners in her basement. When she got pregnant with Gertie, she and Jack wanted to prove that life didn’t end with a baby. But she needed a job with more flexibility that would eventually allow Jack to attend in-person seminary. In 2022, Waters approached the Heritage Foundation, the most influential conservative think tank. Heritage had recently shed its intellectual bona fides to become a MAGA mouthpiece; the next year, it would release Project 2025, the playbook for Trump 2.0.

Waters pitched Heritage that she would cover emerging fertility tech as an analyst: crafting policy briefs, penning op-eds, whispering into politicians’ ears. Waters found traditional pro-life policy banal—everything was about abortion. Debates around IVF started and ended with “Are embryos people?” She wanted to apply her dual major in political science and biblical studies to cutting-edge science. At the time, it seemed like “the least popular policy issue,” she says, but she promised the bosses it would soon be a big deal. They were sold.

Waters found her conservative colleagues ignorant about the state of assisted baby-making. One Hill staffer emailed Waters about a test that counts embryos’ chromosomes, asking, “Will this be around in 10 years?” It had been around for decades. At that point, a Chinese scientist had already embryo-­Crispr’d babies, gone to jail for it, and gotten out. Sex selection had become a standard part of American IVF; the first sex-selected people were in their thirties. It was easier to open a surrogacy agency than an ice cream cart or a tanning salon.

Then there was China. In 2023, more than two years before mainstream media outlets reported on Sino-US infant import-exports, Waters was on Fox News, accompanied by an article headlined “Chinese ‘Rent-a-Womb’ Industry Using American Surrogates Is a National Security Threat.” She called it “the new face of birth tourism.” Intended parents didn’t even have to leave the country. Our nation’s lax laws meant that you could ship sperm over and get an American citizen shipped back.

WIRED Women Nobody wants to talk about women in tech anymore—not even women in tech. Is that progress?

Waters hates it when people harp on what she’s anti. Instead, she wants people to focus on what she’s pro: pro-“human flourishing”; pro-“the human person,” including embryos; pro-man-woman marriage; pro-life (duh); pro-Natural Procreative Technology, by which infertile heteros of breeding age clean up their diets, reduce their plastics, and ultimately get knocked up according to God’s will. Pronatalist? She prefers “pro-family,” which implies more straight marriages where straight penises and vaginas produce tons of babies. (Critics would add that the goal is really white Christian babies.)

Waters never says she’s against IVF per se. She doesn’t talk about “murdering” embryos; she makes it sound more like negligent manslaughter. She mostly argues that IVF doesn’t work. It encourages young women to postpone their true calling by falsely reassuring them that there’s still time.

To Waters, IVF is the conduit for many horrors. Ranking and selecting embryos tricks parents into thinking they can choose and control what kind of children they have, cheapening God’s handmade gift into an off-brand dustmop plucked off an Amazon wish list. It allows you to outsource reproduction to surrogates, objectifying women and commoditizing babies. Decoupling sex, marriage, and procreation distorts the natural order. Infertility explodes. Civilizations collapse. In her work, Waters fastidiously avoids mentioning gays, singles, or women over 40. When I ask her about this omission, she gets defensive: “It’s not about the desires of adults. It’s about the rights and well-being of children.”

Tech.title: The Organization Fighting Ebola Has Never Been More Worried
Tech.content:
Ebola hasn’t gone away. In fact, the ongoing outbreak in Africa is among the most concerning epidemics the organization trying to tame it has ever seen.

“Other than Covid, which affected the whole world, this is the thing that has frightened me the most,” says Nicole Lurie, who has worked for Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations since 2017 and now serves as executive director for preparedness and response and the US director.

More than 7,000 people have contracted the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo since May, around half of whom have died, according to government data compiled by the World Health Organization.

“This is the most rapidly growing Ebola outbreak that we’ve seen. It’s probably on pace to be the worst the world has ever seen,” Lurie tells WIRED, “and it’s quite terrifying.”

While health officials were able to end the outbreak in Uganda through contact tracing, isolation, and clinical care, instability in the DRC means cases continue to climb. Millions of people have been displaced by ongoing violence, which has made contact tracing a “struggle,” according to Lurie. Matters have only been made harder by a distrust of outside humanitarian workers, which has made isolating and treating cases difficult. Locals have attacked Red Cross volunteers, destroyed medical equipment including ambulances, and delayed safe burial teams.

“I don’t think we’re going to be able to bring this to an end without a vaccine,” Lurie says.

Shortly after the first Bundibugyo cases were reported in May, nonprofit CEPI redirected $100 million of internal funding to develop a vaccine. That money helped fund scientists at the Serum Institute of India to manufacture doses of Oxford University’s ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine at record speed. That and Moderna’s vaccine candidate, also supported by CEPI, have entered safety trials, with efficacy trials expected to start this month.

Though CEPI sees a vaccine as key to ending the epidemic, it’s likely that any trials, which require contact tracing, will still face challenges in the communities. "The thing that worries me is vaccine distrust and mistrust,” says vaccinology and immunology professor Teresa Lambe, who is the lead scientific investigator in the Oxford safety trials. “And even if we get vaccines that are fabulous, will they be used?”

Tech.title: Apple’s Clever New iPhone Feature Will Cost $5 on T-Mobile, Is Coming to Verizon – and AT&T Isn’t Interested
Tech.content:
You might not need to use it much, but Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27 is certainly convenient: Easily switch between two iPhones using a single phone number, activating it on whichever phone is unlocked. Your texts, calls, voicemails and Find My location automatically follow you to the phone in use.

At launch, however, the feature is supported only by T-Mobile in the US, and the carrier is charging $5 a month to use it. And while Verizon support is expected by the end of the year, AT&T appears to be sitting this feature out for now.

iPhone Handoff is similar to what the Apple Watch has done with data for a few generations, where taking off one watch and putting on another automatically switches all of your information, such as activity tracking, to it. For example, some people use one watch during the day — perhaps the rugged Apple Watch Ultra — and switch to a slimmer, older Apple Watch at night, allowing the first to charge for the morning.

But replicating that behavior to the iPhone requires coordination with cellular providers. Each phone’s eSIM needs to be configured for iPhone Handoff by a carrier, and service needs to switch cleanly on the network side.

Ironically, the Apple Watch gets left out of the iPhone Handoff transaction: Your watch remains paired with just one watch, communicating with it via Wi-Fi or cellular (if that’s an option). “If neither is available,” Apple writes, “calls, messages, notifications, certain health and fitness features, Siri AI or other app experiences relayed from your paired iPhone may not be available.”

In its press release about offering the iPhone 18 Pro, T-Mobile writes, “iPhone Handoff is available on any iPhone with iOS 27 via iPhone settings and ready to use from day one on the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iPhone Duo. T-Mobile is introducing the feature at $5/month.”

When I reached out to T-Mobile asking about the charge, a spokesperson wrote via email, “The $5/month charge reflects the added service that powers the experience on both devices.”

While iPhone Handoff appears to seamlessly switch your eSIM just by picking up the phone you want to use, it’s not yet clear what else is different with this process versus just transferring your eSIM manually using your iPhone’s settings menu.

Notably absent from Apple’s news was the other major US carrier, AT&T. I contacted a spokesperson there to learn more about the company’s plans for the feature, but it sounds like it’s not a priority.

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

In addition to T-Mobile, iPhone Handoff is currently supported by Telekom in Germany. The UK carrier EE will also support the feature later this year, according to Apple.

A Verizon representative confirmed the projected timeline for support but did not have further details to share.

Tech.title: Eight Sleep Launches Pod 6 With Smaller Hub and Cheaper Entry Price
Tech.content:
Eight Sleep, a sleep tech company, launched the Pod 6 bed-cooling system on Wednesday with meaningful hardware changes, including a hub that’s half the size of its predecessor, new solo-size configurations and a $1,999 starting price for the solo sizes — the lowest the company has offered. The entry price for standard sizes will be $2,699.

“We redesigned the hub, so it is 50% shorter than Pod 5, while increasing thermal power. That requires a more efficient approach to the system’s internal architecture, thermal management, fluid movement and overall packaging,” Matteo Franceschetti, CEO and co-founder of Eight Sleep, told CNET. The smaller hub can slide under most standard bed frames.

For the first time since the Pod launched in 2019, customers can choose solo-size options like twin XL and half sizes for queen, king and California king. Until now, the Pod has been built for couples with standard mattress sizes.

“For six generations, the Pod’s dual-zone design has been extremely valuable for couples, because each person can independently control their temperature and receive their own sleep data. But there are many people who want that same experience for just one side of the bed, or in a bedroom with a twin XL or split-mattress configuration,” Franceschetti said.

The Pod 6 has 80% more sensors per side and AI-powered tracking for more accurate sleep insights. The redesigned hub delivers 40% to 50% more thermal power for faster temperature response.

Eight Sleep

Franceschetti said that the main advantage of having more sensors is improved precision and consistent tracking across different sleep positions. “People move throughout the night, and a higher density of sensors gives the system more opportunities to maintain a reliable signal, whether someone is on their back, side or shifting position.”

With these updates, the Pod 6 aims to make advanced sleep technology more accessible and versatile for individual sleepers and couples alike.

Tech.title: Qualcomm Wants You to Let AI Agents Spend Your Money
Tech.content:
The keynote kicking off Snapdragon Summit 2026 in Maui had the latest forecast for how AI agents will organize our lives through the phones in our pockets. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon spent some time walking viewers through how the agents will buy things for them, preparing for the day when AI will have access to our bank accounts or credit cards — and why that’s a good idea.

For years, Qualcomm has pitched a future where AI agents on your devices know your habits and preferences well enough to make informed decisions on your behalf. Eventually, this will include the capability to spend your money on things such as necessities, gifts and travel. The question is how agents will decide whether or not to pull the trigger on a purchase — and how much input you’ll have on what decisions they make.

Nobody’s figured this out yet, and might not for some time. The fear is that an AI agent would run off with your bank account numbers, clear out your savings and run up your credit card. But at this year’s summit, Qualcomm suggested how this might actually work, wherein agents would repeatedly check in before they spend your money.

“When an agent is acting as a proxy of you, you need to trust the agent, and you need to trust the device, especially for something like shopping,” Amon said on the keynote stage.

Naturally, the CEO was pitching a method with his company’s technology at the center, but it was at least sensitive to the uncertainties people likely have about an AI buying things for them. He said that the company is developing technologies to protect personal information and provide a secure device environment.

“The agent needs to authenticate and operate and keep you in control,” Amon said.

Around 45 minutes into the keynote, Qualcomm presented a way this might go. A woman wearing smart glasses walks past a store when the AI agent suggests that, in the past, she’d bought sunscreen and lip balm from that location — did she want to buy more? She okays the purchase, and the AI agent says she can go pick up her goods. She then proceeds down the street and asks the agent about getting a laptop, and the AI agent guides her to a shop where she can view several on display. She decides on one, but the agent asks her to confirm the purchase first.

I didn’t love everything about the demo, as her purchase was followed by a reminder about her credit card rewards points in what felt like a nagging ad, but that’s probably a personal preference I could tell my AI agent to avoid. From a consumer standpoint, the most important part was waiting for confirmation before making a purchase — especially when plunking down several thousand dollars for a pricey computer.

Qualcomm featured a prerecorded video from MasterCard’s CEO reassuring viewers that the financial institution could ensure trust in AI agent payments made on behalf of consumers. David Lumb/CNET

Qualcomm is treading carefully here, and shrewdly brought in execs from a trusted purchasing platform to reassure viewers that the financial institutions they already trust will be part of the process. MasterCard CEO Michael Miebach, speaking in a prerecorded video, reaffirmed that people will only use processes they trust to keep their payments and data secure; on stage, Amon was joined by MasterCard senior fellow Raja Rajamannar, who spoke plainly about the implicit trust that an AI agent would work on their behalf — which will come from a brand they already trust, such as Mastercard.

This is all self-promotional, but they’re speaking to relatable uncertainty. Over the past decades, people have become a lot more comfortable with online shopping, with the initial skepticism thawing as the process became trustworthy. AI agents further separate people from the act of handing over their hard-earned cash, so another bridge of trust must be built. Envisioning the next process with clear moments when an AI agent will stop to ask people before making purchases on their behalf is reassuring amid uncertainty about a new way to spend money.

A screenshot from the Snapdragon Summit 2026 keynote showing an AI agent reminding a person that they could get 5% off a purchase today. David Lumb/CNET

The long road to letting AI agents pay for you

The technology at the center of the process is the AI agent itself, which runs on your smartphone. In a media roundtable discussion after the keynote, Chris Patrick, Qualcomm SVP and general manager of handsets, emphasized that building consumer trust in the process would take time.

Dino Bekis, Qualcomm SVP of premium mobile and AI business unit, reasoned that the answer will include a lot of reassurance by making financial institutions a central part of the process. Just as institutions now take care of fraudulent charges or other mistaken purchases when your credit card is stolen, there will need to be reassurances if AI agents wrongly buy something that consumers didn’t approve.

“Financials [will need to] do some level of backstop to say, hey, you as a consumer, if this happens, there’s going to be some level of consumer protection for you, right?” Bekis said.

Later on, I wandered into a demo room where Qualcomm showed off concepts revealed on stage, one of which simulated how an AI agent would buy something for you. The demonstration followed three clear steps: identifying something to buy, the AI agent finding a relevant suggestion to ask about buying it and the actual purchase process.

Francisco Cheng, Qualcomm senior director of product marketing, had a demo walking through how an AI agent would make purchases. David Lumb/CNET

Qualcomm’s Francisco Cheng, senior director of product marketing, wearing off-the-shelf TCL Rayneo smart glasses, looked at a poster for an experience (aptly, a Hawaiian volcano). The AI agent recommended a particular tour of a nearby volcano, and when Cheng confirmed that he’d like to buy it, the agent — running on a connected smartphone — handed the transaction over to Mastercard to make the purchase. Any disputes could, in theory, be resolved by the credit card company.

“I think if there’s a level of mistrust by letting an agent handle things through and through, at least Mastercard can step in as a trusted payment provider to handle that piece of it,” Cheng said.

People will still surely be gunshy about the whole process, Cheng admitted, but at least there are trusted brands handling every step of the process. And that’s exactly how it went with online shopping.

“I’m old enough to remember when I was skeptical about making online payments, about doing banking transactions online. I was comfortable writing a check to somebody,” Cheng said. “But today, I wouldn’t even think twice about paying bills online. It’s a learning process.”

Tech.title: How to File a Claim in the $7.85 Million PlayStation Antitrust Settlement Before the Deadline
Tech.content:
Sony has agreed to pay $7.85 million to settle allegations that it illegally locked PlayStation owners out of buying digital games anywhere but its own store. The lawsuit said Sony violated antitrust law by discontinuing game-specific vouchers that allowed digital game purchases through third-party retailers, effectively eliminating competition and leaving the PlayStation Store as the only viable option. Compensation is coming as PSN wallet credit rather than cash, with distribution expected after a final approval hearing in mid-October. US PlayStation customers who bought digital games during the eligible period can file a claim now.

The class action lawsuit Caccuri v. Sony Interactive Entertainment alleged that Sony’s actions caused “consumers to pay more for certain digital games than they otherwise would have paid on the PlayStation Store.” It alleges that this action violates antitrust laws by forcing PlayStation customers to buy from a single storefront at an inflated price.

Put simply, the lawsuit alleges that Sony limited the sale of digital games on other marketplaces, funneling customers into its own PlayStation Store. Some of these games include PlayStation exclusives such as The Last of Us, as well as third-party titles like the Mass Effect Trilogy and Resident Evil 4.

The lawsuit was initially settled in 2024, but the settlement was rejected twice during the approval process — most recently in July 2025, when the presiding judge said the proposed plan “[did] not provide an estimated recovery or a range of potential recovery for class members.” The approval process was reinitiated in April.

Sony denied any wrongdoing or that settlement class members were damaged by its actions, and the court has not decided if the company violated any laws. Despite this, the court has preliminarily approved the $7.85 million settlement payment, subject to the court’s final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled for Oct. 15, and it’s meant to confirm the settlement amount, allocate up to 25% of the funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute the remainder to eligible class members.

If you fit all of the criteria to be part of the Sony PlayStation game-voucher settlement, you’re automatically a class member in this lawsuit and will be able to collect a portion of the settlement money — added directly to your PlayStation Network account wallet — sometime after the final approval hearing.

Gamers who have deactivated their PlayStation Network accounts can apply for the settlement payment by sending qualifying purchase information to the email address info@PSNDigitalGamesSettlement.com. Customers with deactivated accounts will receive cash payments instead of PSN account accreditation.

The option to opt out of the settlement to retain your right to sue Sony separately in regard to its game-voucher sales practices closed on July 2. A written request to the court opting out of or objecting to the settlement had to be received by then; otherwise, you will remain part of the settlement class.

Who can be part of the Sony PlayStation settlement?

Not every PlayStation owner is automatically eligible. The money is reserved for those who purchased a digital game through the PlayStation Store after Sony ceased selling game-specific vouchers for alternative online storefronts.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual human being in the US or its territories. Have purchased one of the eligible digital games (PDF) through the PlayStation Store between the period of April 1, 2019, and Dec. 31, 2023.

Affected individuals are automatically part of the settlement class and will receive their compensation through their PlayStation Network account wallet, subject to approval at the final hearing, the date and time of which could change. Any updates will be posted to the settlement website.

How much will the Sony PlayStation settlement pay?

It’s unclear how much each settlement class member will receive, though we know affected parties will automatically receive compensation in the form of PlayStation account funds.

Up to a quarter of the $7.85 million settlement will be used to pay attorneys’ fees, taxes and other administrative costs. The remaining settlement money will be administered equally to every settlement class member. Settlement class members will likely see a couple of dollars added to their PlayStation accounts once the funds are fully allocated.

Tech.title: A Barista’s Trick for Making Perfect Water for Coffee. Is It Worth It?
Tech.content:
Depending on where you live and what comes out of your tap, you may need to do damage control with the water that goes into your coffee machine, kettle, or French press. Water quality can greatly affect coffee outcomes, both by preventing off-flavors and aromas and by providing the right mineral composition to interact with the coffee’s aroma and flavor compounds.

When I previously spoke with Jose Lepe, director of sourcing and quality control for Sightglass Coffee, about whether you might need to use filtered water for coffee, he pointed out that “water hardness is part of what is going to make your coffee taste right, so you need some of that minerality in coffee to help pull out the actual flavors.”

The Best Drip Coffee Makers for 2026 See at CNET

High-end coffee shops typically use a water system that relies on reverse osmosis, which distills local water into its purest H2O form, then remineralizes it for the perfect balance. Not every major coffee city relies on a system like this, but in places like Los Angeles, which (according to Lepe) has famously terrible water for coffee, this is definitely in play.

Believe it or not, you can re-create this exact process at home without any five-figure specialized equipment.

Why consider making water for coffee?

Santevia makes a nifty unit that remineralizes water after filtering it. David Watsky/CNET

There are a few good reasons to tackle bespoke coffee water recipes. Consider the mineral composition of New York City tap water, often upheld as the liquid gold standard. NYC’s water is soft, with low concentrations of dissolved minerals such as calcium and magnesium and trace amounts of sodium, according to NYC.gov.

I spend much of the year in London, where the tap water ultimately tastes fine, but the mineral composition can quickly choke the life out of any coffee machine with narrow water conduits if it isn’t treated with a descaler. (Do I know this firsthand? I do. RIP steam wand.) London’s water has about eight to 10 times the calcium content of New York’s. Las Vegas, Indianapolis and San Antonio are just a few US cities where the water is almost as hard as London’s and considered extremely hard.

Best Water Filters and Dispensers, Lab-Tested by CNET See at CNET

Water hardness can be somewhat fixed with filtered water, but filtering water removes most minerals without putting any back in. It’s not as bad as pure, distilled water (more on that below), but you’re not getting the most out of your coffee experience. The real reason to try a “water recipe,” frankly, is to save your devices while nerding out for the best possible cuppa. We’re into that kind of thing here.

You can both distill and remineralize water easily at home. Steve Conaway/CNET

What is remineralized water?

Rather than relying on filtered water, remineralized water is simply distilled or reverse osmosis water that has certain minerals added back in, specifically sodium bicarbonate and magnesium sulfate, according to a precise ratio. You can easily find distilled water in your grocery store or pharmacy shelves, but the other two? You can also find them in the same place. Sodium bicarbonate is commonly known as baking soda, and magnesium sulfate is sold as Epsom salt.

We’ll get into the ratios later, but if you’re not in the mood to turn your kitchen into an ersatz chem lab, brands like Third Wave Water and Lotus also offer simple mineral packets to add to distilled or reverse-osmosis-filtered water.

An actual recipe for coffee water

All the ingredients for remineralized water. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Digging into Reddit reveals a common DIY water recipe: add 0.25 grams of baking soda and 0.76 grams of Epsom salt to 1 gallon of distilled water. (This is the ratio the Specialty Coffee Association suggests.) You’ll notice this recipe relies on a kitchen scale that measures to the hundredth of a gram, unless you can scale up to 10 gallons of water at a time.

Without that particular piece of equipment, another potentially simpler method that doesn’t rely on a scale at all involves using standard measuring spoons to make liter-size batches of mineral water concentrates, one with Epsom salt and one with baking soda, and then adding easier-to-measure portions of the liquid concentrates to a larger quantity of distilled water. (If this is sending you back several paragraphs to look into those ready-to-use packets — I concur.)

The perfect coffee water taste test

I tested coffee made with remineralized water to see what the fuss is about. Pamela Vachon/CNET

To assess the actual flavor difference with remineralized water, I made three cups of coffee in succession, using precise ground and water measurements and an AeroPress: one with pure distilled water, one with regular tap water, and one with remineralized water. I tasted each black once, freshly brewed, then several more times as it cooled. I eventually splashed a little milk into each, since that’s how I normally drink coffee.

First things first, coffee made with pure distilled water was truly terrible. I was already forewarned and therefore forearmed for this, but I was honestly shocked at how bad it was, somehow both hollow in body and with a pronounced tang that was somewhere between acidic and metallic. Do not recommend.

The tap water cup, which I already knew I liked, soared by comparison next to the distilled water version, but was also noticeably heavier in body.

After mixing the remineralized water with microdoses of both baking soda and Epsom salt for the amount of distilled water I was using, I was somewhat dubious that so little could do so much, but I have to admit, it really did. I believe the resulting cup had what can reasonably be described as balance: good body, strength, and brightness, without the weird tang of the distilled water version, or the thud of the tap water.

Does this mean I would go through the trouble regularly? To save my electric coffee makers and enjoy the outcome a little bit more? You know what, I might.

Tech.title: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
Tech.content:
The year’s not nearly over, but 2026 has already delivered a glut of exciting Android phones. Still, we can’t help but think about what might come next. Every phone-maker has distinct ideas about what features they’d like to add and improve with every generation. Some of these things, like design, they can do alone, but others require close collaboration with their partners.

Two such partners are Google and Qualcomm – the former on the software side and the latter on the hardware side. Every summer at Google I/O, we learn about a slew of new software features that will enhance existing and upcoming Android phones. Then, every fall, Qualcomm, which makes the chips, gives us a glimpse of what power and features those companies, like Samsung and Motorola, will have to play with in upcoming releases.

On Tuesday at the Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced a pair of powerful new chips – the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

“We’re just now at the beginning of the agentic age, and Snapdragon is the platform built for it,” added Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, in his Snapdragon Summit keynote.

Qualcomm hosted its first of several keynotes to kick off the 2026 Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii.

Of the new dual chips, it’s the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 that will really take phones to the next level of performance and AI capabilities. The chip “represents the pinnacle of Snapdragon innovation, purpose-built for the most advanced AI workloads and the experiences that will define the agentic era,” said Qualcomm product marketing manager Charlie Beeman in a briefing ahead of the announcement.

The Extreme sees inevitable improvements to speed, connectivity and efficiency, but more interesting are the tweaks Qualcomm has made to enable new experiences and features that it simply wasn’t possible to include on prior Android phones.

“It brings an enormous amount of compute power to a smartphone, and therefore opens up a lot of new opportunities in terms of the applications that could be developed,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. “But it’s a bit of a chicken and egg situation because until that’s enabled on the phones, we won’t know what those applications are going to be.”

A question mark lingers over how different phone-makers will tap the power of the Elite Extreme, but Qualcomm has given us some distinct areas where we can expect to see new experiences. Here are three to look out for and look forward to.

Camera

“How’s the camera?” is pretty much the first question everyone will ask when coming across a new smartphone in the wild. Phone-makers know that image quality and camera capabilities are priorities for any new device, and while a lot of that comes down to choices made by the manufacturer, Qualcomm chips still run the show when it comes to the phone’s imaging pipeline.

Both of the new Snapdragon chips will enable a refined camera experience with intelligent stabilization and every pixel now carrying 16 bits of data. The image signaling processor is also tightly coupled to the NPU, a specialized chip that accelerates AI and machine learning tasks. This will enable AI to work on an image while it’s being captured, instead of after. This allows for a dramatic leap in raw throughput and professional-grade video, and a far deeper understanding of every pixel in your scene.

“Each element of the scene is processed individually, helping ensure every shot looks natural, consistent, and remarkably true to life,” said Lekha Motiwala, Qualcomm’s senior director of product management, speaking at Snapdragon Summit.

The new Snapdragon chips will boost camera capabilities. Katie Collins/CNET

And the Extreme version of the chip offers more capabilities, such as enabling phone cameras to record video in 8K resolution at 60 fps or film in 4K resolution at 240 fps for super-slow-mo footage.

“You’ll see this coming for the first time in Snapdragon-powered smartphones,” said Motiwala. “It’s not just about getting a shot. It’s about preserving a moment as you experienced it.”

Personalized AI

There’s simply no way for AI to be personal without it really getting to know you. Agentic AI that lacks personal context – past, present and future – would be like speaking with a different stranger each time you pick up your phone.

The 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is engineered to collect that context, hold onto it and draw from it whenever needed. This is all thanks to Qualcomm’s new Sensing Hub, which, with its dual micro-NPUs, can support models up to 200 million parameters. The company’s updated Personal Scribe can then remember who said what, why it matters and learn from your messages, emails and conversations to build your private knowledge graph.

It could expand an AI agent’s ability to give you nuanced answers to questions, help you recall when and to whom you made specific promises, and make future plans for you based on a whole range of factors, such as your availability, schedule, travel preferences and need for relaxation or concentrated working time.

With its ability to run over 30 billion different models on device, the Elite Extreme Gen 6 is definitely leading the way when it comes to running agentic AI. “When you have this level of capability, your work starts before you even open your inbox,” said Amon. “Here, an agent digests your [Snapdragon] Summit invitation, understands the dates, the flights, the venue details, key moments inside it, and it builds a plan.”

Gaming

Phones can be overlooked as gaming devices, but for Qualcomm, providing a best-in-class mobile gaming experience remains a priority.

With the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 2, the company is introducing an AI-rendering technology called Adreno Neural Fusion, which is supported across major game engines, including Unreal, Unity and Messiah. It can deliver upscaled images with “rock-solid frame rates” at lower power, according to Matthew Grossman, manager of product marketing at Qualcomm.

Adreno Neural Fusion is “a proprietary technology designed by Qualcomm from the ground up, not an off-the-shelf implementation,” said Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of handsets. “It’s a tightly integrated architecture that brings graphics and AI together to knock a new class of intelligent gaming experiences.”

The 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 opens up new possibilities for gamers. Katie Collins/CNET

In addition, AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores run advanced models, and the chip features 18MB of high-performance memory. So what does this mean for your mobile gaming experience? The answer is better picture quality, higher frame rates and longer play times with games drawing less power than in the past. It’s a win-win-win.

Tech.title: Peloton Launches First Foldable Treadmill, Adds More AI Features
Tech.content:
Fitness enthusiasts who want to save both space and money, it’s your lucky day. Exercise company Peloton on Tuesday launched its first foldable — and least expensive — treadmill, capitalizing on a global running boom and rebuilding momentum from its pandemic-era success.

Peloton also launched two more treadmills, plus new AI tools for runners, walkers and hikers on its Peloton IQ platform. The new treadmills include the foldable Tread Flex ($2,200), Tread Vision ($3,500) and Tread Plus Vision ($6,700) and go on sale Oct. 1.

With marathons across the US enjoying a surge in competitors, Peloton CEO Peter Stern said in a press release that his company hopes to “connect with a much wider audience” through its new treadmill models and AI features.

Peloton, which combines internet-connected exercise machines with streaming and on-demand workout classes, has been on a bit of a roller-coaster ride since launching its first stationary bike in 2014. Revenues climbed quickly in the first few years, driven by online instructors who developed an enthusiastic following among home cyclists. Sales topped $4 billion in 2021 as the COVID pandemic ignited a home-fitness boom.

But after the pandemic ended and exercise enthusiasts went back outside and returned to gyms, Peloton struggled. Slumping revenues, mass layoffs and several safety recalls drove its stock price down from a peak of $151.72 per share in December 2020 to its current price of about $5 per share.

With people buying fewer machines after the pandemic, Peloton focused on selling app subscriptions, which you can use even without a bike or treadmill. For a monthly fee, you can access thousands of digital classes in cycling, running, yoga, Pilates, Barre and more.

App subscriptions now account for nearly 70% of the company’s revenue, up from 20% at the start of the pandemic. Peloton announced at its earnings call last month that fiscal year 2026 was its “first full year of net profitability.”

Folds to half the size

Peloton said the Tread Flex can fold to 50% of its floor footprint, a benefit for people with small apartments or workout rooms. The machine is better suited for walkers, hikers and people seeking lower-impact exercise than runners.

The Tread Flex’s price could be a major lure for fitness shoppers, says Anna Gragert, senior editor on CNET’s Health and Home team.

“That’s where Peloton could gain new users, by releasing its products at prices more people can afford,” Gragert said. “While Peloton might never return to its pandemic peak, I could see more people pay attention to its products based on price alone.”

The Tread Vision model — geared toward walkers, joggers, runners and strength trainers — features a 23.8-inch swivel screen with Sonos-tuned speakers and a camera integrated with Run Analysis, one of the new AI features in Peloton IQ.

The Tread Plus Vision is “built for high-mileage training and elite athletes,” the company says. The machine utilizes a slat-belt deck and a ball-bearing system and includes all the new AI features. It’s an upgraded version of the Tread Plus, which CNET rated as the best luxury treadmill for 2026.

CNET Senior Editor and Peloton loyalist Laura Michelle Davis liked the Tread Plus’s large screen, 15% incline and tread width exceeding 3 feet. But her main complaint was the machine’s bulky size and heavy weight, which made it impossible to fit in smaller spaces.

More AI for Peloton IQ

In addition to the new treadmills, Peloton members will have more AI tools at their disposal with Peloton IQ, the AI-powered software suite and personal training assistant that the company launched last October.

Run Analysis analyzes cadence, vertical oscillation and stride length to help runners increase efficiency. IQ Pace Targets enables runners to set speed targets and receive suggested speeds from the AI. Heart Rate Zone Workouts integrates heart rate data from smart watches or bands to personalize training targets.

Other new AI features include ReRuns, which lets members sync the inclines from their outdoor running routes via the Peloton app, and Sled Mode, which adds up to 300 pounds of resistance to your Tread for strength training.

Peloton also said people who use the Whoop biometric data app can integrate it into Peloton IQ. Customers have already been able to integrate Apple Health, Fitbit and Garmin Connect.

Tech.title: RatHat Malware Can Hijack Your Android by Disguising Itself as a Legitimate App
Tech.content:
A new Android malware strain called RatHat is spreading through unofficial app sources and posing as legitimate downloads, including familiar apps like Google Chrome, to get installed on devices before most users realize what they’ve agreed to. Once it’s in, RatHat uses an AI component to automatically escalate to admin-level control, requiring no further action and giving attackers broad access to the device and everything on it. Here’s how the malware works and what Android users can do to avoid it.

RatHat was discovered by mobile security firm Zimperium, which notes that the program tricks people into downloading what appears to be a legitimate app, such as Google Chrome, via a fake web page that mimics the Google Play Store. Once opened, the app seemingly innocently asks for accessibility permissions, which it then uses to take over your entire device.

RatHat uses the accessibility permissions users grant it to navigate your phone’s menu system and unlock Wireless Debugging, a legitimate developer tool commonly used in app testing, then grants itself ADB Shell permissions. This effectively grants the malware admin access to your device. Next, RatHat installs an AI-assisted agent that runs system commands to steal information and a proxy client that tunnels that stolen information back to the hacker.

“That sort of infection chain isn’t necessarily more complex than, say, following a phishing email on Windows and saying yes when the program asks for administrator permissions,” Sav Wheeler, a research engineer for Malwarebytes, said in an email. “Escalation in the Android landscape often relies on granting apps additional permissions that the OS locks away by default to keep the devices secure.”

Per Zimperium, the malware can be traced to attackers in China and primarily targets apps like WeChat Pay and Alipay, which are as popular in China as Apple Pay and Venmo are in the US. Malwarebytes notes that other financial apps can also be targeted. So far, researchers have found 162 infected apps in the wild, which report back to a dozen servers run by attackers.

What can this malware do?

The worrisome part is that the malware doesn’t do anything wonky the user would notice immediately, unlike with a ransomware attack. Instead, it bides its time, runs in the background, and captures information that appears on the screen, including usernames, passwords and two-factor authentication codes.

It can also steal raw touch input from your touchscreen, allowing it to recreate PIN codes and pattern unlock codes. It can capture SMS messages, too, thereby intercepting security codes. There isn’t much that the app can’t steal if it wants to.

How can I find out if I have RatHat on my phone?

Most folks are likely to never run into RatHat. You have to sideload a malicious app to do this, and so sticking to the Play Store prevents this entire problem.

A Google spokesperson confirmed to CNET in an email that Google Play Protect — which is enabled by default on Android devices with Google Play Services — already recognizes and protects against RatHat and that “no apps containing this malware are found on Google Play.”

The only other way to find it is to run an antivirus scan that detects the software. Malwarebytes on Google Play is a solid choice. It starts with a 14-day free trial of the pro version, which includes real-time protection. But even if you stick with the more limited free version after the 14-day trial, you can still run scans to catch malware. RatHat is publicly documented malware, so most other reputable Android antivirus apps should be able to find it as well.

The bad news is that RatHat is sneaky and difficult to quarantine.

“Unfortunately, because of the behavior of the program itself — remasquerading as other apps, dynamically changing its behavior using the AI endpoint — static analysis and quarantining is not enough to remove the malware,” Wheeler said.

In short, the only way to actually get rid of this malware is a complete factory reset of your device. This effectively removes the hidden secondary files the malware installs, which antivirus apps can’t deal with. Uninstalling the app doesn’t work because the malware retains its admin access through those hidden files, which then let it reinstall the app over and over again.

How do I avoid RatHat?

This is also good news. RatHat’s infection method is complex and can be thwarted at multiple points during the process. First, you should never click a link from an SMS or email from a source you don’t know or trust. That stops almost all social engineering threats right out of the gate, including RatHat. Verify that you’re using the official Google Play app rather than a deceptive imitation website. Look at the top of the screen. If it has an address bar where you type URLs, it’s just a website disguised as an app. Real apps do not have address bars.

Also, note that preinstalled or existing versions of Chrome do not require reinstallation, so if you’re being asked to reinstall an app you know you have, think twice.

Denying accessibility permissions is the critical final line of defense against mobile malware. While downloading a malicious application is risky, the software remains largely powerless until you grant it advanced system privileges.

Wheeler says that SMS phishing is targeted to each specific user, so you won’t see the same phishing attempt as another person, and the tactics the app uses vary from region to region. Following standard antiphishing practices and not enabling accessibility permissions largely removes the threat of RatHat.
